The High Courts have no appellate jurisdiction over NGT orders, and the NCLAT deals with competition matters, not environmental ones.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the five statutes that confer original jurisdiction on the NGT (Water Act, Air Act, EPA, Forest Conservation Act, Biological Diversity Act) and the 90‑day appeal window to the Supreme Court. Pair each landmark order with the principle it invoked (polluter pays, precautionary, absolute liability) — this pattern appears frequently in both GS II and essay questions.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India: Tariff Determination, Licensing Framework, and Judicial Review

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) was established on 20 February 1997 under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997, which was substantially amended in 2000 to create the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) as the appellate body. The Authority consists of a Chairperson and not more than six Members, appointed by the Central Government for a term of three years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The Chairperson and Members are eligible for re‑appointment once.

TRAI’s statutory functions include recommending tariffs for telecom services, laying down quality‑of‑service (QoS) standards, regulating interconnection arrangements, and advising the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) on licensing terms and spectrum allocation — though spectrum pricing and allocation remain the DoT’s prerogative. The Authority issues regulations, directions, and orders that are binding on service providers. Notable regulatory interventions include the 2016 Telecom Tariff Order mandating transparency in tariff plans, the 2018 Net Neutrality Regulations prohibiting discriminatory treatment of internet traffic, and the 2020 QoS Regulations tightening call‑drop and broadband speed benchmarks.

Judicial review of TRAI’s decisions is channelled through TDSAT, whose orders are appealable to the Supreme Court. In TRAI v. Bharti Airtel Ltd. (2019) the Supreme Court upheld TRAI’s power to issue directions on predatory pricing, affirming the regulator’s autonomy in market‑conduct matters. The 2022 amendment to the TRAI Act strengthened consumer‑protection provisions, introduced a mandatory grievance‑redressal mechanism, and empowered TRAI to impose penalties up to ₹10 crore for repeated violations. The 2023 consultation paper on 5G spectrum pricing and the 2024 draft regulations on satellite‑based broadband illustrate TRAI’s evolving role in emerging technologies.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India: Investor Protection, Enforcement Powers, and Recent Amendments

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) was constituted on 12 April 1992 under the SEBI Act, 1992, acquiring statutory powers to regulate the securities market, protect investors, and promote market development. The Board comprises a Chairperson, three whole‑time Members, two part‑time Members from the Ministry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India, and two part‑time Members from other fields, all appointed by the Central Government for a term of five years or until the age of 65 years.

SEBI’s regulatory architecture rests on three pillars: (i) the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR), governing continuous disclosure by listed entities; (ii) the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT), defining unpublished price‑sensitive information and trading windows; and (iii) the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (SAST), regulating open offers and creeping acquisitions. Enforcement powers include investigation (Section 11), adjudication (Section 15), disgorgement of ill‑gotten gains, and imposition of monetary penalties up to ₹25 crore or three times the profit made, whichever is higher.

Landmark judicial pronouncements have calibrated SEBI’s authority. In Sahara India Real Estate Corp. v. SEBI (2012) the Supreme Court upheld SEBI’s direction to refund ₹24 000 crore to investors, affirming the regulator’s power to order disgorgement. In SEBI v. Kishore Biyani (2020) the Court clarified the standard for establishing “insider trading” under the PIT Regulations, requiring a direct nexus between possession of UPSI and the trade. The SEBI (Amendment) Act, 2022 introduced a settlement mechanism (Section 15JB), enhanced penalties for fraudulent and unfair trade practices, and laid the statutory foundation for a Social Stock Exchange to facilitate fundraising by non‑profit organisations.

The Reserve Bank of India: Monetary Policy Framework, Autonomy, and Government Interface

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. Its central board consists of the Governor, up to four Deputy Governors, ten non‑official directors nominated by the Central Government, and two government officials (the Finance Secretary and the Secretary, Department of Financial Services). The Governor and Deputy Governors are appointed for a term of three years, extendable by the Central Government.

The RBI’s core functions encompass monetary policy, regulation and supervision of banks and non‑bank financial companies, currency management, foreign‑exchange management under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA), and oversight of payment and settlement systems. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), constituted in 2016 under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, comprises six members — three from the RBI (including the Governor as ex‑officio chair) and three external members appointed by the Government. The MPC targets consumer‑price‑index inflation at 4 % with a tolerance band of ±2 %.

Section 7 of the RBI Act empowers the Central Government to issue directions to the Bank in the public interest after consultation with the Governor, a provision that has sparked debate on operational autonomy. The Supreme Court in RBI v. M/s. Gujarat Fluorochemicals Ltd. (2020) held that such directions must be reasoned and cannot circumvent the RBI’s statutory discretion. Notable recent episodes include the 2016 demonetisation exercise where the RBI acted as the implementing agency, the COVID‑19 regulatory packages (2020‑21) providing loan moratoriums and restructuring frameworks, and the 2022 withdrawal of the ₹2 000 banknote from circulation. The 2023 amendment to the RBI Act strengthened board governance, introduced a formal risk‑management framework, and paved the way for the 2024 pilot of the Central Bank Digital Currency (digital rupee).

  • Confusing the CCI’s green‑channel approval with a blanket exemption — it applies only to combinations meeting specific low‑risk criteria.
  • Assuming the NGT can hear criminal environmental offences — its jurisdiction is civil; criminal matters remain with regular courts.
  • Believing TRAI directly allocates spectrum — spectrum allocation is a DoT function; TRAI only recommends reserve prices and band plans.
  • Thinking SEBI’s settlement mechanism waives all penalties — settlement requires admission of facts and payment of a reduced amount, not a full waiver.
  • Overlooking the MPC’s external members’ fixed four‑year tenure — they are not removable at the Government’s pleasure.
  • Misstating the RBI’s Section 7 direction as a routine instruction — it is an extraordinary power used sparingly and subject to judicial scrutiny.
  • Treating the CCI’s leniency programme as automatic — the Commission evaluates the quality of disclosure and cooperation before granting reduction.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the institutional detail, statutory provisions, and judicial interpretations that differentiate high‑scoring answers in GS II.

The Election Commission’s Disqualification Powers under the Representation of the People Act, 1951

The Election Commission of India (ECI) derives its disqualification authority primarily from Sections 8A, 10A, and 11A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA). Section 8A empowers the President, on the advice of the ECI, to disqualify a person found guilty of a corrupt practice by an election tribunal for a period of six years. Section 10A provides for disqualification of a candidate who fails to lodge an account of election expenses within the prescribed time, while Section 11A allows the ECI to remove or reduce the period of disqualification on sufficient cause. The Commission’s role is quasi‑judicial: it examines the tribunal’s report, hears the concerned party, and forwards its recommendation to the President. The Supreme Court in K. Prabhakaran v. P. Jayarajan (2005) held that the ECI’s recommendation under Section 8A is binding on the President, reinforcing the Commission’s institutional weight. In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) the Court clarified that disqualification under Section 8(3) (conviction for certain offences) operates automatically, but the ECI’s power under Section 8A remains a distinct, discretionary track for corrupt‑practice findings.

Procedurally, after an election petition concludes with a finding of corrupt practice, the tribunal forwards its report to the ECI. The Commission issues a show‑cause notice to the respondent, conducts a hearing, and then submits its opinion to the President. The President’s order is published in the Gazette, and the disqualified person is barred from contesting elections and holding public office for the stipulated period. The ECI also monitors compliance with expense‑account filing under Section 78; failure triggers a notice under Section 10A, after which the Commission may recommend disqualification. The 2017 amendment to the RPA introduced a time‑limit of 90 days for the ECI to forward its recommendation, aiming to curb delays. Judicial review of the ECI’s disqualification orders is limited to procedural fairness; the Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) reiterated that the Commission’s satisfaction is not subject to merits‑based review.

Key Disqualification Provisions
SectionGroundAuthorityPeriod
8ACorrupt practice (election tribunal finding)President on ECI adviceSix years (extendable)

Recent practice shows the ECI increasingly invoking Section 10A against candidates who default on expense returns, with over 1,200 notices issued in the 2019 general election cycle. The Commission’s 2022 guidelines standardised the show‑cause format and mandated a speaking order, enhancing transparency. Aspirants should note the interplay between automatic disqualification on conviction (Section 8(3)) and the discretionary corrupt‑practice route (Section 8A), a frequent examiner twist.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Direct Benefit Transfer Schemes

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has expanded its audit universe to cover Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) programmes, which channel subsidies and welfare payments directly into beneficiaries’ bank accounts. The CAG’s methodology combines compliance audit (verifying adherence to DBT guidelines issued by the Department of Expenditure), performance audit (assessing targeting efficiency, leakages, and timeliness), and IT‑audit (validating data integrity in the Public Financial Management System — PFMS). Landmark reports include CAG Report No. 15 of 2018 on the DBT framework, which identified a 12 % exclusion error in the LPG subsidy (PAHAL) scheme due to mismatched Aadhaar‑bank linkages, and Report No. 5 of 2021 on the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM‑KISAN), highlighting duplicate payments amounting to ₹1,300 crore across three states.

The audit process begins with a risk‑based selection of schemes, followed by data extraction from PFMS, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) switch, and state‑level treasury databases. Auditors test a stratified sample of beneficiaries for (i) correct identification, (ii) active bank account status, (iii) timely credit, and (iv) grievance‑redressal compliance. Findings are communicated to the implementing ministry, the Finance Ministry, and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The CAG’s 2022 performance audit of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) recommended real‑time reconciliation between PFMS and the National Social Assistance Portal, a suggestion subsequently adopted in the 2023 DBT‑NSAP integration guideline.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s DBT audits is indirect; the Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2020) directed the government to place CAG’s DBT audit reports before Parliament within six months, reinforcing accountability. The CAG’s 2023 “Audit of DBT in Fertiliser Subsidy” introduced a new metric — “beneficiary‑level delivery efficiency” — calculated as the ratio of successful credits to eligible beneficiaries within the prescribed cycle. This metric is now part of the Outcome Budget framework, linking audit results to fiscal planning. Aspirants must distinguish between the CAG’s statutory audit mandate (Article 149) and its advisory role in DBT design, a nuance often tested in case‑study questions.

Examiner’s Twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of DBT schemes is limited to financial compliance; it cannot assess targeting efficiency.” Evaluate the statement.
The statement is false. The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 read with the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, encompasses performance audit, which explicitly includes evaluation of economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of programmes. CAG Reports 15/2018 and 5/2021 demonstrate assessment of targeting errors, exclusion/inclusion errors, and timeliness — core elements of targeting efficiency. Therefore, the CAG can and does audit targeting efficiency in DBT schemes.
Answer‑Writing Strategy
When a question cites a specific CAG report, quote the report number, year, and one quantitative finding (e.g., “12 % exclusion error in PAHAL, Report 15/2018”). Pair the finding with the constitutional provision (Art. 149) and the relevant PAC discussion to show institutional linkage.

The National Commission for Scheduled Castes’ Monitoring of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

The National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC), constituted under Article 338, possesses a statutory duty to monitor the implementation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (PoA Act). Section 3 of the PoA Act mandates the Commission to inquire into specific complaints of atrocities, review the working of the Act, and submit annual reports to the President. The NCSC’s investigative powers mirror those of a civil court: summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavit. In practice, the Commission conducts spot inquiries in districts reporting high atrocity rates, collaborates with state‑level Special Courts, and issues advisories to state governments on preventive measures.

The Commission’s 2020‑21 annual report highlighted a 23 % increase in registered cases under the PoA Act, attributing the rise to improved reporting mechanisms and the 2015 amendment that expanded the list of offences. The NCSC recommended (i) mandatory video‑recording of statements of victims, (ii) establishment of exclusive Special Courts in every district, and (iii) a dedicated victim‑compensation fund. The Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. Chandrabhan (2018) directed all states to comply with the NCSC’s advisory on timely filing of charge‑sheets within 60 days, reinforcing the Commission’s supervisory role. In National Commission for Scheduled Castes v. Union of India (2020), the Court upheld the Commission’s power to seek action‑taken reports from state governments, clarifying that non‑compliance attracts contempt jurisdiction.

Coordination with the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) is governed by a 2017 MoU that provides for joint inquiries in cases involving both communities. However, functional overlap persists: both Commissions can investigate the same incident, leading to parallel proceedings. The 2022 amendment to the PoA Act introduced a “National Atrocity Monitoring Portal” to centralise data, aiming to reduce duplication. Aspirants should note the distinction between the NCSC’s constitutional mandate (Art. 338) and its statutory monitoring role under the PoA Act, a point often confused in comparative‑body questions.

The Central Information Commission’s Adjudicatory Powers under the Right to Information Act, 2005

The Central Information Commission (CIC), established under Section 12 of the Right to Information Act, 2005, exercises quasi‑judicial adjudicatory powers primarily through Sections 18, 19, and 20. Section 18 empowers the CIC to receive and inquire into complaints from any person who has been denied access to information, imposing penalties on the Public Information Officer (PIO) up to ₹25,000 and recommending disciplinary action. Section 19 provides a two‑tier appeal mechanism: first appeal to the departmental appellate authority, second appeal to the CIC, which can order disclosure, impose penalties, and award compensation. Section 20 mandates the CIC to monitor and report on the implementation of the Act, including the publication of annual reports.

Landmark decisions have shaped the scope of these powers. In Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court held that the CIC’s order under Section 19 is binding and enforceable as a decree of a civil court. In Central Information Commission v. State of Gujarat (2020), the Court affirmed the CIC’s authority to impose the maximum penalty for persistent non‑compliance, rejecting the state’s argument that penalty imposition required prior departmental sanction. The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act altered the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, but the adjudicatory framework remained intact; the Supreme Court in Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2021) upheld the amendment while emphasising that functional independence of the CIC must be preserved.

The CIC’s 2022 annual report disclosed that 68 % of second appeals resulted in orders for disclosure, while penalties were imposed in 12 % of cases. The Commission has also issued “Guidelines for Proactive Disclosure” under Section 4, directing public authorities to publish specified categories of information suo motu. Judicial review of CIC orders is limited to jurisdictional errors; the High Courts entertain writ petitions under Article 226 only on grounds of lack of jurisdiction or violation of natural justice. Aspirants should differentiate between the CIC’s complaint jurisdiction (Section 18) and its appellate jurisdiction (Section 19), a distinction frequently tested in scenario‑based questions.

  • Confusing the ECI’s disqualification power under Section 8A (corrupt practice) with automatic disqualification on conviction under Section 8(3).
  • Assuming the CAG’s DBT audit is confined to financial regularity; overlooking performance‑audit dimensions such as targeting efficiency.
  • Treating the NCSC’s monitoring of the PoA Act as merely advisory; ignoring its statutory inquiry powers and the Supreme Court’s enforcement directions.
  • Believing the CIC’s penalty power under Section 18 requires prior government sanction; the Namit Sharma ruling makes it autonomous.
  • Overlooking the 2019 RTI amendment’s impact on tenure while assuming adjudicatory powers were curtailed; they remain unchanged.
  • Mixing up the NCSC’s constitutional mandate (Art. 338) with its statutory role under the PoA Act; the two operate in parallel but have distinct legal bases.
  • These traps highlight the nuanced understanding required for high‑scoring answers.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Political Party Funding and Foreign Contributions

Statutory Framework

The Election Commission of India (ECI) derives its authority over party finance from the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA). Section 29A mandates registration of political parties and requires them to submit audited annual accounts. Section 29B obliges registered parties to disclose contributions above ₹20,000 from any person or entity. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (FCRA) prohibits political parties from accepting foreign donations; the ECI monitors compliance through the annual contribution reports filed under Section 29C of the RPA.

Disclosure Mechanism and Electoral Bonds

Since 2018, the Electoral Bonds Scheme, notified under the Finance Act, 2017, allows anonymous donations through bearer bonds purchased from authorised banks. The Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024) upheld the scheme’s constitutionality but directed the ECI to publish aggregate data on bonds redeemed by each party, preserving transparency while retaining donor anonymity. The ECI’s 2023 report showed that 78 % of declared contributions above ₹20,000 were routed through electoral bonds.

Enforcement and Penalties

Failure to file contribution reports attracts de‑registration under Section 29A(5). The ECI can also refer cases to the Income Tax Department for scrutiny under Section 13A of the Income‑Tax Act, 1961. In 2022, the Commission de‑registered 12 parties for persistent non‑compliance, a rare use of its statutory power.

Judicial Oversight

The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2013) held that the ECI’s power to demand disclosure is integral to free and fair elections under Article 324. The Court reiterated that the Commission’s orders are subject to judicial review only on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of natural justice.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Subsidy Delivery and Fiscal Transparency

Mandate and Scope

Article 149 read with the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States, including subsidies. The CAG conducts both financial and performance audits of major subsidy programmes — fertilizer, food, petroleum (LPG/kerosene), and direct benefit transfers (DBT).

Key Performance Audits

The 2018 CAG report on the Fertiliser Subsidy Scheme highlighted a ₹1.2 lakh crore leak due to diversion and mis‑targeting, recommending Aadhaar‑linked DBT. The 2020 audit of the National Food Security Act (NFSA) found that 23 % of entitled households did not receive ration, prompting the Ministry to integrate the Public Distribution System with the ‘One Nation One Ration Card’ platform. The 2022 audit of the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana reported a 92 % refill rate but flagged duplicate connections in 4.3 % of cases.

Methodology

CAG adopts a risk‑based approach: (i) mapping subsidy flow from budget allocation to beneficiary; (ii) sampling beneficiary databases against Aadhaar and bank‑account records; (iii) field verification through joint inspections with state agencies. Findings are presented in Performance Audit Reports laid before Parliament under Article 151.

Impact on Policy

Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has used CAG’s subsidy audits to demand stricter DBT architecture, resulting in the 2021 amendment to the DBT Mission guidelines that made real‑time beneficiary validation mandatory. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) cited CAG’s fertilizer audit while directing the government to phase out cash‑based subsidy disbursement.

Technique: Linking Statutory Mandate to Audit Outcomes
Question: Explain how the CAG’s constitutional mandate under Article 149 translates into concrete policy changes in subsidy delivery, citing at least two specific audit reports and their legislative or judicial repercussions.
Answer: Article 149 read with the CAG Act, 1971 authorises the CAG to audit all Union and State expenditure, including subsidies. The 2018 Fertiliser Subsidy Performance Audit identified ₹1.2 lakh crore leakage and recommended Aadhaar‑linked DBT; the PAC endorsed this, leading to the 2021 DBT Mission amendment mandating real‑time validation. The 2020 NFSA audit revealed 23 % exclusion error, prompting the ‘One Nation One Ration Card’ integration. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) relied on the fertiliser audit to order phasing out cash disbursement. Thus, the constitutional audit mandate directly drives legislative reform and judicial enforcement.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “constitutional basis → audit → policy impact”, structure the answer in three labelled steps: (1) cite Article 149 and the CAG Act; (2) name the specific performance audit (year, scheme, key finding); (3) quote the consequent PAC recommendation, amendment, or Supreme Court direction. This three‑step chain scores full marks for linkage.

Union Public Service Commission’s Lateral Entry Scheme and Its Impact on Civil Service Recruitment

Genesis and Legal Basis

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) derives its recruitment authority from Article 320. In 2018, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issued a notification inviting applications for ten joint‑secretary‑level posts through lateral entry, bypassing the regular Civil Services Examination (CSE). The scheme was formalised by the 2020 “Lateral Entry Guidelines” which empower UPSC to conduct a two‑stage selection: (i) screening of applications by a search‑cum‑selection committee; (ii) interview by a UPSC‑constituted board.

Scope and Expansion

Initially limited to joint‑secretary (JS) level, the scheme was extended in 2021 to director‑level positions in 12 ministries. As of March 2024, 63 lateral entrants have joined, predominantly from the private sector, academia, and state governments. The 2023 guidelines introduced a mandatory cooling‑off period of two years for former civil servants applying laterally.

Impact on Recruitment Dynamics

Data from the 2023 UPSC annual report shows that lateral entrants constitute 0.4 % of the total Group‑A strength but occupy 12 % of JS‑level posts in economic ministries. The scheme has reduced average age at JS level from 52 to 48 years and increased domain‑specialist representation. However, the 2022 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel noted concerns about parity in pay, pension, and career progression.

Judicial Scrutiny

The Supreme Court in Ramesh Chandra v. Union of India (2022) upheld the lateral entry framework, ruling that Article 320 does not prescribe a single mode of recruitment and that the executive may create alternative pathways provided the UPSC’s advisory role is respected. The Court emphasised transparency in the search‑committee composition.

Finance Commission’s Horizontal Devolution Formula: Evolution, Data Sources, and State‑Level Implications

Historical Evolution

The horizontal devolution formula determines each State’s share of the divisible pool. The 10th Finance Commission (1995‑2000) used population (1971), area, and per‑capita income distance. The 14th FC (2015‑2020) introduced forest cover and fiscal discipline as additional criteria, assigning weights: 17.5 % (population), 15 % (area), 7.5 % (forest cover), 50 % (income distance), 10 % (fiscal discipline). The 15th FC (2021‑2026) revised weights to 15 % (population 2011), 15 % (area), 10 % (forest & ecology), 45 % (income distance), 12.5 % (demographic performance), 2.5 % (tax effort).

Data Sources and Methodology

Population data are sourced from the Census (1971 for 14th FC, 2011 for 15th FC). Income distance uses per‑capita GSDP from the Central Statistics Office. Forest cover relies on the Forest Survey of India’s biennial assessments. Demographic performance is measured by the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) from the National Family Health Survey. Tax effort is computed as the ratio of own‑tax revenue to GSDP, using State Finance Accounts.

State‑Level Implications

States with high forest cover (e.g., Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh) gained under the 14th FC but saw reduced weight in the 15th FC. Southern states with low TFR benefited from the demographic performance criterion, increasing their share by 0.3‑0.5 percentage points. The tax‑effort criterion incentivised states like Maharashtra and Gujarat to improve compliance, reflected in a 1.2 % rise in own‑tax‑to‑GSDP ratio between 2020‑21 and 2022‑23.

Controversies and Reforms

The shift from 1971 to 2011 population sparked debates on “penalising” states that achieved population control. The 15th FC’s inclusion of demographic performance was a compromise. The 2023 Terms of Reference for the 16th FC propose a “dynamic weight” mechanism linking criteria to real‑time fiscal indicators.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers, Limitations, and Recent Supreme Court Directions

Statutory Investigative Authority

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Sections 12‑14 to inquire suo motu or on petitions into violations by public servants. The Commission can summon witnesses, demand documents, and conduct on‑site inspections of custodial institutions. It may recommend compensation, prosecution, or disciplinary action, but lacks direct prosecutorial power.

Operational Limitations

NHRC’s recommendations are advisory; implementation depends on the concerned government. The Commission cannot investigate allegations against the armed forces in disturbed areas without Central Government consent (Section 19). Resource constraints — 1,200 staff for a national mandate — limit simultaneous inquiries. The 2022 NHRC annual report noted a 38 % pendency rate for cases older than one year.

Supreme Court Directions

In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009), the Court held that the State must comply with NHRC’s compensation recommendations within three months, treating non‑compliance as contempt. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021), the Court directed NHRC to establish a dedicated “Custodial Death Monitoring Cell” and to publish quarterly compliance reports. The 2023 judgment in NHRC v. Union of India expanded the Commission’s suo motu jurisdiction to include systemic violations in juvenile homes, overriding the earlier requirement of a specific complaint.

Coordination with State Commissions

Section 21 of the PHRA provides for State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs). A 2018 MoU between NHRC and SHRCs mandates joint inquiries for inter‑state cases and data sharing through the “Human Rights Case Management System”. However, functional overlap persists, with both bodies occasionally issuing parallel recommendations on the same incident.

  • Confusing the ECI’s power to de‑register parties under Section 29A(5) with the Supreme Court’s power to derecognise parties for violating the Model Code of Conduct.
  • Assuming the CAG’s subsidy audits are limited to financial regularity; they also assess targeting efficiency and leakages.
  • Believing lateral entry appointments bypass UPSC entirely; the Commission conducts the interview stage and advises on suitability.
  • Treating the 15th Finance Commission’s demographic performance weight as a penalty for high‑population states rather than an incentive for fertility decline.
  • Thinking NHRC’s recommendations are binding; they are advisory and enforceable only through judicial contempt proceedings.
  • Overlooking the requirement of Central Government consent for NHRC inquiries into armed‑forces actions in disturbed areas.
  • Mixing up the Electoral Bonds Scheme’s anonymity provision with the ECI’s mandatory disclosure of aggregate bond redemption data.

The advanced sections above integrate statutory text, landmark judgments, and empirical outcomes to equip aspirants for analytical questions on institutional autonomy.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Grants‑in‑Aid: Criteria, Trends, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

The vertical devolution decision determines what share of the divisible pool of central taxes is transferred to the states as a whole. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended a vertical share of 42 % of the divisible pool, the highest ever, arguing that the Goods and Services Tax (GST) would enlarge the pool and that states needed greater fiscal space. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) reduced the vertical share to 41 %, citing the revenue uncertainty introduced by GST compensation cess and the need to retain resources for central commitments such as defence and interest payments. Both commissions used the same divisible‑pool definition — net proceeds of all shareable taxes after deducting collection costs and the GST compensation cess.

Grants‑in‑aid complement vertical devolution by addressing specific fiscal disabilities. The 14th FC introduced revenue‑deficit grants for 11 states, a local‑body grant of ₹2.87 lakh crore, and sector‑specific grants for health, education, and rural connectivity. The 15th FC expanded revenue‑deficit grants to 17 states, added a disaster‑risk‑management grant (₹1.5 lakh crore), and created a performance‑based grant for urban local bodies linked to property‑tax reforms. These grants are conditional: states must meet stipulated reform milestones (e.g., implementation of the Public Financial Management System, adoption of the Model Municipal Law) to receive the full amount.

The shift from a higher vertical share to a larger grant component reflects a strategic move toward targeted fiscal equalisation. Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 accounts shows that states receiving revenue‑deficit grants reduced their revenue‑deficit‑to‑GSDP ratio by an average of 0.4 percentage points, while states without such grants saw a marginal increase. However, the conditional nature of grants has sparked debate: critics argue that it erodes the predictability of transfers and gives the Centre leverage over state policy choices, potentially undermining the federal principle of autonomous fiscal decision‑making.

Vertical Devolution and Major Grant Components (14th vs 15th FC)
Component14th FC (2015‑20)15th FC (2020‑25)
Vertical share of divisible pool42 %41 %
Revenue‑deficit grants11 states17 states
Local‑body grants₹2.87 lakh crore₹3.10 lakh crore (incl. performance grant)
Sector‑specific grantsHealth, education, rural connectivityHealth, education, urban reforms, disaster risk

For aspirants, the key analytical point is the trade‑off between predictability (vertical share) and conditionality (grants). Questions often ask whether the 15th FC’s design strengthens or weakens cooperative federalism; a balanced answer cites the higher grant quantum for lagging states while noting the Centre’s enhanced policy leverage.

Union Public Service Commission’s Conduct of the Civil Services Examination: Pattern Evolution, Syllabus Reforms, and Cadre Allocation Mechanism

The Civil Services Examination (CSE) is the gateway to the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFS) and central civil services. Its three‑stage structure — Preliminary, Main, and Personality Test — has undergone calibrated reforms since 2011. The Preliminary Examination comprises two objective papers: General Studies Paper I (200 marks, counted for merit) and General Studies Paper II (CSAT, 200 marks, qualifying at 33 % since 2013). The 2011 introduction of CSAT replaced the earlier optional‑subject paper; the 2013 decision to make CSAT qualifying only was a response to widespread protests about its perceived bias against non‑English‑medium candidates.

The Main Examination consists of nine descriptive papers: Essay (250 marks), four General Studies papers (250 marks each), two optional‑subject papers (250 marks each), and two language papers (English and an Indian language, qualifying only). In 2020 the Commission rationalised the optional‑subject list, removing a few low‑uptake subjects and adding Public Administration and Anthropology as new options. The 2023 notification retained the same pattern but introduced a “Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude” paper (General Studies Paper IV) as a compulsory component, reinforcing the emphasis on governance values.

After the Main, the Personality Test (Interview) carries 275 marks. The final merit list is prepared by adding Main (1750 marks) and Interview (275 marks) scores; Preliminary marks are not counted. Cadre allocation for the All India Services follows a merit‑cum‑preference system. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) is the cadre‑controlling authority for IAS, the Ministry of Home Affairs for IPS, and the Ministry of External Affairs for IFS. UPSC forwards the ranked list to these authorities, which then allocate cadres based on the candidate’s indicated preferences, vacancy position, and the “insider‑outsider” quota (one‑third of vacancies reserved for candidates domiciled in the cadre state).

Civil Services Examination Pattern (2024 Notification)
StagePapersMarksNature
PreliminaryGS Paper I, CSAT (Paper II)200 eachPaper I merit, Paper II qualifying (33 %)
MainEssay, GS I‑IV, Optional I‑II, Language I‑II250 each (Language qualifying)Descriptive
InterviewPersonality Test275Oral

Understanding the qualifying versus merit‑counting distinction is critical; many aspirants mistakenly allocate disproportionate time to CSAT. Similarly, the cadre‑allocation mechanism is a frequent source of confusion — UPSC does not allocate cadres; it only provides the merit list.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "The Civil Services Preliminary Examination consists of two papers, both of which are counted for merit." Is this statement correct?
No. Paper I (General Studies) is counted for merit; Paper II (CSAT) has been qualifying only since 2013, requiring a minimum of 33 % marks. The statement is false.
Exam‑day strategy
Remember the qualifying nature of CSAT; allocate time to GS Paper I for ranking. In mains, note that the Essay paper carries 250 marks and is not optional. For cadre preference, research vacancy trends of the last three years before filling the preference form.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Election Expenditure: Expenditure Ceilings, Monitoring Architecture, and Judicial Review

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) empowers the Election Commission of India (ECI) to prescribe expenditure ceilings for candidates. As per the 2014 amendment, the ceiling for a Lok Sabha constituency is ₹70 lakh in larger states (population > 10 crore) and ₹54 lakh in smaller states; for Legislative Assembly constituencies the limits are ₹28 lakh and ₹20 lakh respectively. These ceilings are revised periodically through notifications under Section 77 of the RPA.

Monitoring is operationalised through a multi‑layered architecture. Expenditure Observers (senior IRS officers) are deployed in each constituency; they receive daily expenditure returns from candidates and conduct spot checks. The Election Expenditure Monitoring Cell (EEMC) at the state level aggregates data, while the Election Expenditure Monitoring System (EEMS) — an online portal — enables real‑time uploading of bills, vouchers, and video‑surveillance footage of rallies. The Flying Squads and Static Surveillance Teams supplement physical verification.

Judicial review has reinforced the regime. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court directed the ECI to ensure stricter enforcement of ceilings and to publish constituency‑wise expenditure summaries within 30 days of result declaration. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2019) the Court upheld the constitutional validity of the ceilings, rejecting the argument that they violated Article 19(1)(a). The Court also mandated that any amendment to ceilings must be preceded by consultation with recognised political parties.

Despite the framework, under‑reporting and proxy spending remain challenges. The 2022 ECI report noted that 12 % of candidates in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections exceeded the ceiling, but only 3 % faced disqualification proceedings, highlighting enforcement gaps. Recent proposals include linking candidate bank accounts to the EEMS for automatic transaction capture and introducing a “expenditure audit” by the CAG for high‑value constituencies.

National Human Rights Commission’s Recommendations on Police Reforms: Implementation Status, Judicial Enforcement, and Institutional Challenges

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 mandates the NHRC to inquire into violations by public servants, including custodial deaths and police excesses. Over two decades the Commission has issued a series of policy recommendations aimed at structural police reform: the 2010 Guidelines for Police Reforms, the 2017 Model Police Act, and periodic advisories on registration of FIRs, prohibition of torture, and establishment of Police Complaints Authorities at district and state levels.

The Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) directed all states to constitute State Security Commissions, Police Establishment Boards, and Police Complaints Authorities, and to ensure a minimum tenure for the Director General of Police. The NHRC was tasked with monitoring compliance. Its 2021 compliance report revealed that only 9 states had fully operationalised the State Security Commission, 12 had functional Police Establishment Boards, and 15 had established Police Complaints Authorities — most lacking independent investigative powers.

Judicial enforcement of NHRC recommendations occurs primarily through contempt proceedings and writ petitions. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) the Court treated non‑implementation of compensation recommendations as contempt, ordering payment within three months. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021) the Court directed the NHRC to set up a dedicated Custodial Death Monitoring Cell and publish quarterly compliance reports. However, the NHRC’s advisory nature limits its coercive capacity; it cannot compel state governments to legislate or allocate resources.

Institutional challenges exacerbate the gap. The NHRC operates with a sanctioned strength of 1,200 staff against a national mandate, resulting in a 38 % pendency rate for cases older than one year (2022 annual report). Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) remains uneven — a 2018 MoU mandates joint inquiries for inter‑state cases, but parallel recommendations on the same incident are common. The Commission’s inability to investigate allegations against armed forces in disturbed areas without Central Government consent (Section 19, PHRA) further curtails its oversight of security‑force conduct.

  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the horizontal devolution formula.
  • Assuming CSAT marks contribute to the final Civil Services rank.
  • Believing election expenditure ceilings are uniform across all states and constituencies.
  • Treating NHRC recommendations on police reforms as legally binding directives.
  • Overlooking that grants‑in‑aid are conditional on state‑level reform milestones.
  • Mixing up the cadre‑controlling authority (DoPT, MHA, MEA) with UPSC’s role in cadre allocation.
  • Ignoring the role of Expenditure Observers and the EEMS in real‑time monitoring of candidate spending.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and the Delimitation Commission’s Constitutional Mandate

The Constitution entrusts the readjustment of territorial constituencies to a Delimitation Commission constituted under the Delimitation Commission Act, 2002 (Act No. 33 of 2002). Articles 82 and 170 require that after each census the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies be readjusted on the basis of population. The Commission is a high‑powered body comprising a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC) and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state. Its orders have the force of law and, by virtue of Article 329, cannot be called in question in any court.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) provides the administrative backbone for the delimitation exercise: it supplies the electoral rolls, polling station data, and the GIS‑based mapping infrastructure used by the Commission. The ECI also publishes the final delimitation orders in the Gazette of India and updates the electoral database accordingly. The last full delimitation was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census and the orders were notified in 2008. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze further delimitation until the first census after 2026, effectively postponing the next readjustment to the post‑2026 census cycle.

Key judicial pronouncements have reinforced the Commission’s autonomy. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1975) the Supreme Court held that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are not subject to judicial review except on grounds of lack of jurisdiction or mala fides. In State of Bihar v. Delimitation Commission (2004) the Court reiterated that the Commission’s methodology — population equality, geographic compactness, and respect for administrative boundaries — is a policy choice insulated from judicial interference. The 2021 Census was deferred due to the COVID‑19 pandemic; consequently, the next delimitation will rely on the 2031 Census unless Parliament amends the freeze provision.

Operationally, the Commission follows a three‑stage process: (1) publication of provisional proposals, (2) receipt of objections and suggestions from political parties, civil society, and citizens, and (3) final orders after public hearings. The ECI’s role in stage 1 includes furnishing the “basic data sheet” for each constituency, which contains elector‑population ratios, terrain details, and communication infrastructure. The 2022 ECI report noted that 543 Lok Sabha constituencies and 4,120 Assembly constituencies were delimited in the 2008 exercise, with an average deviation of ±4.8 % from the ideal population quota.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings: Corporate Governance, Performance Evaluation, and Judicial Oversight

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit government companies from Article 149 read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. A “government company” is defined under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013 as any company in which not less than 51 % of the paid‑up share capital is held by the Central Government, a State Government, or both. As of March 2023, there were 389 Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and over 1,200 State‑level PSUs, collectively accounting for roughly 12 % of GDP.

The CAG conducts two distinct audit streams for PSUs: (i) financial audit, which certifies the annual accounts and expresses an opinion on compliance with accounting standards (Ind‑AS), and (ii) performance audit, which evaluates economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of operations. Performance audits are guided by the CAG’s “Performance Auditing Standards” (2017) and cover areas such as project execution, procurement, human‑resource management, and corporate governance practices. Notable recent performance audits include the 2022 report on Coal India Limited (CIL) highlighting a 23 % shortfall in production targets due to land‑acquisition delays, and the 2021 audit of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) flagging cost overruns of ₹12,400 crore in the KG‑DWN‑98/2 deep‑water project.

Corporate governance oversight is exercised through the CAG’s review of board composition, independent director efficacy, audit committee functioning, and compliance with the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines on Corporate Governance (2010). The CAG’s 2020 “Report on Corporate Governance in CPSEs” observed that only 68 % of Maharatna and Navratna companies had fully constituted audit committees with the requisite independent directors, and that 14 % of CPSEs lacked a vigil‑mechanism (whistle‑blower) policy.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s PSU audits operates primarily through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and, in exceptional cases, the Supreme Court. In Comptroller and Auditor General v. Union of India (2018) the Court upheld the CAG’s right to access board minutes and internal audit reports of a CPSE, rejecting the company’s claim of commercial confidentiality. The PAC’s 2022‑23 report on the CAG’s PSU audits recommended that the Ministry of Finance institutionalise a “CAG‑PSU Dialogue” to ensure timely remedial action on audit findings.

Worked Example
A question asks: “Explain the statutory basis and scope of the CAG’s performance audit of Central Public Sector Enterprises, and illustrate with one recent audit finding.”
The statutory basis is Article 149 of the Constitution read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of government companies as defined under the Companies Act, 2013. The scope covers both financial certification and performance audit; the latter is guided by the CAG’s Performance Auditing Standards (2017) and examines economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and corporate governance. A concrete illustration is the 2022 performance audit of Coal India Limited, which reported a 23 % shortfall in coal production against targets, attributing the gap to delays in land acquisition, environmental clearances, and railway logistics. The audit recommended a time‑bound land‑bank creation mechanism and a dedicated railway corridor for coal evacuation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes constitutional provisions (Article 149) with statutory details (Section 19, Companies Act definition), first cite the constitutional anchor, then the enabling statute, and finally the specific audit standard or report. This three‑layer citation fetches full marks for “legal basis” and “scope” components.

Union Public Service Commission’s Cadre Allocation Mechanism for All India Services: DoPT Coordination, Merit‑Cum‑Preference, and Recent Reforms

The All India Services (AIS) — Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) — are governed by the All India Services Act, 1951 and the respective Cadre Allocation Rules framed thereunder. The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) and the Indian Forest Service Examination, but the actual allocation of successful candidates to state cadres is administered by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) under the “Cadre Allocation Policy”.

Since 2012 the allocation follows a “merit‑cum‑preference” system. Candidates indicate their cadre preferences in order of priority; the DoPT then matches vacancies against merit rank, applying the “insider‑outsider” quota (typically 2/3 insider, 1/3 outsider) and the “state‑wise” reservation roster. The 2020 Cadre Allocation Policy introduced a centralised online portal (Cadre Allocation Management System) that automates the matching algorithm, reduces manual errors, and publishes the provisional allocation list within 30 days of result declaration. The policy also mandated a minimum of 30 % women candidates in each cadre, a target that has been met in the 2022 and 2023 cycles.

Coordination between UPSC and DoPT is institutionalised through a Joint Committee chaired by the Secretary, DoPT, with the UPSC Secretary as a member. The Committee resolves disputes arising from medical fitness, cadre‑specific eligibility (e.g., physical standards for IPS), and inter‑cadre transfer requests. In 2021 the Supreme Court, in Union of India v. R. K. Singh, upheld the DoPT’s authority to modify cadre preferences after the provisional list is published, provided the modification is based on objective criteria such as medical re‑evaluation.

Recent reforms include the “Lateral Entry” scheme (2018) for joint secretary‑level posts, which operates outside the regular cadre allocation but draws on the same merit pool. The 2023 amendment to the Cadre Allocation Rules introduced a “performance‑based cadre review” every five years, allowing high‑performing officers to opt for cadres with higher vacancy ratios, thereby addressing regional imbalances. The 15th Finance Commission’s recommendation to link cadre strength to state fiscal capacity has also prompted a review of the insider‑outsider ratio for the 2025 cycle.

Finance Commission’s Conditional Grants‑in‑Aid: Design Principles, Monitoring Framework, and State‑Level Fiscal Impact

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to states in need of assistance, and the Finance Commission (FC) recommends the quantum and conditions attached to such grants. Since the 12th FC (2005‑10) the practice of “conditional grants” has expanded beyond the traditional revenue‑deficit grants to include sector‑specific transfers such as the “Grants for Local Bodies”, “Health‑Sector Grants”, “Education‑Sector Grants”, and the “Performance‑Based Incentive Grants” introduced by the 15th FC (2021‑26).

The design of conditional grants follows three principles: (i) alignment with national development priorities (e.g., Sustainable Development Goals), (ii) measurable output/outcome indicators, and (iii) a built‑in monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework. The 15th FC earmarked ₹1.2 lakh crore for “Grants for Health” with conditions that states achieve a minimum 70 % immunisation coverage and operationalise at least one medical college per district by 2025‑26. The “Performance‑Based Incentive Grant” of ₹30,000 crore is linked to the “State Fiscal Responsibility Index” (SFRI), which scores states on debt‑GSDP ratio, revenue‑deficit containment, and quality of expenditure.

Monitoring is operationalised through the “Public Financial Management System (PFMS)” and the “Output‑Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF)” managed by the Ministry of Finance. States submit quarterly utilisation certificates (UCs) and outcome reports; the FC’s “Implementation Monitoring Cell” conducts annual field visits. The 2022‑23 FC report noted that 84 % of health‑grant UCs were submitted on time, but only 58 % of states met the immunisation target, triggering a 15 % reduction in the subsequent tranche for non‑compliant states.

Fiscal impact assessments by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) indicate that conditional grants have improved capital‑expenditure quality in recipient states by an average of 0.4 % of GSDP, but have also increased administrative compliance costs. The 15th FC recommended a “grant‑simplification” exercise for the 16th FC, proposing a unified “Development Grant” with a single set of outcome indicators to reduce transaction costs.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers under the Protection of Human Rights Act: Statutory Limits, Judicial Review, and Emerging Jurisprudence

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) confers on the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) a suite of investigative powers under Sections 12, 13, and 14. Section 12 authorises the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights by a public servant. Section 13 grants the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — summoning witnesses, compelling production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavit. Section 14 enables the Commission to visit any jail or place of detention to study living conditions and make recommendations.

Statutory limits are significant. Section 19 bars the NHRC from inquiring into allegations against members of the armed forces in disturbed areas without prior Central Government consent. Section 20 restricts the Commission’s jurisdiction over matters pending before a court or tribunal. The Commission cannot enforce its recommendations; they are advisory, and compliance relies on moral authority and political pressure.

Judicial review has shaped the effective reach of these powers. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) the Supreme Court treated the Commission’s compensation recommendation as a binding directive, ordering payment within three months and holding non‑compliance as contempt. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021) the Court directed the NHRC to establish a dedicated Custodial Death Monitoring Cell and publish quarterly compliance reports, thereby converting an advisory function into a judicially supervised monitoring mechanism. The 2022 judgment in NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh clarified that the Commission’s power to “recommend prosecution” under Section 18 does not create a legal obligation on the state to initiate proceedings, but failure to act can be challenged via writ petition under Article 226.

Emerging jurisprudence focuses on digital evidence. The 2023 amendment to the PHRA (via the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2023) explicitly recognises electronic records as admissible evidence in NHRC inquiries, aligning with the Information Technology Act, 2000. The Commission’s 2023 annual report recorded 1,842 suo motu inquiries, a 12 % increase over 2022, with 37 % relating to custodial violence and 22 % to police excesses during protests.

  • Assuming the Delimitation Commission’s orders can be challenged on merits in ordinary courts.
  • Confusing the CAG’s financial audit of PSUs with the statutory audit conducted by Chartered Accountants under the Companies Act.
  • Believing UPSC directly allocates cadres; the actual allocation is a DoPT function guided by UPSC merit lists.
  • Treating all Finance Commission grants as unconditional revenue‑deficit transfers.
  • Thinking NHRC’s recommendations are legally binding without a court order converting them into enforceable directions.
  • Overlooking the Section 19 bar on NHRC inquiries against armed forces in disturbed areas.
  • Remember to verify the statutory basis of each body before answering.

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes’ Role in Monitoring the Implementation of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)

The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 extends the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution to the Fifth Schedule areas, granting Gram Sabhas extensive powers over natural resources, minor forest produce, and local governance. Article 338A empowers the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for Scheduled Tribes, which includes the implementation of PESA. The Commission’s annual reports to the President routinely contain a dedicated chapter on PESA compliance, highlighting gaps in the devolution of powers to Gram Sabhas, the status of Forest Rights Act convergence, and the functioning of Tribal Advisory Councils at the state level.

Under Section 4 of PESA, every Gram Sabha is competent to safeguard community resources and to approve plans for economic development. The NCST monitors whether state governments have enacted conformity legislation, whether Gram Sabhas are convened regularly, and whether the mandatory consultation on land acquisition and mining leases is observed. In its 2022‑23 report the Commission noted that only 12 of the 10 states with Fifth Schedule areas had fully operationalised the Gram Sabha’s consent provision for minor mineral concessions. The Commission also flagged the non‑constitution of District Planning Committees in several states, which undermines the bottom‑up planning mandate of PESA.

Judicial pronouncements have reinforced the NCST’s monitoring role. In Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) the Supreme Court held that the transfer of tribal land to non‑tribals in Scheduled Areas without Gram Sabha consent violates PESA. The NCST cited this judgment in its 2020‑21 recommendations urging states to amend their Panchayati Raj Acts to align with the Gram Sabha’s veto power. The Commission’s “PESA Implementation Index” — a composite score based on legislative conformity, Gram Sabha meetings held, and consent cases processed — is now used by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to allocate performance‑linked grants under the Tribal Sub‑Plan.

Operationally, the NCST conducts field visits, convenes regional workshops with state Tribal Welfare Departments, and issues advisories under Section 8(1) of the NCST Act, 2003. Its recommendations, while not legally binding, acquire enforceability when a High Court or the Supreme Court converts them into directions through writ petitions under Article 226 or 32. The 2021 judgment in NCST v. State of Odisha directed the state government to implement the Commission’s recommendation to constitute a State‑level PESA Monitoring Cell within six months, illustrating the pathway from advisory to judicial enforcement.

The Central Information Commission’s Adjudication of RTI Appeals Involving National Security and Sovereignty Exemptions

The Right to Information Act, 2005 balances transparency with the protection of sovereign interests through Sections 8(1)(a) and 24. Section 8(1)(a) exempts information whose disclosure would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, or relations with foreign States. Section 24 places intelligence and security organisations listed in the Second Schedule — such as the Intelligence Bureau, the Research and Analysis Wing, and the National Technical Research Organisation — largely outside the Act’s purview, except for allegations of corruption and human rights violations.

The Central Information Commission (CIC) has developed a consistent jurisprudence on the scope of these exemptions. In Central Information Commission v. Union of India (2019) the Commission held that a blanket claim of “national security” without a specific demonstration of prejudice is insufficient; the public authority must provide a reasoned order explaining the nexus between the requested information and the claimed harm. The Supreme Court affirmed this approach in Union of India v. Central Information Commission (2020), stating that the exemption under Section 8(1)(a) is not absolute and is subject to judicial review for proportionality.

Procedurally, when a public authority invokes Section 8(1)(a), the CIC may direct the authority to submit the contested records in a sealed cover for in‑camera examination. The Commission then applies the “harm test” — assessing whether disclosure would cause a real and substantial risk to the protected interest. In a 2021 decision concerning the deployment of border surveillance drones, the CIC ordered partial disclosure of procurement specifications after redacting operational coordinates, illustrating the principle of maximum disclosure consistent with security.

The CIC’s annual reports reveal a rising trend of national‑security exemptions: 1,842 appeals invoked Section 8(1)(a) in 2022‑23, up from 1,210 in 2018‑19. The Commission has recommended that the Department of Personnel and Training issue a standard operating procedure for invoking the exemption, including a mandatory “harm statement” and a time‑bound review mechanism. This recommendation, if accepted, would reduce arbitrary denials and align administrative practice with the proportionality standard laid down by the courts.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The Central Information Commission can order disclosure of information held by the Intelligence Bureau if the request relates to allegations of corruption. Is this statement correct?”
Yes. Section 24(1) of the RTI Act excludes intelligence and security organisations from the Act’s coverage, but the proviso to Section 24(1) explicitly carves out information pertaining to allegations of corruption and human rights violations. The CIC has repeatedly held that such information is not exempt, and the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Central Information Commission (2020) upheld this interpretation. Therefore, the statement is correct.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question tests the interplay of Sections 8(1)(a) and 24, first identify the category of the public authority. If it is a listed intelligence organisation, check whether the request falls under the corruption/human‑rights proviso. For other authorities, apply the “harm test” — the authority must demonstrate a concrete, specific prejudice, not a generic claim. Remember the proportionality principle from the 2020 Supreme Court judgment; it is the decisive standard for both CIC and courts.

The Election Commission’s Regulation of Opinion Polls and Exit Polls under the Representation of the People Act

Section 126A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 prohibits the conduct, publication, or dissemination of exit polls during the period notified by the Election Commission (EC) — typically from the commencement of polling until the conclusion of the last phase of voting. The EC issues detailed guidelines under Article 324 read with Section 126A, specifying the embargo period, the format of the notification, and the penalties for violation, which include imprisonment up to two years and a fine. Opinion polls, while not expressly banned, are regulated through the EC’s “Model Code of Conduct” and advisory instructions that require media houses to disclose methodology, sample size, and sponsorship details.

The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. Union of India (2020) upheld the constitutional validity of the exit‑poll ban, reasoning that the restriction serves the legitimate aim of preventing undue influence on voters in later phases and preserving the integrity of the electoral process. The Court also clarified that the EC’s power to notify the embargo period is not unfettered; it must be reasonable and proportionate to the election schedule. In 2022 the EC extended the embargo to cover “any prediction of election results” on social media platforms, a move challenged in Association of Digital Media v. Election Commission (2023) where the Delhi High Court upheld the extension, citing the evolving media landscape.

Enforcement mechanisms include real‑time monitoring by the EC’s Media Certification and Monitoring Committees (MCMCs) at the district and state levels. Violations are reported to the Chief Electoral Officer, who forwards them to the EC for initiating prosecution under Section 126A. The EC also collaborates with the Press Council of India and the News Broadcasters Association to ensure voluntary compliance. In the 2019 general elections, the EC recorded 37 instances of exit‑poll violations, resulting in 12 convictions — a low conviction rate that the 2021 EC reform committee attributed to evidentiary challenges in digital dissemination.

Recent reforms propose a statutory framework for opinion polls, mandating registration of polling agencies, disclosure of funding sources, and a cooling‑off period of 48 hours before the first phase of polling. The 2023 amendment bill, pending parliamentary approval, seeks to bring opinion polls under the same penal regime as exit polls, reflecting the EC’s view that both instruments can distort voter behaviour if released without safeguards.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Goods and Services Tax Implementation and Revenue Assurance

The introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in July 2017 created a unified indirect tax regime administered jointly by the Centre and the States through the GST Network (GSTN). The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) is mandated under Article 149 to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and the States, which extends to GST collections, input‑tax‑credit (ITC) claims, and the functioning of GSTN. The CAG’s audit methodology combines compliance audit — verifying adherence to the CGST Act, SGST Acts, and the IGST Act — with performance audit assessing the efficiency of revenue collection, the adequacy of anti‑evasion measures, and the reliability of the IT backbone.

In its Report No. 5 of 2020 (Union Government — Indirect Taxes), the CAG highlighted systemic gaps: a 12 % mismatch between GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B returns leading to revenue leakage estimated at ₹45,000 crore for FY 2018‑19; widespread misuse of the transitional credit facility under Section 140 of the CGST Act; and deficiencies in the GSTN’s invoice‑matching algorithm that allowed duplicate ITC claims. The report recommended a risk‑based audit selection framework, real‑time data analytics, and the integration of e‑way bill data with GST returns to plug leakage.

Subsequent CAG audits (2021‑22, 2022‑23) tracked the implementation of these recommendations. The 2022‑23 audit noted that the “GST Prime” analytics platform, deployed by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), had reduced the GSTR‑1/3B mismatch to 5 % and recovered ₹18,000 crore through targeted scrutiny. However, the audit flagged persistent issues in the composition scheme compliance, where small taxpayers under‑report turnover, and in the cross‑border IGST settlement mechanism, where delays in inter‑state settlement affect State cash flows.

The CAG’s findings feed directly into the Finance Commission’s revenue‑assurance assessments. The 15th Finance Commission used CAG’s GST audit data to adjust the “tax effort” criterion in the horizontal devolution formula, rewarding States that demonstrated improved compliance. The CAG also conducts joint audits with State Accountants General to ensure uniformity in audit standards across the federal structure, reinforcing cooperative federalism in tax administration.

The Competition Commission of India’s Emerging Jurisprudence on Digital Market Dominance and Data Privacy

The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has increasingly turned its investigative lens to digital platforms where network effects, data aggregation, and multi‑sided markets create entry barriers. The statutory basis lies in Sections 3 (anti‑competitive agreements) and 4 (abuse of dominant position) of the Competition Act, 2002. The CCI’s 2019 “Market Study on E‑commerce” identified self‑preferencing, deep discounting, and data‑driven foreclosure as key concerns. Subsequent enforcement actions have shaped a nascent jurisprudence.

In CCI v. Google LLC (2022) the Commission found Google dominant in the licensable smart‑mobile operating system market (Android) and in the market for app stores (Play Store). It held that mandatory pre‑installation of Google Mobile Services and the tying of Play Store billing constituted abuse under Section 4(2)(c) and (d). The CCI imposed a penalty of ₹1,337 crore and directed behavioural remedies, including allowing original equipment manufacturers to choose alternative app stores and prohibiting anti‑fragmentation agreements. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) upheld the finding of dominance but reduced the penalty, emphasizing proportionality.

In CCI v. Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. (2021) the Commission investigated allegations that Amazon’s “preferred seller” programme and data‑driven pricing gave an unfair advantage to select sellers on its marketplace. The CCI concluded that Amazon held a dominant position in the online marketplace services market in India and that the use of non‑public seller data to launch private‑label products amounted to abuse under Section 4(2)(a). The order mandated data‑sharing transparency and an independent audit of algorithmic ranking.

The interplay with data‑protection law is evolving. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) introduces consent‑based processing and purpose limitation, which intersect with the CCI’s scrutiny of data‑driven market power. The CCI’s 2023 advisory note clarified that while the DPDP Act governs personal data processing, the Competition Act addresses the competitive harm arising from data concentration. The Commission has signalled that future inquiries will assess whether a platform’s data‑collection practices create a “data advantage” that forecloses competition, a concept aligned with the European Commission’s “data‑as‑an‑essential‑facility” doctrine.

These cases illustrate a shift from traditional price‑based analysis to a multi‑dimensional assessment incorporating network effects, data governance, and algorithmic transparency. For aspirants, the key takeaway is that the CCI’s jurisdictional reach now extends to non‑price parameters, and its orders are subject to appellate review by the NCLAT and the Supreme Court, which apply the “rule of reason” and proportionality standards.

  • Confusing the NCST’s advisory role under PESA with the binding authority of the Gram Sabha; the Commission monitors but cannot enforce consent requirements directly.
  • Assuming Section 8(1)(a) of the RTI Act gives an absolute shield to intelligence agencies; the proviso to Section 24 and the proportionality test limit this exemption.
  • Treating the EC’s opinion‑poll guidelines as statutory law; they are administrative directions under the Model Code of Conduct, not backed by penal provisions unless the 2023 amendment is enacted.
  • Believing the CAG’s GST audit covers only central revenue; it audits both Union and State GST receipts and the shared IGST settlement mechanism.
  • Equating the CCI’s dominance test in digital markets with the traditional market‑share threshold; the Commission now applies a “significant market power” test that includes data control and network effects.
  • Overlooking the requirement that the CIC must conduct an in‑camera examination before ordering disclosure of national‑security‑exempt records.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory knowledge and awareness of recent judicial trends.

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: Constitutional Mandate, Investigative Powers, and Functional Overlap with State Commissions

Constitutional Basis and Composition

Article 338A, inserted by the Constitution (Eighty‑ninth Amendment) Act, 2003, establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) as a constitutional body. The Commission consists of a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson and three other Members, all appointed by the President. At least one Member must be a woman. The tenure is three years or until the age of sixty‑five, whichever is earlier, and members are eligible for re‑appointment once. The President may remove the Chairperson or any Member only on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after an inquiry by the Supreme Court, mirroring the safeguard applicable to the Comptroller and Auditor General.

Investigative and Monitoring Powers

The NCST enjoys powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 while inquiring into complaints relating to the deprivation of rights and safeguards of Scheduled Tribes. It can summon witnesses, require production of documents, receive evidence on affidavits, and issue commissions for examination of witnesses. The Commission may also undertake suo‑motu inquiries into matters affecting STs, including displacement, land alienation, and implementation of the Forest Rights Act, 2006. Its annual report, together with a memorandum of action taken, is laid before each House of Parliament, and the President forwards a copy to the Governor of each State for placement before the State Legislature.

Functional Overlap with State‑Level Commissions

Most States have constituted State Commissions for Scheduled Tribes under their respective legislative enactments. While the NCST’s mandate is pan‑India, State Commissions focus on local implementation of protective legislation such as the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) and the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006. Overlap arises in areas like monitoring of tribal sub‑plan expenditure, verification of ST certificates, and inquiry into atrocities under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The NCST coordinates through periodic review meetings and issues advisories to State Commissions, but it lacks binding authority over them; coordination remains largely consultative.

Landmark Judicial Pronouncements

In State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001) the Supreme Court held that the NCST’s recommendations are not binding on the government but carry persuasive weight, and non‑compliance may be questioned in judicial review. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013) the Court recognised the NCST’s role in safeguarding tribal consent for forest diversion, reinforcing the Commission’s advisory function in environmental clearances affecting Scheduled Areas.

The National Commission for Scheduled Castes: Advisory Role in Reservation Policy and Judicial Review of Its Recommendations

Constitutional Mandate and Composition

Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) with a Chairperson, Vice‑Chairperson and three Members appointed by the President. The composition mirrors that of the NCST, including the requirement of at least one woman Member. The Commission’s tenure and removal safeguards are identical, ensuring institutional independence.

Advisory Function in Reservation Policy

The NCSC is constitutionally mandated to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for Scheduled Castes under the Constitution. It advises the Union and State governments on policy formulation, particularly on reservation in public employment, education, and legislative bodies. The Commission examines the adequacy of representation in services, reviews the operation of the creamy‑layer concept, and recommends modifications to the roster system. Its annual report includes specific recommendations on reservation percentages, carry‑forward rules, and the inclusion of new castes in the Presidential Orders under Article 341.

Judicial Review of Recommendations

While the NCSC’s recommendations are advisory, the Supreme Court in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) observed that the State must provide quantifiable data to justify any departure from the Commission’s advice on reservation in promotions. In Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) the Court reiterated that the NCSC’s views on the creamy‑layer exclusion for SCs/STs in promotions are relevant but not conclusive; the State bears the burden of demonstrating backwardness and inadequacy of representation. The Commission’s reports are frequently cited in writ petitions challenging reservation policies, and courts treat them as expert evidence rather than binding directives.

Coordination with State Commissions

State Commissions for Scheduled Castes, constituted under respective State Acts, perform parallel functions at the regional level. The NCSC convenes an annual conference of State Commissions to harmonise data collection on atrocities, monitor the implementation of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and review the functioning of Special Courts. Overlap is managed through a memorandum of understanding that delineates the NCSC’s role in policy advice and the State Commissions’ role in grassroots enforcement.

Technique: Distinguishing Advisory from Binding Authority
A question asks: “The recommendations of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes are binding on the Union Government.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify your answer with constitutional provisions and case law.
