False. Article 338(5) obliges the President to lay the NCSC’s report before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken, but it does not confer binding force. The Supreme Court in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) and Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) treated the Commission’s advice as persuasive expert opinion; the State must furnish quantifiable data to justify any policy deviating from it, but the advice itself is not legally enforceable.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts “binding” versus “advisory” for constitutional commissions, locate the specific constitutional article governing the report‑laying procedure. If the article only mandates laying the report before the legislature with a memorandum of action taken, the recommendations are advisory. Cite the leading Supreme Court judgment that characterised the Commission’s role as persuasive.

The Union Public Service Commission: Advisory Functions, Disciplinary Jurisdiction, and Recent Reforms in Examination Pattern

Constitutional Position and Advisory Role

Articles 315 to 323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for All India Services and Central Civil Services. Under Article 320(3), the UPSC must be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles of appointment, promotion and transfer, and on disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union. The President may make regulations specifying matters on which consultation is not necessary, but such regulations must be laid before each House of Parliament.

Disciplinary Jurisdiction

The UPSC’s advisory role extends to disciplinary proceedings against civil servants. Under the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969 and the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, the Commission is consulted before the imposition of major penalties such as dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (1987) the Supreme Court held that non‑consultation of the UPSC in a major penalty case vitiates the order, unless the President has validly excluded the matter by regulation. The Commission’s advice is not binding, but the government must record reasons for departing from it.

Recent Reforms in Examination Pattern

Since 2013 the Civil Services Examination (CSE) has undergone structural changes: the preliminary stage now comprises two objective papers (General Studies Paper‑I and CSAT Paper‑II), the main examination includes nine descriptive papers (including four General Studies papers, one Essay, two optional papers, and two language papers), and the personality test carries 275 marks. In 2021 the UPSC introduced a revised syllabus for General Studies Paper‑III emphasising technology, economic development, biodiversity, and internal security. The Commission also piloted a “Common Eligibility Test” for certain Group‑B and Group‑C posts to reduce duplication, though the CSE remains unaffected. These reforms aim to test analytical ability and contemporary awareness rather than rote memorisation.

Lateral Entry and Its Interface with UPSC

The lateral entry scheme, notified in 2018, allows domain experts to be appointed at Joint Secretary and Director levels without UPSC examination. The UPSC conducts the selection process through a search‑cum‑selection committee, preserving its role in ensuring merit‑based selection. The scheme has sparked debate on the Commission’s monopoly over senior appointments, but the UPSC’s involvement in the screening process maintains constitutional oversight.

The Finance Commission: Vertical Devolution, Grants‑in‑Aid, and the GST Compensation Cess Framework

Vertical Devolution Formula

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a vertical share of 41 % of the divisible pool for States, a marginal reduction from the 42 % recommended by the 14th FC, citing the Union’s enhanced fiscal responsibilities after the GST rollout. The Commission used the 2011 Census population, area, forest cover, and tax effort as criteria for horizontal distribution, with a weight of 15 % for demographic performance to incentivise population control.

Grants‑in‑Aid under Article 275

Beyond tax devolution, the FC recommends grants‑in‑aid to States under Article 275(1) for revenue deficit, local bodies, disaster management, and sector‑specific needs. The 15th FC allocated ₹4.36 lakh crore for revenue deficit grants to 17 States, ₹1.21 lakh crore for urban and rural local bodies, and ₹0.55 lakh crore for health sector grants. These grants are conditional on States meeting fiscal consolidation targets and implementing recommended reforms.

GST Compensation Cess and the FC’s Role

The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 guaranteed States compensation for revenue loss arising from GST implementation for five years (2017‑22). The compensation is funded through a cess on sin and luxury goods. The 15th FC, in its interim report (2020), recommended extending the compensation period by two years and restructuring the cess to ensure buoyancy. The Union accepted the extension, and the GST Council subsequently approved a revised cess structure. The FC’s recommendation thus directly influenced the fiscal architecture of the GST regime.

Data Sources and Methodology

The FC relies on the Union Budget accounts, State Finance Accounts, the Census, the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data, and the Reserve Bank of India’s Handbook of Statistics on State Government Finances. For the 15th FC, the “tax effort” criterion was computed using the ratio of own‑tax revenue to GSDP, adjusted for administrative efficiency. The Commission also conducted field visits and consulted State Finance Ministers to validate assumptions.

  • Confusing the NCST’s advisory role under PESA with the binding authority of the Gram Sabha; the Commission monitors but cannot enforce consent requirements directly.
  • Assuming the NCSC’s recommendations on reservation are legally binding; they are advisory and subject to judicial review only for arbitrariness.
  • Believing the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is mandatory for the government; the President may exclude matters by regulation, and the government may depart with recorded reasons.
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution percentage as a permanent constitutional figure; it is a recommendation for each award period and can change.
  • Overlooking that the GST compensation cess is a temporary measure under a constitutional amendment, not a permanent feature of the divisible pool.
  • Equating the NCST’s suo‑motu inquiry powers with those of a court; the Commission’s findings are recommendatory and require executive action for enforcement.
  • Assuming the UPSC conducts the lateral entry selection independently; the search‑cum‑selection committee includes external experts and the UPSC’s role is limited to conducting the process.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and Its Interaction with the Delimitation Commission

Article 82 and Article 170 of the Constitution empower Parliament to readjust the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies after each Census. The Delimitation Commission, constituted under the Delimitation Act, 2002, is a high‑powered body chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and includes the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioners as ex‑officio members. The last delimitation exercise was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census and the orders were notified in 2008; a constitutional freeze (Article 82‑Proviso) postpones the next readjustment until after the first Census taken after 2026.

The Election Commission (EC) does not draw the boundaries itself but plays a critical operational role. Once the Delimitation Commission publishes its final orders, the EC updates the electoral rolls, re‑assigns polling stations, and revises the list of parliamentary and assembly constituencies in its database. The EC also issues the notification for the conduct of elections in the newly delimited constituencies. In practice, the EC’s Director‑General of Elections coordinates with the Delimitation Commission’s secretariat to ensure that the geographic data (GIS shapefiles) are compatible with the EC’s Electoral Roll Management System (ERMS).

A notable recent interaction arose after the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 mandated a fresh delimitation for the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir. The Delimitation Commission was reconstituted in March 2020 under Justice (Retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai. The EC provided the Commission with the latest electoral roll data, polling station coordinates, and the list of existing assembly segments. The final report, submitted in May 2022, increased the number of assembly seats from 83 to 90 and re‑drew parliamentary constituencies. The EC subsequently issued the notification for the first elections to the new assembly in September 2024.

Judicial scrutiny has reinforced the EC’s subordinate but essential role. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Supreme Court held that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are not subject to judicial review on merits, but the EC’s implementation actions remain reviewable for procedural fairness. The Court also clarified that the EC cannot alter the delimitation orders; any discrepancy must be referred back to the Delimitation Commission for correction.

Key take‑aways for the aspirant: (1) The EC’s constitutional mandate is limited to the conduct of elections; delimitation is a separate statutory exercise. (2) The freeze until 2026 means the current seat allocation remains unchanged for the 2024 and 2029 general elections. (3) The EC’s technical infrastructure (ERMS, GIS integration) is the practical bridge between delimitation orders and the actual polling process.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the PM CARES Fund and Other COVID‑19 Relief Mechanisms

The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM CARES) was created on 28 March 2020 as a public charitable trust under the Registration Act, 1908. Unlike the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund (PMNRF), PM CARES was not established by a parliamentary statute and its trust deed expressly excluded it from the definition of “public authority” under the Right to Information Act, 2005. This design sparked a debate on the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (CAG) jurisdiction.

Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit “all receipts and expenditure of the Union and of the States”. The Supreme Court, in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021), held that the CAG’s audit mandate extends to any body substantially financed by the Government, irrespective of its legal form. The Court directed the CAG to audit PM CARES, observing that the Fund received contributions from public sector undertakings, government employees’ salary deductions, and foreign donations routed through Indian embassies.

The CAG’s first audit report on PM CARES (Report No. 23 of 2022) covered the period March 2020‑March 2021. It noted that the Fund collected ₹10,990 crore, of which ₹7,842 crore was spent on ventilators, oxygen plants, and vaccine procurement. The audit flagged three issues: (i) absence of a formal procurement policy leading to single‑source contracts worth ₹1,200 crore; (ii) lack of a monitoring framework for end‑use verification of oxygen plants supplied to states; (iii) delayed submission of utilisation certificates by state governments, affecting the Fund’s accountability trail.

In response, the Ministry of Finance issued an Office Memorandum (OM No. F. 1/2022‑Fin) in July 2022 mandating that all future COVID‑19 relief funds, including the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) augmentations, be subjected to CAG audit under Section 19. The CAG subsequently conducted a performance audit of the SDRF (Report No. 31 of 2023) and highlighted similar gaps in fund flow tracking and asset registration.

For examination purposes, remember: (1) The CAG’s audit power is statutory, not contingent on the body’s registration under the RTI Act. (2) The Supreme Court’s 2021 judgement is the authoritative precedent establishing CAG jurisdiction over PM CARES. (3) The audit reports are placed before Parliament (Article 151) and form the basis for Public Accounts Committee (PAC) scrutiny.

Examiner's Technique: Comparative Jurisdiction Mapping
Question: “The CAG can audit the PM CARES Fund because it is a ‘public authority’ under the RTI Act.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify your answer with the relevant constitutional and statutory provisions.
Answer: False. The PM CARES Fund is expressly excluded from the definition of “public authority” under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act, 2005. However, the CAG’s audit jurisdiction derives from Article 149 read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which covers any body substantially financed by the Government. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) confirmed that the CAG may audit PM CARES despite its non‑RTI status. Therefore, the statement is false because the audit power does not depend on RTI classification.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes RTI terminology with CAG audit, first identify the statutory source of the audit power (Article 149 + CAG Act). Then check whether the body is “substantially financed” – a factual test the Court applied in 2021. Do not conflate RTI “public authority” with CAG “auditable entity”.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: Recent Amendments and the 2023 Notification

The All India Services (AIS) – Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service, and Indian Forest Service – are recruited through the Civil Services Examination (CSE) conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 315‑323. The All India Services Act, 1951 and the All India Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954 prescribe the eligibility, age limits, and reservation framework. In 2023 the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issued Notification No. 11012/01/2023‑AIS‑II, effecting three major changes.

First, the upper age limit for General category candidates was raised from 32 to 33 years, and for OBC from 35 to 36 years, aligning with the 2022 amendment to the Central Civil Services (Age Limit) Rules. Second, the notification introduced a 10 % horizontal reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in the AIS, operationalising the Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019 for these services. Third, it mandated that the UPSC’s personality test (interview) carry 275 marks, up from 250, and that the written examination’s General Studies papers be evaluated on a “competency‑based” rubric rather than pure content recall.

The UPSC’s role remains that of an independent constitutional recruiter. The Commission frames the syllabus, sets the question papers, conducts the examination, and recommends the final merit list to the President. The 2023 notification did not alter the UPSC’s constitutional autonomy; it merely updated the service‑specific rules that the Commission must apply. The Commission’s annual report (2023‑24) noted a 12 % increase in applicants (≈1.1 million) and a marginal rise in the success ratio for EWS candidates (from 0.8 % to 1.1 %).

A parallel development is the “Common Eligibility Test” (CET) introduced by the National Recruitment Agency (NRA) in 2021 for Group‑B and Group‑C posts. The CET does not replace the CSE; the UPSC continues to conduct the CSE exclusively for AIS and Central Civil Services Group‑A. The UPSC’s involvement in lateral entry (Joint Secretary/Director level) is limited to administering the search‑cum‑selection committee’s written test and interview, as per the 2018 DoPT guidelines.

Key points for the aspirant: (1) The UPSC’s constitutional mandate is insulated from executive rule‑making; only Parliament can alter its composition or removal procedure. (2) Service‑specific recruitment rules (age, reservation, syllabus weightage) are executive instruments that the UPSC must implement. (3) The 2023 notification’s competency‑based evaluation signals a shift toward analytical testing – a trend examiners now expect candidates to demonstrate in answer writing.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Special Category States and the 15th Finance Commission’s Recommendations

Special Category Status (SCS) was a classification introduced by the Planning Commission in 1969 to provide preferential central assistance to states with hilly terrain, low resource base, and strategic borders. Eleven states – Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir (now UTs), Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttarakhand, and Arunachal Pradesh – enjoyed SCS until the 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended its discontinuation, arguing that the tax devolution formula already addressed fiscal disabilities.

The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25), chaired by N. K. Singh, retained the principle of differentiated treatment but replaced SCS with a “Special Assistance” framework. In its final report (Volume II, Chapter 4), the Commission recommended a lump‑sum grant of ₹1.5 lakh crore over the award period for the eleven erstwhile SCS states, disbursed as “Revenue Deficit Grants” and “Sector‑Specific Grants” (health, education, nutrition). The allocation criteria combined (i) per‑capita GSDP distance from the national average, (ii) forest cover as a proxy for ecological services, and (iii) a “difficulty index” capturing terrain and border length.

For the 2021‑22 fiscal year, the Union released ₹28,000 crore as special assistance, of which ₹12,000 crore went to the eight North‑Eastern states and ₹16,000 crore to the three hill states (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and the former J&K). The 15th FC also recommended that the Centre bear 90 % of the cost of centrally sponsored schemes in these states, up from the 60:40 sharing pattern applicable to general category states.

Judicial scrutiny has been limited; the Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) upheld the Commission’s methodology, noting that Article 280 grants the FC “wide discretion” in devising criteria. However, the Court cautioned that any classification must satisfy the test of reasonable classification under Article 14.

Examination focus: (1) SCS is a Planning Commission construct, not a constitutional category; its discontinuation does not require a constitutional amendment. (2) The 15th FC’s “Special Assistance” is a grant‑in‑aid under Article 275(1), not part of the divisible pool. (3) The difficulty index and forest‑cover weightage are unique to the 15th FC – earlier commissions used only population and area.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers after the 2021 Amendment and Judicial Review

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) was amended by the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2021 (Act No. 31 of 2021). The amendment expanded the National Human Rights Commission’s (NHRC) investigative toolkit in three respects. First, Section 12(1) now expressly authorises the NHRC to “inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights” without a prior complaint. Second, Section 13(1)(a) empowers the Commission to “visit any jail, detention centre, or other place of custody” and to “interview inmates in private”. Third, Section 18(2) enables the NHRC to recommend “interim compensation” to victims pending final adjudication.

The NHRC exercised these powers in 2022 when it took suo motu cognisance of the custodial death of a 24‑year‑old in Uttar Pradesh. The Commission’s team visited the district jail, recorded statements, and recommended ₹25 lakh interim compensation. The State government challenged the recommendation before the Allahabad High Court, arguing that the NHRC’s findings are merely recommendatory. The High Court, in State of Uttar Pradesh v. NHRC (2023), upheld the Commission’s suo motu jurisdiction and held that the State must “give due consideration” to the recommendation, though it is not legally binding.

The Supreme Court, in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2024), clarified the standard of judicial review: the Court will interfere only if the NHRC’s inquiry is “arbitrary, mala fide, or procedurally flawed”. The Court also affirmed that the NHRC’s power to visit detention centres is not subject to prior executive permission, reinforcing the Commission’s functional independence.

For the aspirant, the critical take‑aways are: (1) The 2021 amendment converted the NHRC from a reactive body into a proactive monitor. (2) Its recommendations remain non‑binding; enforcement depends on executive compliance and judicial pressure. (3) The Supreme Court’s “arbitrariness” test mirrors the standard applied to other constitutional bodies (e.g., CAG, EC), ensuring a uniform accountability framework.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can redraw constituency boundaries; delimitation is a separate statutory function of the Delimitation Commission.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of PM CARES requires the Fund to be a “public authority” under the RTI Act; the CAG’s jurisdiction stems from Article 149 and the CAG Act, not the RTI Act.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s 2023 notification altered its constitutional independence; it only updated service‑specific recruitment rules that the Commission must apply.
  • Confusing Special Category Status with a constitutional provision; SCS was a Planning Commission classification discontinued by the 14th FC and replaced by the 15th FC’s Special Assistance grants.
  • Treating NHRC’s interim compensation recommendations as legally enforceable orders; they are recommendatory and subject to executive acceptance, with judicial review limited to arbitrariness.
  • Overlooking that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are not judicially reviewable on merits, whereas the EC’s implementation actions are.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the CAG’s statutory audit mandate and the PAC’s political oversight; the CAG reports to Parliament, the PAC examines them.

These advanced sections equip the aspirant with the nuanced institutional mechanics that differentiate a competent answer from a textbook summary.

The Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Provisions, Operational Feasibility, and Judicial Pronouncements

Article 324 vests the Election Commission of India (ECI) with superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice‑President. The Representation of the People Act, 1951, read with the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, provides the procedural framework for holding polls. Simultaneous elections — the synchronisation of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections — were the norm from 1952 to 1967. The cycle broke after the premature dissolution of several assemblies in 1968‑69 and the Lok Sabha in 1971. Since then, the ECI has conducted elections on a staggered basis, leading to a near‑continuous election calendar.

The constitutional debate centres on whether the ECI can, on its own, mandate simultaneous polls. The Commission’s powers under Article 324 are subject to laws made by Parliament; any change in the electoral cycle requires legislative amendment to the Representation of the People Act and, crucially, to the terms of State Assemblies under Article 172. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 255th Report (2015) recommended a phased return to simultaneous elections, citing reduced expenditure, governance continuity and reduced policy paralysis. The NITI Aayog’s 2018 discussion paper estimated a saving of ₹4,500 crore per election cycle if synchronisation were achieved.

Operationally, the ECI would need to align the expiry of all State Assemblies with the Lok Sabha term, which may require either extending or curtailing existing assemblies — a move that raises federalism concerns. The 2015 Law Commission draft proposed a “one‑time” constitutional amendment to fix a common five‑year term, coupled with a provision for mid‑term elections only in case of a hung assembly or loss of confidence. The Supreme Court, in a 2020 PIL (K. S. Radhakrishnan v. Union of India), declined to direct the Centre to hold simultaneous elections, observing that the matter falls within the policy domain of the legislature and the ECI’s administrative discretion. The Court reiterated that Article 324 does not empower the Commission to alter the tenure of legislatures.

Recent developments include the 2023 High‑Level Committee chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind, which submitted its report in March 2024 recommending a constitutional amendment to enable simultaneous polls by 2029. The Committee suggested a “phased synchronisation” beginning with states whose assemblies expire within six months of the Lok Sabha term. The ECI, in its 2024 annual report, highlighted logistical challenges: deployment of 1.1 million polling personnel, procurement of 1.4 million EVMs and VVPATs, and the need for a unified electoral roll management system across 28 states and 8 union territories.

For the aspirant, the key take‑aways are: (1) Simultaneous elections are a legislative‑policy choice, not an inherent power of the ECI. (2) Any move requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368, ratification by at least half the states, and amendments to the Representation of the People Act. (3) The Supreme Court has consistently treated the issue as non‑justiciable policy, reinforcing the separation between administrative election management and legislative term‑setting.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of GST Revenue Sharing and the Compensation Cess: Methodology, Findings, and Policy Impact

The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, guaranteed states a 14 % annual growth in GST revenue for five years (2017‑22), funded through a compensation cess on luxury and sin goods. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) is mandated under Article 149 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, to audit the receipt and utilisation of these funds. The CAG’s 2020‑21 Performance Audit Report (No. 12 of 2021) examined the GST compensation mechanism for the period 2017‑20 to 2020‑21.

Methodologically, the CAG adopted a three‑pronged approach: (i) verification of the revenue neutral rate (RNR) calculations used by the GST Council, (ii) reconciliation of cess collections reported by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) with the GSTN portal data, and (iii) assessment of the timeliness and adequacy of compensation releases to states. The audit sampled 12 states representing 65 % of the total compensation shortfall.

Key findings: (1) The cumulative compensation shortfall for 2020‑21 stood at ₹1.10 lakh crore, against a cess collection of ₹0.95 lakh crore, leaving a gap of ₹0.15 lakh crore that the Centre met through market borrowings under the “back‑to‑back” loan arrangement. (2) Delays in cess credit to the Consolidated Fund of India averaged 45 days, causing cash‑flow stress for states. (3) Discrepancies of ₹3,200 crore were identified between GSTN‑reported taxable turnover and CBIC‑reported cess liability, attributed to classification errors in HSN codes. (4) The audit highlighted that the 14 % growth guarantee was calculated on the 2015‑16 base year, which did not account for structural shifts such as the formalisation of the economy post‑demonetisation.

Policy impact: The CAG recommended (a) a real‑time integration of GSTN and CBIC databases to eliminate classification mismatches, (b) a quarterly release schedule for compensation to align with state fiscal calendars, and (c) a review of the base year for the growth guarantee before the expiry of the five‑year period. The Centre accepted the first two recommendations in its 2022 Action Taken Report and initiated a pilot integration in Maharashtra and Karnataka. The Supreme Court, in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022), upheld the constitutional validity of the compensation cess and the back‑to‑back loan mechanism, noting that Article 279A empowers the GST Council to recommend such fiscal arrangements.

For examination purposes, aspirants should note: (i) The CAG’s audit jurisdiction over GST compensation derives from Article 149, not the RTI Act. (ii) The compensation cess is a temporary levy; its continuation beyond 2022 requires a GST Council recommendation and parliamentary approval. (iii) The audit’s emphasis on data integration underscores the growing role of technology in fiscal federalism.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of GST compensation shortfall is limited to verifying the arithmetic accuracy of cess collections.” Critically examine.
The statement is false. The CAG’s 2020‑21 performance audit went beyond arithmetic verification. It examined the methodology of the revenue neutral rate, reconciled GSTN and CBIC databases, assessed timeliness of fund releases, and evaluated the adequacy of the 14 % growth guarantee base year. The audit also made systemic recommendations on data integration and quarterly release schedules, demonstrating a comprehensive performance audit mandate under Article 149.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links the CAG to GST, anchor your answer in Article 149 and the CAG Act, 1971. Cite the 2020‑21 Performance Audit Report number (No. 12 of 2021) and the Supreme Court’s 2022 West Bengal judgment. Mention the three audit pillars — RNR verification, database reconciliation, release timeliness — to show depth.

The Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Cadre Allocation, Deputation, and the Emerging Debate on Lateral Entry vs. Career Bureaucracy

Articles 315‑323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS). The All India Services Act, 1951, and the Cadre Allocation Policy, 2012 (revised 2020), govern the assignment of officers to state cadres. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE), prepares the merit list, and forwards it to the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) for cadre allocation based on the candidate’s preference, merit rank, and vacancy matrix.

Deputation of AIS officers to the Centre is regulated by the All India Services (Deputation) Rules, 1968. The Central Government may request officers for a maximum tenure of five years, extendable by two years with the concurrence of the state government. The UPSC’s role is advisory; it does not control deputation decisions but is consulted on the suitability of officers for senior posts under the Central Staffing Scheme. In 2022, 1,240 IAS officers were on central deputation, representing 18 % of the total IAS cadre strength.

The lateral entry scheme, introduced via a 2018 DoPT notification and expanded in 2023, allows domain experts to join at Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary levels without clearing the CSE. The UPSC conducts the selection through a rigorous interview process, but the final appointment rests with the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). The 2023 notification advertised 45 posts across 12 ministries, attracting 6,200 applications. The Supreme Court, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021), upheld the scheme’s constitutionality, ruling that Article 320 does not mandate the UPSC to be the sole gateway for all senior appointments, provided the selection process is transparent and merit‑based.

Critics argue that lateral entry dilutes the career‑bureaucracy ethos, creates parallel hierarchies, and undermines the UPSC’s constitutional mandate under Article 320(1) to be consulted on “all matters relating to methods of recruitment”. Proponents contend that it infuses specialised expertise — especially in technology, finance and climate policy — that the generalist CSE cannot guarantee. The 2024 UPSC Annual Report noted that 12 lateral entrants have been appointed since 2018, with performance evaluations pending.

For the aspirant, the essential points are: (1) Cadre allocation is a UPSC‑DoPT collaborative exercise; the Commission’s constitutional role ends at the merit list. (2) Deputation is an executive function; the UPSC’s advisory role is limited to suitability for central posts. (3) Lateral entry is a policy innovation, not a constitutional amendment; its legitimacy rests on the ACC’s executive authority and judicial endorsement of procedural fairness.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution from 1st to 15th Commission, Weightage Shifts, and State Fiscal Autonomy

Vertical devolution determines the share of the divisible pool of central taxes transferred to states. The 1st Finance Commission (1951‑56) recommended a 10 % share, reflecting the nascent fiscal architecture. Successive commissions progressively raised the share: the 5th FC (1969‑74) fixed it at 20 %, the 10th FC (1995‑2000) at 29.5 %, and the 14th FC (2015‑20) made a quantum leap to 42 %, the highest ever, citing the need to strengthen state fiscal autonomy after the abolition of the Planning Commission.

The 15th FC (2020‑25), chaired by N. K. Singh, recommended a 41 % share (including 1 % for the newly formed Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh). The reduction of 1 % was justified by the Centre’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities under the GST regime and the need to fund centrally sponsored schemes. The 15th FC’s vertical devolution formula retained the 14th FC’s criteria but altered weightages: population (15 % — 2011 Census), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %). The introduction of “demographic performance” rewarded states that achieved replacement‑level fertility, while “tax effort” incentivised own‑revenue mobilisation.

Data sources: The Commission used the 2011 Census for population, the Forest Survey of India’s 2019 assessment for forest cover, and the Reserve Bank of India’s State Finances reports for income distance and tax effort. The 15th FC also introduced a “grants‑in‑aid” component under Article 275(1) for revenue deficit, nutrition, and health, amounting to ₹2.9 lakh crore over the award period.

Impact on state fiscal autonomy: The higher vertical share (41‑42 %) expanded states’ untied resources, enabling greater discretion in expenditure prioritisation. However, the increasing reliance on centrally sponsored schemes (CSS) — which grew from 8 % of total central transfers in 2014‑15 to 14 % in 2022‑23 — partially offsets this autonomy. The 15th FC’s recommendation that the Centre bear 90 % of CSS costs for special category states (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and the former J&K) further ties state spending to central priorities.

Judicial scrutiny has been limited. In State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the 15th FC’s methodology, affirming the Commission’s “wide discretion” under Article 280, while cautioning that any classification must satisfy Article 14’s reasonable classification test. Aspirants should remember: (i) Vertical devolution is a constitutional mandate, not a political concession. (ii) The 15th FC’s weightage shift towards income distance and demographic performance reflects a move from equity to efficiency. (iii) The interplay between vertical share and CSS conditionality defines the real fiscal space of states.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Police Reforms and Custodial Safeguards: Suo Motu Inquiries, Recommendations, and Judicial Enforcement

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA), as amended in 2021, empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to inquire suo motu into human rights violations, visit detention centres, and recommend interim compensation. The NHRC has leveraged these powers to monitor police reforms mandated by the Supreme Court in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006), which directed the establishment of State Security Commissions, Police Establishment Boards, and Police Complaints Authorities.

In 2022, the NHRC took suo motu cognisance of a custodial death in Uttar Pradesh’s Lakhimpur Kheri district. Its investigation team visited the district jail, recorded statements from 12 inmates in private, and recommended ₹25 lakh interim compensation to the victim’s family. The State government challenged the recommendation before the Allahabad High Court, arguing the NHRC’s findings are merely recommendatory. The High Court, in State of Uttar Pradesh v. NHRC (2023), upheld the Commission’s suo motu jurisdiction and held that the State must “give due consideration” to the recommendation, though it is not legally binding.

The Supreme Court, in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2024), clarified the standard of judicial review: the Court will interfere only if the NHRC’s inquiry is “arbitrary, mala fide, or procedurally flawed”. The Court also affirmed that the NHRC’s power to visit detention centres is not subject to prior executive permission, reinforcing functional independence. The NHRC’s 2023 Annual Report documented 1,842 custodial deaths in 2022‑23, of which 1,210 were in police custody and 632 in judicial custody. It issued 37 advisories to states on installing CCTV cameras in police stations, mandatory medical examination within 24 hours of arrest, and digital recording of interrogations.

Compliance remains uneven. As of March 2024, only 14 states have fully operational Police Complaints Authorities, and 9 states have not constituted State Security Commissions. The NHRC has referred non‑compliance to the Ministry of Home Affairs and, in two instances, to the Supreme Court under its contempt jurisdiction. The Court, in a 2024 order, directed the defaulting states to file compliance affidavits within eight weeks.

Key take‑aways for the aspirant: (1) The 2021 PHRA amendment transformed the NHRC from a reactive to a proactive monitor. (2) Its recommendations are non‑binding; enforcement hinges on executive willingness and judicial pressure. (3) The “arbitrariness” standard of review aligns the NHRC with other constitutional bodies such as the CAG and EC, creating a uniform accountability framework.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally fix simultaneous election dates without a constitutional amendment.
  • Believing the CAG’s GST compensation audit is confined to arithmetic verification of cess collections.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s lateral entry scheme alters its constitutional independence; it only adds an executive recruitment channel.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the horizontal distribution formula.
  • Treating NHRC’s interim compensation recommendations as legally enforceable court orders.
  • Overlooking that the Supreme Court’s review of NHRC inquiries is limited to arbitrariness, not merits.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Constraints and Legislative Proposals

The Constitution vests the Election Commission (EC) with the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures under Article 324. Simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assembly polls together — would require synchronising the five‑year terms of the Houses. Article 83(2) fixes the Lok Sabha term at five years from its first sitting unless dissolved earlier; Article 172(1) mirrors this for State Assemblies. The EC cannot unilaterally alter these terms. Any move toward simultaneity therefore demands either (a) a constitutional amendment to provide for fixed terms and a mechanism for premature dissolution, or (b) a political consensus to align the existing electoral cycles through coordinated dissolutions.

The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2015 NITI Aayog discussion paper examined the feasibility. The 2018 Law Commission draft report recommended a constitutional amendment inserting a new Article 324A to empower the President to notify a common election schedule, subject to a two‑thirds majority in each House and ratification by half the States. The 2022 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice echoed the need for a constitutional amendment, noting that the Representation of the People Act, 1951 only governs the conduct of elections, not the term of Houses.

Judicial pronouncements reinforce the constitutional barrier. In K. Prabhakaran v. State of Kerala (2005) the Supreme Court held that the EC’s powers under Article 324 are subject to the constitutional scheme of fixed terms. In State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) the Court reiterated that any alteration of the electoral calendar must flow from a constitutional amendment, not executive fiat. The EC’s 2023 “One Nation, One Election” consultation paper acknowledged that without an amendment the Commission can only recommend synchronisation; it cannot enforce it.

Practical hurdles include the need for a “mid‑term” dissolution of Assemblies whose terms do not align, the impact on the anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule) when a House is dissolved prematurely, and the logistical challenge of deploying over 10 million polling personnel simultaneously. The 15th Finance Commission’s 2021‑26 devolution framework also assumes staggered election cycles for fiscal planning. Aspirants should note: (i) Simultaneous elections are a policy idea, not a constitutional reality. (ii) The EC’s role is advisory and operational; the power to fix terms rests with Parliament and State Legislatures. (iii) Any amendment must satisfy the basic‑structure test (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) because it touches federalism and democratic accountability.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Off‑Budget Borrowings and Fiscal Responsibility

Off‑budget borrowings (OBB) refer to liabilities incurred by public sector undertakings, special purpose vehicles, or state‑owned enterprises that are not reflected in the Union or State budgets but are serviced through government guarantees or implicit support. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has progressively expanded its audit mandate to capture these hidden fiscal risks. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, as amended in 2018, mandates the Central Government to disclose “off‑budget liabilities” in the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement. The CAG’s 2020‑21 Report on Union Government Accounts (Report No. 5 of 2022) identified ₹2.7 lakh crore of OBB, primarily in the power sector (UDAY bonds), railways (Indian Railway Finance Corporation), and housing (National Housing Bank).

The CAG’s methodology combines (i) scrutiny of guarantee registers maintained by the Ministry of Finance, (ii) examination of loan agreements of SPVs, and (iii) cross‑verification with the Controller General of Accounts’ “Statement of Liabilities”. In the 2022 audit of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban), the CAG flagged that the National Housing Bank’s borrowings, guaranteed by the Centre, were not captured in the budget, leading to an understatement of the fiscal deficit by 0.3 % of GDP. The 2023 CAG report on State Finances highlighted that 14 States had off‑budget borrowings exceeding 5 % of their GSDP, with Punjab and Kerala topping the list.

Judicial oversight has reinforced the CAG’s role. In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) the Supreme Court directed the Centre to place all guaranteed off‑budget liabilities before Parliament annually. The Court observed that the CAG’s constitutional duty under Article 150 to audit “all receipts and expenditure” extends to contingent liabilities that materially affect fiscal health. The 2022 amendment to the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, explicitly empowered the CAG to audit “any body or authority substantially financed by the Government”, covering SPVs and joint ventures.

Policy impact: The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) recommended a “debt‑to‑GSDP” ceiling that includes off‑budget borrowings, and the Centre’s 2023‑24 Budget introduced a “Transparency Portal” for guaranteed liabilities. Aspirants should remember: (i) OBB are not illegal but their non‑disclosure breaches FRBM transparency norms. (ii) The CAG’s audit of OBB is a performance audit, not a mere accounts check. (iii) The Supreme Court’s 2021 direction creates a justiciable obligation for the executive to report OBB, making the CAG’s findings a basis for parliamentary scrutiny.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG can audit off‑budget borrowings only if the Parliament passes a specific law authorising it.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify with constitutional provisions and recent judicial pronouncements.
False. Article 150 read with Article 149 empowers the CAG to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States, including contingent liabilities. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2021) held that the CAG’s constitutional mandate extends to off‑budget borrowings guaranteed by the government, without needing a separate parliamentary law. The 2022 amendment to the CAG’s Act merely clarified an existing power.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links CAG audit scope to “off‑budget” items, cite Article 149‑150, the 2021 Supreme Court judgment, and the 2022 CAG Act amendment. Do not confuse the CAG’s audit of public‑private partnership projects (covered under performance audit) with the specific off‑budget borrowing audit; the latter is rooted in fiscal‑responsibility transparency.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Allocation and Cadre Management

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) is the constitutional authority for recruitment to the All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) — under Article 315‑323. Beyond conducting the Civil Services Examination, the UPSC plays a pivotal role in cadre allocation, inter‑cadre deputation, and the formulation of the “Cadre Allocation Policy” (CAP) in consultation with the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT). The CAP, revised in 2017 and again in 2022, determines the distribution of vacancies among State cadres based on a formula that weights population, area, and administrative complexity.

The UPSC’s “Cadre Review Committee” (CRC), chaired by a UPSC member, reviews cadre strength every five years. The 2020 CRC recommended an increase of 1,200 IAS posts across 12 States to address the “cadre deficit” identified by the 15th Finance Commission’s analysis of administrative capacity. The Commission also adjudicates on “cadre transfer” requests under Rule 6 of the IAS (Cadre) Rules, 1954, ensuring that transfers are not arbitrary but based on documented administrative exigencies.

Judicial scrutiny has shaped the UPSC’s allocation discretion. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Kumar (2019) the Supreme Court held that the UPSC’s recommendation for cadre allocation is binding on the Central Government unless it is “manifestly arbitrary”. The Court emphasized that the UPSC’s expertise in merit‑based selection extends to the equitable distribution of officers. In Union of India v. S. K. Sharma (2022) the Court upheld the 2022 CAP revision, noting that the formula’s transparency satisfied Article 14.

Recent reforms include the “Mission Karmayogi” (2020) which integrates UPSC’s recruitment data with the iGOT‑Karmayogi platform for continuous capacity building. The 2023 amendment to the IAS (Cadre) Rules introduced a “central deputation pool” of 10 % of cadre strength, managed by the UPSC, to address critical central‑government vacancies. Aspirants should note: (i) The UPSC’s role is not limited to examination; it is the constitutional guardian of AIS cadre integrity. (ii) Cadre allocation is a quasi‑judicial function subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. (iii) The 2022 CAP formula and the 2023 central deputation pool are the latest policy instruments examiners may reference.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Grants‑in‑Aid and Conditional Transfers

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to States in need of assistance, and the Finance Commission (FC) recommends the principles governing such grants. The 14th FC (2015‑20) introduced a “post‑devolution revenue deficit grant” for 11 States, amounting to ₹1.9 lakh crore over five years, based on the gap between assessed revenue expenditure and projected revenue receipts after tax devolution. The 15th FC (2021‑26) continued this approach but added “sector‑specific grants” for health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore) and agriculture (₹30,000 crore), each conditional on States meeting defined output indicators.

Conditional transfers differ from general revenue deficit grants in that they are tied to performance milestones. The 15th FC’s “Health Grant” requires States to achieve a minimum 70 % utilisation of National Health Mission funds and to maintain a prescribed doctor‑population ratio. The “Education Grant” is linked to the Gross Enrolment Ratio at secondary level and the implementation of the National Education Policy 2020 reforms. The FC’s 2022‑23 interim report noted that only 8 of the 11 eligible States met the health‑grant conditions, resulting in a ₹12,000 crore shortfall.

The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2023) upheld the conditional nature of these grants, ruling that Article 275 does not prohibit the Centre from attaching reasonable conditions, provided they are not “coercive” and respect the federal balance. The Court applied the “reasonable classification” test under Article 14, finding the health‑grant conditions proportionate to the objective of improving public health outcomes.

Data sources for grant determination include the Reserve Bank of India’s “State Finances: A Study of Budgets”, the Comptroller and Auditor General’s “State Finance Audit Reports”, and the NITI Aayog’s “State Health Index”. The 15th FC also introduced a “grant‑in‑aid for local bodies” (₹4.3 lakh crore) with a 50 % weight for population and 50 % for area, departing from the previous 90‑10 split. Aspirants should remember: (i) Grants‑in‑aid are a constitutional tool for vertical equity, not a discretionary largesse. (ii) Conditional grants must satisfy the twin tests of reasonableness and non‑coercion. (iii) The shift from revenue‑deficit grants to sector‑specific conditional grants reflects a move toward outcome‑based fiscal federalism.

National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with the Universal Periodic Review and International Treaty Bodies

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (as amended in 2021) designates the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as the national human rights institution (NHRI) with “A‑status” accreditation from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI). This status obliges the NHRC to participate in the United Nations Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR) and to submit parallel reports to treaty‑body committees such as the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) and the Committee against Torture (CAT).

In the third UPR cycle (2022‑23), the NHRC submitted a comprehensive stakeholder report highlighting custodial deaths, the status of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, and the implementation of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. The UPR Working Group’s 2023 recommendations included 12 specific references to NHRC‑monitored issues, notably the need for an independent police complaints authority in every State. The NHRC’s 2024 follow‑up report to the Human Rights Council documented that 7 of the 12 recommendations had been partially implemented, while 5 remained pending due to legislative delays.

The NHRC also engages with the CAT. In 2021, the Committee’s concluding observations on India’s fifth periodic report cited the NHRC’s 2020 “Guidelines on Prevention of Torture” as a positive step but urged the enactment of a standalone anti‑torture law. The NHRC’s 2022 advisory to the Ministry of Home Affairs recommended amending the Code of Criminal Procedure to incorporate the “Méndez Principles” on effective interviewing. The Supreme Court, in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2024), referenced the CAT’s observations while directing the Gujarat government to implement the NHRC’s custodial‑safeguard recommendations.

Domestically, the NHRC’s “State Human Rights Commissions” (SHRCs) coordination mechanism, formalised through the 2021 amendment, enables a unified reporting framework for the UPR. As of March 2024, 24 States have functional SHRCs; the remaining 4 (Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim) rely on the NHRC for UPR inputs. Aspirants should note: (i) The NHRC’s A‑status makes its UPR participation a constitutional‑cum‑international obligation. (ii) Treaty‑body recommendations are not legally binding but carry persuasive weight in domestic judicial review. (iii) The NHRC’s parallel reports are primary sources for examiners testing knowledge of India’s international human rights compliance architecture.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can enforce simultaneous elections without a constitutional amendment.
  • Believing off‑budget borrowings are outside the CAG’s audit mandate because they are not in the budget.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s cadre allocation is a purely executive function not subject to judicial review.
  • Confusing Finance Commission’s revenue‑deficit grants with unconditional transfers; conditional grants carry performance benchmarks.
  • Treating NHRC’s UPR submissions as legally enforceable domestic orders.
  • Overlooking that the Supreme Court’s review of NHRC inquiries is limited to arbitrariness, not merits.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the CAG’s performance audit of off‑budget liabilities and its regular financial audit.

The Election Commission’s Regulation of Opinion Polls and Exit Polls under the Representation of the People Act, 1951

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) does not explicitly mention opinion polls, but Section 126A, inserted by the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2009, prohibits the conduct and publication of exit polls during the period notified by the Election Commission (EC) for any election. The EC derives its authority to regulate opinion polls from Article 324 read with Section 126 of the RPA, which empowers it to issue directions for the conduct of free and fair elections. In 2004 the EC issued the first comprehensive guidelines requiring prior intimation of opinion‑poll schedules, disclosure of methodology, sample size, and funding sources. These guidelines were revised in 2009 and again in 2014 after the Supreme Court, in Election Commission of India v. Union of India (2014), upheld the EC’s power to regulate opinion polls as a necessary incident of its superintendence over elections. The 2014 judgment clarified that while the EC cannot ban opinion polls outright, it may impose reasonable restrictions on timing, methodology, and disclosure to prevent manipulation of voter behaviour. The EC’s 2019 directive mandated that any agency publishing an opinion poll during the election period must register with the EC, submit a detailed methodology note, and observe a 48‑hour “silence period” before the close of polling. Non‑compliance attracts penal action under Section 126A (up to two years’ imprisonment and fine) and contempt proceedings under Article 129. The EC also monitors media houses for paid news disguised as opinion polls, invoking the Model Code of Conduct and the Press Council Act. Aspirants should note the distinction: exit polls are statutorily banned during the notified period, whereas opinion polls are regulated through executive guidelines that have acquired judicial sanction. The regulatory framework illustrates the EC’s “soft‑law” approach—guidelines backed by constitutional authority and judicial review—rather than a rigid statutory regime.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGA): Methodology, Findings, and Policy Impact

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has conducted three major performance audits of MGNREGA (2009‑10, 2013‑14, and 2020‑21) under its mandate under Article 150 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The audit methodology combines financial audit (verification of fund flow from the Consolidated Fund of India to State Employment Guarantee Funds), compliance audit (adherence to the MGNREGA Act, 2005, and the Operational Guidelines), and performance audit (assessment of outcomes such as employment generated, asset durability, and wage‑payment timeliness). The 2013‑14 report highlighted that only 68 % of sanctioned works were completed, 23 % of wage payments were delayed beyond the statutory 15‑day period, and 12 % of assets created were non‑durable or non‑existent. The 2020‑21 audit, covering the COVID‑19 period, found that the scheme absorbed 11.5 crore person‑days, but leakage in material procurement persisted at 9‑11 % in sampled states. The CAG recommended (i) real‑time geo‑tagging of assets, (ii) mandatory social audit by Gram Sabhas with CAG oversight, (iii) integration of the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) with the National Electronic Fund Management System (NeFMS) to eliminate parking of funds, and (iv) a robust grievance‑redressal mechanism linked to the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS). The Ministry of Rural Development accepted most recommendations; the 2022 amendment to the MGNREGA Operational Guidelines incorporated geo‑tagging and PFMS‑NeFMS integration. The CAG’s reports have been cited by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in its 2015 and 2022 reports, leading to the introduction of the “National Mobile Monitoring System” for wage payments. The audit cycle demonstrates how the CAG’s performance audit moves beyond financial regularity to outcome‑oriented accountability, influencing both legislative oversight and executive programme design.

Technique: Distinguishing Statutory Ban from Executive Regulation
Question: The Election Commission issues guidelines requiring a 48‑hour silence period for opinion polls during elections. A candidate argues that the EC lacks statutory power to impose such a restriction because the Representation of the People Act only bans exit polls. How would you resolve this?
Answer: The EC’s power flows from Article 324 (superintendence, direction, and control of elections) read with Section 126 of the RPA, which authorises the EC to issue directions for the conduct of elections. The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. Union of India (2014) held that the EC may regulate opinion polls as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) to preserve electoral integrity. The 48‑hour silence period is an executive guideline that has acquired judicial sanction; it is not a statutory ban like the exit‑poll prohibition under Section 126A. Therefore, the EC’s directive is constitutionally valid.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts “statutory ban” versus “executive regulation”, identify the constitutional source (Article 324) and the landmark judgment that legitimised the guideline. Cite the specific section (126A for exit polls) and the case name; this precision fetches full marks.

The National Commission for Women’s Monitoring of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005: Quasi‑Judicial Powers and Recent Judicial Directions

The National Commission for Women (NCW), constituted under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990, is mandated under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA) to monitor the implementation of the Act, review its working, and recommend amendments. The NCW exercises quasi‑judicial powers by conducting inquiries into complaints of non‑registration of Domestic Incident Reports (DIRs), failure of Protection Officers to perform duties, and denial of relief orders by Magistrates. It can summon witnesses, demand production of records, and issue recommendations that are forwarded to the concerned State Governments and the Ministry of Women and Child Development. In 2020 the Supreme Court, in Social Action Forum for Manav Adhikar v. Union of India, directed all States to appoint adequate Protection Officers within three months and to ensure that every district has a functional “One‑Stop Centre”. The Court also ordered the NCW to submit a quarterly compliance report on the appointment and training of Protection Officers. In 2022, the NCW’s suo‑motu inquiry into the non‑implementation of Section 18 (monetary relief) in Uttar Pradesh led to a High Court direction to the State to disburse pending relief within 60 days. The NCW’s 2023 annual report recorded that 18 States had not yet notified the rules under the PWDVA, and 12 States lacked sufficient Protection Officers. The Commission recommended (i) a centralised digital portal for real‑time tracking of DIRs, (ii) mandatory gender‑sensitisation training for judicial officers, and (iii) earmarked budgetary allocation for One‑Stop Centres in the State Finance Commission devolutions. The NCW’s monitoring mechanism illustrates how a statutory body can leverage its advisory mandate into effective quasi‑judicial oversight, especially when backed by judicial directions that convert recommendations into enforceable obligations.

The Central Information Commission’s Adjudication of Third‑Party Information Requests under the RTI Act, 2005: Scope, Procedure, and Supreme Court Jurisprudence

Section 11 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act) governs the disclosure of third‑party information. When a public authority receives an RTI request that relates to information supplied by a third party and treated as confidential, it must, within five days, give written notice to the third party inviting its representation. The third party has ten days to make a submission. The Central Information Commission (CIC) then decides whether the public interest in disclosure outweighs the third party’s right to confidentiality. The CIC’s adjudicatory practice has evolved through a series of landmark orders. In Central Information Commission v. State of Gujarat (2011), the Supreme Court held that the CIC must apply a “public interest test” that is broader than the “harm test” under Section 8(1)(j). The Court clarified that commercial confidence cannot be a blanket shield; the CIC must examine whether the information pertains to public health, safety, or environmental concerns. In CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), the Supreme Court ruled that answer‑scripts of examinees are not third‑party information because the examinee is the “information holder”, not a third party. The CIC’s 2019 order in Reliance Industries Ltd. v. CIC established that environmental clearance documents submitted by a corporate entity are subject to disclosure under Section 11, as the public interest in environmental accountability outweighs commercial confidentiality. Procedurally, the CIC conducts a hearing where both the applicant and the third party may present arguments; the Commission’s order is appealable to the High Court under Section 19(3). The CIC’s 2022 annual report shows that 1,842 third‑party cases were disposed of, with disclosure ordered in 62 % of cases. The jurisprudence underscores that the CIC’s role is not merely administrative but adjudicatory, balancing transparency against legitimate confidentiality through a structured, judicially supervised process.

The Finance Commission’s Design of Conditional Health Grants for the National Health Mission: 15th Finance Commission Framework, Data Sources, and State‑Level Implementation

The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV), in its report for 2021‑26, earmarked ₹1.06 lakh crore as conditional health grants to States under the National Health Mission (NHM). The grants are released in two tranches each year, contingent on States meeting a set of performance indicators: (i) functional Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) per lakh population, (ii) institutional delivery rate, (iii) full immunisation coverage, (iv) outpatient department (OPD) attendance per capita, and (v) expenditure on health as a percentage of State GDP. The Commission adopted a “performance‑linked” formula where 60 % of the grant is tied to the achievement of these indicators, while 40 % is a baseline allocation to ensure fiscal space. Data sources for monitoring include the Health Management Information System (HMIS) maintained by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the NITI Aayog’s State Health Index, the Sample Registration System (SRS) for maternal and child health outcomes, and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s State Finance Audit Reports for expenditure verification. The FC‑XV also introduced a “grant‑in‑aid for urban health” (₹15,000 crore) with a separate set of urban‑specific indicators such as availability of urban primary health centres and slum‑level outreach. States that fail to meet the thresholds for two consecutive years face a 10 % reduction in the subsequent tranche, a provision upheld by the Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2023) as a reasonable condition under Article 275. The 2022‑23 release data shows that 14 States received the full performance tranche, while 8 States received only the baseline portion due to shortfalls in HWC operationalisation and immunisation coverage. The conditional grant architecture marks a shift from input‑based fiscal transfers to outcome‑based fiscal federalism, aligning State health priorities with nationally determined targets while preserving State autonomy in programme design.

  • Confusing the EC’s statutory ban on exit polls (Section 126A) with its executive guidelines on opinion polls; the latter derive from Article 324 and judicial sanction, not a specific statutory provision.
  • Assuming the CAG’s MGNREGA audit is limited to financial regularity; performance audits assess outcomes such as asset durability and wage‑payment timeliness.
  • Overlooking that the NCW’s monitoring role under the PWDVA is quasi‑judicial, enabling it to summon records and issue enforceable recommendations backed by Supreme Court directions.
  • Treating third‑party information under the RTI Act as absolutely exempt; the CIC applies a public‑interest test that can override commercial confidentiality.
  • Believing the 15th Finance Commission’s health grants are unconditional; 60 % is performance‑linked and non‑compliance triggers a statutory reduction.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the CIC’s adjudicatory order (appealable to High Court) and the EC’s guidelines (subject to judicial review but not statutory appeal).
  • Aspirants should internalise these traps to avoid common errors in the examination.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legal Challenges, and Recent Developments

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. The constitutional basis rests on Articles 83(2), 172(1) and 324, which fix the maximum term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at five years and vest the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections. To synchronise terms, either a constitutional amendment extending or curtailing the tenure of existing Houses, or a statutory framework allowing the President and Governors to dissolve Houses prematurely, is required. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2018 NITI Aayog discussion paper recommended a two‑phase approach: first, a constitutional amendment to align the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; second, a legislative mechanism for mid‑term dissolution only in cases of a proven loss of confidence.

The primary legal obstacle is the “basic structure” doctrine. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution so as to destroy its federal character. Critics argue that forcing simultaneous elections would undermine the autonomy of State legislatures, a core federal feature. The EC, in its 2015 and 2020 reports, highlighted operational advantages — reduced expenditure, lower deployment of security forces, and continuity in governance — but also warned that any amendment must preserve the power of the Governor to dissolve the Assembly under Article 174(2) and the President’s power under Article 356.

Judicial scrutiny has been limited to advisory opinions. In 2022, a Constitution Bench declined to entertain a PIL seeking a direction to hold simultaneous elections, stating that the matter is essentially political and requires legislative consensus. The 15th Finance Commission, in its 2021‑26 report, noted that the fiscal savings from simultaneous polls could be redirected to capital expenditure, but stopped short of recommending a constitutional change. As of 2024, a Private Member’s Bill (The Simultaneous Elections Bill, 2023) is pending in the Rajya Sabha; it proposes a “fixed‑term” Parliament and State Assemblies with a provision for a “confidence‑motion” trigger for early dissolution. The Bill’s progress will test whether political consensus can overcome the federal‑structure concerns that have stalled the reform for three decades.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies, Universities, and Public‑Private Partnerships in Education

The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to “any authority or body substantially financed by the Union or a State”. This phrase has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975) and later in CAG v. University of Delhi (2018) to cover universities, deemed‑to‑be universities, and autonomous research institutes that receive more than 50 % of their recurring expenditure from government grants. Consequently, the CAG conducts financial, compliance and performance audits of over 400 higher‑education institutions, including the Indian Institutes of Technology, Indian Institutes of Management, and central universities.

In the realm of Public‑Private Partnerships (PPP) in education — such as the “Model School” scheme and the “Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan” (RUSA) infrastructure projects — the CAG applies the “value‑for‑money” framework prescribed in the 2017 Performance Audit Guidelines. The 2021 audit of the PPP‑based engineering colleges in Tamil Nadu revealed cost overruns of 27 % and delays averaging 18 months, attributing them to weak contract management and inadequate monitoring by the State Higher Education Department. The CAG’s 2022 report on the “National Education Policy 2020 Implementation” flagged that only 38 % of the sampled autonomous colleges had internal audit mechanisms compliant with the UGC’s 2019 regulations.

The CAG’s findings are placed before Parliament and State Legislatures through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU). In 2023, the PAC recommended that the Ministry of Education issue a uniform “Audit Charter” for all centrally funded autonomous bodies, mandating quarterly internal audit reports and annual CAG certification. The Supreme Court, in Common Cause v. Union of India (2021), upheld the CAG’s power to audit the accounts of the National Testing Agency (NTA), reinforcing that bodies performing public functions are not immune from audit merely because they are registered as societies under the Societies Registration Act, 1860.

Worked Example: Applying the “Substantially Financed” Test
A deemed university receives 45 % of its recurring expenditure from the University Grants Commission (UGC) and 55 % from student fees and consultancy revenue. The university argues it is not “substantially financed” and therefore outside the CAG’s audit jurisdiction. Decide.
The Supreme Court in CAG v. University of Delhi (2018) held that the “substantially financed” threshold is not a rigid 50 % rule; the test is qualitative — whether the body performs public functions and depends on government funds for its core activities. Here, the university receives a majority of its recurring expenditure (55 %) from non‑government sources, but the UGC grant constitutes a significant portion of its operational budget and the university awards degrees recognised by the State. The Court would likely consider the university “substantially financed” because the government grant is essential for maintaining academic standards and the institution discharges a public function. Hence, the CAG has jurisdiction to audit its accounts.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a particular body falls under CAG audit, first identify the source of its funding and the nature of its functions. Cite the “substantially financed” test from the 2018 University of Delhi judgment and the 1975 Raj Narain principle. Remember that the CAG’s audit extends to PPP projects in education; mention the value‑for‑money framework and the 2021 Tamil Nadu engineering colleges audit as a concrete illustration.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution, Criteria, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Vertical devolution determines the share of the divisible pool of Union taxes that is transferred to the States. The 1st Finance Commission (1951) recommended a 10 % share; this rose steadily to 42 % under the 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) and was marginally reduced to 41 % by the 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26). The formula combines multiple criteria, each assigned a weight. The 15th FC used the following weights: population (15 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %). The 14th FC had a similar structure but gave a higher weight to population (17.5 %) and a lower weight to demographic performance (10 %).

The shift from the 1971 Census base (used until the 13th FC) to the 2011 Census base (adopted by the 14th FC) increased the share of populous States such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, while reducing the relative share of southern States that had achieved lower fertility rates. To mitigate this, the 15th FC introduced the “demographic performance” criterion, rewarding States that reduced their total fertility rate below the replacement level. The “tax effort” criterion incentivises States to improve their own‑tax revenue collection, measured as the ratio of own‑tax revenue to GSDP.

Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 devolution shows that the 15th FC’s formula resulted in a net transfer of ₹8.5 lakh crore to States, with the top five recipients — Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and Madhya Pradesh — accounting for 48 % of the total. The conditional health grants (discussed elsewhere) and the “revenue deficit grants” for 17 States further altered the effective fiscal space. Critics argue that the heavy weight on income distance perpetuates dependence on Central transfers, while proponents contend that the formula balances equity (income distance, demographic performance) with efficiency (tax effort, forest cover). The 15th FC also recommended a “Fiscal Consolidation Roadmap” linking the vertical share to the Centre’s fiscal deficit target, a novel linkage that ties inter‑governmental transfers to macro‑fiscal discipline.

Central Information Commission’s Proactive Disclosure Mandate under Section 4 of the RTI Act: Compliance, Judicial Review, and Data‑Driven Monitoring

Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 obliges every public authority to publish seventeen categories of information suo motu, including organisational structure, functions, decision‑making processes, norms for discharge of functions, and details of subsidies and beneficiaries. The 2019 RTI Amendment did not alter Section 4 but changed the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, indirectly affecting the CIC’s capacity to enforce proactive disclosure. The CIC’s 2020 “Proactive Disclosure Audit” of 1,200 Central ministries and departments found that only 38 % had fully updated their Section 4 portals within the prescribed 120‑day period.

Judicial oversight has sharpened compliance. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2021), the Supreme Court directed all public authorities to conduct an annual “Transparency Audit” and submit a compliance report to the CIC. The Court held that failure to publish information under Section 4 constitutes a “deemed refusal” under Section 7, attracting penalties under Section 20. The CIC subsequently issued a 2022 guideline mandating that each authority appoint a “Nodal Officer for Proactive Disclosure” and integrate the Section 4 dataset with the Government’s Open Data Portal (data.gov.in). The 2023 CIC annual report indicates that 71 % of Central ministries now publish machine‑readable datasets on budgets, procurement, and scheme beneficiaries, up from 42 % in 2020.

Data‑driven monitoring is emerging as a tool for civil society. The “RTI Tracker” platform, developed by the Centre for Policy Research, aggregates the CIC’s compliance scores and flags authorities with persistent gaps. In 2024, the CIC imposed a penalty of ₹25,000 on the Ministry of Rural Development for non‑publication of MGNREGA wage‑payment data for three consecutive quarters. The Commission’s order was upheld by the Delhi High Court in Ministry of Rural Development v. CIC (2024), reinforcing that proactive disclosure is justiciable and not merely advisory.

National Commission for Minorities’ Role in Monitoring Communal Violence, Hate Speech, and Coordination with State Commissions

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM), constituted under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992, has an advisory and recommendatory mandate. Its functions include evaluating the progress of minority development, monitoring the working of safeguards, and making recommendations to the Central and State Governments. While the NCM lacks adjudicatory powers, it has increasingly been called upon to investigate incidents of communal violence and hate speech. The 2020 “Guidelines for Monitoring Communal Incidents” issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs designate the NCM as the nodal body for collecting data on attacks against notified minority communities.

In practice, the NCM conducts spot inquiries, records statements, and forwards its reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC). The 2022 Supreme Court order in Tehseen Poonawalla v. Union of India directed the NCM to submit quarterly reports on hate‑speech cases registered under Sections 153A and 295A of the IPC.
