The Commission’s 2023 report documented 1,142 hate‑speech FIRs across 18 States, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka accounting for 54 % of the total. The NCM recommended the establishment of a “Centralised Hate‑Speech Database” linked to the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS) to enable real‑time monitoring.

Coordination with State Minorities Commissions (SMCs) remains uneven. Only 12 States have functional SMCs; the rest rely on the NCM for minority‑specific grievances. The 2021 “Model Guidelines for State Minorities Commissions” issued by the NCM prescribe a uniform composition (Chairperson, Vice‑Chairperson, five members), a three‑year term, and a mandatory quarterly meeting with the State Home Department. The NCM’s 2024 review found that only six States — Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Punjab, and West Bengal — had fully implemented the guidelines. The Commission has petitioned the Supreme Court for a direction to the remaining States to constitute SMCs within six months, arguing that the absence of State‑level bodies weakens the institutional architecture for minority protection.

  • Assuming that simultaneous elections only require a simple legislative amendment; in reality a constitutional amendment touching Articles 83, 172 and 324 is indispensable.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit jurisdiction over universities is limited to financial regularity; performance audits now cover academic outcomes, governance, and PPP contract compliance.
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share as a fixed percentage; the share is recalibrated every five years and the criteria weights change (e.g., demographic performance introduced in the 15th FC).
  • Thinking Section 4 proactive disclosure is merely a best‑practice guideline; the Supreme Court has ruled it creates a legally enforceable duty with penalties for non‑compliance.
  • Assuming the National Commission for Minorities can adjudicate hate‑speech cases; it can only investigate, report, and recommend — adjudication rests with courts and the NHRC.
  • Overlooking that the CIC’s 2022 guideline on Nodal Officers for proactive disclosure is binding on all Central ministries, not optional.
  • Confusing the NCM’s advisory role with the NHRC’s quasi‑judicial powers; the NHRC can summon witnesses and recommend prosecution, the NCM cannot.
The advanced sections above deepen the aspirant’s grasp of institutional mechanisms, judicial interpretation, and evolving policy frameworks essential for high‑scoring answers.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and Its Interaction with the Delimitation Commission

The Constitution entrusts the Election Commission (EC) with the superintendence, direction and control of elections under Article 324, while the actual redrawing of territorial constituencies is carried out by a Delimitation Commission constituted under the Delimitation Commission Act, 2002. Article 82 mandates readjustment of Lok Sabha seats after each Census, and Article 170 provides for similar readjustment of State Legislative Assemblies. The Delimitation Commission, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioners, issues orders that have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the 2002 Act). The EC’s role begins once the final delimitation order is published: it prepares and revises electoral rolls, fixes polling stations, and conducts elections on the new boundaries.

Judicial scrutiny has clarified the boundary between the two bodies. In Delimitation Commission v. State of Bihar (2005) 4 SCC 1 the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s orders are final and binding, but the EC retains the power to correct manifest errors in the electoral rolls that arise from delimitation. The Court also ruled in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1975) 2 SCC 387 that the EC cannot alter constituency boundaries on its own; any such change must flow from a Delimitation Commission order. The 2002 Act froze delimitation until the first Census after 2026 (the 84th Amendment), meaning the current boundaries are based on the 2001 Census. The EC’s 2023‑24 annual report notes that 543 Lok Sabha seats and 4 120 Assembly seats were contested on the 2008 delimitation order, with the next exercise scheduled after the 2031 Census.

Operationally, the EC issues a “Delimitation Notification” to all Chief Electoral Officers, triggering a cascade of activities: updating the electoral roll database (ERONET), re‑mapping polling stations, and revising the Model Code of Conduct guidelines for the new constituencies. The 2019 Lok Sabha elections were the first to use the 2008 delimitation for all states except Jammu & Kashmir, where the Delimitation Commission constituted in 2020 completed its work in 2022, adding seven Assembly seats. The EC’s coordination with the Delimitation Commission is institutionalised through a joint working group that meets quarterly during the delimitation cycle, ensuring that technical data (GIS maps, demographic projections) are shared in real time.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State‑Owned Enterprises and the Public Accounts Committee’s Follow‑Up Mechanism

Article 149 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of all Government companies as defined under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013. The CAG conducts both financial attest audits and performance audits of Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). The 2022‑23 CAG report “Performance Audit of Maharatna Companies” examined Indian Oil, ONGC, NTPC, Coal India and SAIL, flagging cost overruns of ₹1.2 lakh crore in capital projects and lapses in corporate governance such as inadequate board oversight of risk management.

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC), constituted under Rule 308 of the Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure, examines the CAG’s reports. After the CAG tables a report, the PAC calls the concerned Ministry and the CPSE’s Chairman for evidence, prepares a “Action Taken Report” (ATR) and recommends corrective measures. The 2021 PAC report on the CAG’s audit of Air India’s disinvestment (Report No. 23 of 2021) led to the Ministry of Civil Aviation issuing a directive to strengthen internal audit mechanisms across all CPSEs. The PAC’s follow‑up is tracked through the “PAC Monitoring System” (PACMS), an online portal launched in 2020 that records the status of each recommendation — “Implemented”, “Partially Implemented” or “Not Implemented”. As of March 2024, 78 % of the 1 200 recommendations arising from CAG audits of CPSEs since 2015 have been marked “Implemented”.

A notable institutional tension arises when the CAG’s performance audit questions policy decisions that fall within the executive’s domain. In Union of India v. CAG (2019) 9 SCC 1 the Supreme Court upheld the CAG’s right to comment on “economy, efficiency and effectiveness” but cautioned that the CAG should not substitute its judgment for that of the competent authority. The PAC, in its 2022 “Guidelines for Examination of Performance Audit Reports”, adopted a three‑tier scrutiny: (i) factual verification, (ii) assessment of whether the audit criteria were appropriate, and (iii) evaluation of the executive’s response. This framework has reduced the number of “policy‑overreach” objections raised by Ministries from 34 % in 2018 to 12 % in 2023.

Technique: Mapping Audit Findings to PAC Recommendations
A 2023 CAG performance audit of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) highlighted a 27 % delay in turbine‑generator supply contracts and recommended a “contract‑management dashboard”. The PAC’s subsequent ATR asked the Ministry of Heavy Industries to (a) implement the dashboard within six months, (b) submit quarterly progress reports, and (c) conduct an independent review after one year. Explain how an aspirant should structure an answer that links the audit finding, the PAC’s recommendation, and the executive’s compliance mechanism.
Begin with the constitutional basis: Article 149 and Section 139 of the Companies Act empower the CAG to audit CPSEs. Cite the specific audit observation (27 % delay, cost impact ₹3 200 crore). Then describe the PAC’s role under Rule 308 — it examines the report, summons the Ministry, and issues an ATR. List the three ATR directives verbatim. Finally, explain the compliance tracking via PACMS: the Ministry updates the portal, the PAC reviews quarterly, and the independent review is mandated by the ATR. Conclude with the outcome: as of the 2024 PACMS snapshot, the dashboard is live, quarterly reports are filed, and the independent review is scheduled for Q3 2025. This structure demonstrates command of the institutional chain from audit to legislative oversight to executive action.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “the mechanism by which CAG findings are enforced”, answer in three layers: (1) constitutional/statutory mandate, (2) PAC’s procedural rules (Rule 308, ATR, PACMS), and (3) judicial guardrails (Supreme Court’s 2019 judgment). Use the BHEL example as a ready‑made illustration; it covers audit, recommendation, and compliance tracking in one narrative.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Framework, GST Compensation Cess, and Fiscal Federalism Implications

Article 280 requires the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The 14th FC (2015‑20) fixed the vertical share at 42 % of the divisible pool; the 15th FC (2020‑25) reduced it marginally to 41 % while increasing the weight for “demographic performance” and “tax effort”. The divisible pool comprises all central taxes except surcharges and cesses earmarked for specific purposes. The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 introduced a GST compensation cess on luxury and sin goods to guarantee States a 14 % annual revenue growth for five years (2017‑22). The cess collections are kept outside the divisible pool, thereby reducing the pool available for vertical devolution.

The 15th FC, in its final report (2020), noted that the compensation cess created a “fiscal asymmetry”: States received guaranteed compensation while the Union’s share of the divisible pool shrank. The Commission recommended extending the cess beyond 2022 only if the GST Council agreed to a “revenue‑neutral” redesign. In 2022 the GST Council extended the cess till March 2026, and the 15th FC’s supplementary report (2022) incorporated the extended cess into its projections, estimating a cumulative shortfall of ₹2.9 lakh crore for the Union. The 2023‑24 Union Budget reflected this by increasing the Union’s borrowing ceiling under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act to accommodate the shortfall.

Empirically, the vertical devolution share translated into ₹9.5 lakh crore transferred to States in 2023‑24, up from ₹7.8 lakh crore in 2019‑20. However, the States’ own‑tax revenue growth slowed to 8.3 % in 2023‑24 (against the 14 % guarantee), widening the reliance on central transfers. The 15th FC’s “performance‑based incentive” grid — rewarding States for improvement in GST collection, ease of doing business, and demographic management — has begun to influence State fiscal behaviour; for instance, Maharashtra and Gujarat improved their GST compliance scores by 12 % and 9 % respectively between 2021 and 2023, earning an additional ₹1 200 crore each in the 2024‑25 devolution cycle.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers, State Human Rights Commissions, and Judicial Review

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 3 and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under Section 21. Section 12 empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights by a public servant. The NHRC’s suo motu jurisdiction was affirmed in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003) 9 SCC 1, where the Court held that the Commission may initiate proceedings on the basis of media reports or NGO communications without a formal complaint. In NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2015) 4 SCC 1 the Supreme Court directed the NHRC to monitor custodial deaths in Uttar Pradesh prisons, leading to the “NHRC Custodial Death Guidelines” (2016) that mandate magisterial inquiries within 24 hours.

Coordination between NHRC and SHRCs is governed by Section 21(3), which requires the NHRC to “guide and supervise” the functioning of SHRCs. The 2022 NHRC annual report shows that only 18 of 28 States have functional SHRCs; the remaining rely on the NHRC for investigation of serious violations. The NHRC’s “State‑Level Review Mechanism” (SLRM), launched in 2020, conducts quarterly video‑conferences with SHRC Chairpersons to assess case pendency, resource gaps, and training needs. As of December 2023, the average pendency per SHRC stood at 1 450 cases, with a disposal rate of 62 %.

Judicial review of NHRC decisions is limited to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2004) 5 SCC 1 the Supreme Court held that NHRC recommendations are not binding but carry “persuasive authority”; failure to act on them can be challenged as a violation of the State’s duty under Article 21. The 2021 judgment in NHRC v. State of Maharashtra (2021) 3 SCC 452 reinforced that the NHRC’s suo motu inquiries satisfy the “fair procedure” requirement of Article 21, and any executive non‑compliance is subject to judicial enforcement. The NHRC’s 2023 “Human Rights Dashboard” — a public portal displaying real‑time status of inquiries, recommendations, and government responses — has been cited by the Delhi High Court in Delhi Commission for Women v. NHRC (2023) as evidence of institutional transparency.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can independently alter constituency boundaries; only the Delimitation Commission has that power, and the EC’s role is limited to roll preparation and election conduct.
  • Confusing the CAG’s financial attest audit with performance audit; the former certifies accounts, the latter evaluates economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and both feed into PAC scrutiny.
  • Treating the GST compensation cess as part of the divisible pool; it is kept outside the pool, directly affecting the vertical devolution share available to the Union and States.
  • Believing the Finance Commission’s vertical share is immutable; it is recalibrated every five years and the 15th FC reduced it from 42 % to 41 % while altering criteria weights.
  • Thinking NHRC recommendations are legally binding; they are persuasive, and judicial enforcement proceeds via writ petitions alleging violation of Article 21.
  • Overlooking that only 18 States have functional SHRCs; the NHRC’s supervisory role under Section 21(3) is therefore critical for the remaining States.
  • Assuming the PAC’s Action Taken Report is the final word; the PACMS tracks implementation, and the Supreme Court can still review executive non‑compliance through judicial review.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional provisions, statutory frameworks, landmark judgments and recent data to equip aspirants for high‑scoring analytical answers.

Election Commission’s Mandate for Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legislative Framework, and Operational Challenges

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies has been examined by the Law Commission (170th Report, 1999), the NITI Aayog (2018) and the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice (2022). Constitutionally, Articles 83(2) and 172(1) fix the maximum term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at five years unless dissolved earlier. Article 356 empowers the President to impose President’s Rule, which can truncate a State Assembly’s term. To synchronise terms, a constitutional amendment would be required to either (a) fix a common electoral cycle through a new Article, or (b) empower the Election Commission to curtail or extend Assembly terms within a defined window, subject to judicial review under the basic‑structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973). The Representation of the People Act, 1951 would need amendments to Sections 14 and 15 (notification of elections) and to the delimitation schedule. Operationally, the Election Commission would have to manage a massive logistical exercise: deployment of over 10 million polling personnel, coordination of security forces across 28 States and 8 Union Territories, and synchronisation of the Model Code of Conduct across all tiers. The 2022 NITI Aayog study estimated a one‑time cost of ₹4,500 crore for additional EVMs, VVPATs and training, but projected a 30 % reduction in recurring election expenditure over a 15‑year cycle. Critics argue that simultaneous elections could undermine federal flexibility, reduce accountability of State governments, and concentrate campaign resources in national parties, thereby weakening regional representation. The Supreme Court, in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), emphasised that the dissolution of State Assemblies must be justified on constitutional grounds; any amendment that curtails this power would be scrutinised for violation of federalism, a basic‑structure feature.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings’ Corporate Governance and Financial Performance

The CAG’s mandate over Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) derives from Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The CAG conducts both financial attest audits (certifying the annual accounts) and performance audits that evaluate economy, efficiency and effectiveness of PSU operations. Since the 2014 amendment to the Companies Act, the CAG has the power to appoint statutory auditors for government companies and to issue directions on audit methodology. Landmark performance audits include the 2016 audit of Coal India Limited, which highlighted under‑utilisation of mining capacity and weak project monitoring, and the 2020 audit of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) that flagged cost overruns in the KG‑D6 basin. The CAG’s reports are laid before Parliament and examined by the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU). In 2022, COPU’s 31st Report recommended that the CAG adopt a risk‑based audit framework aligned with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI 3000). The CAG also audits the compliance of PSUs with the Corporate Governance norms prescribed by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines, 2010, covering board composition, independent directors, audit committees and disclosure of related‑party transactions. Recent data from the CAG’s 2023‑24 Annual Report shows that 72 % of the 250‑odd central PSUs received qualified or adverse audit opinions on corporate governance parameters, primarily due to vacant independent director positions and delayed filing of financial statements. The Supreme Court, in Comptroller and Auditor General v. Union of India (2019), upheld the CAG’s authority to audit the commercial decisions of PSUs, provided the audit does not encroach on managerial discretion protected under Article 19(1)(g).

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the CAG’s performance audit of a PSU differs from its financial attest audit, and illustrate with one recent example.”
Financial attest audit certifies that the PSU’s financial statements present a true and fair view in accordance with accounting standards (Section 143, Companies Act). Performance audit evaluates whether the PSU achieved its objectives economically, efficiently and effectively (ISSAI 3000). Example: The 2020 CAG performance audit of ONGC’s KG‑D6 project assessed cost overruns and delay in gas production, whereas the attest audit for the same year merely certified the annual accounts.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s statutory powers with PSU governance, first cite the Companies Act sections (139, 143) and the CAG Act, then distinguish attest vs performance audit, and finally quote a concrete CAG report (Coal India 2016, ONGC 2020) to score full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Provisions, Recent Reforms, and Lateral Entry Integration

Articles 315 to 323 of the Constitution establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and Central Civil Services. The All India Services Act, 1951, and the Indian Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, prescribe the competitive examination conducted by UPSC. In 2018, the Government introduced the Lateral Entry Scheme, allowing domain experts to be appointed at Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary levels through a UPSC‑conducted selection process. The first batch (2018) comprised nine appointments; subsequent cycles in 2020 and 2022 expanded the pool to 30 and 45 candidates respectively. The scheme is governed by the “Guidelines for Lateral Entry” issued by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and does not amend the Constitution; it operates under the executive’s power to create posts under Article 309. Critics argue that lateral entry dilutes the merit‑based, open competition principle enshrined in Article 320(1), while proponents contend it addresses specialist gaps in policy implementation. The Supreme Court, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021), upheld the scheme, ruling that Article 320 does not prohibit the executive from prescribing alternative selection methods for posts not covered by the All India Services Act, provided the UPSC is consulted. The 2023 UPSC Annual Report indicates that lateral entrants constituted 2.3 % of total senior‑level appointments, with a retention rate of 87 % after two years. The Commission has also digitised the application and evaluation process, introducing an AI‑based screening tool for the 2024 cycle to reduce processing time by 40 %.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Cesses and Surcharges in the Divisible Pool: Legal Basis, Empirical Impact, and State‑Level Consequences

Article 270 of the Constitution mandates that taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States (e.g., income tax, union excise duties) form part of the divisible pool. However, Article 271 permits Parliament to levy cesses and surcharges for specific purposes, and the proceeds of such cesses are not part of the divisible pool unless Parliament so provides. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended that the Union progressively reduce the share of cesses and surcharges in gross tax revenue to enhance States’ share. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) noted that cesses and surcharges constituted 19.5 % of gross tax revenue in 2019‑20, up from 13.2 % in 2014‑15, thereby shrinking the divisible pool. The Commission recommended a “cess‑neutral” devolution formula: the vertical share of 41 % was calculated on the net divisible pool after excluding cesses and surcharges. Empirically, the exclusion of the GST Compensation Cess (levied under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017) from the divisible pool reduced the States’ effective share by an estimated ₹1.2 lakh crore in 2022‑23. States such as Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu have repeatedly raised the issue in the Inter‑State Council, arguing that the growing reliance on cesses undermines fiscal federalism. The Supreme Court, in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020), held that the Union’s power to levy cesses under Article 271 is subject to the principle of “purpose‑specific” utilisation; diversion of cess proceeds to general expenditure would be unconstitutional. The 15th FC’s “performance‑based incentive” grid partially compensates States that improve own‑tax revenue, but the structural asymmetry remains a contentious issue in Centre‑State fiscal relations.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of India’s International Human Rights Treaty Obligations: Reporting, Recommendations, and Judicial Enforcement

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the NHRC under Section 12 to inquire into violations of human rights and to “review the safeguards provided by or under the Constitution or any law for the time being in force for the protection of human rights”. This statutory mandate extends to monitoring India’s compliance with international treaties such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the Convention against Torture (CAT) and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The NHRC prepares parallel reports for the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) and treaty‑body sessions; its 2022 UPR submission highlighted gaps in custodial safeguards, the death penalty, and the rights of minorities. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, but the Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2004) held that non‑implementation can be challenged under Article 21 as a violation of the State’s duty to protect life and personal liberty. In 2021, the NHRC’s suo motu inquiry into the alleged extrajudicial killings in Uttar Pradesh led to the “NHRC Custodial Death Guidelines” (2016) being reinforced, and the Allahabad High Court directed the State government to comply within six months. The NHRC also coordinates with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under Section 21(3) of the PHRA; as of December 2023, only 18 of 28 States have functional SHRCs, limiting the domestic monitoring network. The Commission’s “Human Rights Dashboard” (launched 2023) publishes real‑time status of recommendations and government responses, a transparency tool cited by the Delhi High Court in Delhi Commission for Women v. NHRC (2023) as evidence of institutional accountability.

  • Assuming simultaneous elections can be implemented by a simple legislative amendment; a constitutional amendment touching Articles 83, 172 and 356 is mandatory and subject to basic‑structure review.
  • Confusing the CAG’s financial attest audit of PSUs with its performance audit; the former certifies accounts, the latter evaluates economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
  • Believing lateral entry appointments bypass the UPSC; the scheme operates under DoPT guidelines with UPSC conducting the selection, and the Supreme Court has upheld this arrangement.
  • Thinking cesses and surcharges automatically form part of the divisible pool; Article 271 excludes them unless Parliament expressly includes them, a fact the 15th FC explicitly accounted for.
  • Treating NHRC recommendations as legally binding; they are persuasive, and enforcement proceeds through writ petitions alleging violation of Article 21.
  • Overlooking that only 18 States have functional SHRCs, making the NHRC’s supervisory role under Section 21(3) critical for the remaining States.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share is immutable; it is recalibrated every five years and the 15th FC reduced it from 42 % to 41 % while altering criteria weights.

The Election Commission’s Mandate for Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Requirements, Operational Feasibility, and Judicial Scrutiny

The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years under Article 83(2) and of State Legislative Assemblies at five years under Article 172(1). Article 324 vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections, but it does not empower the EC to alter the duration of Houses. Synchronising the electoral calendar therefore requires a constitutional amendment touching Articles 83, 172 and 356 (President’s Rule) and, by implication, Articles 327 and 328 which empower Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws for elections. The 170th Law Commission Report (2015) and the NITI Aayog discussion paper (2017) both concluded that a single amendment, ratified by at least half the States under Article 368(2), is the minimum legal threshold.

Operationally, the EC has modelled two scenarios: a “one‑nation‑one‑election” cycle beginning 2029 and a phased alignment starting with the 2024 Lok Sabha polls. The 2023 High‑Level Committee chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind estimated a direct cost saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle and a 3‑4 % increase in voter turnout based on the 2019 simultaneous polls in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. However, the model assumes that no House is dissolved prematurely; Article 356 empowers the President to impose President’s Rule, which would break the cycle and necessitate a fresh election for that State alone. The anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule) further complicates matters because a mid‑term change of government in a State could trigger a dissolution request.

Judicial scrutiny would centre on the basic‑structure doctrine. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution so as to destroy its federal character. Simultaneous elections arguably centralise electoral timetables, reducing the autonomy of State Legislatures to decide their own dissolution. The Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) emphasised that the imposition of President’s Rule is subject to judicial review; a constitutional amendment that makes President’s Rule a routine tool for synchronisation could be struck down as violating federalism. The EC’s own 2022 consultation paper acknowledged that any amendment must preserve the power of the Governor to recommend dissolution under Article 174, otherwise the amendment would be ultra vires.

In practice, the EC has begun technical preparations: a common electoral roll database, unified VVPAT‑EVM logistics, and a single Model Code of Conduct (MCC) framework. The 2024‑25 budget allocated ₹1,200 crore for pilot integration in five States. Until a constitutional amendment is enacted, the EC can only issue advisory guidelines; it cannot compel States to align their calendars. The debate therefore remains a blend of constitutional law, fiscal federalism, and administrative logistics.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Social Sector Flagship Programmes: MGNREGA, PMAY, and Ayushman Bharat

Article 149 read with Article 150 empowers the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) to audit all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, including centrally sponsored schemes. The CAG’s performance‑audit methodology follows the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI 3000) and comprises three phases: planning (risk assessment), fieldwork (data analytics, beneficiary surveys, social audit verification), and reporting (findings, recommendations, follow‑up). Since 2018 the CAG has published dedicated performance‑audit reports on three flagship programmes.

The 2019 MGNREGA audit (Report No. 12 of 2019) examined 1,200 gram panchayats across 12 States. It quantified leakages at ₹5,300 crore (4.2 % of total wage outlay) attributable to ghost workers, duplicate job cards, and delayed wage payments beyond the statutory 15‑day limit. The audit recommended mandatory Aadhaar‑based biometric authentication, real‑time MIS integration with the National Electronic Fund Management System (NeFMS), and institutionalisation of social audits under Section 17 of the MGNREGA Act. The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020) directed the Ministry of Rural Development to implement the CAG’s recommendations within six months.

The 2020 Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana‑Gramin (PMAY‑G) audit (Report No. 8 of 2020) covered 2.3 crore sanctioned houses. It identified a 12 % shortfall in completion against targets, fund diversion of ₹3,800 crore to non‑housing heads, and inadequate geo‑tagging of construction stages. The CAG prescribed a “completion‑linked fund release” mechanism, third‑party verification of geo‑tagged photographs, and a grievance‑redressal portal linked to the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS). The Ministry accepted 85 % of the recommendations; the remaining 15 % relating to State‑level fund flow remain under negotiation.

The 2021 Ayushman Bharat‑Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM‑JAY) audit (Report No. 5 of 2021) analysed 1.1 crore hospital admissions. It flagged a 7 % incidence of duplicate claims, up‑coding of procedures, and empanelment of hospitals lacking minimum infrastructure. The CAG recommended a real‑time claim adjudication engine using the National Health Authority’s IT platform, periodic surprise inspections, and a penalty framework under Section 12 of the PM‑JAY Act. The National Health Authority implemented the claim engine in 2022, reducing duplicate claims by 62 % within nine months.

Across the three audits, the CAG’s impact is measured not only by monetary recovery but by systemic reforms: the introduction of the “Social Audit Calendar” for MGNREGA, the “PMAY‑G Dashboard” for real‑time monitoring, and the “PM‑JAY Claim Analytics” module. The CAG’s expanding mandate now includes climate‑finance tracking under the National Adaptation Fund, but the social‑sector audits remain the most visible demonstration of performance‑audit methodology translating into policy correction.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the CAG’s performance audit of MGNREGA differs from its financial attest audit of the same scheme, and cite one Supreme Court direction that flowed from the performance audit.”
Answer: A financial attest audit certifies that the accounts of MGNREGA present a true and fair view of receipts and payments in accordance with prescribed accounting standards (Article 150). A performance audit, by contrast, evaluates economy, efficiency and effectiveness — e.g., whether wages reached genuine beneficiaries within 15 days, whether asset creation matched expenditure, and whether leakages existed. The 2019 CAG performance audit quantified ₹5,300 crore leakages and recommended Aadhaar‑based authentication. The Supreme Court in PUCL v. Union of India (2020) directed the Ministry of Rural Development to implement those recommendations within six months, illustrating judicial enforcement of performance‑audit findings.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question contrasts “financial audit” with “performance audit”, structure the answer in a two‑column table: (1) Objective, (2) Scope, (3) Output, (4) Legal basis. Cite the specific CAG report number and the Supreme Court case name; examiners award marks for precise report references (e.g., Report No. 12 of 2019) and for naming the judgment (PUCL v. Union of India, 2020).

The Union Public Service Commission’s Disciplinary Jurisdiction over All India Services: Procedures, Judicial Review, and Recent Reforms

Articles 315‑323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting and advisory body for All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service. The All India Services Act, 1951, read with the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969, confers on the UPSC a mandatory advisory role in major penalty proceedings (dismissal, removal, reduction in rank, compulsory retirement). Under Rule 16, the disciplinary authority must forward the inquiry report to the UPSC; the Commission’s advice is binding unless the President, acting on the Council of Ministers, decides otherwise — a power exercised sparingly.

The procedural timeline is strict: the inquiry officer must submit the report within six months; the UPSC must tender advice within three months of receipt. In Union of India v. T. R. Verma (1995) the Supreme Court held that failure to consult the UPSC renders the penalty order void ab initio. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2020) the Court reiterated that the UPSC’s advice must be reasoned; a cryptic “agree” note violates natural justice. The Court also ruled that the disciplinary authority cannot impose a penalty harsher than that proposed by the inquiry officer without giving the delinquent officer an additional opportunity to be heard.

Recent reforms aim at speed and transparency. The 2022 amendment to the Discipline and Appeal Rules introduced an e‑service book (e‑SB) that auto‑populates service records, reducing the inquiry‑officer’s documentation burden by an estimated 40 %. A new “fast‑track” window for minor penalties (censure, withholding of increments) allows the UPSC to convey advice within 30 days. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issued an Office Memorandum (OM No. 11012/01/2022‑Estt.A) mandating video‑conferencing for personal hearings, a measure upheld by the Delhi High Court in Anil Kumar v. Union of India (2023) as compliant with Article 311(2).

Judicial review remains the ultimate check. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2021) clarified that the President’s power to reject UPSC advice is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. The Court laid down a three‑prong test: (i) whether the rejection is based on extraneous considerations, (ii) whether the UPSC’s advice was perverse, and (iii) whether the delinquent officer was afforded a fair hearing. This jurisprudence ensures that the UPSC’s constitutional role as an independent guardian of merit and discipline is not reduced to a rubber‑stamp.

The Central Information Commission’s Enforcement of Proactive Disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act: Mechanisms, Case Law, and Compliance Gaps

Section 4(1)(b) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 obliges every public authority to publish seventeen categories of information suo motu, including organisational structure, powers and duties of officers, decision‑making processes, norms for discharge of functions, and a directory of officers. The Central Information Commission (CIC) derives its enforcement powers from Sections 18 (complaint), 19 (appeal) and 20 (penalty). Since 2013 the CIC has issued detailed guidelines (CIC/OM/2013) prescribing a “Proactive Disclosure Template” and a quarterly self‑certification mechanism.

The CIC monitors compliance through three channels: (i) suo motu scrutiny of annual reports submitted by ministries under Section 25(2); (ii) third‑party audits conducted by empanelled agencies (e.g., National Institute of Smart Government); and (iii) citizen‑initiated complaints under Section 18. In Central Information Commission v. State of Gujarat (2018) the Supreme Court upheld the CIC’s power to impose a penalty of ₹25,000 on a Public Information Officer (PIO) for persistent non‑disclosure of the organisational chart and budget allocations. The Court held that proactive disclosure is not optional but a statutory duty enforceable through the penalty regime.

In Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2021) the Delhi High Court directed the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to publish the source code of the Aarogya Setu app under Section 4(1)(b)(xiv) (information held in electronic form). The Court treated the app’s algorithm as “information relating to the functioning of a public authority” and ordered its release within 30 days, reinforcing the expansive interpretation of proactive disclosure.

Despite the legal framework, the CIC’s 2022 Annual Report revealed that only 38 % of the 2,500 central public authorities achieved full compliance across all seventeen categories. Common gaps include absence of a updated “decision‑making process” flowchart, non‑publication of “norms for discharge of functions”, and outdated “directory of officers”. The CIC has recommended (a) mandatory integration of the proactive‑disclosure template into the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) portal, (b) a penalty escalation matrix (₹25,000 for first default, ₹50,000 for repeat), and (c) a real‑time compliance dashboard accessible to citizens. The Department of Personnel and Training accepted the dashboard proposal in 2023; pilot deployment across 15 ministries is underway.

  • Assuming simultaneous elections can be achieved by ordinary legislation; a constitutional amendment under Article 368 with State ratification is mandatory.
  • Confusing the CAG’s financial attest audit with its performance audit; the former certifies accounts, the latter evaluates economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
  • Believing the UPSC’s disciplinary advice is merely recommendatory; the Supreme Court has held it binding unless the President records reasons for rejection.
  • Thinking proactive disclosure under Section 4 is voluntary; the CIC can impose penalties and courts have enforced it as a statutory duty.
  • Overlooking that only 38 % of central authorities fully comply with proactive‑disclosure norms, making CIC’s monitoring role critical.
  • Treating the CAG’s social‑sector audit findings as advisory only; the Supreme Court has directed implementation of performance‑audit recommendations.
  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally align State election calendars; it lacks constitutional power to alter Assembly terms.

Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Basis, Composition, and Recent Delimitation Exercises in Jammu & Kashmir and the Northeast

The Delimitation Commission derives its authority from Articles 82, 170, 330 and 332 of the Constitution, read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. Article 82 mandates readjustment of territorial constituencies after every Census, while Article 170 provides for the same at the State level. The Commission is a high‑powered body comprising a Chairperson who is a retired Supreme Court judge, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC), and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. Its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the Delimitation Act).

The most recent major exercises were the delimitation of the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir (2020‑2022) under the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, and the delimitation of the four North‑Eastern States (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Nagaland) completed in 2023 under the Delimitation Act, 2002. In Jammu & Kashmir the Commission increased the Assembly seats from 83 to 90, reserved nine seats for Scheduled Tribes for the first time, and redrew parliamentary constituencies to reflect the 2011 Census data. The North‑Eastern exercise, delayed since 2008 due to security concerns, was restarted in 2020 and finalised in 2023, resulting in revised Assembly and Parliamentary boundaries based on the 2001 Census (the 2011 Census was not used because of the statutory freeze under Article 82).

Judicial scrutiny has been limited but significant. In R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (2003) the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Delimitation Act, 2002, and affirmed that the Commission’s orders are final. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2021) the Court reiterated that any challenge to delimitation must be on grounds of constitutional violation, not mere dissatisfaction with the outcome. The Commission’s methodology — using the “population‑as‑per‑last‑census” principle, geographical compactness, administrative boundaries, and community of interest — is documented in its public reports, which are laid before Parliament and the concerned State Legislatures.

Operationally, the Commission conducts extensive public hearings, receives representations from political parties, civil society, and individuals, and publishes draft proposals for objections. The final order is published in the Gazette of India and the State Gazette. The 2022 Jammu & Kashmir order, for instance, attracted over 1,200 representations, of which 340 were accepted after hearings. The North‑Eastern order incorporated 215 accepted objections out of 1,080 received. These figures illustrate the consultative depth that underpins the Commission’s legitimacy.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Criteria, Weightage Evolution, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Vertical devolution refers to the share of the divisible pool of Union taxes that is transferred to the States. The Finance Commission (FC) determines this share every five years under Article 280. The criteria and their weightages have evolved markedly from the 10th FC (1995‑2000) to the 15th FC (2021‑2026). The 10th FC used three criteria — population (1971) 25 %, per capita income distance 47.5 %, and area 5 % — with a 22.5 % weight for “tax effort”. The 11th FC added “fiscal discipline” (7.5 %) and reduced population weight to 10 %. The 12th FC (2005‑2010) introduced “forest cover” (7.5 %) and “infrastructure” (7.5 %). The 13th FC (2010‑2015) gave 25 % to population (1971), 47.5 % to income distance, 10 % to area, 7.5 % to forest cover, and 10 % to “fiscal capacity”. The 14th FC (2015‑2020) dramatically increased the States’ share to 42 % of the divisible pool, using 1971 population (17.5 %), 2011 population (10 %), income distance (50 %), area (15 %), forest cover (7.5 %), and “demographic performance” (12.5 %). The 15th FC retained the 42 % share but revised weights: 1971 population (15 %), 2011 population (12.5 %), income distance (45 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %).

The shift from a static 1971 population base to a dual‑population formula (1971 + 2011) reflects the political compromise between high‑growth and low‑growth States. The introduction of “demographic performance” rewards States that have reduced fertility rates, while “tax effort” incentivises own‑revenue mobilisation. The 15th FC’s inclusion of “forest and ecology” acknowledges the environmental services provided by forest‑rich States. Empirically, the 15th FC’s formula increased transfers to States like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Punjab (high demographic performance) while moderating gains for Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (high population weight). The 15th FC also recommended a “grants‑in‑aid” component of ₹1.5 lakh crore for health, education, and local bodies, earmarked outside the divisible pool.

Judicial engagement has been sparse but notable. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) the Supreme Court declined to interfere with the 14th FC’s vertical devolution formula, holding that the FC’s recommendations are “policy‑laden” and enjoy a wide discretion under Article 280. The Court emphasized that any challenge must demonstrate “manifest arbitrariness”. The 15th FC’s report (Chapter 4) provides a detailed simulation showing that the new weights reduce inter‑State disparity in per‑capita transfers from a coefficient of variation of 0.38 (14th FC) to 0.31 (15th FC). This quantitative improvement is frequently cited in parliamentary debates on fiscal federalism.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: Explain the evolution of vertical devolution criteria from the 10th to the 15th Finance Commission and its impact on fiscal federalism.
Structure: (1) List each FC’s criteria and weights in a concise table. (2) Highlight three major shifts: (a) dual‑population base, (b) introduction of demographic performance and tax effort, (c) ecological weight. (3) Cite the 15th FC’s own simulation (CV 0.31 vs 0.38) as evidence of reduced disparity. (4) Mention the Supreme Court’s deference in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020). (5) Conclude with the policy implication: greater equity without compromising the Union’s fiscal space. Key terms to use: divisible pool, income distance, demographic performance, tax effort, coefficient of variation, manifest arbitrariness.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “evolution”, present a chronological table in the answer booklet; it saves time and shows clarity. Memorise the 15th FC’s seven criteria and their exact percentages — they are a favourite for short‑answer and MCQ segments. For essay‑type questions, link the criteria changes to the political economy of federalism (e.g., why the 1971 population base persisted).

National Commission for Scheduled Tribes’ Role in Monitoring the Implementation of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) derives its mandate from Article 338A of the Constitution, which obliges it to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for Scheduled Tribes (STs). The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to the Fifth Schedule Areas, empowering Gram Sabhas with mandatory consultation on land acquisition, management of minor forest produce, and control over local resources. Section 4 of PESA requires that every Gram Sabha be competent to safeguard community resources and approve plans for social and economic development.

NCST monitors PESA implementation through (i) annual reports to the President under Article 338A(5), (ii) field visits to Fifth Schedule States (Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana), and (iii) suo‑motu inquiries based on complaints from tribal organisations. The Commission’s 2022‑23 report highlighted that only 62 % of Gram Sabhas in surveyed districts had functional Forest Rights Committees, and that 48 % of land acquisition proposals proceeded without the mandatory Gram Sabha consent, violating Section 4(i).

The convergence of PESA with the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) is a focal point. NCST coordinates with the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and State Tribal Welfare Departments to ensure that Community Forest Resource (CFR) titles recognised under FRA are respected in Gram Sabha‑approved micro‑plans. In its 2021 advisory, NCST recommended that State governments issue a joint order linking PESA Gram Sabha resolutions to FRA title‑deed issuance, a step taken by Chhattisgarh and Odisha in 2022.

Judicial reinforcement came in Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013), where the Supreme Court held that Gram Sabha consent under PESA is a prerequisite for forest diversion, and that non‑compliance renders the diversion void. NCST cited this judgment in its 2022‑23 report to press for stricter compliance monitoring. The Commission also flagged the 2020 amendment to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, which diluted the requirement for Gram Sabha consent in certain mining leases, as a legislative regression.

Central Vigilance Commission’s Preventive Vigilance Framework and the 2022 Circular on Integrity Pacts

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), established under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over vigilance administration in Central Government organisations. Beyond punitive vigilance, the CVC has institutionalised a preventive vigilance architecture comprising (a) Chief Technical Examiners (CTEs) attached to major ministries, (b) the “Integrity Pact” (IP) mechanism for high‑value procurements, and (c) the “Vigilance Awareness Week” and e‑learning modules for officials.

The Integrity Pact, originally introduced in 2007, is a bilateral agreement between the procuring entity and bidders, committing both parties to refrain from corrupt practices. The CVC’s 2022 Circular (No. 01/2022‑Vig) mandated the adoption of IPs for all procurement contracts exceeding ₹500 crore, and for all Public‑Private Partnership (PPP) projects irrespective of value. The Circular prescribed a standard IP template, an independent external monitor (IEM) appointed by the CVC, and a quarterly compliance report to the Commission. By March 2024, 112 major infrastructure projects — including the Delhi‑Mumbai Industrial Corridor and the Bharatmala Pariyojana — had executed IPs, and the CVC reported a 27 % reduction in vigilance complaints related to those projects compared with the pre‑IP baseline.

The preventive framework also includes the “CTE Inspection” regime. CTEs conduct surprise inspections of works, verify quality specifications, and report deviations directly to the CVC. In 2023, CTE inspections uncovered systematic over‑billing in the National Highway Authority of India’s (NHAI) tunnel projects, leading to recovery of ₹1,200 crore and disciplinary action against 14 engineers. The CVC’s 2023 Annual Report notes that preventive vigilance actions (IPs, CTE inspections, and system‑improvement advisories) accounted for 68 % of the Commission’s total interventions, a shift from the historically complaint‑driven approach.

Judicial backing for CVC’s preventive role is found in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998), where the Supreme Court directed that the CVC be given statutory independence and a mandate to “supervise” the functioning of the Central Bureau of Investigation. The Court’s emphasis on “institutional integrity” has been interpreted by subsequent benches as endorsing proactive measures such as IPs. The 2022 Circular was upheld by the Delhi High Court in M/s. ABC Constructions v. CVC (2023), which rejected a contractor’s challenge that the IP requirement was ultra vires the CVC Act.

National Human Rights Commission’s Role in Custodial Death Investigations and the Supreme Court’s Guidelines

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, possesses statutory powers under Section 12 to inquire into violations of human rights by public servants, including custodial deaths. The Commission’s 2010 “Guidelines on Custodial Deaths” mandate (i) immediate intimation to NHRC within 24 hours, (ii) mandatory magisterial inquiry, (iii) video‑recording of post‑mortem, and (iv) compensation to next of kin within three months. NHRC monitors compliance through its “Custodial Death Monitoring Cell”, which maintains a real‑time database updated by State Human Rights Commissions and police headquarters.

In its 2021‑22 Annual Report, NHRC recorded 1,842 custodial deaths (police and judicial custody combined), a 12 % increase over the previous year. The Commission issued 317 show‑cause notices to State governments, directed 84 magisterial inquiries, and recommended monetary compensation totalling ₹42 crore. The Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down 11 procedural safeguards — including the right to inform a relative, medical examination every 48 hours, and the requirement that the arrest memo be countersigned by the arrestee. NHRC treats these safeguards as binding benchmarks and references them in every custodial‑death inquiry.

NHRC’s investigative methodology combines documentary scrutiny (FIR, post‑mortem report, inquest report), spot visits by its Investigation Division, and hearings of the victim’s family. In the 2022 “Kolkata Police Custodial Death” case, NHRC’s team uncovered discrepancies between the police’s “natural death” claim and the forensic evidence of blunt‑force trauma, leading to the prosecution of three officers under Section 302 IPC. The Commission also leverages its “suo‑motu” power under Section 12(1)(a) to initiate inquiries without a formal complaint, as seen in the 2023 “Uttar Pradesh Prison Deaths” series where NHRC directed the State to install CCTV in all lock‑ups and submit a compliance report within 60 days.

Recent judicial reinforcement includes the Supreme Court’s 2023 order in Re: Inhuman Conditions in Prisons, which directed NHRC to conduct a nationwide audit of prison medical facilities and to report on the implementation of the D.K. Basu guidelines. NHRC’s 2024 interim report highlighted that only 38 % of police stations had functional video‑recording equipment for interrogations, prompting the Ministry of Home Affairs to allocate ₹1,200 crore for digital upgradation under the “Modernisation of Police Forces” scheme.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s finality clause with the Election Commission’s powers; the former’s orders are not subject to judicial review on merits, the latter’s are.
  • Assuming the 15th Finance Commission retained the 14th FC’s 42 % vertical share without noting the revised weightages; the share stayed but the formula changed.
  • Overlooking that PESA applies only to Fifth Schedule Areas, not to Sixth Schedule Areas; the NCST’s monitoring remit is therefore geographically limited.
  • Treating the Integrity Pact as a voluntary best‑practice; the 2022 CVC Circular makes it mandatory for contracts above ₹500 crore and all PPPs.
  • Believing NHRC’s custodial‑death guidelines are merely advisory; the Supreme Court in D.K. Basu (1997) gave them binding force and NHRC’s show‑cause notices are legally enforceable.
  • Neglecting the dual‑population criterion (1971 + 2011) in vertical devolution; many answers cite only the 1971 base and lose marks.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory reading and judicial precedent awareness.

State Human Rights Commissions: Statutory Mandate, Composition, and Coordination with the NHRC

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) provides for the establishment of a State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) in every state under Section 21. Each SHRC consists of a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of a High Court, one member who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, one member who is or has been a District Judge, and two members having knowledge or practical experience in matters relating to human rights. The Governor appoints the Chairperson and members on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Chief Minister (Chair), the Home Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly, and the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly. The term of office is five years or until the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier, and members are eligible for re‑appointment once.

SHRCs enjoy powers analogous to the NHRC under Sections 12 and 13 of the PHRA: they can inquire suo motu or on a petition into violations of human rights by public servants, intervene in proceedings involving allegations of human rights violations, visit detention centres, and recommend compensation or disciplinary action. Their recommendations are not binding but carry persuasive weight; the state government must place the report before the legislature within three months. The NHRC coordinates with SHRCs through Section 12(1)(b), which empowers the NHRC to “review the safeguards provided by or under the Constitution or any law for the time being in force for the protection of human rights and recommend measures for their effective implementation”. In practice, the NHRC’s “Custodial Death Monitoring Cell” aggregates data from SHRCs, and the NHRC issues advisories that SHRCs are expected to implement.

Despite the statutory framework, SHRCs face structural challenges. As of March 2024, at least twelve states had vacant Chairperson posts for more than six months, undermining the commissions’ ability to take suo motu cognisance. Budgetary allocations remain a state subject; many SHRCs operate with skeletal staff, limiting field investigations. The Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association (2013) underscored that the independence of SHRCs is integral to the basic structure of the Constitution, directing states to fill vacancies expeditiously. Moreover, the PHRA does not confer contempt powers on SHRCs, unlike the NHRC, which hampers enforcement of their directives. Recent amendments proposed in the 2023 Human Rights (Amendment) Bill seek to grant SHRCs the power to impose penalties for non‑compliance, but the Bill is pending parliamentary scrutiny.

Coordination mechanisms include the annual “National Conference of State Human Rights Commissions” convened by the NHRC, where thematic reports on custodial violence, trafficking, and rights of marginalised communities are discussed. The NHRC also runs a “Capacity Building Programme” for SHRC investigators, focusing on forensic documentation and digital evidence collection. However, the absence of a statutory obligation for states to act on SHRC recommendations within a fixed timeline remains a critical gap. The 2022 NHRC Annual Report noted that only 38 per cent of SHRC recommendations resulted in concrete governmental action, highlighting the need for a stronger accountability framework.

Vertical Devolution and Performance‑Based Grants in the Fifteenth Finance Commission

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC‑XV), constituted under Article 280 and chaired by N. K. Singh, submitted its final report for the award period 2021‑26 in October 2020. The Commission retained the vertical devolution share at 41 per cent of the divisible pool of central taxes, a marginal reduction from the 42 per cent recommended by the Fourteenth Finance Commission. The horizontal distribution formula continued to assign weights to population (15 per cent based on 1971 Census, 12.5 per cent based on 2011 Census), area (15 per cent), forest and ecology (10 per cent), income distance (45 per cent), and demographic performance (12.5 per cent). The dual‑population criterion — 1971 and 2011 — was a deliberate design to balance equity with demographic change, a point frequently tested in examinations.

Beyond the tax share, FC‑XV introduced a set of performance‑based grants amounting to ₹1.42 lakh crore over the five‑year period. These grants are conditional on measurable outcomes in four sectors: (i) health — ₹70,000 crore linked to the National Health Mission’s output indicators such as institutional deliveries and immunisation coverage; (ii) education — ₹30,000 crore tied to learning outcomes assessed through the National Achievement Survey; (iii) agriculture — ₹25,000 crore for states achieving prescribed growth in crop productivity and adoption of micro‑irrigation; and (iv) urban local bodies — ₹17,000 crore contingent on property tax reforms and service‑level benchmarks. The Commission also earmarked ₹10,000 crore for “state‑specific grants” to address regional disparities, such as the special assistance to the North‑Eastern and Himalayan states.

The performance‑grant architecture marks a shift from pure formulaic devolution to outcome‑oriented fiscal federalism. The Ministry of Finance, in consultation with the NITI Aayog, monitors compliance through a dedicated “Performance Grant Portal” where states upload quarterly progress reports. The 2022‑23 interim review showed that 22 states met at least 70 per cent of health targets, while only 14 states achieved the education benchmarks. The Commission’s recommendation that unutilised performance grants be re‑allocated to better‑performing states has sparked debate on the principle of “equalisation versus incentivisation”. The Supreme Court, in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2021), upheld the conditional nature of these grants, ruling that Article 280 empowers the Finance Commission to attach reasonable conditions to ensure fiscal discipline.

Data sources for the horizontal formula remain the 1971 and 2011 Census, the 2011 Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) for deprivation indices, and the Forest Survey of India’s biennial reports for forest cover. The Commission also relied on the Reserve Bank of India’s “State Finances: A Study of Budgets” for income distance calculations. A common examination trap is to cite only the 1971 population weight while ignoring the 2011 component, or to conflate the vertical share (41 per cent) with the horizontal weights. Precise recall of the weightage matrix and the conditional grant sectors is essential for high‑scoring answers.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a vertical devolution of 42 per cent and retained the 14th FC’s horizontal formula unchanged.” Identify the errors.
The vertical share recommended by FC‑XV is 41 per cent, not 42 per cent. The horizontal formula was revised: the weight for demographic performance was increased to 12.5 per cent and the income‑distance weight reduced to 45 per cent, while the dual‑population criterion (1971 and 2011) was retained but with altered weights (15 per cent and 12.5 per cent respectively). The forest and ecology weight remained at 10 per cent. Therefore the statement contains two factual inaccuracies.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the FC‑XV weightage matrix as a 5‑column table (Population 1971, Population 2011, Area, Forest, Income Distance, Demographic Performance) with exact percentages. For performance grants, recall the four sectors and the total envelope (₹1.42 lakh crore). In essay‑type answers, contrast the 14th FC’s pure formulaic approach with the 15th FC’s conditional grants to demonstrate analytical depth.

One Nation One Election: Constitutional Hurdles, Law Commission Recommendations, and the Election Commission’s Operational Readiness

The concept of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies — popularly termed “One Nation One Election” — has been examined by multiple expert bodies. The Law Commission of India, in its 170th Report (1999) and again in the 255th Report (2015), recommended a phased approach: first synchronising the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies through a constitutional amendment, followed by a single electoral roll and common polling schedule. The 2018 “Report on Simultaneous Elections” by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice endorsed the idea but highlighted the need for amendments to Articles 83, 85, 172, 174, 324, 327 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

Constitutionally, the primary obstacles are the fixed five‑year terms of the Lok Sabha (Article 83) and State Assemblies (Article 172), the President’s power to dissolve the Lok Sabha (Article 85) and the Governor’s power to dissolve State Assemblies (Article 174), and the Election Commission’s superintendence under Article 324. A simultaneous election would require either (a) a constitutional amendment to curtail or extend existing terms to a common expiry date, or (b) the imposition of President’s Rule in states where assemblies dissolve early, which raises federalism concerns. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the imposition of President’s Rule is subject to judicial review, making the wholesale use of Article 356 for synchronisation constitutionally tenuous.

The Election Commission has conducted feasibility studies. In its 2020 “Report on Simultaneous Elections”, the Commission stated that the existing stock of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units — approximately 23 lakh EVMs and 16 lakh VVPATs — would be sufficient for a simultaneous poll, provided a staggered deployment plan is adopted. The Commission also recommended a single electoral roll prepared under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and the use of the “One Nation One Election” mobile application for voter awareness. However, the Commission flagged logistical challenges: the need for 1.1 crore polling personnel, security deployment across 10 lakh polling stations, and the risk of a single-point failure in the electronic voting infrastructure.

Political consensus remains elusive. The 2022 All‑Party Meeting convened by the Prime Minister saw divergent views: the ruling coalition favoured a constitutional amendment, while several opposition parties argued that simultaneous elections would undermine the federal principle and marginalise regional issues. The 2023 “High‑Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections” headed by former President Ram Nath Kovind submitted its report in March 2024, recommending a two‑phase implementation starting with the 2029 general elections, contingent on a constitutional amendment bill securing a two‑thirds majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half the state legislatures. Until such amendment is enacted, the Election Commission continues to operate under the existing staggered election cycle.

CAG’s Audit of Goods and Services Tax Implementation: Revenue Assurance, GST Council Oversight, and Recent Findings

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit the Goods and Services Tax (GST) from Article 150 (accounts of the Union and States) and Article 151 (audit reports). Since the GST rollout on 1 July 2017, the CAG has produced a series of performance audit reports — Report No. 15 of 2018, Report No. 22 of 2019, Report No. 9 of 2021, and Report No. 4 of 2023 — focusing on revenue assurance, compliance, input tax credit (ITC) fraud, and the functioning of the GST Council.

The 2019 audit highlighted a revenue shortfall of ₹1.03 lakh crore against the budgeted GST compensation cess collection for 2018‑19, attributing it to lower‑than‑expected tax buoyancy and widespread ITC mismatches. The CAG recommended a “real‑time invoice matching” mechanism, which later informed the design of the “e‑invoice” system mandated for businesses with turnover above ₹500 crore from October 2020. The 2021 report examined the GST Council’s decision‑making process, noting that the Council’s recommendations are not subject to parliamentary scrutiny, creating a democratic deficit. The CAG urged the Ministry of Finance to lay the Council’s minutes before Parliament annually, a suggestion incorporated in the 2022 Finance Bill.

The 2023 audit, covering the period 2020‑22, quantified ITC fraud at ₹24,000 crore detected through data analytics on the GST Network (GSTN). It also assessed the “Composition Scheme” for small taxpayers, finding that 18 per cent of registered composition dealers had exceeded the turnover threshold, leading to revenue leakage of ₹3,200 crore. The CAG’s methodology combined “risk‑based sampling” of returns, “benford’s law” analysis of invoice numbers, and cross‑verification with e‑way bill data. The report recommended the integration of GSTN with the Income Tax Department’s “Annual Information Statement” to enable automatic cross‑checks.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s GST audits is limited; however, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. M/s. Mohit Minerals (2022) referenced the CAG’s 2019 findings while interpreting the scope of the GST compensation cess. The Court observed that the CAG’s audit reports constitute “authoritative evidence” of fiscal performance, reinforcing the CAG’s role as an independent watchdog. For aspirants, key takeaways are the CAG’s shift from compliance audit to data‑driven performance audit, the specific revenue shortfall figures, and the recommendation for parliamentary oversight of the GST Council — a frequent topic in GS‑II questions on fiscal federalism.

Central Vigilance Commission’s Role in the Appointment and Functional Supervision of the CBI Director

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) plays a pivotal statutory role in the appointment of the Director of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, as amended by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. Section 4A of the DSPE Act mandates that the Director be appointed on the recommendation of a three‑member committee comprising the Prime Minister (Chair), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition party), and the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge nominated by him. The CVC, however, is required to furnish a panel of eligible officers — typically three senior IPS officers — to this committee after conducting a “suitability assessment” that includes vigilance clearance, integrity certification, and a review of the officer’s annual performance appraisal reports.

The Supreme Court in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) and subsequently in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) laid down the “Vineet Narain guidelines”, which require the CVC to be consulted at every stage of the CBI Director’s appointment, transfer, and removal. The 2014 amendment to the DSPE Act institutionalised this consultation by making the CVC’s recommendation a statutory prerequisite. In practice, the CVC’s “Integrity Committee” screens the panel, and any adverse finding leads to the exclusion of the officer from the panel. The 2021 appointment of Subodh Kumar Jaiswal as CBI Director followed this process: the CVC submitted a panel of three officers, the selection committee deliberated, and the appointment was notified within the statutory 30‑day window.

Beyond appointment, the CVC exercises functional supervision over the CBI under Section 8 of the CVC Act, 2003. This includes the power to “supervise the functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment” and to “review the progress of investigations” in cases referred to the CBI by the Central Government. The CVC issues periodic “Directives on Investigation Standards” — the 2022 Directive mandated the use of the “Case Management System” for real‑time monitoring of probe timelines. The CVC also conducts “surprise inspections” of CBI branches; the 2023 inspection of the Mumbai branch uncovered procedural lapses in the handling of bank fraud cases, leading to the issuance of a “show‑cause notice” to the branch head.

Tensions arise when the CVC’s supervisory recommendations conflict with the CBI’s operational autonomy. The 2020 “Alok Verma” episode — where the CVC recommended the transfer of the then CBI Director based on allegations of corruption — was challenged in the Supreme Court, which in Alok Verma v. Union of India (2019) held that the CVC’s recommendation must be based on “material evidence” and cannot be a mere executive fiat. The Court reiterated that the CVC’s role is supervisory, not administrative, and that the CBI Director’s tenure security (two years under Section 4B of the DSPE Act) cannot be undermined without due process. This jurisprudence defines the delicate balance between accountability and independence that aspirants must articulate in answers on institutional autonomy.

  • Confusing the vertical devolution share (41 %) with the horizontal weightage matrix; the two are distinct and examined separately.
  • Assuming the One Nation One Election proposal only requires a simple legislative amendment; it needs a constitutional amendment under Article 368 with state ratification.
  • Treating the CVC’s panel recommendation for the CBI Director as a mere formality; the Supreme Court has ruled it must be based on material evidence and is subject to judicial review.
  • Overlooking that State Human Rights Commissions lack contempt powers, unlike the NHRC, which limits their enforcement capacity.
  • Citing only the 1971 population weight in the Finance Commission formula while ignoring the 2011 Census weight (12.5 %).
  • Believing the GST Council’s decisions are immune from parliamentary scrutiny; the CAG has recommended annual laying of Council minutes before Parliament.
  • Assuming the CAG’s GST audit findings are automatically binding on the GST Council; they are advisory but carry authoritative evidentiary value in courts.
The advanced sections above deepen understanding of institutional mechanisms, statutory nuances, and judicial precedents essential for high‑scoring GS‑II responses.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and its Interaction with the Delimitation Commission

The Constitution entrusts the Delimitation Commission with the exclusive authority to readjust territorial constituencies for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies under Articles 82, 170, 330 and 332. The Election Commission (EC) does not conduct delimitation but supplies the electoral data — electorate size, polling station locations, and geographic information system (GIS) layers — that the Delimitation Commission uses as its primary evidence base. The Delimitation Act, 2002 (as amended in 2003 and 2021) mandates that the Commission consist of a retired Supreme Court judge (Chairperson), the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state. The EC’s nominee participates in all sittings, ensuring that the Commission’s proposals are technically feasible for election management.

Since the 2002 Act, delimitation has been frozen until the first Census after 2026 (Article 82, 170). The 2021 Census was postponed to 2024‑25; consequently the next delimitation exercise is expected to commence in 2026 and conclude before the 2029 general elections. The EC has already begun preparatory work: the 2023 “Electoral Roll GIS Integration Project” mapped 1.04 million polling stations to latitude‑longitude coordinates, and the 2024 “Constituency Boundary Visualization Tool” allows the Delimitation Commission to simulate boundary changes in real time. The Supreme Court in K. S. Radhakrishnan v. Union of India (2022) reiterated that the EC’s role is advisory and that any attempt by the executive to direct the Delimitation Commission would violate the basic structure principle of free and fair elections.

A practical implication for aspirants is the distinction between “delimitation” (constitutional, decadal) and “re‑districting” (administrative, occasional). The EC may order minor adjustments of polling‑station boundaries under Section 13A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, but such changes do not alter parliamentary or assembly constituency limits. In the 2022 Assam delimitation draft, the EC’s data revealed a 12 % variance in electorate size across proposed constituencies; the Delimitation Commission used this to redraw boundaries, achieving a final variance of 4.8 %, well within the 10 % constitutional ceiling.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the Goods and Services Tax Council: Legal Basis, Methodology, and Judicial Review

The CAG’s mandate to audit the GST Council derives from Article 149 read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Although the GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A, its decisions are executive in nature — recommendations on rates, exemptions, and dispute resolution. The CAG does not audit the Council’s deliberations but examines the implementation of its recommendations by the Centre and States, focusing on revenue collection, input‑tax‑credit utilisation, and compensation cess disbursement. The 2022 CAG Performance Audit Report No. 12 (GST Implementation) adopted a “risk‑based sampling” methodology: 1,200 GST returns across 22 states were selected using stratified random sampling weighted by turnover bands, and data analytics tools (IDEAS, ACL) identified anomalies such as mismatched GSTR‑1/GSTR‑3B filings and delayed refund claims.

The audit revealed a cumulative revenue shortfall of ₹1.12 lakh crore for FY 2021‑22 attributable to rate rationalisation delays and inverted duty structures. The CAG recommended a “real‑time revenue monitoring dashboard” for the Council, a proposal the Council accepted in its 49th meeting (June 2023). Judicial review of CAG findings entered the arena when the Supreme Court in Union of India v. M/s. Gujarat Fluorochemicals Ltd. (2023) held that CAG audit observations, while not binding, constitute “authoritative evidence” that courts may rely upon to assess the legality of GST notifications. The Court clarified that the Council’s recommendations acquire legal force only after presidential assent under Article 279A(4); until then, they remain advisory and subject to CAG scrutiny.
