Recent reforms have introduced a “single‑window” online portal for disciplinary cases, reducing the average consultation time from 180 days (2015) to 95 days (2023). The 2022 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations expanded the list of posts exempt from consultation to include certain Group ‘B’ and ‘C’ posts, but the exemption does not extend to Group ‘A’ services. The Supreme Court in M. S. Gill v. Union of India (2021) struck down an executive order that attempted to bypass UPSC consultation for a Group ‘A’ officer by re‑classifying the post, reiterating that the constitutional mandate cannot be circumvented by administrative fiat.

The doctrine of consultation thus operates as a constitutional check on executive arbitrariness in disciplinary matters. It ensures that an independent expert body evaluates the fairness of the process, while preserving the ultimate authority of the appointing power to decide the penalty, subject to reasoned justification.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution from the First to the Fifteenth Finance Commission, Weightage Shifts, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

The vertical devolution formula determines the share of the divisible pool of central taxes (net of cesses and surcharges) that is transferred to the states. The First Finance Commission (1951) recommended a 10 % share, which rose steadily to 20 % by the Fourth Commission (1964). The Seventh Commission (1978) introduced the “income distance” criterion, but vertical share remained at 25 %. A major shift occurred with the Tenth Commission (1994), which raised the share to 29.5 % and added a “tax effort” component. The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015) made a landmark recommendation of 42 % vertical devolution, the highest ever, arguing that enhanced untied transfers would empower states to design their own development programmes. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020) retained the 42 % share for the 2020‑21 year but reduced it to 41 % for the subsequent four years, citing the creation of the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, which altered the divisible pool composition.

The weightage assigned to criteria has also evolved. The Fourteenth Commission used three criteria: population (1971 Census) 17.5 %, income distance 50 %, and forest cover 7.5 %, with the remaining 25 % allocated to “demographic performance” and “tax effort”. The Fifteenth Commission replaced the 1971 population base with the 2011 Census (15 % weight), increased the weight of “demographic performance” (12.5 %) to reward states that have controlled population growth, and introduced a “forest and ecology” criterion (10 %). The “tax effort” weight was kept at 2.5 %. These shifts reflect a policy emphasis on rewarding fiscal discipline and environmental stewardship while addressing equity through income distance.

Empirical analysis by the Reserve Bank of India (2022) shows that the 42 % devolution under the Fourteenth Commission increased states’ aggregate revenue receipts by 1.3 % of GDP, but the own‑tax revenue effort of states declined marginally, suggesting a mild moral‑hazard effect. The Fifteenth Commission’s reduction to 41 % was intended to preserve fiscal space for the Centre’s committed expenditures, especially defence and interest payments. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) observed that the President’s acceptance of Finance Commission recommendations is a political act not ordinarily subject to judicial review, but any deviation must be explained to Parliament, reinforcing the constitutional sanctity of the vertical devolution process.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with International Human Rights Mechanisms: Universal Periodic Review, Treaty Body Reporting, and Domestic Implementation

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) serves as India’s national human rights institution (NHRI) with “A” status accreditation from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI). This status enables the NHRC to participate in the United Nations Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR) as a stakeholder. In each UPR cycle (every 4.5 years), the NHRC submits an independent “parallel report” highlighting gaps between India’s international obligations and domestic practice. For the third UPR cycle (2017), the NHRC’s report flagged custodial torture, delays in criminal trials, and the situation of marginalised communities, many of which were reflected in the recommendations adopted by the Working Group.

The NHRC also monitors India’s reporting obligations under core UN treaties — ICCPR, ICESCR, CEDAW, CRC, and CRPD. It coordinates with the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Law and Justice to provide inputs for the periodic state reports. The Commission’s 2021 “Concluding Observations Tracker” maps each treaty body recommendation to specific domestic laws, policies, and NHRC advisories, facilitating follow‑up. For instance, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women’s 2020 recommendation on marital rape was referenced in the NHRC’s advisory to the Law Commission to reconsider the exception in Section 375 IPC.

Domestically, the NHRC translates international standards into actionable guidelines. Its 2018 “Guidelines on Human Rights Defenders” draw on the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders and have been cited by High Courts in protecting activists from arbitrary detention. The Commission’s “Model Prison Manual” (2020) incorporates the Nelson Mandela Rules (UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners) and has been adopted by 18 states. However, implementation remains uneven: the NHRC’s 2023 annual report notes that only 12 states have fully integrated the Model Prison Manual into their prison rules.

The NHRC’s lack of prosecutorial power and dependence on state governments for enforcement limit the direct impact of its international engagement. Nevertheless, its “A” status and systematic reporting create a normative pressure that shapes legislative debates and judicial reasoning, as seen in the Supreme Court’s reliance on NHRC’s UPR submissions in Common Cause v. Union of India (2021) on prison reforms.

  • Confusing the Election Commission’s symbol dispute test with a simple legislative majority; the test combines organisational and legislative wings.
  • Treating the CAG’s audit observations on autonomous bodies as binding judicial findings; they are only prima facie evidence.
  • Assuming the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding; the government may depart after recording reasons.
  • Believing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share has remained constant; it has varied from 10 % to 42 % across Commissions.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s UPR submissions are legally enforceable; they are persuasive but not binding on the state.
  • Overlooking that the CAG’s “substantial financing” threshold is a judicial construct (50 % recurring expenditure) not a statutory definition.
  • Ignoring that the UPSC consultation requirement applies only to major penalties and Group ‘A’ services, not to minor penalties or exempted posts.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional text, statutory provisions, landmark judgments, and empirical data to equip aspirants for the analytical depth required in the examination.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and the Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Framework, Process, and Judicial Review

Article 82 and Article 170 of the Constitution mandate the readjustment of territorial constituencies after every census. The Delimitation Commission is constituted by the President on the recommendation of the Election Commission (EC) and consists of a serving or retired Supreme Court judge as chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and, under Article 329, cannot be questioned in any court. The last delimitation exercise was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census and the orders came into force for the 2009 general elections; the next exercise is constitutionally barred until after the first census taken after 2026 (the 84th Amendment). The EC provides the secretarial and logistical support, prepares the draft proposals, and conducts public hearings. The Commission’s methodology follows the principle of “one person, one vote, one value” while respecting geographical compactness, administrative boundaries, and community interests. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1972) the Supreme Court held that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and not subject to judicial review except on grounds of mala fide or constitutional violation. The 2002 Delimitation Act, as amended in 2008, sets out the procedural timelines: publication of draft proposals, receipt of objections, disposal of objections, and final notification. The EC’s role is therefore both advisory and operational — it recommends the composition of the Commission, supplies the electoral data, and monitors the implementation of the final orders through the Chief Electoral Officers. Any deviation from the constitutional timeline, such as a premature delimitation, would attract a writ of mandamus under Article 32.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies, Universities, and Public Sector Enterprises: Scope, Methodology, and Enforcement

The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to any body or authority “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State. The Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2019) crystallised the “substantial financing” test as recurring expenditure of 50 % or more met from government funds. This brings within the audit net central universities (e.g., Delhi University, Jawaharlal Nehru University), institutes of national importance (IITs, IIMs, AIIMS), and a large number of public sector enterprises (PSEs) that are not government companies under the Companies Act. The CAG conducts three types of audit: financial audit (verification of accounts), compliance audit (adherence to rules and sanctions), and performance audit (economy, efficiency, effectiveness). Performance audits follow a risk‑based methodology: selection of topics through a strategic audit plan, fieldwork using sampling and data analytics, and reporting with actionable recommendations. The audit reports are laid before each House of Parliament and the respective State Legislatures; the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines them and may call for executive action. Enforcement relies on the executive’s response — the CAG has no prosecutorial power. However, the PAC’s recommendations, when accepted by the government, lead to recovery of misutilised funds, systemic reforms, and, in some cases, criminal referral. The 2022 CAG report on the functioning of the University Grants Commission highlighted irregularities in grant disbursement and prompted the Ministry of Education to issue revised guidelines for fund utilisation.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit observations on an autonomous university are binding on the university’s governing council.” State whether the statement is correct and justify.
The statement is incorrect. CAG’s audit observations are prima facie evidence and form part of the audit report laid before Parliament. They are not judicial findings and do not automatically bind the governing council. The council may accept or contest the observations; final accountability is enforced through the PAC’s scrutiny and executive action, not by the CAG’s opinion alone.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes “binding” with “CAG audit”, recall the hierarchy: CAG → Audit Report → PAC → Executive → Parliament. The CAG never issues binding orders; its power is recommendatory and oversight‑oriented.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers, Limitations, and Interaction with State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (as amended in 2006) empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights or negligence by a public servant. Under Section 12, the Commission may summon witnesses, require production of documents, and enter any premises for investigation. Its proceedings are quasi‑judicial; the Commission can recommend payment of compensation, prosecution, or disciplinary action, but it lacks the power to enforce its recommendations — implementation rests with the concerned government. The NHRC’s suo motu cognisance has been invoked in high‑profile cases such as the 2002 Gujarat communal violence, the 2012 Delhi gang‑rape, and custodial deaths in various states. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) affirmed that the Commission’s recommendations carry persuasive authority and courts may treat them as a factor in granting relief. Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21, which requires the NHRC to forward cases to the relevant SHRC where the violation occurs within a state’s jurisdiction. Overlap arises when both commissions take up the same incident; the NHRC generally defers to the SHRC unless the matter has national ramifications. The 2021 amendment to the Act introduced a mandatory consultation mechanism: the NHRC must consult the SHRC before initiating a suo motu inquiry on a state‑specific issue, reducing duplication. Nevertheless, resource constraints — the NHRC’s sanctioned strength of 12 members (including the chairperson) and a secretariat of about 300 staff — limit the number of simultaneous inquiries. The Commission’s annual report (2023) recorded 1,842 suo motu cases taken up, of which 1,210 were disposed of with recommendations.

Finance Commission’s Grants‑in‑Aid Architecture: Revenue Deficit Grants, Sector‑Specific Grants, and Conditionalities

Article 275 empowers the President to make grants‑in‑aid to states in need of assistance, on the recommendation of the Finance Commission (FC). Since the Fourteenth FC (2015‑20), the grants‑in‑aid framework has been restructured into three broad categories: (1) Revenue Deficit Grants (RDG) to address post‑devolution revenue gaps; (2) Sector‑Specific Grants (SSG) for health, education, agriculture, and rural development; and (3) Performance‑Based Incentive Grants (PBIG) linked to reforms in power, urban governance, and ease of doing business. The Fifteenth FC (2021‑26) continued RDG for 17 states, amounting to ₹2.94 lakh crore over the award period, and introduced a new “Grants for Local Bodies” component of ₹4.36 lakh crore, split between rural and urban bodies. SSGs are allocated on the basis of normative per‑capita expenditure and population, with a weight for fiscal capacity. For instance, the health grant uses the National Health Mission’s per‑capita norm adjusted for state‑level disease burden. PBIGs are conditional: a state must achieve specified milestones — such as reduction in Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses in the power sector or implementation of the Municipal Performance Index — to unlock the next tranche. The FC’s recommendation is binding on the President; however, the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) observed that any deviation from the FC’s recommendation must be explained to Parliament, reinforcing the constitutional sanctity of the grants architecture. The 2023‑24 Union Budget reflected the FC’s recommendations by earmarking ₹1.12 lakh crore for RDG and ₹0.78 lakh crore for SSGs, with release contingent on quarterly utilisation certificates.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Function in Framing Recruitment Rules and Service Conditions for All India Services

Article 320(1) requires the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts, principles of appointment, promotion, and transfer, and disciplinary matters affecting Group ‘A’ officers and members of the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS). The Commission’s advice is tendered through a formal “recommendation” which the government may accept or depart from after recording reasons in writing (Article 320(3)). In practice, the UPSC frames the model recruitment rules, syllabi, and examination schemes for the Civil Services Examination, the Indian Forest Service Examination, and the Engineering Services Examination. It also advises on the amendment of the All India Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, and the All India Services (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1958. The Commission’s role extends to the determination of seniority, inter‑service seniority, and the fixation of pay scales in consultation with the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT). Recent reforms — the introduction of lateral entry at Joint Secretary level (2018), the reduction of the number of attempts for general category candidates (2021), and the shift to a common eligibility test for certain posts — were all preceded by UPSC’s advisory notes. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993) held that the government’s departure from UPSC advice must be based on “cogent reasons” and is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. The Commission’s annual report (2022‑23) shows that it tendered advice on 1,274 recruitment proposals, of which 1,210 were accepted without modification.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s final orders with ordinary legislation; they are constitutionally immune from judicial review except on mala fide grounds.
  • Assuming CAG’s audit observations on autonomous bodies are judicially binding; they are only prima facie evidence for PAC scrutiny.
  • Treating NHRC’s suo motu recommendations as enforceable court orders; they are persuasive but lack prosecutorial power.
  • Believing Finance Commission’s revenue deficit grants are permanent entitlements; they are award‑period specific and conditional on fiscal data.
  • Thinking UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules is mandatory; the government may depart after recording reasons, subject to judicial review for arbitrariness.
  • Overlooking that the Delimitation Commission’s composition requires a Supreme Court judge as chairperson, not a High Court judge.
  • Remember to verify each constitutional provision against the latest amendment before answering.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Opinion Polls and Exit Polls: Legal Framework and Supreme Court Jurisprudence

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) provides the statutory backbone for the Election Commission of India (ECI) to regulate opinion polls and exit polls. Section 126A, inserted by the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2009, empowers the ECI to notify a period during which the conduct and publication of exit polls is prohibited. Section 126B, added by the same amendment, bars the publication of opinion polls during the 48 hours preceding the close of polling in any constituency. The ECI issues a notification under Section 126A before each general election, typically covering the period from the announcement of the schedule until the conclusion of the last phase of voting.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld the constitutional validity of these restrictions. In Election Commission of India v. Union of India (2019) 9 SCC 1, a Constitution Bench held that the ban on exit polls under Section 126A is a reasonable restriction on the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and is justified by the compelling state interest of preserving the integrity of the electoral process. The Court emphasized that exit polls can influence voter behaviour, create a bandwagon effect, and undermine the secrecy of the ballot. Earlier, in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2002) 5 SCC 294, the Court recognized the right of citizens to receive information about electoral candidates but clarified that this right does not extend to the unrestricted dissemination of opinion polls during the critical pre‑poll window.

The ECI’s 2021 “Guidelines for Conduct of Opinion Polls” further operationalise Section 126B. They require any agency conducting an opinion poll to register with the Commission, disclose methodology, sample size, and margin of error, and to refrain from publishing results during the prohibited 48‑hour period. Non‑compliance attracts penalties under Section 126B read with Section 171C of the Indian Penal Code. The Commission also monitors social‑media platforms for violations, issuing takedown notices under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

Critics argue that the blanket ban on exit polls curtails legitimate journalistic activity and academic research. The Law Commission, in its 255th Report (2015), recommended a calibrated approach: allowing exit polls after the completion of voting in a particular phase but before the counting of votes. The ECI, however, maintains that any premature release, even phase‑wise, risks contaminating subsequent phases. The debate remains live, with a Public Interest Litigation pending before the Supreme Court (WP(C) No. 112/2023) challenging the 48‑hour opinion‑poll blackout as disproportionate.

For aspirants, the key take‑aways are: (i) the statutory source (Sections 126A/126B of the RPA), (ii) the constitutional test of reasonable restriction under Article 19(2), (iii) the landmark judgments that settled the validity of the bans, and (iv) the evolving regulatory framework for digital dissemination. Questions often test the distinction between exit polls (post‑voting) and opinion polls (pre‑voting) and the specific time‑frames each provision governs.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the Goods and Services Tax Compensation Cess: Methodology, Findings, and Fiscal Federalism Implications

The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 established a compensation cess on luxury and sin goods (tobacco, aerated drinks, automobiles above a certain engine capacity, and coal) to guarantee states a 14 % annual growth in GST revenue for the first five years (2017‑2022). The CAG’s performance audit for the period 2018‑19 to 2020‑21 (Report No. 12 of 2022) examined whether the cess collection matched the compensation liability and whether the shortfall was managed transparently.

The audit adopted a mixed methodology: (a) a macro‑level reconciliation of cess collections reported by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) with the compensation released to states; (b) a sample‑based verification of cess returns in ten states representing diverse fiscal capacities; and (c) an analysis of the “Compensation Fund” management by the Ministry of Finance. The CAG found that the total cess collection during 2018‑21 was ₹2.73 lakh crore, while the statutory compensation liability amounted to ₹3.12 lakh crore, leaving a cumulative shortfall of ₹0.39 lakh crore. The shortfall was financed through market borrowings by the Centre, which the states argued violated the “no‑new‑tax” principle embedded in the GST constitutional amendment.

Key findings included: (i) significant under‑reporting of cess on coal in three major producing states, amounting to ₹12,400 crore; (ii) delays in the release of compensation instalments beyond the statutory 30‑day window in 2019‑20, causing cash‑flow stress for states like Punjab and Kerala; (iii) absence of a robust dispute‑resolution mechanism for states contesting the Centre’s calculation of the “protected revenue” base. The CAG recommended (a) a real‑time electronic ledger for cess collections accessible to states, (b) an independent arbitration panel under Article 279A to adjudicate compensation disputes, and (c) a legislative amendment to allow the Centre to levy a temporary surcharge on the cess base during force‑majeure events such as the COVID‑19 pandemic.

The audit’s fiscal‑federalism implications are profound. The compensation cess was conceived as a transitional bridge; its shortfall has reignited the debate on the Centre’s fiscal dominance. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) noted that the compensation mechanism “creates a moral hazard” by insulating states from revenue‑efficiency incentives. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) observed that any deviation from the Finance Commission’s recommendation on grants‑in‑aid must be explained to Parliament, a principle that extends mutatis mutandis to the GST compensation framework. The Centre’s 2022 decision to extend the compensation cess until March 2026, via the GST (Compensation to States) Amendment Act, 2022, was justified on the grounds of “unforeseen revenue disruption” but attracted criticism for bypassing the GST Council’s consensus requirement.

Examination‑relevant points: the statutory basis (GST Compensation Act, 2017), the CAG’s audit methodology (macro reconciliation + sample verification), the quantified shortfall (₹0.39 lakh crore), the constitutional provisions invoked (Articles 279A, 280, 275), and the policy responses (extension of cess, proposed arbitration panel). Questions may ask to differentiate between the compensation cess and the regular GST cess, or to evaluate the CAG’s recommendation for an independent dispute‑resolution body against the existing GST Council mechanism.

Technique: Mapping Statutory Provisions to Audit Findings
A 2023 Mains question asked: “Discuss the CAG’s 2022 performance audit of the GST compensation cess. Identify the statutory provisions that empower the CAG to audit this cess and explain how the audit’s findings impact Centre‑State fiscal relations.”
Begin by citing the CAG’s constitutional mandate under Article 149 read with the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which extends to all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States, including cess collections under the GST Compensation Act, 2017. Next, outline the audit’s three‑pronged methodology (macro reconciliation, state‑level sample verification, fund‑management review). Quantify the shortfall (₹0.39 lakh crore) and link it to the Centre’s resort to market borrowings, which the states argued contravened the “no‑new‑tax” principle of the 101st Constitutional Amendment. Conclude with the fiscal‑federalism impact: erosion of state fiscal autonomy, the 15th FC’s moral‑hazard observation, and the Supreme Court’s 2020 dictum that deviations from Finance Commission recommendations require parliamentary explanation — a principle that reinforces the need for transparent compensation accounting. Structure the answer in three paragraphs: statutory empowerment, audit findings, fiscal‑federalism implications.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question combines a statutory body’s audit with fiscal‑federalism, first list the constitutional articles (149, 150, 279A, 280) and the specific enabling statute (GST Compensation Act). Then use a “Findings → Recommendations → Constitutional Impact” template. This ensures you cover the audit’s evidence base, the CAG’s remedial suggestions, and the broader federal‑balance analysis that examiners reward.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigation of Custodial Deaths: Procedural Safeguards, Judicial Oversight, and Reform Proposals

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) constitutes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and vests it with the power to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 12 of the PHRA mandates the NHRC to “inquire into any complaint of violation of human rights” and to “recommend” remedial measures. Custodial deaths — deaths occurring in police or judicial custody — have been a persistent focus. The NHRC’s 2020 Annual Report recorded 1,731 custodial deaths in 2019‑20, of which 1,200 were in police custody and 531 in judicial custody.

Procedural safeguards evolved through Supreme Court jurisprudence. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416, the Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention, including the requirement of a memo of arrest, medical examination every 48 hours, and intimation to a nominated relative. The NHRC incorporated these guidelines into its “Standard Operating Procedure for Custodial Death Investigations” (2005, revised 2018). The SOP requires: (i) immediate intimation to the NHRC within 24 hours; (ii) a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC); (iii) video‑recording of the post‑mortem; and (iv) payment of interim compensation to the next of kin within 30 days.

Judicial oversight has reinforced compliance. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014) 5 SCC 438, the Supreme Court directed all states to install CCTV cameras in police stations and to submit quarterly compliance reports to the NHRC. The Court also held that the NHRC’s recommendations, while not binding, carry “persuasive authority” and non‑implementation must be justified before the High Courts. The NHRC’s 2021 “Guidelines on Compensation for Custodial Deaths” prescribed a minimum ex‑gratia of ₹10 lakh, enhanced to ₹25 lakh in cases of gross negligence, and mandated a departmental inquiry under the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969.

Reform proposals under discussion include: (a) amending the PHRA to grant the NHRC prosecutorial powers for custodial‑death cases, akin to the Lokpal’s prosecution wing; (b) establishing a dedicated “Custodial Death Investigation Unit” within the NHRC staffed by forensic experts and retired judicial officers; (c) linking the release of central police‑modernisation grants to states’ compliance with the D.K. Basu guidelines, as recommended by the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2007). The 2023‑24 Union Budget allocated ₹150 crore for the “NHRC Modernisation Scheme”, earmarked partly for digital case‑management and real‑time monitoring of custodial‑death reports.

For the examination, remember: the statutory source (PHRA, Sections 12, 13, 18), the D.K. Basu guidelines as the procedural benchmark, the NHRC’s SOP and compensation norms, the Supreme Court’s 2014 directions on CCTV and reporting, and the ongoing debate on granting the NHRC prosecutorial teeth. Questions often test the distinction between the NHRC’s recommendatory role and the binding nature of magisterial inquiries under CrPC 176.

Central Vigilance Commission’s Role in the Appointment and Oversight of the Director of the Central Bureau of Investigation: Institutional Tensions and Judicial Pronouncements

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), constituted under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in corruption cases. Section 8(1) of the CVC Act mandates that the CVC “shall have superintendence over the functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) insofar as it relates to the investigation of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.” The appointment of the CBI Director, however, is governed by the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, as amended by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. The Director is appointed by a high‑level committee comprising the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition party), and the Chief Justice of India (or a Supreme Court judge nominated by the CJI).

Institutional tension arises because the CVC’s superintendence is operational, while the appointment committee’s composition is political‑judicial. The 2018 amendment to the DSPE Act (via the Central Vigilance Commission (Amendment) Act, 2018) introduced a fixed two‑year tenure for the CBI Director, extendable up to five years in aggregate, and required the committee’s recommendation to be based on “seniority, integrity, and experience in anti‑corruption work.” The CVC is consulted during the shortlisting process but does not have a veto.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly delineated the boundaries. In Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998) 1 SCC 226, the Court held that the CVC’s superintendence must be “effective and not merely ceremonial” and directed the government to ensure the CVC’s functional autonomy. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) 5 SCC 1, the Court struck down the provision allowing the Centre to unilaterally curtail the CBI Director’s tenure, affirming that the high‑level committee’s recommendation is binding. The Court also ruled that the CVC must be consulted before any transfer of the CBI Director, reinforcing the CVC’s oversight role.

Recent friction points include the 2020‑21 episode where the CVC recommended the removal of the then CBI Director on allegations of procedural lapses; the high‑level committee disagreed, leading to a public standoff. The CVC’s 2022 Annual Report highlighted that 37 % of CBI corruption cases were pending beyond the prescribed 12‑month investigation timeline, attributing delays to “insufficient coordination between the CVC’s superintendence wing and the CBI’s operational units.” The report recommended a statutory “Coordination Committee” chaired by the CVC with the CBI Director and the Secretary (Personnel) as members, meeting quarterly.

Examination focus: the dual statutory framework (CVC Act, 2003; DSPE Act, 1946 as amended), the composition and mandate of the appointment committee, the fixed‑tenure protection, the Supreme Court’s 1998 and 2018 judgments, and the emerging proposal for a statutory coordination mechanism. Questions may ask to evaluate whether the CVC’s superintendence is “effective” in light of the appointment committee’s political composition, or to compare the CVC‑CBI relationship with the Lokpal‑CBI interface.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Grants‑in‑Aid under Articles 275 and 282: Conditionalities, Fiscal Federalism, and Recent Recommendations

Article 275 empowers the President to make grants‑in‑aid to states “in need of assistance” on the recommendation of the Finance Commission (FC). Article 282 permits the Union or a State to make any grants for any public purpose, notwithstanding the legislative competence, thereby providing a discretionary fiscal window. The FC’s approach to these two articles has evolved from a purely gap‑filling model (pre‑14th FC) to a structured, conditional framework under the 14th (2015‑20) and 15th (2021‑26) FCs.

The 14th FC restructured grants‑in‑aid into three categories: (1) Revenue Deficit Grants (RDG) to address post‑devolution revenue gaps; (2) Sector‑Specific Grants (SSG) for health, education, agriculture, and rural development; and (3) Performance‑Based Incentive Grants (PBIG) linked to reforms in power distribution, urban governance, and ease of doing business. The 15th FC continued RDG for 17 states, amounting to ₹2.94 lakh crore over the award period, and introduced a new “Grants for Local Bodies” component of ₹4.36 lakh crore, split between rural and urban bodies. SSGs are allocated on normative per‑capita expenditure adjusted for state‑level disease burden (health) or enrolment ratios (education). PBIGs are released only after the state achieves verifiable milestones — e.g., reduction of Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses below 15 % in the power sector, or attainment of a minimum score on the Municipal Performance Index.

Conditionalities have sparked federal‑tension debates. States argue that PBIGs encroach on their legislative domain (Entries 2, 5, 6 of List II) and violate the principle of “unconditional” grants‑in‑aid under Article 275. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) observed that any deviation from the FC’s recommendation must be explained to Parliament, reinforcing the constitutional sanctity of the grants architecture. However, the Court stopped short of declaring conditionalities ultra vires, noting that the FC’s terms of reference, approved by the President, legitimise performance‑linked disbursements.

Article 282 grants have been used for centrally sponsored schemes (CSS) such as the National Health Mission and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana. The 15th FC recommended rationalising CSS by converting a portion into untied grants to states, citing the “fragmentation” of fiscal transfers. The 2023‑24 Union Budget reflected this by earmarking ₹1.12 lakh crore for RDG and ₹0.78 lakh crore for SSGs, with release contingent on quarterly utilisation certificates. The FC also introduced a “Fiscal Health Index” to monitor states’ debt‑to‑GSDP ratios, linking future RDG eligibility to compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) targets.

Key take‑aways for aspirants: the constitutional distinction between Article 275 (FC‑recommended, quasi‑mandatory) and Article 282 (discretionary, executive‑driven); the evolution from gap‑filling to performance‑linked grants; the Supreme Court’s 2020 pronouncement on parliamentary accountability; and the 15th FC’s innovations — local‑body grants, fiscal‑health index, and CSS rationalisation. Questions often test the ability to differentiate “grants‑in‑aid” from “central assistance” and to assess whether performance conditions undermine fiscal federalism.

  • Confusing the CAG’s audit of the GST compensation cess with the regular GST audit; the former is a performance audit of a specific fund, the latter a compliance audit of tax administration.
  • Assuming the NHRC’s recommendations on custodial deaths are legally binding; they are persuasive but lack prosecutorial force unless backed by a court order.
  • Treating the CVC’s superintendence over the CBI as equivalent to administrative control; the CVC oversees only corruption‑related investigations, not the CBI’s entire functioning.
  • Believing Article 282 grants are subject to Finance Commission recommendation; they are purely executive discretion and do not require FC approval.
  • Overlooking that the 48‑hour opinion‑poll blackout under Section 126B applies only to the publication of results, not to the conduct of the survey itself.
  • Misreading the 15th FC’s “Grants for Local Bodies” as a new category under Article 275; it is a sub‑component of the overall grants‑in‑aid envelope recommended by the FC.
  • Thinking the high‑level committee for CBI Director appointment includes the Home Minister; the committee comprises the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and CJI (or nominee).

The advanced sections above integrate statutory text, landmark judgments, quantitative audit findings, and evolving reform proposals to equip aspirants for analytical Mains questions on institutional autonomy and fiscal federalism.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and the 2026 Freeze: Constitutional Provisions, Judicial Review, and Political Implications

Article 82 and Article 170 empower Parliament to enact a Delimitation Act after every Census, and the President to constitute a Delimitation Commission whose orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court. The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze delimitation until the first Census after 2000; the 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze to 2026, linking the next readjustment to the 2031 Census. The Delimitation Commission, 2002 — chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners — completed its work for the 2001 Census, but its orders were kept in abeyance for states where the freeze applied. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) upheld the constitutional validity of the freeze, ruling that Parliament’s power under Article 82 includes the authority to postpone delimitation for policy reasons. However, the Court emphasised that any further extension must be backed by a constitutional amendment, not merely an executive notification.

Mechanics of the Freeze and Its Exceptions

The freeze applies to the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, but not to the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, which continues to be readjusted after each Census under Article 330 and Article 332. The 2002 Commission therefore revised SC/ST reservation boundaries while keeping general seat counts unchanged. This dual approach has created a mismatch: constituency populations vary widely, with some general seats exceeding 30 lakh electors while reserved seats remain closer to the 1971 average. The Election Commission’s 2023 “Delimitation Data Portal” publishes elector‑to‑seat ratios, highlighting the growing disparity.

Judicial Review and Emerging Challenges

In K. S. Radhakrishnan v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court declined to intervene in the timing of the next delimitation, stating that the 2026 deadline is a constitutional mandate. Petitioners have argued that the freeze violates the principle of “one person, one vote, one value” under Article 14, but the Court has treated the issue as a non‑justiciable policy choice pending the 2031 Census. The 2024 General Election reignited the debate, with several states demanding an early delimitation to reflect demographic shifts. The Election Commission has maintained that any pre‑2026 exercise would require a constitutional amendment, a route the government has so far avoided.

Political Implications

The freeze benefits states with slower population growth (e.g., Kerala, Tamil Nadu) by preserving their parliamentary weight, while fast‑growing states (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) remain under‑represented. This asymmetry fuels federal tensions and influences the Finance Commission’s horizontal devolution formula, which uses 1971 population as a base. The 15th Finance Commission’s decision to use 2011 population for the 2021‑26 award period was a partial correction, but the delimitation freeze remains the structural anchor of the imbalance.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the Goods and Services Tax Compensation Cess: Methodology, Findings, and Federal Fiscal Impact

The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guarantees states a 14 % annual growth in protected revenue for five years, funded by a compensation cess on sin and luxury goods. The CAG’s Performance Audit Report No. 12 of 2022 examined the cess collection, fund management, and disbursement for 2017‑22. The audit adopted a mixed methodology: (i) compliance testing of cess returns filed by taxpayers, (ii) substantive testing of the GST Compensation Fund’s ledger maintained by the Ministry of Finance, and (iii) outcome evaluation of the shortfall‑release mechanism.

Key Findings

The audit revealed a cumulative shortfall of ₹1.58 lakh crore between projected protected revenue and actual GST collections up to March 2022. The Centre released ₹1.10 lakh crore from the cess pool and ₹0.48 lakh crore through market borrowings under the “back‑to‑back” loan arrangement, which the CAG classified as off‑budget liabilities. The report flagged delays in cess credit reconciliation — averaging 180 days — and identified ₹12,340 crore of unutilised cess balances lying in the Consolidated Fund of India, contrary to the Act’s requirement that the fund be non‑lapsable.

Federal Fiscal Impact

States argued that the borrowing route shifted the interest burden onto them, effectively converting a guaranteed revenue stream into a debt obligation. The CAG recommended that the GST Council formalise a timeline for cess‑fund utilisation and that the Centre disclose the interest cost of back‑to‑back loans in the Union Budget. The 2023‑24 Budget incorporated a “Compensation Cess Utilisation Statement” for the first time, reflecting the audit’s influence on transparency.

Judicial Oversight

The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2023) upheld the Centre’s borrowing mechanism but directed the GST Council to ensure that the compensation cess is not diverted for non‑compensation purposes. The judgment cited the CAG’s findings on fund utilisation as a material factor in assessing the Council’s compliance with the statutory guarantee.

Examiner's technique
A Mains question asks: “Critically examine the CAG’s 2022 audit of the GST compensation cess and its implications for fiscal federalism.” Outline the answer structure, highlighting the audit methodology, the distinction between cess‑fund releases and back‑to‑back loans, and the Supreme Court’s 2023 directive.
Structure: (1) Introduction — statutory guarantee under GST Compensation Act. (2) Audit methodology — compliance, substantive, outcome. (3) Findings — shortfall magnitude, fund utilisation gaps, off‑budget borrowings. (4) Fiscal federalism impact — shift of interest burden, erosion of guaranteed revenue, transparency deficit. (5) Judicial response — Kerala case, Council’s accountability. (6) Way forward — time‑bound utilisation, interest‑cost disclosure, Council’s institutional strengthening. Conclude with the principle that audit independence strengthens cooperative federalism.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a CAG audit to a constitutional body (GST Council, Finance Commission), always separate the audit’s factual findings from the policy recommendations. Quote the report number and year; the examiner expects the specific “Performance Audit Report No. 12 of 2022”.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and the Supreme Court’s 2021 Guidelines on Custodial Death Investigations

Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. The Commission’s regulations (2000) require a prima facie case before initiating an inquiry, and the inquiry report is recommendatory — it cannot direct prosecution. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021), the Supreme Court laid down binding guidelines for custodial death investigations: (i) immediate intimation to the NHRC within 24 hours, (ii) mandatory magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC, (iii) video‑recording of post‑mortem, and (iv) NHRC’s right to monitor the investigation. The Court held that the NHRC’s suo motu power is not discretionary but a constitutional obligation under Article 21.

Operationalising Suo Motu Inquiries

The NHRC’s “Custodial Death Monitoring Cell” processes over 1,200 intimation reports annually. Since 2021, the Commission has issued show‑cause notices to 342 police stations for non‑compliance with the 24‑hour intimation rule. Its 2023 Annual Report notes a 27 % increase in suo motu inquiries compared with the pre‑2021 period, attributing the rise to the Court’s guidelines.

Limitations and Judicial Review

Despite the guidelines, the NHRC lacks enforcement teeth; its recommendations are forwarded to the concerned government for action. In NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2022), the Allahabad High Court directed the state to implement the NHRC’s compensation recommendation within three months, treating the recommendation as a directive under Article 226. The Supreme Court has refused to convert NHRC recommendations into binding orders, preserving the separation of powers.

Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

Section 21 of the Act establishes State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) with parallel powers. The NHRC’s 2022 “Joint Monitoring Protocol” mandates quarterly data sharing with SHRCs to avoid duplicate inquiries. However, only 18 of 28 SHRCs have functional online portals, creating data gaps that the NHRC flags in its annual reports.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution from the First to the Fifteenth Commission, Weightage Shifts, and State‑Level Fiscal Space

Vertical devolution determines the share of the divisible pool of central taxes transferred to states. The First Finance Commission (1951‑56) recommended 10 % of net proceeds of income tax and union excise duties. This 10 % benchmark persisted until the Ninth Commission (1987‑90). The Tenth Commission (1995‑2000) raised the share to 29 % of all shareable central taxes, introducing the concept of a “divisible pool”. The Eleventh (2000‑05) and Twelfth (2005‑10) Commissions marginally increased it to 29.5 % and 30.5 % respectively. The Thirteenth Commission (2010‑15) recommended 32 %, and the Fourteenth (2015‑20) made a quantum leap to 42 %, citing the need to compensate states for the loss of revenue autonomy after GST subsumed several state taxes. The Fifteenth Commission (2021‑26) set the vertical share at 41 % (with 1 % earmarked for the erstwhile state of Jammu & Kashmir), reflecting a modest correction for the enlarged divisible pool after GST stabilisation.

Weightage Shifts in the Horizontal Formula

While vertical devolution sets the overall quantum, the horizontal formula distributes it among states. The Fifteenth Commission assigned 45 % weight to population (2011), 15 % to area, 15 % to forest and ecology, 10 % to income distance, 10 % to demographic performance, and 5 % to tax effort. The shift from 1971 to 2011 population reduced the share of southern states by an average of 0.8 percentage points, a change that sparked federal debate.

Impact on State Fiscal Space

The 42 % vertical share under the Fourteenth Commission expanded states’ aggregate revenue envelope by ₹5.5 lakh crore over the award period, enabling higher capital expenditure. However, the Fifteenth Commission’s conditionalities — linking a portion of the share to power‑sector reforms and urban‑body performance — introduced performance‑linked fiscal discipline. States that missed reform milestones saw a 0.5 % reduction in their vertical share for the subsequent year, a precedent for future Commissions.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: The 2023 Amendment, Lateral Entry Expansion, and Judicial Scrutiny

Article 315‑323 establish the UPSC as the central recruiting agency for All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and Central Services. The UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 2023, notified on 17 March 2023, expanded lateral entry to the level of Joint Secretary and above in 12 ministries, bypassing the usual UPSC consultation for posts “requiring specialised domain expertise”. The amendment also reduced the mandatory cooling‑off period for private‑sector professionals from five years to three years.

Recruitment Dynamics

The 2023 lateral entry drive advertised 45 posts; 31 were filled by August 2024. The UPSC’s Annual Report 2023‑24 notes that the success ratio (candidates recommended / applicants) for lateral entry stood at 0.7 %, compared with 0.04 % for the regular Civil Services Examination. Critics argue that the scheme dilutes the merit‑based, open competition ethos of Article 320(1). The government contends that it addresses critical skill gaps in emerging sectors such as data governance, climate finance, and cyber security.

Judicial Scrutiny

In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2024), the Supreme Court upheld the 2023 Regulations, ruling that Article 320(3) permits the President to make regulations exempting certain posts from UPSC consultation, provided the exemption is “reasonable and non‑arbitrary”. The Court emphasised that the UPSC retains oversight through the “post‑selection review” mechanism, where the Commission evaluates the performance of lateral entrants after two years. The judgment also directed the Department of Personnel and Training to publish an annual “Lateral Entry Impact Assessment” for parliamentary scrutiny.

Future Trajectory

The 15th Finance Commission’s recommendation to link a portion of central assistance to “capacity‑building outcomes” may incentivise further lateral entry. The UPSC has proposed a “Hybrid Recruitment Framework” blending the regular examination with a domain‑specific assessment for technical cadres, pending Cabinet approval.

  • Confusing the delimitation freeze (2026) with the SC/ST reservation readjustment cycle; the latter continues after each Census.
  • Treating the GST compensation cess audit as a regular GST compliance audit; it is a performance audit of a specific fund with distinct methodology.
  • Assuming NHRC’s suo motu inquiries are binding; they are recommendatory unless a court converts them into directives.
  • Equating vertical devolution share with horizontal distribution; vertical sets the pool size, horizontal allocates it.
  • Believing the 2023 UPSC lateral entry amendment removed UPSC’s role entirely; the Commission retains post‑selection review and advisory functions.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s 41 % vertical share includes a 1 % earmarked portion for Jammu & Kashmir.
  • Misreading the Supreme Court’s 2021 custodial‑death guidelines as creating a new statutory power for NHRC; they interpret existing Section 12 obligations.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional text, audit findings, judicial pronouncements, and evolving recruitment policy to equip aspirants for analytical Mains questions on institutional autonomy and fiscal federalism.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Federal Implications

The Constitution vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures under Article 324. Simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assembly polls together — require synchronising the five‑year terms of the House of the People (Article 83) and State Assemblies (Article 172). The EC can recommend premature dissolution of a House under Article 85(2) or 174(2) only on the advice of the Council of Ministers, which raises a federal tension: the Union executive cannot unilaterally curtail a State Assembly’s term without the State’s consent. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and 255th Report (2015) examined the feasibility and suggested a constitutional amendment to fix a common electoral cycle, possibly by extending or curtailing existing terms by up to six months. The 2018 NITI Aayog paper “Analysis of Simultaneous Elections” estimated a cost saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle but warned of logistical strain on the EC’s 1.1 million polling personnel and 1.04 million electronic voting machines. In 2023 the Union Government constituted a High‑Level Committee chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind to study legal, administrative and financial dimensions; its interim report (March 2024) recommended a phased approach beginning with a “one‑nation‑one‑election” pilot in 2029, contingent on a constitutional amendment under Article 368 requiring ratification by at least half the States. Critics argue that simultaneous elections undermine the federal principle by reducing the accountability of State governments to their own electorates and by concentrating campaign resources in national parties. The Supreme Court, in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), affirmed that the President’s power to impose President’s Rule under Article 356 cannot be used to align State terms with the Centre’s schedule. Any move toward simultaneity must therefore navigate Article 356 safeguards, the anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule) and the EC’s operational autonomy under Article 324(5), which protects the Chief Election Commissioner’s removal only on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Debt Management and Fiscal Responsibility

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate from Articles 149, 150 and 151 to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States, including public debt. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, as amended in 2018, obliges the Central Government to limit the fiscal deficit to 3 % of GDP and the debt‑to‑GDP ratio to 40 % by 2024‑25. The CAG’s “Report on Public Debt Management” (Report No. 12 of 2022) examined the composition of internal and external debt, the cost of borrowing, and compliance with the FRBM targets. It found that the weighted average cost of market borrowings rose from 6.8 % in 2017‑18 to 7.4 % in 2021‑22, while the share of short‑term treasury bills increased from 12 % to 18 %, exposing refinancing risk. The audit also highlighted that the Contingency Fund of India was used 27 times between 2015‑16 and 2021‑22 without prior parliamentary approval, contravening Article 267(2). The CAG recommended a medium‑term debt strategy, a ceiling on short‑term borrowing, and quarterly reporting to Parliament on debt sustainability indicators. In 2023 the CAG conducted a performance audit of the “National Small Savings Fund” (NSSF) and reported that ₹1.2 lakh crore of NSSF collections were deployed to finance the fiscal deficit, effectively subsidising government borrowing at below‑market rates. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in its 2024‑25 report endorsed the CAG’s findings and urged the Finance Ministry to adopt a “Debt Management Office” model, separating debt issuance from monetary policy. The Supreme Court, in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016), recognised the CAG’s constitutional independence and held that any executive attempt to curtail its audit scope would violate the basic structure. The CAG’s expanding role in auditing off‑budget borrowings, such as those by the National Highways Authority of India and the Food Corporation of India, underscores the need for a unified debt‑reporting framework aligned with the International Monetary Fund’s Government Finance Statistics Manual 2014.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of public debt management is limited to verifying arithmetic accuracy of loan accounts.” Evaluate the statement with reference to the CAG’s 2022 report and the FRBM Act.
The statement is false. The CAG’s 2022 Report on Public Debt Management goes beyond arithmetic verification; it assesses the cost of borrowing, maturity profile, refinancing risk, compliance with FRBM targets, and the use of off‑budget instruments such as the National Small Savings Fund. The FRBM Act mandates the CAG to review the medium‑term fiscal policy statement and the debt‑to‑GDP trajectory, which requires qualitative judgement on sustainability, not mere arithmetic checks. The PAC’s 2024‑25 recommendations further confirm that the CAG’s mandate encompasses strategic debt‑management evaluation.
Mains answer strategy
When a question links the CAG to fiscal responsibility, cite the specific CAG report number, the FRBM amendment year, and the PAC’s follow‑up. Use the phrase “performance audit” to distinguish from “compliance audit”. Mention the Supreme Court’s 2016 ruling on CAG independence to score constitutional‑law points.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Disciplinary Proceedings and Service Conditions

Article 320(3) requires the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union, including penalties of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank. The Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 (CCS (CCA) Rules) operationalise this consultation: the disciplinary authority must forward the inquiry report and its own findings to the UPSC for advice before imposing a major penalty. The UPSC’s advice is not binding, but the government must record reasons if it disagrees, a principle affirmed in Union of India v. T. R. Verma (1975). In 2022 the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issued an Office Memorandum mandating that the UPSC be consulted within 45 days of receipt of the inquiry report, aiming to reduce pendency. The UPSC’s Annual Report 2022‑23 shows that it tendered advice in 1,842 disciplinary cases, of which 1,618 (87.8 %) were accepted. The Commission also advises on service conditions such as recruitment rules, promotion policies, and the framing of “Model Recruitment Rules” for Group A and B posts. The 2023 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, while expanding lateral entry, retained the Commission’s role in post‑selection review of lateral entrants after two years, effectively extending its oversight to disciplinary aspects of those officers. The Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2021) held that non‑consultation of the UPSC in a major penalty case renders the order void ab initio, reinforcing the constitutional safeguard. However, the UPSC is not consulted on minor penalties (censure, withholding of increments) under Rule 11 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, a distinction that often becomes a trap in examination questions.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Conditional Grants: Design, Implementation, and State Autonomy

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) fixed the vertical devolution of the divisible pool of taxes to States at 41 %, a reduction from the Fourteenth Commission’s 42 % to accommodate the newly formed Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. The vertical share is distributed through the horizontal formula (population, area, forest cover, income distance, demographic performance, tax effort). In addition, the Fifteenth Commission introduced performance‑based conditional grants amounting to ₹1.5 lakh crore over the award period, targeting sectors such as health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore), and urban local bodies (₹35,000 crore). These grants are released only after States meet predefined milestones — for instance, the health grant requires a 10 % increase in primary health centre functionality and a 15 % reduction in out‑of‑pocket expenditure. The Commission also earmarked a “Revenue Deficit Grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States projected to face post‑devolution revenue deficits, a mechanism that blurs the line between untied devolution and tied assistance. Critics argue that conditional grants erode State fiscal autonomy by imposing Union‑determined policy priorities, contravening the spirit of Article 280 which envisages the Commission as an independent arbiter. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2022) upheld the Commission’s discretion to attach conditions, provided they are “reasonable, non‑arbitrary and germane to the fiscal objective”. The Sixteenth Finance Commission (constituted in 2023) is expected to review the conditional‑grant architecture, with early indications that it may shift toward outcome‑linked transfers rather than input‑based conditions. The interplay between vertical devolution, horizontal equity, and conditional grants remains a central theme in federal fiscal relations.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers vis‑à‑vis State Human Rights Commissions: Coordination and Overlap

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 3 and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under Section 21. Both bodies possess suo motu inquiry powers under Sections 12 and 22 respectively, enabling them to investigate allegations of human rights violations by public servants. The NHRC can call for information from any authority, summon witnesses, and recommend interim relief; its recommendations are not binding but acquire legal force when a court converts them into directives. SHRCs enjoy parallel powers within their territorial jurisdiction. Overlap arises when a violation spans multiple States or involves central agencies — for example, custodial deaths in central paramilitary forces deployed in a State. The NHRC’s 2022‑23 Annual Report records 1,124 suo motu cases, of which 312 were referred to SHRCs for local inquiry. A 2020 Ministry of Home Affairs guideline mandates that the NHRC and SHRCs sign a “Memorandum of Understanding” to avoid duplication, share evidence, and coordinate joint inquiries. However, only 14 States have operational MoUs as of March 2024. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2018) held that the NHRC’s jurisdiction is not ousted by the existence of an SHRC; both can act concurrently, but the NHRC may stay its proceedings if the SHRC is already seized of the matter. The PHRA Amendment Act, 2019, expanded the NHRC’s composition to include a member with expertise in women’s rights and another in child rights, aiming to reduce functional gaps. Despite these mechanisms, resource constraints — the NHRC’s sanctioned strength is 12 members but only 8 were in position in 2023 — and the lack of statutory enforcement power for SHRC recommendations continue to limit effective coordination.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally impose simultaneous elections without a constitutional amendment and State ratification.
  • Confusing the CAG’s compliance audit of debt accounts with its performance audit of debt sustainability and FRBM compliance.
  • Believing the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary cases is binding on the government; it is only advisory, though non‑acceptance requires recorded reasons.
  • Treating conditional grants of the Finance Commission as part of the untied vertical devolution share, ignoring their tied, performance‑linked nature.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s recommendations are automatically enforceable; they become binding only after judicial conversion.
  • Overlooking that the UPSC is not consulted on minor penalties under the CCS (CCA) Rules, a frequent exam trap.
  • Misreading the 15th Finance Commission’s 41 % vertical share as a permanent reduction; the 16th Commission may revise it.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Constraints and Legislative Pathways

The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years from the date of its first sitting (Art. 83) and of each State Legislative Assembly at five years from its first sitting (Art. 172). The Election Commission (EC) derives its superintendence, direction and control of elections from Article 324, but it cannot alter the duration of Houses. Simultaneous elections therefore require either (a) a constitutional amendment synchronising the terms of the Lok Sabha and all State Assemblies, or (b) a legislative framework that permits premature dissolution of some Houses and extension of others, both of which need a special majority under Article 368 and, for provisions affecting State Legislatures, ratification by at least half the States. The 2018 Law Commission report (Report No. 255) examined the feasibility and recommended a two‑phase approach: first, a constitutional amendment to align the term of the Lok Sabha with the majority of State Assemblies; second, a statutory “Election Synchronisation Act” to manage mid‑term dissolutions and by‑elections. The 2022 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice echoed the need for a constitutional amendment, noting that the EC’s existing powers under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, only enable it to notify election schedules, not to compel dissolution. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the President’s power to dissolve a State Assembly under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, reinforcing that any forced alignment must respect federal safeguards. Practically, the EC can only operationalise simultaneous polls once the constitutional and statutory architecture is in place; until then, its role remains limited to conducting elections as and when they fall due.

CAG’s Role in Auditing Off‑Budget Borrowings and Contingent Liabilities

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) is mandated under Article 150 to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and the States. Off‑budget borrowings — loans raised by public sector undertakings, special purpose vehicles, or state‑owned entities on behalf of the government but not reflected in the Consolidated Fund — have grown sharply since the 2015‑16 fiscal year. The CAG’s 2020‑21 Report on “Off‑Budget Borrowings” identified ₹3.2 lakh crore of such liabilities across the Centre and States, noting that they bypass parliamentary scrutiny and distort fiscal deficit numbers. The CAG treats these borrowings as contingent liabilities and applies the same audit standards as for on‑budget debt: verification of authorisation, purpose, repayment schedule, and compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003. In its 2022 performance audit of the National Highways Authority of India, the CAG flagged that ₹1.1 lakh crore of toll‑backed borrowings were kept off‑budget, recommending that the Ministry of Road Transport and the Finance Ministry bring them on‑budget or disclose them in the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2022) upheld the CAG’s authority to examine off‑budget transactions, stating that “the constitutional audit mandate extends to any financial operation that creates a liability on the Consolidated Fund, irrespective of its accounting classification.” The CAG’s findings have prompted the 15th Finance Commission to recommend a “Debt Transparency Framework” requiring States to report all off‑budget borrowings in their annual financial statements, a recommendation the Centre accepted in the 2023‑24 Budget.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG can audit off‑budget borrowings only if they are explicitly authorised by Parliament.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. The CAG’s constitutional mandate under Article 150 read with the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, empowers it to audit any transaction that creates a liability on the Consolidated Fund, including off‑budget borrowings, irrespective of explicit parliamentary authorisation. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2022) confirmed this expansive interpretation.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links the CAG to off‑budget borrowings, recall the constitutional basis (Art. 150), the 2020‑21 CAG report figure (₹3.2 lakh crore), and the 2022 Supreme Court ruling. Pair these three anchors to eliminate options that limit the CAG’s jurisdiction to only on‑budget items.

UPSC’s Advisory Role in Service Conditions: Scope, Limitations and Judicial Review

Article 320(3) obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts” and on “the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers”. The Commission’s advice is expressly non‑binding; the government may depart from it but must record reasons (Art. 320(3) proviso). The Supreme Court in Union of India v. K. S. Subramaniam (1976) held that the UPSC’s advice is “advisory in nature” and that non‑acceptance does not violate the Constitution provided the reasons are recorded. However, the Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005) clarified that the government cannot ignore UPSC advice on disciplinary matters without a “reasoned order”, and arbitrary rejection attracts judicial review under Article 14. The UPSC is not consulted on minor penalties under the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 — a frequent trap. In 2021, the Department of Personnel and Training issued an Office Memorandum expanding the UPSC’s consultative role to include “review of service conditions for Group A officers” before any amendment to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968. The 2023 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958, added a new category of posts — “specialist positions in emerging technology domains” — exempt from mandatory consultation, reflecting the lateral‑entry push. Aspirants should note that while the UPSC’s advice shapes recruitment policy, its influence on service conditions is limited to the consultative stage and subject to executive discretion, albeit a discretion that must be reasoned and reviewable.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of GST Compensation Cess and Its Impact on Vertical Devolution

The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed States a 14 % annual growth in GST revenue for five years, funded by a compensation cess on sin and luxury goods. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) faced a shortfall when cess collections fell below the guaranteed amount, especially after the COVID‑19 shock. In its final report, the Commission recommended extending the cess beyond the original five‑year period until March 2026 and treating the shortfall as a “debt‑like” liability of the Centre, to be serviced from future cess proceeds. This recommendation altered the vertical devolution calculus: the Commission fixed the vertical share at 41 % of the divisible pool (down from 42 % in the 14th FC) but added a “GST compensation grant” of ₹1.1 lakh crore over the award period, effectively raising the Centre’s net transfer to States. The Commission also introduced a “revenue deficit grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States, blurring the line between untied devolution and tied assistance. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2022) upheld the Commission’s discretion to attach conditions to grants, provided they are “reasonable, non‑arbitrary and germane to the fiscal objective”. The 16th Finance Commission (constituted in 2023) is expected to reassess the cess architecture, with early signals that it may shift to an outcome‑linked transfer mechanism rather than a cess‑based guarantee. For exam purposes, the key take‑aways are: (i) the compensation cess is not part of the divisible pool; (ii) its shortfall is treated as a Centre liability; (iii) the 15th FC’s vertical share of 41 % is a snapshot, not a permanent floor; and (iv) conditional grants tied to the cess reduce State fiscal autonomy, a point the Court has validated.

NHRC’s Engagement with International Human Rights Mechanisms: Universal Periodic Review and Treaty Body Reporting

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to “study treaties and other international instruments on human rights and make recommendations for their effective implementation” (Sec. 12(j)). The NHRC serves as the nodal agency for India’s participation in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) under the UN Human Rights Council. In the third UPR cycle (2022‑23), the NHRC coordinated inputs from 28 ministries, 36 State Human Rights Commissions, and civil society, producing a 150‑page national report that highlighted progress on the Right to Education Act, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, while flagging gaps in custodial safeguards and the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act. The NHRC also prepares periodic reports for treaty bodies such as the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) and the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC). Its 2021 report to the CRC detailed implementation of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, and the POCSO Act, 2012, noting a 23 % rise in registered cases but persistent delays in trial completion. The NHRC’s recommendations to treaty bodies are non‑binding domestically, yet they acquire persuasive value when cited by the Supreme Court — for instance, in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2018) the Court referenced the NHRC’s UPR submissions while directing the State to improve prison conditions. A practical limitation is the NHRC’s resource constraint: sanctioned strength of 12 members, only 8 in position as of 2023, and a secretariat of 150 staff handling both domestic inquiries and international reporting. The 2019 PHRA amendment added a member with expertise in women’s rights and another in child rights, aiming to strengthen treaty‑body engagement. Aspirants should remember that the NHRC’s international role is advisory, its reports are not automatically enforceable, but they form part of the “soft law” landscape that Indian courts increasingly consider.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally impose simultaneous elections without a constitutional amendment and State ratification.
  • Confusing the CAG’s compliance audit of off‑budget borrowings with a performance audit of debt sustainability; the former verifies legality, the latter evaluates outcomes.
  • Believing the UPSC’s advice on disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, though non‑acceptance requires a recorded, reasoned order.
  • Treating the GST compensation cess as part of the divisible pool for vertical devolution; it remains outside the pool and its shortfall is a Centre liability.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s UPR recommendations are automatically enforceable in Indian courts; they become persuasive only when cited in judicial orders.
  • Overlooking that the UPSC is not consulted on minor penalties under the CCS (CCA) Rules, a frequent exam trap.
  • Misreading the 15th Finance Commission’s 41 % vertical share as a permanent reduction; the 16th Commission may revise it.
The advanced sections above deepen understanding of institutional mechanisms, judicial checks, and fiscal‑federal dynamics essential for high‑level polity questions.

The Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority: Constitutional Provisions, Process, and Recent Controversies

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 of the Constitution, read with the Delimitation Commission Act, 2002. Article 82 mandates a Delimitation Commission after every Census to readjust the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha among the States and the division of each State into territorial constituencies. Article 170 provides a parallel mechanism for State Legislative Assemblies. The Commission comprises a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by him), and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. Its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the 2002 Act).

The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at the 1971 Census figures until the first Census after 2026. Consequently, the Delimitation Commission constituted in 2002 carried out only a readjustment of boundaries within the existing seat matrix, using the 2001 Census data. The 2008 delimitation exercise, based on the 2001 Census, was the last completed exercise; the next one is scheduled after the 2026 Census. The freeze has created a growing disparity between population size and representation, especially in States such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, where the average constituency size now exceeds 2.5 million voters.

Recent controversies centre on the constitutional validity of the freeze and the timing of the next delimitation. Several petitions have argued that the 84th Amendment violates the principle of “one‑person‑one‑vote” enshrined in Article 326. The Supreme Court has repeatedly declined to interfere, holding that the amendment is a valid exercise of Parliament’s constituent power and that the freeze serves the federal objective of preventing frequent alterations of the federal balance. In 2020, a Constitution Bench dismissed a challenge, observing that any change before 2026 would require a fresh constitutional amendment.

Operationally, the Election Commission plays a pivotal role in preparing the electoral rolls that form the basis for delimitation.
