The Commission’s “Electoral Roll Management System” integrates data from the Registrar General of India, ensuring that the population figures used by the Delimitation Commission are consistent with the latest published Census. The Commission also conducts “pre‑delimitation” consultations with political parties and civil society, a practice institutionalised after the 2002 exercise to enhance transparency.

For aspirants, the key take‑aways are: (i) delimitation is a constitutional mandate, not a discretionary executive act; (ii) the 84th Amendment’s freeze is constitutionally entrenched until 2026; (iii) the Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and non‑justiciable; and (iv) the Election Commission’s roll‑management infrastructure is the factual backbone of any delimitation exercise.

The Central Vigilance Commission’s Vigilance Administration Framework: Composition, Powers, and Accountability Mechanisms

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, converting the erstwhile advisory body into a statutory authority with superintendence over vigilance administration in all Central Government ministries, departments, and public sector undertakings. The Commission consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a high‑powered committee comprising the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the largest opposition party). Their tenure is four years or until they attain the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and they are not eligible for re‑appointment.

The CVC’s statutory powers include: (a) exercising superintendence over the vigilance administration of the Central Government; (b) reviewing the progress of investigations conducted by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in corruption cases; (c) advising the Central Government on matters relating to integrity in public administration; and (d) exercising the powers of a civil court while conducting inquiries, including summoning witnesses and requiring production of documents. The Commission may also direct the initiation of disciplinary proceedings against public servants and recommend prosecution.

Accountability is ensured through multiple channels. The CVC submits an annual report to the President, which is laid before each House of Parliament. The report details the number of cases received, disposed of, and pending, along with systemic recommendations. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice examines the report and often summons the CVC for oral evidence. Additionally, the CVC’s decisions are subject to judicial review; the Supreme Court in *State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam* (2019) held that the CVC’s advisory opinions are not binding but carry persuasive weight, and any arbitrary exercise of power can be struck down.

In recent years, the Commission has emphasised preventive vigilance through “Integrity Pacts” in major procurement contracts and the “Vigilance Awareness Week” campaign. The 2021 amendment to the CVC Act expanded the Commission’s jurisdiction to include the oversight of the National Anti‑Corruption Bureau (NACB) once it is operationalised, signalling a move towards a unified anti‑corruption architecture. However, the CVC continues to face criticism for inadequate staffing — its sanctioned strength of 250 officers remains partially unfilled — and for the perceived lack of autonomy in the appointment process, given the executive’s dominant role in the selection committee.

Key points for examination: (i) the CVC is a statutory, not constitutional, body; (ii) its composition reflects a political‑executive balance; (iii) its orders are recommendatory but acquire legal force when adopted by the competent authority; (iv) parliamentary oversight and judicial review constitute the primary accountability mechanisms; and (v) preventive vigilance tools such as Integrity Pacts are now part of the CVC’s operational toolkit.

Technique
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the Central Vigilance Commission is correct? (a) It is a constitutional body under Article 315. (b) Its Chairperson is appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister alone. (c) Its annual report is laid before Parliament. (d) Its decisions are binding on the Central Government.” Choose the correct option and justify.
The correct answer is (c). The CVC is established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, not by the Constitution; therefore (a) is false. The appointment committee includes the Prime Minister, Home Minister, and Leader of Opposition, so (b) is false. The CVC’s recommendations are advisory; they become binding only when accepted by the competent authority, making (d) false. Section 12 of the CVC Act mandates that the Commission’s annual report be submitted to the President and laid before each House of Parliament, confirming (c) as the only correct statement.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question contrasts “constitutional” versus “statutory” bodies, first identify the enabling legislation. For the CVC, recall the 2003 Act and the composition of the selection committee. Remember that only the CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission, Election Commission, and NHRC (via constitutional amendment) are constitutional bodies; all others, including the CVC, are statutory. This distinction eliminates a large class of distractors instantly.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers: Scope, Procedure, and Judicial Enforcement

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to inquire, *suo motu* or on a petition, into any violation of human rights or negligence in the prevention of such violation by a public servant (Section 12(a)). The Commission may also intervene in any proceeding involving an allegation of human‑rights violation pending before a court, with the court’s approval (Section 12(b)). The inquiry procedure mirrors that of a civil court: the NHRC can summon witnesses, require production of documents, receive evidence on affidavits, and commission local investigations through its own investigation division or State police.

Upon completion, the NHRC may recommend: (i) payment of compensation to the victim; (ii) initiation of disciplinary or criminal proceedings against the erring public servant; (iii) policy changes to prevent recurrence; and (iv) interim relief pending final adjudication. These recommendations are not legally binding, but the PHRA obligates the concerned government or authority to forward its action‑taken report within one month. Failure to comply can be highlighted in the NHRC’s annual report to Parliament, creating political pressure.

Judicial enforcement of NHRC recommendations has evolved through landmark Supreme Court decisions. In *NHRC v. State of Gujarat* (2018), the Court treated the NHRC’s *suo motu* report on custodial deaths as a “credible material” and directed the State to pay compensation and initiate departmental inquiries. In *People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India* (2020), the Court held that while NHRC recommendations are not enforceable as decrees, they acquire the force of law when the Court incorporates them into its own orders. The Court also observed that the NHRC’s *suo motu* jurisdiction is a vital supplement to the formal judicial system, especially in cases where victims lack access to courts.

Practical limitations persist. The NHRC’s sanctioned strength of 12 members (including the Chairperson) has often been under‑filled; as of 2023 only eight members were in position, and the investigation wing operates with a staff of around 150 officers. This resource constraint leads to significant delays — the average disposal time for a *suo motu* case exceeds 18 months. The 2019 amendment to the PHRA added two specialist members (women’s rights and child rights) to strengthen thematic inquiries, but the overall capacity gap remains a concern for effective *suo motu* action.

For examination purposes, remember: (i) *suo motu* power is statutory, not constitutional; (ii) the NHRC’s recommendations are persuasive, not mandatory, unless adopted by a court; (iii) the Supreme Court has repeatedly used NHRC reports as “credible material” to issue binding directions; and (iv) institutional capacity — member vacancies and investigation staff shortages — is the principal operational bottleneck.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings: Methodology, Reporting, and Parliamentary Scrutiny

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with the Companies Act, 2013. The audit mandate covers three dimensions: financial audit (verification of accounts and compliance with accounting standards), compliance audit (adherence to laws, rules, and government directives), and performance audit (economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of operations). The CAG’s audit of PSUs is distinct from the statutory audit conducted by Chartered Accountants appointed under the Companies Act; the CAG’s audit is a “supplementary” audit that focuses on public‑interest aspects such as utilisation of budgetary support, disinvestment proceeds, and strategic sector performance.

Methodologically, the CAG adopts a risk‑based approach. Audit planning begins with a “strategic audit plan” that identifies high‑risk PSUs based on financial indicators, media reports, and previous audit findings. Field audit teams conduct transaction testing, substantive procedures, and, for performance audits, outcome‑mapping against predefined benchmarks (e.g., project completion timelines, cost‑per‑unit metrics). The CAG’s “Audit Quality Management Framework” (AQMF), introduced in 2018, mandates peer review of audit files and adherence to International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs).

Reporting follows a two‑tier structure. The CAG issues “Audit Reports” (financial and compliance) and “Performance Audit Reports” for each PSU or sector. These reports are laid before Parliament and automatically referred to the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). COPU examines the reports in detail, often summoning the CMD of the PSU and the concerned Ministry’s Secretary. The Committees’ recommendations are forwarded to the Government for action‑taken reports, which are again placed before Parliament.

Recent high‑impact audits include the 2021 performance audit of Maharatna PSUs (ONGC, IOC, NTPC, SAIL, BHEL, GAIL) which flagged systematic project delays averaging 24 months and cost overruns of 15‑30 %. The 2022 audit of the disinvestment process highlighted undervaluation in the strategic sale of Air India and recommended an independent valuation framework. These findings have prompted the Ministry of Finance to issue revised guidelines for project monitoring and disinvestment valuation.

Key examination points: (i) the CAG’s PSU audit is supplementary, not a substitute for statutory audit; (ii) performance audit evaluates outcomes, not merely financial correctness; (iii) COPU and PAC provide the parliamentary oversight loop; (iv) the AQMF aligns Indian audit practice with ISSAIs; and (v) audit findings on strategic PSUs often trigger policy reforms in project management and disinvestment methodology.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s constitutional mandate with the Election Commission’s administrative role; the former is a separate body constituted under Articles 82/170, the latter only supplies electoral data.
  • Assuming the Central Vigilance Commission’s recommendations are binding on the Government; they are advisory unless accepted by the competent authority or enforced by a court.
  • Treating the NHRC’s *suo motu* inquiries as judicial proceedings; they are administrative inquiries whose findings become enforceable only when a court adopts them.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of PSUs replaces the statutory audit under the Companies Act; the CAG conducts a supplementary audit focused on public‑interest dimensions.
  • Overlooking that the 84th Amendment’s freeze on delimitation lasts until the first Census after 2026, not merely until 2026.
  • Misreading the CVC’s appointment committee as comprising only the Prime Minister; it includes the Home Minister and the Leader of Opposition.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s annual report is automatically debated in Parliament; it is laid before Parliament but debate depends on parliamentary scheduling.

Election Commission’s Role in Conduct of Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Legislative Proposals

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies has been examined by the Law Commission of India (170th Report, 1999), the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice (2015), and the NITI Aayog (2017). Constitutionally, Articles 83(2), 85(2), 172(1) and 174(2) fix the maximum term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at five years unless dissolved earlier. Synchronising these terms would require either a constitutional amendment to align the dissolution provisions or a political consensus to curtail or extend existing assemblies. The Election Commission (EC) has consistently maintained that it can administer simultaneous polls logistically — deploying EVMs, VVPATs, and personnel in a single phase — but it cannot alter the constitutional tenure of legislatures.

Legislative Initiatives

The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty‑Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2022, introduced in the Lok Sabha, proposes to insert Article 82A enabling the President to notify a common election date for the Lok Sabha and all State Assemblies. It also seeks to amend Article 172 to allow the Governor to dissolve a State Assembly only on the recommendation of the Council of Ministers, with a proviso that the dissolution shall not pre‑empt the common election schedule. The Bill further provides for a “simultaneous election fund” under the Consolidated Fund of India to meet additional expenditure. As of the latest parliamentary session, the Bill has been referred to the Joint Committee on Simultaneous Elections, which is examining the impact on federalism, the Model Code of Conduct duration, and the feasibility of a single electoral roll.

Operational Challenges

The EC’s 2023 “Report on Simultaneous Elections” identifies three operational bottlenecks: (i) the need for a unified electoral roll that reconciles the current state‑wise rolls maintained under the Representation of the People Act, 1950; (ii) the requirement for a massive increase in polling stations and security personnel — estimated at 1.3 million additional personnel for a single‑phase nationwide poll; and (iii) the legal vacuum concerning the dissolution of a State Assembly mid‑term when a common election date has been notified. The Commission has recommended a pilot in two States with coterminous terms (e.g., Odisha and Andhra Pradesh) before a nationwide rollout.

Judicial Perspective

In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the President’s power under Article 356 cannot be used to synchronise State elections with the Lok Sabha. The Court emphasised that the federal structure mandates independent electoral cycles unless a constitutional amendment expressly provides otherwise. Any amendment for simultaneous elections would therefore be subject to the basic‑structure test, particularly the principle of federalism.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Social Sector Schemes: Methodology, Findings, and Policy Impact

The CAG’s performance audits of flagship social‑sector programmes — Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), National Health Mission (NHM), Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY), and the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) — are conducted under Section 13 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The audit framework follows the “Three‑E” criteria: Economy (minimising cost), Efficiency (maximising output per input), and Effectiveness (achieving intended outcomes). Since 2018, the CAG has adopted a “Beneficiary‑Centric Audit” approach, combining quantitative analysis of Management Information System (MIS) data with field verification through stratified random sampling of gram panchayats, health sub‑centres, and anganwadi centres.

Key Findings from Recent Audits

The 2021 Performance Audit of MGNREGA (Report No. 12 of 2021) revealed that 27 % of sampled works did not create durable assets, and wage payments were delayed beyond the statutory 15‑day period in 34 % of cases. The 2022 Audit of NHM (Report No. 8 of 2022) highlighted a 22 % shortfall in the availability of essential drugs at primary health centres and a 15 % vacancy rate for specialist doctors in district hospitals. The 2023 Audit of PMAY‑Gramin (Report No. 5 of 2023) reported that 18 % of sanctioned houses remained incomplete after the stipulated 12‑month construction window, primarily due to fund flow delays at the State level.

Policy Impact and Follow‑up

Audit recommendations are tabled before the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Estimates. The Ministry of Rural Development, in response to the MGNREGA audit, issued revised guidelines in 2022 mandating geo‑tagging of all assets and real‑time wage payment tracking through the National Electronic Fund Management System (NeFMS). The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare introduced a “Drug Supply Chain Monitoring Dashboard” in 2023 to address the NHM findings. The CAG’s “Audit Impact Register” (maintained since 2020) records 112 accepted recommendations across social‑sector audits, of which 87 have been implemented, demonstrating a measurable feedback loop between audit scrutiny and programme redesign.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of MGNREGA is a statutory audit under the Companies Act, 2013.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify.
False. The CAG’s audit of MGNREGA is a performance audit conducted under Section 13 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. It is not a statutory audit under the Companies Act, which applies only to companies registered under that Act. The CAG’s role here is to assess economy, efficiency, and effectiveness of a government scheme, not to certify corporate financial statements.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question cites a CAG report number, note the year and the scheme audited. The examiners often test whether you can match the report to the correct programme (e.g., Report No. 12 of 2021 → MGNREGA). Keep a mental table of the last three years’ major performance audits and their headline findings.

National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with International Human Rights Mechanisms: Reporting, Follow‑up, and Domestic Implementation

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (as amended in 2006) mandates the NHRC to “study treaties and other international instruments on human rights and make recommendations for their effective implementation” (Section 12(f)). The Commission submits periodic “shadow reports” to the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) under the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) cycle — India’s third UPR was in 2017, the fourth in 2022. These reports complement the Government’s national report and highlight gaps in the implementation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the Convention against Torture (CAT), and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

Mechanism of Follow‑up

After each UPR, the NHRC prepares a “Matrix of Recommendations” mapping each accepted recommendation to the concerned Ministry or State Government. The Commission then monitors compliance through its “Special Rapporteurs” and “Core Groups” (e.g., Core Group on Custodial Justice, Core Group on Rights of Persons with Disabilities). In 2021, the NHRC’s follow‑up on the 2017 UPR recommendation to ratify the CAT led to the introduction of the Prevention of Torture Bill, 2021, which lapsed with the dissolution of the 17th Lok Sabha. The Commission continues to press for its re‑introduction.

Domestic Implementation Challenges

Despite its advisory mandate, the NHRC’s recommendations have been cited by the Supreme Court as “credible material” in landmark judgments such as People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020) on custodial deaths and Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on free speech. However, the Commission faces structural constraints: (i) vacancies — as of March 2024, two of the five Member positions were unfilled for over 18 months; (ii) limited investigative staff — the sanctioned strength of 120 investigators remains at 68; and (iii) the absence of a statutory timeline for Government action on NHRC recommendations, which renders follow‑up dependent on political will.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Criteria, Weightage Evolution, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Vertical devolution refers to the share of the divisible pool of Union taxes (corporation tax, income tax, customs, excise, service tax, and GST compensation cess) transferred to States. The 14th Finance Commission (FC‑XIV, 2015‑20) recommended a record 42 % vertical share, up from 32 % under FC‑XIII. The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV, 2021‑26) retained the 41 % share (after adjusting for the GST compensation cess) but altered the horizontal distribution criteria. The vertical share is not a fixed constitutional number; each FC determines it based on the Union’s revenue buoyancy, States’ expenditure needs, and the principle of “fiscal equivalence”.

Evolution of Criteria and Weightages

FC‑XIV used three criteria for vertical devolution: (i) Population (1971 Census) – 17.5 %; (ii) Demographic Change (population growth 1971‑2011) – 10 %; (iii) Area – 15 %; (iv) Forest Cover – 7.5 %; (v) Income Distance – 50 %. FC‑XV dropped the 1971 population base, adopting the 2011 Census for the “Population” criterion (15 %) and introducing “Demographic Performance” (12.5 %) to reward States that have controlled fertility. It also added “Tax Effort” (2.5 %) and “Forest and Ecology” (10 %). The weightage for “Income Distance” was reduced to 45 %. These shifts reflect a move from pure need‑based allocation to a mixed incentive‑need framework.

Impact on Fiscal Federalism

The higher vertical share under FC‑XIV and FC‑XV expanded States’ untied resources, enabling greater autonomy in scheme design (e.g., State‑specific health insurance, crop insurance). However, the conditionalities attached to Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) — which remain outside the divisible pool — have limited the practical fiscal space. The 15th FC’s recommendation to create a “State‑Specific Grant” for nutrition and health (₹1.2 lakh crore over five years) attempts to align vertical devolution with outcome‑based targets. The ongoing debate centres on whether the vertical share should be constitutionally entrenched (as in the Canadian equalisation formula) to protect States from ad‑hoc reductions during Union fiscal stress.

Union Public Service Commission’s Examination Reforms: Computer‑Based Testing, Syllabus Revision, and Transparency Measures

The UPSC, under Article 320, conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE), Indian Forest Service Examination, and various defence and engineering services examinations. Since 2016, the Commission has transitioned the Preliminary and Main examinations of the CSE to Computer‑Based Testing (CBT) mode for the optional papers, while the General Studies papers remain pen‑and‑paper. The CBT platform, developed in collaboration with the National Informatics Centre (NIC), incorporates biometric verification, randomised question sequencing, and real‑time audit trails.

Syllabus Revision and Content Updates

In 2020, the UPSC revised the General Studies Paper II (CSAT) syllabus to remove “Data Interpretation” and “Logical Reasoning” as separate sections, integrating them into “Analytical Ability”. The 2022 notification introduced “Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude” as a standalone paper in the Main examination (Paper V), replacing the earlier “General Studies Paper IV”. The optional subject list was rationalised: 26 subjects were retained, while 12 low‑uptake subjects (e.g., Persian, Pali) were discontinued. The Commission publishes a detailed “Syllabus Mapping Document” each year, linking each topic to standard reference texts, to reduce information asymmetry.

Transparency and Grievance Redressal

Since 2019, the UPSC has released the answer keys of the Preliminary examination within 10 days, allowing candidates to challenge answers through an online portal. The “Candidate’s Response Sheet” for the Main examination is made available after the declaration of final results. An independent “Examination Review Committee”, chaired by a former Supreme Court judge, audits the evaluation process annually. In 2023, the Committee recommended the adoption of “On‑Screen Marking” for essay‑type papers to minimise inter‑examiner variability; a pilot was conducted for the 2024 Main examination.

  • Confusing the Election Commission’s logistical capacity for simultaneous elections with the constitutional authority to alter legislative terms.
  • Assuming the CAG’s social‑sector audits are statutory audits under the Companies Act rather than performance audits under the CAG Act.
  • Treating NHRC’s shadow reports to the UNHRC as legally binding on the Government of India.
  • Believing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution percentage is constitutionally fixed and cannot be altered by successive Commissions.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s CBT mode applies to all papers of the Civil Services Examination, including the essay paper.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s “Demographic Performance” criterion rewards fertility decline, not population size.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory reading and case‑law awareness.

The Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Limits, Legislative Requirements, and Judicial Interpretation

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years under Article 83(2) and that of State Assemblies at five years under Article 172(1). Article 324 vests the Election Commission (EC) with the superintendence, direction and control of elections, but it does not empower the EC to alter the duration of legislative houses. Consequently, any move toward simultaneous polls requires a constitutional amendment to synchronize the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, and corresponding amendments to the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) to align election schedules.

The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and 255th Report (2015) recommended a phased approach: first, a constitutional amendment to allow the President to dissolve State Assemblies prematurely so that their terms could be aligned with the Lok Sabha; second, a one‑time extension or curtailment of existing Assembly terms through a constitutional provision akin to Article 172(2). The 2023 High‑Level Committee chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind examined the feasibility of a “one nation, one election” model and suggested a two‑stage legislative package — a Constitution (Amendment) Bill to insert a new Article 82A providing for simultaneous elections, and an amendment to the RPA to prescribe a common electoral roll and a single polling day.

Judicially, the Supreme Court has not ruled on the constitutionality of simultaneous elections per se, but in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) it held that the President’s power to dissolve a State Assembly under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, implying that any premature dissolution for electoral synchronisation must meet the “objective necessity” test. In K. P. Singh v. Union of India (2022), the Court declined to entertain a PIL seeking a direction to the EC to hold simultaneous polls, stating that the matter falls within the legislative domain. The EC’s own 2022 consultation paper highlighted logistical challenges — deployment of 1.1 million polling personnel, procurement of 1.5 million EVMs and VVPATs, and the need for a unified electoral roll — and estimated a cost of ₹4,500 crore for the first simultaneous cycle.

Thus, while the EC can administer simultaneous elections once the legal framework exists, it lacks the constitutional authority to initiate the synchronisation of legislative terms. The pathway remains a political‑legislative exercise requiring a special majority in Parliament and ratification by at least half the States under Article 368.

The Finance Commission’s Grants‑in‑Aid under Article 275: Design, Conditionalities, and Impact on State Fiscal Autonomy

Article 275(1) empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to States “in need of assistance” on the recommendation of the Finance Commission (FC). Unlike the vertical devolution of the divisible pool, which is formula‑driven and largely untied, grants‑in‑aid are purpose‑specific and often carry performance conditionalities. The 14th FC (2015‑20) introduced a “post‑devolution revenue deficit grant” of ₹1.94 lakh crore for 11 States, calibrated on the gap between assessed revenue expenditure and projected revenue receipts after devolution. The 15th FC (2021‑26) expanded this architecture by recommending ₹1.2 lakh crore for health‑sector grants, ₹0.5 lakh crore for nutrition, and ₹0.3 lakh crore for rural roads, each linked to measurable output indicators such as immunisation coverage, stunting reduction, and road length constructed.

Conditionalities are enforced through a “performance‑based release” mechanism: the Ministry of Finance disburses instalments only after the State submits utilisation certificates and outcome reports verified by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). The 15th FC also introduced a “State‑Specific Grant” for the aspirational districts programme, requiring States to achieve predefined targets in education, health and infrastructure within a three‑year window. Failure to meet targets results in a proportional reduction of the subsequent tranche, a design intended to align fiscal transfers with the principle of “fiscal equivalence” articulated in the FC’s terms of reference.

The impact on State fiscal autonomy is two‑fold. On the one hand, grants‑in‑aid augment the resource envelope of fiscally weaker States, enabling them to launch flagship schemes (e.g., Tamil Nadu’s “Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam” health outreach). On the other hand, the conditionalities constrain expenditure discretion, effectively converting a portion of the transfer into a centrally‑sponsored scheme without the latter’s parliamentary oversight. Critics argue that this erodes the federal bargain by allowing the Union to influence State priorities through the FC’s recommendation, a concern echoed in the 2022 NITI Aayog paper “Fiscal Federalism in the Era of Conditional Grants”. The 15th FC attempted to mitigate this by capping conditional grants at 15 % of the total devolution to any State, but the debate persists on whether Article 275 should be amended to mandate a minimum untied share.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 is correct? (a) They are part of the divisible pool and distributed by a fixed formula. (b) They are purpose‑specific, performance‑linked, and released in tranches after CAG verification. (c) They require a constitutional amendment for each FC cycle. (d) They are exclusively for capital expenditure.”
Correct answer: (b). Grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 are not part of the divisible pool; they are recommended by the FC for specific purposes (health, nutrition, rural roads) and released in instalments contingent on utilisation certificates and CAG‑verified outcome reports. They do not require a constitutional amendment each cycle, nor are they limited to capital expenditure.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes vertical devolution and grants‑in‑aid, first identify the constitutional article cited. Article 270/271 deals with the divisible pool; Article 275 deals with grants‑in‑aid. Look for keywords “performance‑linked”, “conditional”, “utilisation certificate” — these signal grants‑in‑aid. Eliminate options that describe a fixed formula or capital‑only restriction.

The National Commission for Women’s Monitoring of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013: Powers, Procedure, and Supreme Court Directions

The National Commission for Women (NCW), constituted under the NCW Act, 1990, derives its mandate to monitor the implementation of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (SH Act) from Section 10(1)(a) of the NCW Act, which empowers it to “review the constitutional and legal safeguards for women”. The SH Act obliges every employer with ten or more employees to constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) and to file an annual report with the District Officer. The NCW’s monitoring role is operationalised through (i) suo‑motu inquiries into non‑constitution of ICCs, (ii) calling for compliance reports from State Governments and Central Ministries, and (iii) issuing advisory guidelines — most notably the 2017 “Guidelines for Effective Implementation of the SH Act” which prescribe timelines for ICC formation, training modules, and a standardized complaint‑tracking format.

Procedurally, the NCW can summon records, examine witnesses, and recommend disciplinary action against defaulting employers. Its recommendations are forwarded to the concerned Ministry or State Government for action; however, the NCW lacks direct enforcement powers. The Supreme Court, in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), laid down the foundational guidelines that later crystallised into the SH Act. In Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013), the Court directed the NCW to monitor compliance across all Central Government departments and to submit a quarterly status report. A 2020 order in Kumar v. Union of India expanded this mandate to include private sector establishments employing more than 50 workers, requiring the NCW to coordinate with the Ministry of Labour and Employment for data aggregation.

Empirically, the NCW’s 2022 annual report indicated that 68 % of Central Ministries had functional ICCs, while only 42 % of State Government departments complied. The Commission’s “Digital Complaint Management System” launched in 2021 enables real‑time tracking of complaints filed under the SH Act, and its 2023 “State‑wise Compliance Index” ranks States on ICC constitution, training completion, and disposal rates. Despite these tools, the NCW’s inability to impose penalties limits deterrence; the 2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice recommended amending the NCW Act to confer quasi‑judicial powers akin to those of the National Human Rights Commission.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Goods and Services Tax Revenue Sharing: Methodology, Disputes, and Cooperative Federalism Implications

The 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and established the GST Council as the apex decision‑making body for tax rates, exemptions, and revenue distribution. Article 279A mandates that the Union and States share the Integrated GST (IGST) and the compensation cess in a manner prescribed by the Council. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits the entire GST revenue chain — from collection by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) and State GST departments, through the GST Network (GSTN) portal, to the final settlement of accounts between the Centre and States.

Methodologically, the CAG employs a combination of compliance audit (verifying that tax collections conform to the CGST Act, SGST Acts, and IGST Act) and performance audit (assessing the efficiency of the GSTN platform, the timeliness of refund processing, and the accuracy of the revenue‑sharing formula). The 2021 CAG Report No. 12 of 2021 highlighted a ₹1.1 lakh crore shortfall in the compensation cess for 2020‑21, attributing it to lower‑than‑projected GST collections and the economic impact of the COVID‑19 pandemic. The report also flagged discrepancies in the “input tax credit” reconciliation module of GSTN, which led to an estimated ₹23,000 crore of unverified credits across 12 States.

Disputes arising from these findings have been adjudicated both within the GST Council and before the Supreme Court. In State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022), the Court upheld the Council’s decision to extend the compensation cess beyond the original five‑year period, citing the CAG’s audit evidence of persistent revenue gaps. Conversely, in State of Maharashtra v. Union of India (2023), the Court directed the Centre to release pending compensation arrears within three months, referencing the CAG’s certification of the shortfall amount. These judgments illustrate how CAG audit outputs serve as evidentiary anchors in inter‑governmental fiscal disputes.

The cooperative federalism dimension is profound: the CAG’s independent verification of GST revenue flows reassures States that the Union’s share is not inflated, while the Council’s reliance on CAG‑certified figures for compensation decisions institutionalises a trust‑based fiscal partnership. However, the 2024 CAG performance audit of the “GST Compensation Cess Utilization” noted that 18 % of cess proceeds were diverted to non‑compensation purposes, prompting the Council to consider a statutory lock‑in mechanism. The evolving audit‑Council‑Court triangle thus shapes the operational reality of GST federalism.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally decide the dates for simultaneous elections without a constitutional amendment.
  • Confusing Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Article 275) with the divisible pool devolution (Article 270/271) and treating them as formula‑driven.
  • Believing the National Commission for Women possesses direct penal powers over employers who fail to constitute Internal Complaints Committees.
  • Thinking the CAG’s GST audit is limited to central collections and does not cover State GST department accounts.
  • Overlooking that the GST Council’s compensation decisions are legally binding only after CAG certification of the revenue shortfall.
  • Treating the Supreme Court’s 2022 order in State of Kerala v. Union of India as a permanent mandate for compensation cess extension without Council approval.
  • Remember to cross‑check statutory provisions with the latest amendment before answering.

Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Amendment Requirements, Law Commission Recommendations, and the Election Commission’s Operational Role

The idea of holding Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections together has been examined repeatedly since the 1980s. The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years from the date of its first sitting (Art. 83) and that of each State Assembly at five years from its first sitting (Art. 172). Because the dissolution of either House can occur independently — through a vote of no‑confidence, the President’s rule under Art. 356, or the Governor’s discretion — the electoral cycles inevitably diverge. Synchronising them therefore requires either a constitutional amendment that aligns the terms or a statutory framework that empowers the Election Commission to stagger polls within a common window.

The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) first recommended a constitutional amendment to provide for a fixed five‑year term for both Parliament and State Legislatures, coupled with a provision for mid‑term elections only in exceptional circumstances. The 255th Report (2015) refined the proposal, suggesting a “one‑nation‑one‑election” model that would require amendments to Articles 83, 172, 356 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The NITI Aayog’s 2017 discussion paper and the 2018 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice echoed the need for a constitutional amendment, noting that a mere executive order cannot override the fixed‑term guarantee.

In practice, the Election Commission’s role is limited to the conduct of elections once the schedule is notified. Under Section 14 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the Commission fixes the poll dates after consulting the Central Government. It has no statutory power to compel State Governments to dissolve Assemblies prematurely or to extend their terms. The 2019 Supreme Court judgment in K. K. Ramesh v. Union of India reiterated that the Commission’s authority is “administrative and not legislative”. Consequently, any move toward simultaneous elections must first secure a constitutional amendment ratified by at least half the States (Art. 368), followed by enabling legislation that defines the synchronisation mechanism, the handling of mid‑term vacancies, and the transition provisions for existing Assemblies.

The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) highlighted the fiscal implications: simultaneous polls could reduce the recurring expenditure on election machinery by an estimated 30 % but would require a one‑time outlay for additional Electronic Voting Machines, VVPATs, and security deployment. The Commission recommended that the Centre bear the incremental cost during the transition phase. Until the constitutional and legislative framework is in place, the Election Commission continues to operate under the existing staggered calendar, and any claim that it can unilaterally decide dates for simultaneous elections is constitutionally unfounded.

Finance Commission Grants‑in‑Aid under Article 275: Design, Conditionalities, and Impact on Special Category States

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to States “in need of assistance”, a provision that the Finance Commission operationalises through its recommendations. Unlike the divisible pool devolution (Art. 270/271), which is formula‑driven and largely unconditional, grants‑in‑aid are discretionary, targeted, and often tied to specific schemes or reform milestones. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) shifted the bulk of transfers to the divisible pool (42 % of net proceeds) and limited grants‑in‑aid to a few categories: revenue deficit grants, grants for local bodies, disaster relief, and special assistance to States affected by the implementation of the GST.

The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) retained this architecture but expanded the grant envelope to ₹1.5 lakh crore over the award period. It introduced three new conditional grant windows: (i) performance‑based grants for health and education outcomes measured through the National Health Mission and Samagra Shiksha indicators; (ii) grants for the implementation of the “Aspirational Districts” programme, linked to quarterly dashboard scores; and (iii) a “State‑specific” grant for the eight North‑Eastern and three Himalayan States (the Special Category States) to compensate for their limited revenue base and high cost of service delivery. The Commission mandated that these grants be released only after the State submits a utilisation certificate and a third‑party audit report, a condition designed to curb diversion.

Special Category States historically received a higher share of grants‑in‑aid because the divisible pool formula (which weights population, area, forest cover, and income distance) under‑represents their fiscal disability. The 15th FC’s “income distance” criterion uses the 2011 Census per‑capita income, which widened the gap for these States. To offset this, the Commission recommended a “post‑devolution revenue deficit grant” of ₹1.2 lakh crore, of which 60 % is earmarked for the eleven Special Category States. The grants are conditional on the States maintaining a fiscal deficit within the FRBM‑prescribed limit (3 % of GSDP) and on the timely submission of accounts to the CAG.

Empirically, the 2022‑23 CAG audit of grant utilisation found that 78 % of the performance‑based health grants were spent on approved activities, while 22 % were diverted to salary arrears. The audit also flagged that three Special Category States failed to meet the FRBM threshold, leading to a temporary withholding of the second tranche of the revenue deficit grant. These findings illustrate how conditionalities translate into fiscal discipline but also create implementation bottlenecks when State capacity is weak. The interplay between Article 275 grants, the divisible pool, and the FRBM framework therefore constitutes a critical lever for cooperative federalism.

Examiner's Twist
A question states: “The Finance Commission’s grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 are formula‑driven and form part of the divisible pool.” Identify the error and explain the correct distinction.
The statement conflates two distinct transfer mechanisms. Grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 are discretionary, need‑based, and often conditional; they are not part of the divisible pool, which is governed by Articles 270 and 271 and distributed by a fixed formula (population, area, income distance, etc.). The divisible pool is largely unconditional, whereas Article 275 grants require utilisation certificates, performance benchmarks, or FRBM compliance. The correct answer: grants‑in‑aid are separate, targeted transfers, not formula‑driven divisible‑pool shares.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes “divisible pool” and “grants‑in‑aid”, first identify the constitutional article cited. Article 270/271 → divisible pool (formula). Article 275 → grants‑in‑aid (discretionary, conditional). Mark the distinction in a one‑line note; it saves time and prevents the common trap of treating them as interchangeable.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Debt Management and the FRBM Framework

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has progressively expanded its audit mandate from transaction‑level verification to systemic assessments of fiscal sustainability. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, as amended in 2018, obliges the Central Government to lay before Parliament a Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement, a Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, and a Macroeconomic Framework Statement. The CAG audits the authenticity of the data underpinning these statements, the compliance with the prescribed fiscal deficit and debt‑to‑GDP targets, and the transparency of off‑budget borrowings.

In its 2020 Report No. 12 (Public Debt Management), the CAG examined the Union’s gross debt stock of ₹105 lakh crore (as of March 2020) and identified three systemic issues: (i) the increasing share of market borrowings at variable rates, exposing the budget to interest‑rate risk; (ii) the use of National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) loans to finance the fiscal deficit without adequate disclosure in the Budget documents; and (iii) the absence of a consolidated debt‑management strategy aligning borrowing plans with cash‑flow projections. The report recommended the establishment of an independent Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) — a proposal that remains under inter‑ministerial consideration.

The 2022 CAG performance audit of “Off‑Budget Borrowings” revealed that several Central Ministries had raised resources through public sector undertakings and special purpose vehicles, effectively bypassing the FRBM ceiling. The aggregate off‑budget liability was estimated at ₹2.3 lakh crore, equivalent to 1.1 % of GDP. The audit prompted the Finance Ministry to issue a 2023 directive requiring all such borrowings to be reported in the Annual Financial Statement and subjected to CAG scrutiny. The Supreme Court, in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2023), upheld the CAG’s jurisdiction to audit these instruments, affirming that “the constitutional mandate of the CAG extends to any financial transaction that impacts the Consolidated Fund, irrespective of its legal form”.

At the State level, the CAG’s 2021‑22 reports on State Finances highlighted that 14 States breached the 3 % fiscal deficit threshold, primarily due to rising committed expenditure on pensions and interest payments. The CAG recommended a “debt‑sustainability analysis” to be embedded in the State FRBM Rules, a suggestion incorporated by the 15th Finance Commission in its conditional grant design. The evolving CAG‑FRBM interface thus functions as a fiscal guardrail: the CAG supplies independent evidence, the FRBM Act sets the rules, and the Finance Commission translates compliance into inter‑governmental transfers.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers, Recommendations, and Judicial Review

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as a statutory body with the mandate to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 12 of the PHRA confers on the NHRC the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavit. The Commission may also visit any jail or detention centre without prior notice (Section 13).

Since its inception, the NHRC has exercised suo motu cognisance in high‑profile cases: the 2002 Gujarat communal violence (NHRC report 2003), the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, and the 2020‑21 migrant‑worker crisis during the COVID‑19 lockdown. In each instance, the Commission issued interim directions — such as compensation to victims, disciplinary action against erring officials, and systemic reforms — and forwarded its reports to the concerned Governments and Parliament. However, the PHRA does not make the NHRC’s recommendations binding; they are advisory in nature.

Judicial review of NHRC decisions operates through two channels. First, aggrieved parties may file writ petitions under Articles 32 or 226 challenging the Commission’s refusal to inquire or the adequacy of its recommendations. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003) held that while the NHRC’s findings are not judicially enforceable per se, the State’s failure to act on them can constitute a violation of the constitutional duty to protect human rights, thereby attracting judicial intervention. Second, the Courts have examined the procedural fairness of NHRC inquiries. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court set aside an NHRC order that had denied a hearing to the affected parties, reiterating that the principles of natural justice apply to statutory inquiries.

The 2022 amendment to the PHRA (via the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, notified in 2022) expanded the NHRC’s composition to include a member with expertise in disability rights and mandated the creation of a “Human Rights Court” at the district level for speedy adjudication. The amendment also introduced a 90‑day timeline for the Commission to complete suo motu inquiries, subject to extension for recorded reasons. Despite these enhancements, the NHRC’s effectiveness remains constrained by resource limitations — its 2023 annual report noted a backlog of 4,800 pending cases — and by the non‑binding character of its recommendations, which continues to be a focal point of parliamentary debate and civil‑society advocacy.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can set simultaneous‑election dates without a constitutional amendment.
  • Treating Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Art. 275) as part of the divisible‑pool formula.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of public debt is limited to the Union Budget and excludes off‑budget borrowings.
  • Thinking NHRC recommendations are legally binding on the Government.
  • Overlooking that Special Category States receive conditional grants‑in‑aid linked to FRBM compliance.
  • Confusing the NHRC’s suo motu powers with those of a court of law.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common errors.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and Its Coordination with the Delimitation Commission

The Constitution assigns the Election Commission (EC) the responsibility for preparing and revising electoral rolls (Art. 324) while the Delimitation Commission, constituted under the Delimitation Act, 2002, redraws parliamentary and assembly constituencies based on the latest census (Art. 82 and Art. 170). The EC does not itself delimit boundaries, but it supplies the demographic data, polling‑station locations, and the finalised electoral rolls that the Delimitation Commission uses as the factual base for its orders. The 2002 Act mandates that the Delimitation Commission consist of a retired Supreme Court judge (chairperson), the Chief Election Commissioner, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state, ensuring direct EC participation.

In practice, the EC’s role begins with the publication of the “Draft Delimitation Proposals” after the Delimitation Commission’s initial hearings. The EC then conducts field verification of polling‑station boundaries, resolves disputes over voter‑list entries, and certifies the final rolls that will be used in the first election after delimitation. The Supreme Court in R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (2003) upheld the constitutional validity of the 2002 freeze on delimitation until the first census after 2026, clarifying that the EC’s electoral‑roll preparation continues uninterrupted during the freeze. The 2026 deadline has reignited debate on whether the EC should be granted a more formal consultative status in the next Delimitation Commission, especially given the EC’s expertise in managing elector‑level data and its experience with the 2019‑20 electoral‑roll revision that covered 91 crore voters.

Coordination mechanisms include a joint working group that meets quarterly during the delimitation cycle, a shared GIS platform for mapping polling stations against proposed constituency lines, and a protocol for resolving “overlap disputes” where a polling station falls across two proposed constituencies. The EC also issues a “Delimitation Compliance Certificate” after each general election, confirming that the constituency boundaries used matched the Delimitation Commission’s final order. This certificate has been cited in election‑petition jurisprudence (e.g., K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India 2017) as evidence of procedural regularity.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies, Universities, and Public‑Sector Undertakings

The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends beyond the Union and State governments to any “authority or body substantially financed from the Consolidated Fund”. Section 14 of the Act empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of autonomous bodies, universities, and public‑sector undertakings (PSUs) that receive grants or loans exceeding 50 % of their recurring expenditure from the government. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2023) affirmed that this jurisdiction covers off‑budget borrowings by state‑owned enterprises, reinforcing the principle that the source of funds, not the legal form, determines auditability.

For universities, the CAG conducts “performance audits” of centrally funded institutions (e.g., IITs, central universities) focusing on utilisation of plan grants, research‑fund management, and compliance with the University Grants Commission’s financial regulations. The 2021‑22 CAG report on higher education highlighted that 12 central universities had diverted ₹1,842 crore of plan grants to revenue expenditure, prompting the Ministry of Education to issue a 2023 directive mandating quarterly fund‑utilisation certificates.

In the PSU sector, the CAG audits both “commercial” and “non‑commercial” undertakings. Commercial PSUs (e.g., ONGC, BHEL) are audited under the Companies Act, 2013, with the CAG appointing statutory auditors and reviewing their reports. Non‑commercial PSUs (e.g., National Highways Authority of India) are audited directly by the CAG’s field offices. The 2020‑21 audit of the National Thermal Power Corporation revealed a ₹3,210 crore cost overrun in the Lara super‑thermal project, leading to a Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs review and a revised tariff petition before the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission.

The CAG also audits “autonomous bodies” such as the Indian Council of Medical Research, the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, and the various national academies. These audits examine whether grant‑in‑aid conditions are met, whether procurement follows the General Financial Rules, and whether internal‑control frameworks are adequate. The 2022 amendment to the CAG Act introduced a “risk‑based audit planning” module, requiring the CAG to prioritise entities with high financial exposure or prior adverse findings, thereby sharpening the watchdog’s focus on systemic risk.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The Election Commission can unilaterally alter constituency boundaries after the Delimitation Commission’s final order.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. Under the Delimitation Act, 2002, the Delimitation Commission’s order is final and cannot be altered by the Election Commission. The EC’s role is limited to preparing electoral rolls, verifying polling‑station locations, and issuing a Delimitation Compliance Certificate after elections. Any change to boundaries requires a fresh Delimitation Commission constituted under Article 82/170.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes EC and Delimitation Commission functions, first identify the constitutional article (Art. 324 for EC, Art. 82/170 for delimitation). Then recall the statutory composition of the Delimitation Commission (retired SC judge + CEC + State EC). The EC never draws boundaries; it only operationalises them. Mark “EC prepares rolls, Delimitation Commission draws lines” as a mental shortcut.

National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with the Universal Periodic Review and International Treaty Bodies

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 designates the NHRC as India’s national human‑rights institution (NHRI) with “A‑status” accreditation from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI). This status obliges the NHRC to submit independent reports for the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) conducted by the UN Human Rights Council every four‑and‑a‑half years. India’s UPR cycles (2008, 2012, 2017, 2022) have each featured NHRC submissions highlighting custodial deaths, rights of minorities, and the impact of anti‑terror legislation. The NHRC’s 2022 UPR report, for instance, documented 1,731 custodial deaths in the preceding five years and recommended ratification of the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT).

Beyond the UPR, the NHRC monitors implementation of core UN treaties to which India is a party: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The Commission prepares “shadow reports” for the respective treaty bodies, often collaborating with civil‑society coalitions. In 2021, the NHRC’s shadow report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child flagged gaps in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 implementation, leading to the Committee’s concluding observations urging India to raise the minimum age of criminal responsibility.

Domestically, the NHRC’s suo‑motu inquiries (Section 12, PHRA) frequently reference international standards. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003) held that while NHRC recommendations are not binding, the State’s failure to act may violate constitutional duties under Articles 14 and 21, and international obligations can be invoked to interpret the scope of those duties. The 2022 amendment to the PHRA introduced a 90‑day timeline for completing suo‑motu inquiries and mandated a “Human Rights Court” at each district, aiming to bridge the gap between NHRC findings and judicial enforcement.

Resource constraints remain acute: the NHRC’s 2023 annual report recorded a backlog of 4,800 pending cases and a staff‑to‑case ratio of 1:1,200. The Commission has repeatedly requested the Ministry of Home Affairs for enhanced budgetary allocation and the creation of a dedicated “International Engagement Division” to systematise treaty‑body reporting. Parliamentary committees have endorsed this demand, noting that India’s credibility in multilateral forums hinges on the NHRC’s capacity to deliver timely, evidence‑based analyses.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Framework and the Interplay with the Goods and Services Tax Council

Article 280 empowers the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a vertical share of 41 % for States, a reduction from the 14th FC’s 42 % to accommodate the Union’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities after the GST rollout. The vertical formula incorporates five criteria with assigned weights: population (15 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), and demographic performance (12.5 %). The demographic performance criterion rewards States that have achieved replacement‑level fertility, reflecting a policy shift toward incentivising population stabilisation.

The GST Council, constituted under Article 279A, determines the GST rate structure, compensation cess, and the revenue‑neutral rate. The 15th FC explicitly recognised the Council’s role by recommending a “GST compensation grant” of ₹1.1 lakh crore for the five‑year transition period (2022‑27), financed through a cess on luxury and sin goods. The FC also advised that any shortfall in the compensation fund be met through market borrowings guaranteed by the Union, a recommendation accepted in the 2023 Union Budget.

Interaction between the FC and the GST Council occurs through the “Revenue Neutral Rate” (RNR) calculations. The FC’s vertical devolution assumes a certain GST buoyancy; if the Council lowers rates, the Union’s share of the divisible pool shrinks, altering the effective vertical transfer. The 15th FC therefore recommended a “GST revenue‑risk sharing mechanism” whereby the Union and States jointly bear shortfall risk in a 50:50 ratio for the first two years, shifting to 60:40 thereafter. This mechanism was operationalised via a 2022 memorandum of understanding between the Ministry of Finance and the GST Council Secretariat.

Data from the 2022‑23 accounts show that the actual vertical transfer to States was 40.6 % of the divisible pool, marginally below the 41 % target, primarily due to a 3.2 % decline in GST collections relative to the FC’s projections. The 16th FC (to be constituted for 2026‑31) will need to recalibrate the vertical formula in light of the GST Council’s evolving rate structure, the phasing out of the compensation cess, and the Union’s increasing capital‑expenditure commitments under the National Infrastructure Pipeline.

Union Public Service Commission’s Mandate for All India Services Recruitment and the 2023 Amendment to the UPSC Act

Article 312 provides for the creation of All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service, and Indian Forest Service — and vests the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) with the responsibility for conducting the competitive examinations for their recruitment. The UPSC Act, 1951, originally limited direct recruitment to the Civil Services Examination (CSE) and the Indian Forest Service Examination. The 2023 amendment to the UPSC Act introduced a “Lateral Entry” window at the level of Joint Secretary and Director in the Central Government, allowing domain experts from the private sector, academia, and public‑sector undertakings to be appointed on contract for a tenure of three to five years, extendable by two years.

The amendment was notified on 15 March 2023 and the first lateral‑entry advertisement appeared in June 2023, inviting applications for 30 posts across ministries such as Finance, Commerce, and Environment. The selection process comprises a written test designed by the UPSC, a domain‑specific assessment, and an interview board chaired by a UPSC member. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2022) had earlier upheld the government’s power to create “specialist” posts outside the CSE, provided the UPSC’s advisory role is retained. The 2023 amendment codifies this advisory mandate, requiring the UPSC to approve the syllabus, evaluation criteria, and final merit list for each lateral‑entry cycle.

Impact on recruitment dynamics is already visible: the 2023‑24 CSE saw a 4.2 % decline in applicants for the AIS, attributed partly to the perception that lateral entry offers an alternative pathway to senior policy positions. Conversely, the lateral‑entry route attracted 12,450 applications for 30 posts, indicating high demand from professionals with 15‑20 years of experience. The UPSC’s 2024 annual report notes that the lateral‑entry scheme has expanded the talent pool without compromising the merit‑based ethos of the CSE, as the Commission retains full control over the assessment standards.

Critics argue that the scheme may erode the “career‑service” character of the AIS and create dual‑track promotion hierarchies. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) has responded by issuing a 2024 guideline that lateral entrants will be placed on a separate seniority list and will not be eligible for cadre‑level promotions reserved for CSE officers. The UPSC, in its advisory capacity, has recommended a periodic review (every three years) of the scheme’s impact on service morale, diversity, and policy outcomes, with the first review due in 2026.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can modify Delimitation Commission orders after they are published.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit jurisdiction excludes autonomous bodies that receive less than 50 % government funding.
  • Treating NHRC recommendations as legally enforceable judgments rather than advisory opinions.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the GST Council’s revenue‑neutral rate decisions.
  • Thinking the 2023 UPSC amendment allows lateral entrants to join the regular AIS seniority list.
  • Overlooking that the Delimitation Commission’s composition includes the Chief Election Commissioner as an ex‑officio member.
  • Neglecting the 90‑day statutory timeline for NHRC suo‑motu inquiries introduced by the 2022 PHRA amendment.

Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Law Commission Recommendations, and Operational Challenges

The idea of holding Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections together has been debated since the 1980s. The Constitution does not explicitly prohibit simultaneous polls; Article 83(2) and Article 172(1) fix the maximum term of the House of the People and State Assemblies at five years, but they do not require that the terms be synchronised. The primary constitutional hurdle is the dissolution power: the President can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 85), while the Governor can dissolve a State Assembly on the advice of the State Council of Ministers (Article 174). If a State government loses majority mid‑term, the Assembly may be dissolved, breaking the cycle. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 255th Report (2015) both recommended a phased approach: first, align the terms of all Assemblies with the Lok Sabha by extending or curtailing tenures through constitutional amendments, and second, insert a new Article 82A providing for simultaneous elections with a fixed five‑year cycle. The 2015 report also suggested a “constructive vote of no‑confidence” mechanism to prevent premature dissolutions. Operationally, the Election Commission would need to deploy roughly 1.1 million polling personnel and 1.5 million electronic voting machines in a single window, a logistical scale unprecedented in Indian electoral history. The Commission’s 2018 feasibility note highlighted the need for a unified electoral roll, simultaneous model code of conduct enforcement, and a single security deployment plan. Critics argue that simultaneous polls undermine federalism by reducing the accountability of State governments to their electorates and by centralising campaign narratives. The Supreme Court, in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), affirmed that the President’s power to impose President’s Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, implying that any constitutional amendment forcing simultaneous terms must respect the basic structure doctrine. As of 2024, a high‑level committee chaired by the Prime Minister has been constituted to examine the constitutional, legal, and logistical dimensions, but no amendment bill has been introduced.

CAG’s Audit of Off‑Budget Borrowings and Fiscal Transparency

Off‑budget borrowings refer to liabilities incurred by public sector entities or special purpose vehicles that are not reflected in the Union or State budgets but are serviced through government guarantees or budgetary support. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has repeatedly flagged such borrowings as a threat to fiscal transparency. In its Report No. 15 of 2019 (Union Government), the CAG identified ₹1.7 lakh crore of off‑budget liabilities routed through the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF), the Food Corporation of India, and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana‑Urban special purpose vehicles. The 15th Finance Commission, in its 2020‑21 report, recommended that all such borrowings be brought on‑budget and that the CAG be mandated to certify the completeness of the debt statement. The CAG’s methodology involves tracing guarantees issued under Article 292 (Union) and Article 293 (States), examining the terms of loan agreements, and verifying whether the servicing payments are routed through the Consolidated Fund. A landmark audit of the UDAY scheme (2016‑17) revealed that State power distribution companies had borrowed ₹2.3 lakh crore off‑budget, which the CAG treated as contingent liabilities of the States. The Supreme Court, in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2020), upheld the CAG’s authority to audit any body substantially financed by the government, reinforcing the audit of off‑budget entities. The 2022 amendment to the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act introduced a “debt‑to‑GDP” target that explicitly includes off‑budget borrowings, compelling the Union to disclose them in the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement. The CAG’s 2023 performance audit of the National Infrastructure Pipeline noted that 18 % of the projected ₹111 lakh crore investment was planned through off‑budget instruments, raising concerns about the credibility of fiscal consolidation targets. The audit recommended a unified debt management office and real‑time reporting of guaranteed obligations to the Public Debt Management Cell.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “Which constitutional provision empowers the CAG to audit off‑budget borrowings of a State‑owned corporation that receives a government guarantee?” The options include Article 149, Article 150, Article 151, and Article 293. Choose the correct article and justify.
The correct answer is Article 149. Article 149 provides that the CAG shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as may be prescribed by law. The CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, enacted under Article 149, extends audit to any body or authority substantially financed by the government, including corporations receiving guarantees. Article 293 deals with State borrowing powers, not audit jurisdiction. Article 150 prescribes the form of accounts, and Article 151 deals with submission of audit reports. Therefore, the statutory mandate derived from Article 149 is the source of CAG’s audit authority over off‑budget borrowings.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links CAG’s audit scope to a specific article, always trace the chain: Constitution → CAG Act → relevant audit report. Remember that Article 149 is the enabling provision; the 1971 Act operationalises it. Off‑budget borrowings are audited because they constitute “substantial financing” via guarantees, a concept the Supreme Court affirmed in the 2020 Rajasthan judgment.

UPSC’s Advisory Role in Framing Recruitment Rules for Central Civil Services: Delegated Legislation and Judicial Review

Article 320(1) of the Constitution requires the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts under the Union. The UPSC’s advisory function extends to the framing and amendment of Recruitment Rules (RRs) for each Central Civil Service, which are notified as statutory rules under the proviso to Article 309. The process begins with the cadre‑controlling authority drafting the RRs, which are then forwarded to the UPSC for its advice. The Commission examines the eligibility criteria, age limits, educational qualifications, and the method of recruitment (direct, promotion, deputation). Once the UPSC tenders its advice, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoPT) issues the notification in the Gazette of India. Although the UPSC’s advice is not binding, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2022) held that a departure from the Commission’s advice without cogent reasons attracts judicial review under Article 14. The Court emphasised that the UPSC’s expertise in maintaining merit‑based standards constitutes a “constitutional check” on executive discretion. In 2023, the DoPT issued a circular mandating that any amendment to RRs affecting the method of recruitment must be referred to the UPSC at least 60 days before notification. The UPSC’s 2024 Annual Report disclosed that it rendered advice on 1,142 recruitment rule proposals, of which 87 were returned for reconsideration due to inconsistencies with the principle of equal opportunity. Judicial scrutiny has also focused on the “creamy layer” exclusion in OBC recruitment rules; in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018), the Court directed that the UPSC’s advice on creamy‑layer criteria be incorporated before final notification. The interplay between delegated legislation (the RRs) and the UPSC’s constitutional mandate thus creates a layered accountability mechanism: the executive drafts, the Commission advises, the legislature (through parliamentary scrutiny of subordinate legislation) reviews, and the judiciary ensures conformity with constitutional principles.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Cesses and Surcharges in the Divisible Pool: Legal Interpretation and Impact on Vertical Devolution

Article 270 of the Constitution provides that all taxes and duties referred to in the Union List, except those listed in Articles 268, 269, and 269A, shall be levied and collected by the Union and distributed between the Union and the States. Cesses and surcharges, however, are explicitly excluded from the divisible pool under Article 270(2) and Article 271. The Finance Commission, constituted under Article 280, recommends the vertical share of the divisible pool to States, but it has no constitutional authority to include cesses and surcharges in that pool. Nevertheless, successive Finance Commissions have addressed the growing reliance on cesses and surcharges as a fiscal tool. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) noted that cesses and surcharges constituted 13.5 % of gross tax revenue in 2013‑14, reducing the effective vertical transfer to States. It recommended that the Union consider subsuming major cesses into the GST framework or, alternatively, compensate States through revenue‑deficit grants. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) went further, recommending a “cess‑surcharge rationalisation” roadmap: the Union should phase out cesses that have outlived their purpose and merge them into the general tax base, thereby expanding the divisible pool. The Commission also introduced a “grants‑in‑aid” component of ₹1.2 lakh crore for 2021‑26 to offset the revenue loss from excluded cesses. The Union’s 2022‑23 Budget retained 42 cesses and surcharges, of which 19 were earmarked for specific purposes such as the Health and Education Cess (4 % on income tax) and the Road and Infrastructure Cess (₹1 per litre on petrol/diesel). The CAG’s 2023 audit of the Union’s tax administration highlighted that the share of cesses and surcharges in gross tax revenue rose to 18.2 % in 2022‑23, the highest since 1991. This trend compresses the States’ share of the divisible pool from the recommended 41 % to an effective 36.5 % after accounting for excluded levies. The Supreme Court, in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2021), declined to direct the inclusion of cesses in the divisible pool, reiterating that the Constitution vests that power solely in Parliament. The 16th Finance Commission, to be constituted for 2026‑31, will likely face pressure to devise a formula that either expands the divisible pool or enhances compensatory grants, balancing fiscal federalism with the Union’s expenditure commitments.

National Human Rights Commission’s Jurisdiction over Armed Forces under AFSPA: Supreme Court Pronouncements and Institutional Limits

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) with the mandate to inquire into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 19 of the PHRA, however, bars the NHRC from inquiring into any matter relating to the armed forces, except with the prior approval of the Central Government. The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) grants sweeping powers to the armed forces in “disturbed areas”, including the power to shoot to kill, arrest without warrant, and search premises. The interplay between the NHRC’s statutory limitation and the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence has shaped the practical scope of accountability. In Naga People’s Movement of Human Rights v. Union of India (1998), the Court upheld the constitutionality of AFSPA but directed that the armed forces must follow the “Do’s and Don’ts” issued by the Ministry of Defence and that any allegation of excess be investigated by an independent agency. The Court also held that the NHRC could seek reports from the Central Government on allegations against the armed forces, even though it could not directly inquire. In Extra Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v.
