Union of India (2016), the Supreme Court mandated that all encounters in AFSPA areas be subjected to a magisterial inquiry and that the NHRC be informed of the outcome. The 2019 amendment to the PHRA (Section 19) retained the prior‑approval requirement but added a 90‑day timeline for the Central Government to respond to NHRC’s request for permission to inquire. The NHRC’s 2022 annual report stated that it had sought permission in 27 cases involving alleged violations by security forces in Jammu & Kashmir and the Northeast; the Central Government granted permission in 12 cases, denied in 8, and did not respond within 90 days in 7. The Commission recommended that the statutory bar be replaced by a “consultative mechanism” whereby the NHRC can independently initiate inquiries subject to a national security review by a high‑level committee. The Supreme Court, in a 2023 order, reiterated that the NHRC’s inability to directly investigate armed forces does not absolve the State of its obligation under Article 21 to protect life and liberty, and directed the Union to place before Parliament a report on the implementation of the 2016 guidelines. The institutional limit thus remains: the NHRC can monitor, recommend, and report, but direct investigative jurisdiction over the armed forces continues to be contingent on executive consent.

  • Assuming that simultaneous elections can be implemented without a constitutional amendment to Articles 83 and 172.
  • Believing that off‑budget borrowings are outside the CAG’s audit mandate because they are not part of the Consolidated Fund.
  • Treating the UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules as merely recommendatory with no judicial consequence for non‑compliance.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the Union’s discretion to levy cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool.
  • Thinking the NHRC can independently investigate armed forces personnel under AFSPA without Central Government approval.
  • Overlooking that the 90‑day statutory timeline for NHRC suo‑motu inquiries applies only after the 2022 PHRA amendment and not to armed‑forces cases.
  • Neglecting that the 15th Finance Commission’s cess‑surcharge rationalisation roadmap is a recommendation, not a binding directive on the Union.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Cesses, Surcharges and the Divisible Pool

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The “divisible pool” is defined in Article 270 as all taxes and duties levied by the Union except those expressly excluded — principally the surcharge on income‑tax (Article 271) and the cesses levied for specific purposes such as the Health and Education Cess (4 % on income‑tax) and the Road and Infrastructure Cess (₹1 per litre on petrol and diesel). The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) recommended a vertical share of 41 % of the divisible pool for States, the same as the 14th Commission, but flagged that the growing share of cesses and surcharges — 18.2 % of gross tax revenue in 2022‑23 according to the CAG’s 2023 audit — effectively reduces the States’ real share to about 36.5 %.

The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2021) held that the Constitution vests the power to decide the composition of the divisible pool solely in Parliament; the Court declined to direct inclusion of cesses. Consequently, the Union can increase cesses without altering the vertical share, a lever that has been used repeatedly since 2015‑16. The 15th Commission recommended a “cess‑surcharge rationalisation roadmap” and suggested that the 16th Commission (to be constituted for 2026‑31) consider expanding the divisible pool or enhancing compensatory grants. However, the roadmap is advisory; the Union is not constitutionally bound to implement it. The interplay between Article 270 (divisible pool), Article 271 (surcharge) and the Finance Commission’s recommendations creates a dynamic where fiscal federalism is negotiated through political‑budgetary choices rather than a rigid constitutional formula.

Key data points for answer‑writing: the 15th Commission’s vertical share (41 %), the CAG‑reported cess‑surcharge share (18.2 % in 2022‑23), the effective State share after exclusions (≈36.5 %), and the Supreme Court’s 2021 judgment confirming Parliamentary primacy. Aspirants should be able to distinguish between the Constitution’s mandatory vertical devolution (Article 280) and the Union’s discretionary power to levy cesses outside the pool (Article 271).

Election Commission’s Delimitation Mandate: Constitutional Framework, Delimitation Commission and Judicial Review

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. Article 82 requires the President to constitute a Delimitation Commission after every Census; the Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Article 329). The Election Commission (EC) supplies the electoral data — electorate size, polling station locations, and geographic information — but the Delimitation Commission, headed by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners, exercises independent authority to fix boundaries.

The last delimitation exercise was based on the 2001 Census and completed in 2008; the next is constitutionally barred until after the 2026 Census (the 84th Amendment froze the total number of seats until 2026). The 2002 Act prescribes a methodology: each State’s territorial constituencies are divided so that the population per seat is as equal as practicable, with a permissible deviation of ±10 % (extended to ±15 % for certain hill and tribal areas). The EC’s role is consultative; it may file objections during the draft stage, but the final order is issued by the Delimitation Commission.

Judicial review is extremely limited. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2002) the Supreme Court upheld the finality clause of Article 329, ruling that courts cannot entertain challenges to the Delimitation Commission’s orders on grounds of malafide or procedural irregularity unless there is a patent violation of constitutional provisions. However, the Court has entertained petitions where the Commission acted without jurisdiction — for instance, when it attempted to alter the total number of seats contrary to the freeze. The EC’s own power to delimit local body wards under the 73rd/74th Amendments is separate and subject to State legislation.

For mains, remember: (i) the constitutional freeze (84th Amendment) and its expiry; (ii) the ±10 %/±15 % deviation rule; (iii) the EC’s data‑provision role versus the Delimitation Commission’s decision‑making role; (iv) the near‑absolute bar on judicial review under Article 329, with the narrow exception of jurisdictional error.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The Election Commission can independently alter parliamentary constituency boundaries after the 2021 Census.” Identify the error and cite the correct constitutional provision.
The statement is false. Under Article 82 read with the Delimitation Act, 2002, the power to fix parliamentary constituency boundaries rests with the Delimitation Commission, not the Election Commission. The EC only supplies electoral data. Moreover, the 84th Amendment freezes any fresh delimitation until after the 2026 Census. The relevant provisions are Articles 82, 170, 329 and the Delimitation Act, 2002.
Answer‑writing tip
When a question mixes the EC’s administrative functions with the Delimitation Commission’s statutory mandate, first separate the two bodies. Quote Article 82 and the Delimitation Act, then note the 84th Amendment freeze. This two‑step structure (constitutional provision → statutory freeze) fetches full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Disciplinary Jurisdiction over Civil Servants: Constitutional Basis, Procedure and Supreme Court Precedents

Article 320(3) obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union, including the imposition of penalties such as dismissal, removal or reduction in rank. Article 311 provides the procedural safeguards — reasonable opportunity of being heard, inquiry by an independent authority, and the right to representation. The UPSC’s advice is mandatory but not binding; the President (or the Governor for State services) may accept or reject it, but must record reasons for deviation.

The disciplinary procedure typically follows the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. After a preliminary inquiry, a charge‑sheet is issued, an inquiring authority conducts a departmental inquiry, and the findings are forwarded to the UPSC for advice. The Commission examines the record, hears the charged officer if requested, and tenders its recommendation on the quantum of penalty. In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2013) the Supreme Court held that the UPSC’s advice is a constitutional prerequisite; non‑consultation renders the disciplinary order void. However, in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2009) the Court clarified that the government may disagree with the UPSC’s recommendation provided it records cogent reasons, preserving the executive’s ultimate authority.

Recent reforms have introduced a “single‑window” online portal for disciplinary cases to reduce pendency, and the 2022 amendment to the CCS (CCA) Rules mandated that the UPSC be consulted within 45 days of receipt of the inquiry report. The Commission’s annual report (2022‑23) shows it tendered advice in 1,842 disciplinary cases, with the government accepting 92 % of recommendations. The jurisprudence underscores a balance: the UPSC safeguards merit‑based, non‑partisan discipline, while the executive retains the final decision‑making power subject to judicial review for arbitrariness.

National Human Rights Commission’s Oversight of Custodial Deaths: D.K. Basu Guidelines, Suo‑Motu Inquiries and Institutional Limits

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo‑motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants (Section 12). Custodial deaths have been a persistent focus. The Supreme Court in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention, including immediate medical examination, intimation to a relative, and a magistrate’s inquiry within 24 hours. The NHRC monitors compliance through its “Custodial Deaths” database; its 2022 annual report recorded 1,642 custodial deaths nationwide, of which 1,102 were in police custody and 540 in judicial custody.

The NHRC can issue directions to the concerned State government, recommend prosecution, and seek compensation for victims’ families. However, its recommendations are not binding; implementation depends on the executive. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court directed all States to institutionalise the D.K. Basu guidelines and to report compliance to the NHRC quarterly. The NHRC’s suo‑motu powers were strengthened by the 2019 PHRA amendment, which introduced a 90‑day timeline for the Commission to complete an inquiry after taking cognisance, but this timeline does not apply to cases involving the armed forces (Section 19 bar).

Institutional limits remain: the NHRC lacks prosecutorial power, cannot enforce its orders, and its jurisdiction over security forces is contingent on Central Government approval. The 2023 Supreme Court order in NHRC v. State of Gujarat reiterated that the State’s obligation under Article 21 to protect life and liberty is non‑derogable, urging Parliament to consider granting the NHRC independent investigative authority over all public servants.

  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical share (41 %) with the effective share after cess‑surcharge exclusions.
  • Attributing delimitation authority to the Election Commission instead of the Delimitation Commission.
  • Assuming the UPSC’s disciplinary advice is binding on the government.
  • Believing the NHRC can independently prosecute custodial‑death cases without State cooperation.
  • Overlooking the 84th Amendment freeze on fresh delimitation until after the 2026 Census.
  • Neglecting the 90‑day inquiry timeline under the 2019 PHRA amendment applies only to non‑armed‑forces cases.

Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Provisions, Legislative Hurdles, and Judicial Interpretation

The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years under Article 83(2) and of State Legislative Assemblies at five years under Article 172(1). Simultaneous elections would require synchronising these terms, which can be achieved only through constitutional amendment or a series of legislative measures that either extend or curtail existing tenures. Article 356 empowers the President to impose President’s Rule, effectively dissolving a State Assembly, but the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that such power cannot be exercised arbitrarily to align election cycles. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2015 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice both recommended a constitutional amendment to enable a common electoral roll and a single election schedule, citing cost savings and governance continuity. However, the 2018 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951, introduced the “one nation, one election” pilot for a few States, but the Election Commission clarified that without a constitutional amendment the Commission cannot unilaterally postpone or advance elections beyond the five‑year limit. The Commission’s 2022 consultation paper highlighted logistical challenges — deployment of over 10 lakh polling personnel, security forces, and EVM‑VVPAT units — and warned that any forced synchronisation could violate the basic structure doctrine by undermining federalism. Judicial interpretation remains cautious: in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) the Court refused to direct the Centre to hold simultaneous elections, stating that the power to amend the Constitution rests with Parliament. Consequently, any move toward simultaneous polls must pass the twin tests of constitutional validity and federal consensus.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Institutions and Universities: Scope, Methodology, and Recent Findings

Section 14 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of any body or authority substantially financed by the Union or State governments. This provision brings centrally funded universities, Indian Institutes of Technology, Indian Institutes of Management, and research councils within the CAG’s purview. The audit methodology follows the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) — financial audit, compliance audit, and performance audit. In the 2021‑22 audit of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) system, the CAG flagged irregularities in procurement of laboratory equipment worth ₹312 crore, non‑adherence to General Financial Rules, and delays in utilisation of grants under the Higher Education Financing Agency. The 2022‑23 report on the University Grants Commission highlighted that 27 % of sanctioned faculty positions remained vacant across central universities, affecting the student‑teacher ratio mandated by the UGC Regulations, 2018. The CAG also conducts “theme‑based” audits; the 2020 audit of the National Rural Health Mission’s funding to autonomous health institutes revealed diversion of ₹1,045 crore to non‑scheduled activities. Findings are tabled in Parliament and referred to the Public Accounts Committee, which can summon the heads of these institutions. The CAG’s recommendations have led to the Ministry of Education issuing revised guidelines for grant utilisation in 2023, mandating quarterly expenditure returns and independent internal audit cells. However, the CAG lacks enforcement power; compliance depends on executive action and parliamentary oversight.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “Which constitutional provision enables the CAG to audit autonomous universities?” The options include Article 149, Article 150, Section 14 of the CAG Act, and Article 151. Identify the correct answer and explain why the others are incorrect.
The correct answer is Section 14 of the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Article 149 defines the CAG’s duties in relation to the accounts of the Union and States, not autonomous bodies. Article 150 prescribes the form of accounts, and Article 151 deals with audit reports being laid before Parliament. Only Section 14 explicitly extends audit jurisdiction to bodies “substantially financed” by government, covering autonomous universities.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes constitutional articles with statutory sections, first locate the statutory provision that operationalises the constitutional mandate. The CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is a classic example: the Constitution gives the CAG broad authority (Art. 149), but the specific extension to universities is in Section 14 of the 1971 Act. Memorise the pairing “Art. 149 → Section 14” for quick recall.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Human Rights in Armed Conflict Areas: Legal Constraints and Operational Practices

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the NHRC with the mandate to inquire into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 12 grants suo‑motu inquiry powers, but Section 19 imposes a bar on investigating allegations against the armed forces unless the Central Government grants prior approval. This statutory limitation has shaped the NHRC’s operational footprint in conflict‑affected regions such as Jammu & Kashmir, the North‑East, and areas affected by Left‑Wing Extremism. The Commission relies on “spot inquiries” conducted by its own investigation division, supplemented by reports from State Human Rights Commissions and civil society organisations. In its 2021 annual report, the NHRC documented 1,274 cases of alleged excesses by security forces in the North‑East, of which only 312 received Central Government clearance for full inquiry. The Commission can recommend compensation, disciplinary action, and policy changes, but its recommendations are non‑binding. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2023) reiterated that the State’s obligation under Article 21 to protect life and liberty is non‑derogable and urged Parliament to consider amending Section 19 to grant the NHRC independent investigative authority over all public servants. Meanwhile, the NHRC has developed a “conflict‑zone monitoring framework” that includes real‑time data collection from district magistrates, mandatory reporting of custodial deaths within 24 hours, and periodic review meetings with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The 2019 amendment to the PHRA introduced a 90‑day timeline for completing inquiries, but this timeline does not apply to cases involving the armed forces, preserving the Section 19 bottleneck. Consequently, the NHRC’s effectiveness in conflict zones remains contingent on executive cooperation and legislative reform.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Mandate, Cadre Allocation, and Recent Reforms

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All India Services (AIS) common to the Union and the States. The Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service, and Indian Forest Service are constituted under the All India Services Act, 1951. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) — a three‑stage process comprising Preliminary, Main, and Personality Test — to select candidates for these services. The Commission’s constitutional mandate under Article 320(1) requires it to be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts. The Cadre Allocation Policy, revised in 2022, introduced a “zone‑based” preference system where candidates rank cadres within five zones; allocation is then done by a computerised algorithm that balances merit, preference, and vacancy. The 2023 UPSC annual report shows that 1,056 candidates were recommended for AIS, with a success rate of 0.18 % of applicants. The Commission also advises on promotion, deputation, and disciplinary matters concerning AIS officers under Article 320(3). In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2013) the Supreme Court held that the UPSC’s advice on disciplinary proceedings is a constitutional prerequisite, though not binding. Recent reforms include the introduction of a common foundation course at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration for all AIS probationers, and the 2024 amendment to the CSE notification allowing candidates to choose an optional subject from a revised list of 48 disciplines. The UPSC’s online “Single Window System” for cadre allocation and service allocation has reduced processing time from 45 days to 12 days. These measures aim to enhance transparency, reduce litigation, and align the recruitment pipeline with the evolving governance requirements of the Union and the States.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can postpone elections beyond the five‑year constitutional limit without an amendment.
  • Confusing the CAG’s audit jurisdiction over autonomous bodies with its audit of government departments; the former rests on Section 14 of the CAG Act, not Article 149 alone.
  • Believing the NHRC can independently investigate armed‑forces excesses in conflict zones without Central Government approval.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice on disciplinary matters is binding on the government; it is mandatory but not binding.
  • Overlooking that the Cadre Allocation Policy for All India Services is a statutory policy, not a constitutional provision.
  • Neglecting the 90‑day inquiry timeline under the 2019 PHRA amendment does not apply to armed‑forces cases.
  • Assuming simultaneous elections can be implemented through ordinary legislation; a constitutional amendment is required to alter the fixed terms of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the nuanced understanding needed to tackle high‑difficulty polity questions in the mains examination.

The Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Constraints and Legislative Pathways

The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years from the date of its first sitting (Article 83) and of each State Legislative Assembly at five years from its first sitting (Article 172). Any proposal to hold simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Assemblies therefore requires either a constitutional amendment altering these articles or a legislative mechanism that synchronises the existing terms without violating the fixed‑term guarantee. The 2018 Law Commission report (Report No. 255) examined three models: (i) a one‑time amendment to extend or curtail Assembly terms to align with the Lok Sabha cycle; (ii) a “phased” approach where elections are held in two or three clusters over a five‑year window; and (iii) a permanent constitutional provision for simultaneous polls. The first model would need a special majority under Article 368 and ratification by at least half the States because it affects the federal distribution of legislative powers. The second model can be pursued through ordinary legislation amending the Representation of the People Act, 1951, but it still requires the President’s assent and may be challenged as a colourable exercise of power if it effectively shortens or lengthens Assembly terms beyond the constitutional limit. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the President’s power under Article 356 to impose President’s Rule cannot be used to dissolve Assemblies prematurely for political convenience, a principle that extends to any executive‑driven synchronisation. The Election Commission, under Article 324, has the superintendence, direction and control of elections but no independent authority to alter constitutional term limits. In 2023 the Commission submitted a “feasibility note” to the Ministry of Law and Justice outlining logistical requirements — additional EVMs, VVPATs, polling personnel, and security forces — and highlighted that a constitutional amendment remains the only legally watertight route. Until such amendment is enacted, any attempt to enforce simultaneous elections through executive order would be ultra vires the Constitution.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies under Section 14 of the CAG Act: Scope, Limitations, and Judicial Interpretation

Section 14 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of any body or authority “substantially financed” by the Union or a State government. The phrase “substantially financed” has been the focal point of litigation. In Comptroller and Auditor General of India v. State of Gujarat (2001) the Supreme Court held that a body receiving more than 50 % of its annual budget from government grants qualifies as substantially financed, but the Court also emphasised that the test is qualitative — the degree of control exercised by the government over the body’s functioning matters as much as the quantum of funds. Subsequent judgments (Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, 2019) clarified that autonomous universities, research institutes, and statutory regulators (e.g., the University Grants Commission, the Medical Council of India before its replacement) fall within the CAG’s audit jurisdiction when they receive majority government funding. However, bodies that generate a significant portion of their revenue from fees, consultancy, or commercial activities — such as the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) after the 2016 fee‑autonomy reforms — have contested CAG audits, arguing that “substantial financing” no longer applies. The CAG’s 2022 audit report on “Autonomous Bodies under the Ministry of Education” listed 112 entities, of which 37 were audited under Section 14; the remaining 75 were excluded because their government share fell below the 50 % threshold. The CAG’s methodology combines financial audit (verification of receipts and expenditure) with performance audit (assessment of outcomes against objectives). The 2020 amendment to the CAG Act introduced a “risk‑based” selection framework, allowing the CAG to prioritize high‑value or high‑risk entities. Judicial review remains available: any audit finding can be challenged before the High Court under Article 226, and the Supreme Court has entertained Special Leave Petitions on questions of jurisdiction. The key limitation is that the CAG cannot audit purely private entities or bodies that receive only incidental grants, a line the courts have consistently upheld.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG can audit any autonomous body that receives any government grant.” Is this statement correct? Explain with reference to the statutory provision and case law.
The statement is incorrect. Section 14 of the CAG Act limits audit to bodies “substantially financed” by government. The Supreme Court in CAG v. State of Gujarat (2001) interpreted “substantially financed” as requiring a majority (generally >50 %) of the body’s budget to come from government grants, coupled with a qualitative assessment of governmental control. Mere receipt of a small grant does not attract CAG audit. Therefore, the CAG’s jurisdiction is not triggered by any grant but only by substantial financing.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “autonomous body” and “CAG audit”, first identify the funding pattern. Cite Section 14, the 50 % benchmark, and the qualitative control test from the Gujarat judgment. Distinguish between financial audit (accounts) and performance audit (outcomes). Remember that the CAG’s report is advisory; the executive decides on follow‑up.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Custodial Deaths: Statutory Mandate, Procedural Safeguards, and Supreme Court Directions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) mandates the NHRC to inquire into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 19 of the PHRA requires the Central Government’s prior approval before the Commission can investigate allegations against members of the armed forces, a provision that has created a practical bottleneck in conflict‑zone custodial deaths. The NHRC’s 2021 annual report recorded 1,274 alleged excesses by security forces in the North‑East, of which only 312 received clearance for full inquiry. To mitigate delays, the 2019 amendment to the PHRA introduced a 90‑day timeline for completing inquiries, but explicitly excluded cases involving the armed forces from this deadline. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2023) reiterated that the State’s obligation under Article 21 to protect life and liberty is non‑derogable and urged Parliament to amend Section 19 to grant the NHRC independent investigative authority over all public servants. In response, the NHRC developed a “conflict‑zone monitoring framework” comprising real‑time data collection from District Magistrates, mandatory reporting of custodial deaths within 24 hours, and quarterly review meetings with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Commission also issues “spot inquiry” guidelines empowering its own investigation division to visit detention centres, record statements, and preserve forensic evidence. Despite these measures, the NHRC’s recommendations remain non‑binding; compliance depends on executive willingness. The 2022 “National Human Rights Action Plan” proposed a statutory amendment to make NHRC recommendations enforceable through a dedicated compliance cell, but the Bill has not yet been introduced in Parliament. Consequently, the effectiveness of custodial‑death monitoring remains contingent on political will and legislative reform.

The Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Disciplinary Proceedings: Constitutional Requirement versus Executive Discretion

Article 320(3) of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union in a civil capacity. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2013) held that this consultation is a constitutional prerequisite — the government cannot finalise a disciplinary order without seeking the UPSC’s advice — but the advice itself is not binding. The Court distinguished between “mandatory consultation” and “binding opinion”, emphasizing that the executive retains the final decision‑making authority. In practice, the UPSC examines the inquiry report, the chargesheet, the defence submissions, and the inquiry officer’s findings before tendering advice. The 2022 UPSC annual report shows that the Commission rendered advice in 1,842 disciplinary cases, of which the government accepted the recommendation in 1,617 instances (87.8 %). Where the government deviates, it must record reasons, a requirement reinforced by the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. The UPSC also advises on penalties ranging from censure to dismissal, and its advice is sought even when the disciplinary authority is a Minister. A notable exception arises under Article 311(2)(c), where the President may dispense with consultation in the interest of national security; this power has been invoked sparingly, most recently in 2019 for a case involving a senior intelligence officer. The Commission’s “Single Window System” for disciplinary advice, launched in 2021, reduced average processing time from 68 days to 22 days. Nevertheless, critics argue that the non‑binding nature of the advice dilutes the Commission’s role as an independent safeguard against arbitrary executive action.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Criteria: Evolution of Weightage, Data Sources, and Fiscal Federalism Implications

The vertical devolution formula determines the share of the divisible pool of Union taxes that is transferred to the States. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended a 42 % share, a sharp increase from the 32 % recommended by the 13th Commission, citing the need to enhance States’ fiscal autonomy after the abolition of the Planning Commission. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) retained the 41 % share (slightly reduced to accommodate the newly created Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh) but restructured the weightage among criteria: population (15 % based on 2011 Census), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), tax effort (2.5 %), and demographic performance (12.5 %). The 14th Commission had used 1971 Census population (17.5 %) and 2011 Census (10 %); the shift to 2011 Census alone in the 15th Commission sparked controversy among southern States, which argued that it penalised successful population control. Data sources include the Census, the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) consumption expenditure surveys, the Forest Survey of India for forest cover, and the Reserve Bank of India’s State‑level tax collection data. The 15th Commission also introduced a “performance‑based incentive” of 1 % of the divisible pool for States achieving targets in GST compliance, ease of doing business, and sustainable development goals. The horizontal distribution (inter‑State) uses the same criteria but with different weightages. The vertical share directly influences the fiscal space of States for capital expenditure, social sector spending, and debt servicing. Empirical analysis by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (2023) shows that the 42 % vertical share under the 14th Commission increased States’ aggregate revenue receipts by ₹3.2 lakh crore over five years, but the composition shifted towards revenue expenditure rather than capital formation. The ongoing debate centres on whether the vertical share should be linked to a fiscal responsibility framework, ensuring that enhanced transfers translate into productive investment.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can postpone elections beyond the five‑year constitutional limit without a constitutional amendment.
  • Confusing the CAG’s audit jurisdiction over autonomous bodies (Section 14 of the CAG Act) with its audit of government departments under Article 149 alone.
  • Believing the NHRC can independently investigate armed‑forces excesses in conflict zones without Central Government approval under Section 19 of the PHRA.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice on disciplinary matters is binding on the government; it is mandatory but not binding.
  • Overlooking that the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share is a recommendation, not a constitutional mandate, and requires Presidential acceptance.
  • Neglecting that the 90‑day inquiry timeline under the 2019 PHRA amendment does not apply to armed‑forces cases.
  • Assuming simultaneous elections can be implemented through ordinary legislation; a constitutional amendment is required to alter the fixed terms of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.

Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Basis, Composition, and Impact on Electoral Representation

The Delimitation Commission derives its authority from Articles 82, 170, 330 and 332 of the Constitution. Article 82 mandates readjustment of territorial constituencies after each Census, while Article 170 requires the same for State Legislative Assemblies. Articles 330 and 332 provide for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies respectively, linking the quantum of reserved seats to the proportion of SC/ST population in each State. The Delimitation Act, 2002 operationalises these provisions and empowers the President to constitute a Commission for each delimitation exercise.

The Commission is chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge. Its other members are the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC) and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. For the 2002 exercise, Justice Kuldip Singh served as Chairperson. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the Delimitation Act). The last delimitation was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census and its orders came into force for the 2009 general elections. A constitutional amendment (the 84th Amendment, 2001) froze further delimitation until the first Census after 2026, thereby postponing the next exercise to the 2031 Census.

The impact of delimitation on electoral representation is twofold. First, it equalises the population size of constituencies, ensuring the principle of “one person, one vote, one value”. The 2002 exercise reduced the average Lok Sabha constituency size from roughly 1.5 million to about 1.3 million electors. Second, it recalibrates the number of reserved seats. For instance, Uttar Pradesh saw its SC reserved Lok Sabha seats increase from 17 to 20, while Kerala’s ST reserved seats remained at zero because the ST population fell below the threshold. The freeze has created a growing disparity: States with faster population growth (e.g., Bihar, Uttar Pradesh) are under‑represented relative to States that have stabilised (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Kerala). This disparity fuels the debate on whether the freeze should be lifted or whether a new formula linking representation to population should be adopted.

Judicial scrutiny of delimitation orders is limited to procedural compliance. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2008), the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s satisfaction regarding the correctness of Census data is not justiciable. However, the Court can intervene if the Commission exceeds its statutory mandate, as illustrated in State of Bihar v. Union of India (2015) where the Court set aside an order that altered constituency boundaries after the notification of elections. The Commission’s work also intersects with the Election Commission’s roll‑out of electoral rolls; any change in constituency boundaries triggers a revision of the electoral roll under Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.

Finance Commission’s GST Compensation Mechanism and Its Fiscal Federalism Implications

The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 established a five‑year compensation regime (July 2017‑June 2022) to protect States from revenue loss arising from the transition to GST. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) had recommended a guaranteed 14 % annual growth in States’ GST revenue, with the shortfall to be met from a compensation cess levied on sin goods and luxury items. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) examined the post‑compensation landscape and recommended that the Centre continue to provide a “revenue‑neutral” grant for an additional two years (2022‑24) to smooth the fiscal adjustment, a recommendation accepted by the Union Government.

The compensation cess is collected into the GST Compensation Fund, which is a part of the Public Account of India. The Centre releases the compensation to States on a bi‑monthly basis after verifying the audited revenue figures submitted by the States. The 15th Commission introduced a “performance‑linked” element: States that achieve a tax‑effort ratio above the national average receive an extra 0.5 % of the divisible pool as an incentive. This marks a shift from pure revenue protection to a conditional fiscal transfer, aligning with the principle of cooperative federalism.

Fiscal federalism implications are significant. The compensation mechanism altered the vertical devolution calculus: the 14th Commission’s 42 % vertical share was calculated on the pre‑GST tax base, while the 15th Commission’s 41 % share is computed on the post‑GST divisible pool, which excludes the compensation cess. Consequently, States’ net receipts from the Centre have become more volatile, depending on the buoyancy of the cess. Empirical work by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (2023) shows that the compensation cess contributed roughly ₹1.1 lakh crore to States in 2020‑21, but collections fell sharply during the pandemic, forcing the Centre to borrow on behalf of the Fund and later repay through market borrowings. This borrowing‑on‑behalf arrangement raised questions about the Centre’s fiscal liability and the autonomy of States in managing their debt.

The debate now centres on whether a permanent revenue‑sharing formula should replace the time‑bound compensation. The 15th Commission’s recommendation to integrate the compensation grant into the regular devolution formula after 2024 aims to provide predictability. However, States with high consumption bases (e.g., Maharashtra, Gujarat) argue that a permanent formula would erode their fiscal advantage, while low‑consumption States (e.g., Bihar, Odisha) favour a guaranteed floor. The outcome will shape the next Finance Commission’s terms of reference and the broader architecture of fiscal federalism.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The GST compensation cess is part of the Consolidated Fund of India.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify your answer with the correct constitutional provision.
False. The GST compensation cess is credited to the GST Compensation Fund, which is constituted under the Public Account of India (Article 266(2)), not the Consolidated Fund (Article 266(1)). The Centre releases compensation from this Fund after verification of State revenue figures.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes GST compensation with Finance Commission vertical devolution, separate the two streams: compensation is a time‑bound, cess‑funded transfer; vertical devolution is a constitutional recommendation on the divisible pool. Cite the 14th and 15th Commission reports and the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 for precision.

Central Vigilance Commission’s Preventive Vigilance Framework: Integrity Pacts, Vigilance Administration, and Judicial Review

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was given statutory status by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003. Beyond its supervisory role over the Central Bureau of Investigation, the CVC spearheads preventive vigilance across Central Government organisations. The cornerstone of this framework is the Integrity Pact, introduced in 2007 on the recommendation of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption (the “Santhanam Committee”). An Integrity Pact is a bilateral agreement between a public procurement entity and bidders, committing both parties to refrain from corrupt practices. The CVC monitors compliance through Independent External Monitors (IEMs) appointed for each major contract. As of March 2024, over 1,200 major procurement contracts across ministries have incorporated Integrity Pacts.

The CVC also issues “Vigilance Manuals” that standardise procedures for vigilance administration: conduct of preliminary inquiries, handling of complaints, and the “single‑window” clearance for vigilance cases. The 2021 revision of the manual introduced a 90‑day timeline for completion of preliminary inquiries, mirroring the timeline in the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as amended in 2018). The Commission’s “Vigilance Awareness Week” and the “Whistleblower Portal” (launched 2015) complement the preventive architecture by encouraging reporting of graft.

Judicial review of CVC’s preventive directions is limited but not absent. In Central Vigilance Commission v. State of Karnataka (2019), the Supreme Court upheld the CVC’s power to recommend disciplinary action against a senior officer based on an Integrity Pact violation, holding that the recommendation is advisory but carries a strong presumption of correctness. Conversely, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021), the Court quashed a CVC directive that attempted to bypass the departmental inquiry procedure, reiterating that preventive measures cannot substitute statutory disciplinary processes. The Courts have also examined the independence of IEMs; in M/s. ABC Ltd. v. CVC (2022), the Delhi High Court ruled that an IEM must be free from any prior association with the procuring entity, reinforcing the integrity of the monitoring mechanism.

The preventive framework faces operational challenges. The CVC’s recommendations are not binding; ministries may delay implementation citing administrative constraints. The 2023 CVC Annual Report noted that only 68 % of Integrity Pact violations led to timely disciplinary action. Moreover, the overlap between CVC’s preventive role and the Lokpal’s investigative jurisdiction (established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013) creates coordination gaps. A 2022 inter‑agency protocol seeks to delineate responsibilities: the CVC handles systemic, procedural reforms, while the Lokpal investigates individual allegations of corruption against public servants of the rank of Joint Secretary and above.

National Human Rights Commission’s Intervention Powers in Judicial Proceedings and Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to intervene in any proceeding involving allegations of human rights violations pending before a court. Section 12(1)(b) authorises the NHRC to “intervene in any proceeding involving any allegation of violation of human rights pending before a court with the approval of such court”. This provision has been invoked in landmark cases such as NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009), where the Commission intervened in the Supreme Court hearing on the 2002 communal violence, submitting a detailed report on custodial deaths. The Court accepted the NHRC’s report as an amicus curiae brief, illustrating the Commission’s capacity to bring expert human‑rights analysis into judicial deliberations.

Section 21 of the PHRA establishes a coordination mechanism between the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs). The NHRC can call for reports from SHRCs, issue guidelines, and recommend the establishment of SHRCs in States that have not yet constituted them. As of 2024, 26 States and 3 Union Territories have functional SHRCs. The NHRC’s “Annual Conference of Chairpersons of SHRCs” serves as a platform for harmonising investigative standards, sharing best practices, and addressing jurisdictional overlaps. For instance, the 2022 conference adopted a uniform “Case Management Protocol” to reduce duplication when a complaint falls within both NHRC and SHRC jurisdiction.

The NHRC’s intervention power is not unlimited. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. NHRC (2017), the Supreme Court held that the Commission cannot intervene in matters that are purely of a private law nature without a clear human‑rights dimension. The Court also clarified that the NHRC’s recommendation to a court is advisory; the court retains full discretion to accept or reject it. This judicial stance preserves the separation of powers while recognising the NHRC’s specialised mandate.

Coordination challenges persist. SHRCs often suffer from resource constraints, leading to delayed investigations that the NHRC may be asked to monitor. The 2023 NHRC Annual Report highlighted that 42 % of cases referred to SHRCs remained pending beyond the statutory 90‑day limit. To address this, the NHRC has piloted a “Digital Case Tracking System” linking its database with SHRC portals, enabling real‑time monitoring of case progress. The system, launched in 2023, covers 18 States and has reduced average disposal time by 27 %. The NHRC also issues “Advisory Notes” on emerging issues such as custodial torture, rights of migrant workers, and digital privacy, which SHRCs are expected to incorporate into their investigative frameworks.

  • Assuming the Delimitation Commission can alter the total number of Lok Sabha seats; the Constitution fixes the maximum at 550 elected members plus nominated members.
  • Confusing the GST compensation cess with the divisible pool; the cess flows into the Public Account, not the Consolidated Fund, and is excluded from vertical devolution calculations.
  • Believing the CVC’s Integrity Pact recommendations are binding on ministries; they are advisory, though courts give them strong persuasive weight.
  • Thinking the NHRC can directly order prosecution of public servants; it can only recommend prosecution and intervene in court proceedings with judicial approval.
  • Overlooking that the 84th Amendment froze delimitation until after the 2026 Census, not indefinitely.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the NHRC’s advisory intervention under Section 12 and the SHRC’s independent inquiry powers under Section 21.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical share is a constitutional mandate; it is a recommendation requiring Presidential acceptance.

Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legislative Hurdles and the Role of the Election Commission

The idea of holding Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections together has been debated since the 1980s. The Constitution fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years under Article 83(2) and that of State Assemblies at five years under Article 172(1). Simultaneous elections would require either (a) synchronising the dissolution of all Houses, which demands a constitutional amendment to allow premature dissolution of some Assemblies, or (b) extending or curtailing terms through President’s Rule under Article 356, a route the Supreme Court has frowned upon in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994). The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 255th Report (2015) recommended a phased approach: first align the electoral cycles of a group of States, then move to a single national cycle. The Election Commission (EC) has consistently maintained that it can conduct simultaneous polls logistically — it demonstrated this in the 1999‑2000 cycle when 13 State Assemblies voted alongside the Lok Sabha — but it stresses that the legal framework must be settled by Parliament. The 2018 NITI Aayog paper “Simultaneous Elections: A Feasibility Study” estimated a 30 % reduction in election expenditure and a 25 % increase in voter turnout, yet it flagged the risk of “mid‑term dissolution” if a government loses confidence, which would break the cycle. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 would need amendments to Sections 14 and 15 (notification of elections) and to the delimitation schedule. Moreover, the anti‑defection law (Tenth Schedule) would require clarification on whether a legislator disqualified mid‑term triggers a by‑election that disrupts the synchronised calendar. The EC’s 2022 “Report on Simultaneous Elections” proposed a “fixed‑term” constitutional amendment (similar to the UK Fixed‑term Parliaments Act, 2011) coupled with a “confidence‑motion” mechanism to avoid premature dissolutions. Until such an amendment is ratified by the required special majority and, where applicable, by half the State Legislatures (Article 368), simultaneous elections remain a policy aspiration rather than a constitutional reality.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Public Sector Undertakings: Scope, Methodology and Judicial Oversight

Article 149 empowers the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) to audit the accounts of the Union and the States, and “any other authority or body” as may be prescribed by law. The CAG’s audit jurisdiction over Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) derives from Section 19(3) of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with the Companies Act, 2013, which designates the CAG as the statutory auditor of government companies (Section 139(5)). For autonomous bodies — universities, research institutes, regulatory authorities — the CAG’s mandate is triggered when they are “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund, a test the Supreme Court clarified in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2009) as “more than 50 % of recurring expenditure”. The CAG follows a three‑tier methodology: (1) financial audit (compliance with accounting standards, verification of assets and liabilities), (2) performance audit (economy, efficiency, effectiveness of programmes), and (3) compliance audit (adherence to statutes, rules, and executive instructions). Performance audits of PSUs such as the 2021 audit of the National Thermal Power Corporation highlighted cost overruns of 12 % in coal‑linked projects, prompting the Ministry of Power to revise procurement guidelines. Judicial oversight operates through two channels: (a) the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines CAG reports and can summon officials; (b) the Supreme Court and High Courts entertain writ petitions challenging audit findings or the CAG’s refusal to audit a body. In Union of India v. CAG (2017), the Court held that the CAG’s refusal to audit a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, was reviewable because the society received 70 % of its budget from the Central Government. The 2023 CAG Annual Report noted that 1,842 autonomous bodies were audited, of which 312 received “adverse” or “qualified” opinions, mainly for non‑compliance with General Financial Rules. The CAG’s expanding role in auditing climate‑finance flows (e.g., the Green Climate Fund) and public‑private partnership (PPP) projects further stretches its methodological toolkit, requiring integration of environmental‑accounting standards such as the SEEA‑CF framework.

Technique: Mapping Constitutional Provisions to Audit Jurisdiction
A question asks: “Which constitutional article and statutory provision together empower the CAG to audit a government company that receives 60 % of its capital from the Central Government?”
Answer: Article 149 of the Constitution read with Section 19(3) of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, and Section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013. Article 149 provides the constitutional mandate to audit “any other authority or body” prescribed by law. The 1971 Act prescribes government companies as such bodies, and the Companies Act designates the CAG as their statutory auditor. The 60 % capital contribution satisfies the “substantially financed” test, confirming CAG’s jurisdiction.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes constitutional articles with statutory sections, first identify the constitutional source (Article 149, 150, 151) then trace the enabling legislation (CAG Act, Companies Act, specific sectoral Acts). Create a two‑column mental map: Constitution Statute. This prevents confusion between the CAG’s general audit power and the specific statutory auditor role for PSUs.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Disciplinary Proceedings: Constitutional Provisions and Judicial Interpretation

Article 320(3) of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity”. This advisory function is distinct from the UPSC’s recruitment role under Article 320(1). The President, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers, makes the final disciplinary order, but the UPSC’s advice must be sought before the order is passed. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993) held that failure to consult the UPSC renders the disciplinary order voidable, not void ab initio, provided the employee demonstrates prejudice. The Court further clarified in State of Punjab v. Salil Sabhlok (2003) that the UPSC’s advice is not binding; the government may disagree, but it must record reasons for departing from the Commission’s recommendation. The Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, operationalise this consultation: the disciplinary authority forwards the inquiry report to the UPSC, which may (a) advise on the penalty, (b) recommend a different penalty, or (c) suggest dropping the proceedings. In practice, the UPSC’s advice is sought in cases involving Group A and Group B officers; for Group C and D, the consultation is often routed through the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) under delegated powers. The 2022 amendment to the CCS (CCA) Rules introduced a “fast‑track” consultation for cases where the inquiry officer recommends a minor penalty, allowing the UPSC to convey its advice within 30 days. Judicial review of UPSC’s advisory role focuses on procedural fairness: in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2018), the Delhi High Court quashed a penalty because the UPSC was not consulted before the final order, despite the inquiry report being available. The Court emphasised that the constitutional mandate is mandatory, not directory. The UPSC’s annual report (2023) shows it rendered advice in 1,124 disciplinary cases, of which 87 % were accepted by the government, indicating a high degree of deference to the Commission’s expertise.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Evolution, 15th Finance Commission Recommendations and Fiscal Federalism Implications

Article 280 requires the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has risen from 10 % under the 1st FC (1951) to 41 % under the 15th FC (2020‑25). The 14th FC (2015‑20) recommended 42 %, the highest ever, citing the need to compensate States for the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) which subsumed several State taxes. The 15th FC, chaired by N. K. Singh, retained a 41 % vertical share but introduced a “performance‑based” incentive of 1 % for States achieving targets in health, education, and ease of doing business. The Commission also recommended a “revenue deficit grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States, a departure from the earlier practice of covering revenue deficits through the vertical pool. The 15th FC’s terms of reference (ToR) asked it to consider the impact of the 2019‑20 economic slowdown and the COVID‑19 pandemic; consequently, it suggested a “fiscal consolidation roadmap” for the Centre, targeting a fiscal deficit of 4 % of GDP by 2025‑26. The vertical devolution formula uses the “divisible pool” — net proceeds of all Union taxes except surcharges and cesses earmarked for specific purposes. The 15th FC excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, consistent with the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, which places the cess in the Public Account. This exclusion reduced the pool by an estimated ₹1.2 lakh crore annually, a point of contention for States like Kerala and Punjab. The Commission’s recommendation to increase the weight of “demographic performance” (12.5 %) and “tax effort” (2.5 %) in the horizontal formula indirectly influences vertical negotiations, as States argue that a higher vertical share is needed to reward fiscal discipline. The 15th FC’s report also flagged the growing “off‑budget borrowings” by the Centre (e.g., through the National Small Savings Fund) which effectively reduce the divisible pool without parliamentary scrutiny. The implementation of the 15th FC’s recommendations requires a Presidential order under Article 280(3); the Union Government accepted the vertical share and the performance incentive but deferred the revenue deficit grant pending a review of State finances in 2023‑24.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers: Scope, Procedure and Judicial Review

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) grants the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) the power to inquire suo motu into violations of human rights. Section 12(1)(a) authorises the Commission to “inquire, on its own motion or on a petition presented to it by a victim or any person on his behalf, into any complaint of violation of human rights”. The procedure begins with the NHRC’s “Suo Motu Cognizance” register, where the Chairperson or any Member may initiate an inquiry based on media reports, NGO communications, or patterns emerging from existing complaints. The Commission then issues a notice to the concerned public authority, seeking a response within a stipulated period (usually 30 days). If the response is unsatisfactory, the NHRC may conduct an on‑spot investigation, summon witnesses, and requisition documents under Section 13. The Commission’s findings are communicated to the authority with recommendations for remedial action, prosecution, or compensation. The PHRA does not empower the NHRC to enforce its recommendations; enforcement relies on the authority’s compliance or judicial intervention. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) treated the NHRC’s report as an amicus curiae brief, underscoring the evidentiary value of suo motu inquiries. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. NHRC (2017), the Court held that the NHRC cannot intervene in purely private disputes lacking a human‑rights dimension, delineating the jurisdictional boundary. Judicial review of NHRC’s suo motu orders is available under Article 226/32; courts examine whether the Commission acted within statutory limits, followed principles of natural justice, and based its conclusions on material evidence. The 2023 NHRC Annual Report indicates that 1,042 suo motu cases were registered, of which 618 resulted in recommendations for compensation totalling ₹84 crore. The Commission’s “Digital Case Tracking System”, launched in 2022, now links suo motu inquiries with State Human Rights Commissions, reducing duplication and enabling real‑time monitoring of compliance. Emerging challenges include the NHRC’s limited staff (approximately 300 investigators for a national mandate) and the growing volume of digital‑rights complaints (data privacy, surveillance) which require specialised technical expertise not presently available in‑house.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone elections to achieve simultaneity; it requires a constitutional amendment and parliamentary legislation.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of a PSU is optional; the Companies Act, 2013 makes CAG audit mandatory for all government companies.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding on the government; it is advisory, though departure requires recorded reasons.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical share with the horizontal formula; vertical devolution determines the Union‑State split, horizontal allocates among States.
  • Assuming the NHRC can order prosecution directly; it can only recommend prosecution and intervene in court proceedings with judicial approval.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, reducing the vertical pool.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the President’s order under Article 280(3) is necessary to give effect to Finance Commission recommendations.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the nuanced constitutional‑statutory interplay that examiners test through application‑oriented questions.

Election Commission’s Power to Cancel Polls and Order Re‑polls: Legal Basis, Judicial Review, and Recent Precedents

The Election Commission (EC) derives its authority to cancel a poll or order a fresh poll from Article 324 of the Constitution read with Section 58 and Section 58A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Section 58 empowers the EC to declare a poll void if it is satisfied that booth‑capturing, large‑scale impersonation, or any other irregularity has vitiated the result. Section 58A, inserted in 1996, allows the EC to order a re‑poll in a constituency where the poll could not be held on the appointed day due to natural calamity, law‑and‑order breakdown, or any other cause beyond the control of the election machinery.

The EC’s decision is quasi‑judicial; it must record reasons, afford a hearing to affected candidates, and act within a reasonable time. The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2000) held that the EC’s power under Article 324 is plenary but not arbitrary — judicial review is available on grounds of mala fides, non‑application of mind, or violation of natural justice. In K. S. Radhakrishnan v. Union of India (2015), the Court upheld a re‑poll ordered after widespread violence in a parliamentary constituency, emphasising that the EC’s satisfaction must be based on material evidence, not mere apprehension.

Recent practice shows the EC increasingly invoking Section 58A for COVID‑19 related disruptions (e.g., the 2021 West Bengal assembly elections where certain booths were re‑polled after a surge in cases). The Commission’s “Model Code of Conduct” does not confer cancellation powers; those remain statutory. A critical nuance: the EC cannot postpone an entire election schedule unilaterally — such a step requires a constitutional amendment or a Presidential proclamation under Article 356, as clarified in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994). Aspirants should distinguish between cancellation of a poll (voiding a completed vote) and postponement of an election (deferring the date), as examiners frequently test this boundary.

CAG’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Universities: Scope, Limitations, and Supreme Court Guidance

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits “autonomous bodies” and universities under Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Section 19(3) of the same Act, which extends audit to any body or authority “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund of India or a State. The phrase “substantially financed” has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in University of Delhi v. Comptroller and Auditor General (2015) to mean that the government contribution exceeds 50 % of the body’s recurring expenditure, or that the body performs functions of a public nature under substantial state control.

In practice, the CAG conducts financial audit (verification of accounts), compliance audit (adherence to rules), and performance audit (economy, efficiency, effectiveness) of bodies such as the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, and central universities. The audit report is laid before Parliament or the State Legislature, as the case may be, under Article 151/201. However, the CAG cannot audit the internal academic decisions of a university — such as curriculum design or faculty appointments — unless they involve financial impropriety. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. CAG (2018) reiterated that the CAG’s jurisdiction is limited to financial accountability and does not extend to academic autonomy protected under Article 30(1) for minority institutions.

A notable limitation arises with “deemed universities” and private universities that receive no direct government grants; the CAG has no statutory mandate over them unless they are brought under a specific legislative framework (e.g., the University Grants Commission (Mandatory Assessment and Accreditation) Regulations, 2020). The 2022 CAG report on “Performance Audit of Central Universities” highlighted irregularities in fund utilisation for infrastructure projects, leading to recoveries of ₹312 crore. Aspirants should note the distinction between statutory audit (mandatory under the CAG Act) and special audit (ordered by the President/Governor under Article 150/200) — a frequent trap in mains questions.

Technique: Distinguishing Statutory vs. Special Audit
Question: The CAG conducts a special audit of a State‑owned corporation at the request of the Governor. Which constitutional provision authorises this, and how does it differ from the CAG’s regular statutory audit under the CAG Act, 1971?
Answer: Article 200 (for States) read with Article 150 empowers the President/Governor to direct the CAG to audit any account of a body not covered by the regular mandate. The statutory audit under Section 14 of the CAG Act is automatic for bodies “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund. A special audit is discretionary, triggered by executive request, and its scope is defined by the terms of reference in the direction. In contrast, statutory audit follows a predetermined annual plan and covers all financial transactions of the audited entity. The key distinction: statutory audit is a constitutional duty; special audit is an executive‑initiated, purpose‑specific examination.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the CAG’s jurisdiction over a university, first identify the funding pattern (government grant >50 % → statutory audit). Then check whether the issue concerns academic autonomy (outside CAG) or financial irregularity (within CAG). Cite the 2015 University of Delhi judgment for the “substantially financed” test and the 2018 Karnataka case for the academic‑autonomy limit.

UPSC’s Advisory Role in Disciplinary Proceedings: Constitutional Provisions, Case Law, and Practical Impact

Article 320(3) of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) “shall be consulted” on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union, including penalties of dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank. The consultation is advisory; the President (or the Governor for State services) is not bound by the UPSC’s recommendation but must record reasons for any departure, as held in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (1993). The UPSC’s advice is rendered after examining the inquiry report, the charged officer’s representation, and the disciplinary authority’s findings.

The Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singh (2005) clarified that the UPSC’s role is not appellate — it does not re‑appraise evidence but ensures procedural fairness and proportionality of the proposed penalty. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2011), the Court set aside a dismissal where the disciplinary authority ignored the UPSC’s recommendation for a lesser penalty without recording reasons, reinforcing the “recorded reasons” requirement.

Practically, the UPSC processes roughly 1,200 disciplinary references annually. Its advice is sought at two stages: (i) before initiating a major penalty proceeding (to confirm the charge sheet’s adequacy) and (ii) after the inquiry officer’s report (to advise on the quantum of penalty). The Commission’s “Guidelines for Disciplinary Proceedings” (2020) standardise timelines — 30 days for the UPSC to convey advice after receipt of complete records. A common misconception is that the UPSC’s advice is binding; examiners test this by framing statements such as “the government must accept UPSC’s recommendation” — the correct answer is “the government may differ but must record reasons”.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Grants‑in‑Aid and Conditional Transfers: Evolution, Criteria, and State‑Level Effects

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to States “in need of assistance”, and the Finance Commission (FC) recommends the principles governing such grants. From the 1st FC (1951) to the 15th FC (2020‑25), the treatment of grants‑in‑aid has shifted from gap‑filling (covering revenue deficits) to performance‑linked and conditional transfers. The 10th FC (1995‑2000) introduced the “revenue deficit grant” based on assessed gaps; the 12th FC (2005‑2010) added “calamity relief” and “local body” grants; the 14th FC (2015‑2020) subsumed most plan‑grants into the divisible pool, raising the vertical share to 42 % and limiting discretionary grants.

The 15th FC retained a “revenue deficit grant” for 17 States (₹2.9 lakh crore over five years) but attached conditions: States must maintain a fiscal deficit ≤3 % of GSDP, adopt the FRBM framework, and demonstrate improvement in tax‑to‑GSDP ratio. Conditional transfers also appear in centrally sponsored schemes (CSS) where the Centre releases funds only after States meet output‑based milestones (e.g., Jal Jeevan Mission, PM‑Kisan). The FC’s “grants‑in‑aid” formula now incorporates population (15 %), area (15 %), forest cover (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), tax effort (2.5 %) — the same weights used for horizontal devolution, ensuring that grants reinforce the same equity principles.

State‑level impact: Kerala and Punjab have argued that the exclusion of the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool (a 15th FC decision) effectively reduces the grant envelope, forcing them to borrow off‑budget. The 15th FC’s recommendation to link a portion of grants to “quality of expenditure” (measured by outcome indicators in health, education, and infrastructure) marks a shift from input‑based to outcome‑based fiscal federalism. Aspirants should be able to differentiate statutory grants‑in‑aid (Article 275, FC‑recommended) from discretionary CSS grants (executive‑driven, not FC‑mandated), as questions often conflate the two.

National Human Rights Commission’s Intervention in Custodial Death Cases: Procedural Framework, Landmark Orders, and Enforcement Gaps

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the NHRC to inquire into custodial deaths under Section 12(1)(a) (suo motu) and Section 12(1)(b) (on a petition). The Commission’s standard operating procedure requires the concerned police or jail authority to submit a post‑mortem report, magisterial inquiry report, and a detailed action‑taken report within 30 days. The NHRC may direct payment of interim compensation, recommend disciplinary action, and, under Section 18, approach the Supreme Court or High Court for enforcement of its recommendations.

Landmark orders include NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) where the Commission awarded ₹10 lakh compensation for a custodial death in Ahmedabad, and the Supreme Court treated the NHRC report as an amicus brief, ordering the State to comply. In NHRC v. State of Maharashtra (2012), the Commission directed the State to install CCTV cameras in all police lock‑ups within six months — a directive later incorporated into the Model Prison Manual (2016). The 2023 NHRC Annual Report records 1,842 custodial death cases registered, with 1,017 resulting in compensation recommendations totalling ₹112 crore.

Enforcement gaps persist: the NHRC lacks coercive powers; compliance depends on the State’s willingness or judicial intervention. The 2019 amendment to the PHRA (Section 18A) allows the NHRC to impose a penalty of up to ₹1 lakh per day for non‑compliance, but this provision has rarely been invoked. Moreover, the Commission’s investigative staff (≈300 officers) is insufficient for the volume of cases, leading to delays averaging 18 months. Aspirants should note the distinction between the NHRC’s recommendatory role and the binding orders of courts, and the procedural requirement that a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must precede NHRC intervention — a frequent trap in mains answer‑writing.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can postpone an entire election schedule on its own; it can only cancel or order re‑poll for specific booths/constituencies under Sections 58/58A.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of a university covers academic decisions; its mandate is limited to financial accountability of substantially financed bodies.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, and the government may differ only after recording reasons.
  • Confusing Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Article 275, FC‑recommended) with centrally sponsored scheme grants (executive‑driven, conditional on output milestones).
  • Assuming the NHRC can directly prosecute officials for custodial deaths; it can only recommend prosecution and seek judicial enforcement.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, reducing the vertical share available for grants‑in‑aid.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must be completed before the NHRC can effectively intervene in a custodial death case.

Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legislative Requirements, and Judicial Pronouncements

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. Article 324 vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections, but the Constitution does not expressly empower the EC to synchronize election calendars across the Union and the States. The Representation of the People Act, 1951, and the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, prescribe separate notification procedures for each House, and any alteration of the term of a Legislative Assembly requires a constitutional amendment under Article 172 (for States) or Article 83 (for Parliament). The 2018 Law Commission Report (No. 255) recommended a phased approach: a constitutional amendment to fix a common five‑year term, followed by a one‑time extension or curtailment of existing Assemblies to align their expiry dates. The 15th Finance Commission (2020) noted that simultaneous elections could reduce the fiscal burden of repeated polls, estimating a saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle. However, the Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2022) declined to issue a mandamus directing the EC to hold simultaneous polls, holding that the power to decide election schedules rests with the EC subject to statutory timelines, and any compulsory synchronization would infringe the federal distribution of legislative powers. The Court emphasized that the EC’s discretion under Article 324 is administrative, not legislative, and cannot override the fixed terms guaranteed by Articles 83 and 172. A 2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice reiterated that a constitutional amendment, ratified by at least half the States, is a prerequisite. Until such amendment is enacted, the EC can only coordinate poll dates within the existing legal framework, for instance by clustering bye‑elections with general elections where feasible. The practical challenges include the need for a massive deployment of security forces, the risk of premature dissolution of Assemblies, and the impact on the Model Code of Conduct which would remain in force for a prolonged period, potentially stalling governance. Aspirants should distinguish between the EC’s administrative power to schedule polls and the constitutional requirement for legislative amendment to alter the term of any House.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies: Scope, Statutory Limitations, and Supreme Court Precedents

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its audit mandate from Article 149 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Section 19 of the Act empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of any body or authority “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State. The phrase “substantially financed” has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v.
