Rajesh Gautam (2019) to mean that the government’s contribution exceeds 50 % of the body’s total expenditure, or that the body performs functions of a governmental character. Consequently, premier institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), and the National Law Universities fall within the CAG’s audit jurisdiction. However, the CAG’s remit does not extend to academic or administrative decisions — only to financial regularity, propriety and performance. In CAG v. Union of India (2021), the Court upheld a CAG performance audit of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) that flagged irregularities in grant utilisation, affirming that performance audit is a legitimate extension of the CAG’s constitutional duty. The CAG’s 2022 report on autonomous bodies highlighted that 1,142 entities were audited, with ₹3,200 crore of irregular expenditure identified, of which 68 % related to non‑compliance with General Financial Rules. A notable limitation arises with bodies created under special statutes that explicitly exclude CAG audit — for instance, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) under the RBI Act, 1934, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) under the SEBI Act, 1992. In such cases, the CAG can only conduct a “supplementary audit” if the statute permits, or rely on the audit reports of the statutory auditors appointed by the body itself. The 2023 amendment to the CAG Act introduced a provision for “joint audit” with the internal audit wings of large autonomous bodies to improve coverage. Aspirants must remember that the CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is financial, not academic; the “substantial financing” test is the judicial benchmark; and statutory exclusions operate as a hard limit unless overridden by a specific legislative provision.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG can audit the academic curriculum of an IIT because it is substantially financed by the Centre.” State whether the statement is correct and justify your answer in two sentences.
The statement is incorrect. The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and Section 19 of the CAG Act, 1971, is confined to financial accountability — regularity, propriety and performance of expenditure — and does not extend to academic or administrative policy decisions such as curriculum design, even for bodies that are substantially financed.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes “audit” with “policy”, instantly flag the functional boundary: CAG = financial audit only. Cite Article 149, Section 19 CAG Act, and the 2019 Supreme Court “substantial financing” test to secure full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Mandate, Recent Amendments, and Judicial Scrutiny

Articles 315 to 323 of the Constitution establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and Central Services. Under Article 320, the UPSC must be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles of promotion, and disciplinary matters affecting civil servants. The All India Services Act, 1951, and the Indian Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, operationalise this mandate. In 2022, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) introduced a lateral entry scheme for joint secretary‑level posts, allowing domain experts from the private sector to be appointed on contract for three to five years. The UPSC was tasked with conducting the selection process, including a written test and interview, marking the first time the Commission handled recruitment outside the traditional competitive examination route. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021) upheld the UPSC’s advisory role in disciplinary proceedings, reiterating that the government may differ from the Commission’s advice only after recording reasons in writing, a safeguard derived from Article 320(3). The 2023 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations expanded the list of posts exempt from mandatory consultation, prompting criticism that the executive is eroding the Commission’s constitutional check. The UPSC’s Annual Report 2023‑24 shows that 1,205 candidates were recommended for the Civil Services Examination, while 42 lateral entry appointments were made, reflecting a modest but growing diversification of the talent pool. A key judicial pronouncement, UPSC v. State of Bihar (2020), clarified that the Commission’s recommendation on promotion panels is binding unless the government demonstrates a “palpable error of law or fact”. Aspirants should note the distinction between the UPSC’s constitutional advisory function (which the executive may depart from with recorded reasons) and its statutory role in conducting examinations (which is mandatory and non‑delegable). The lateral entry scheme, while not a constitutional amendment, tests the flexibility of Article 320 and has been the subject of a pending Public Interest Litigation questioning its compatibility with the merit‑based recruitment principle enshrined in the Constitution.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Framework: Evolution of Criteria, Fiscal Federalism Implications, and 15th Finance Commission Recommendations

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has evolved from 10 % (1st FC, 1951) to 41 % (14th FC, 2015‑20) and was retained at 41 % by the 15th FC (2021‑26). The 15th FC introduced a refined criteria matrix for horizontal devolution: population (15 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %). For vertical devolution, the 15th FC recommended a “revenue deficit grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States, conditional on maintaining fiscal deficit ≤3 % of GSDP, adopting the FRBM framework, and improving the tax‑to‑GSDP ratio. The Commission also excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, a decision that reduced the effective vertical envelope for States like Kerala and Punjab, compelling them to resort to off‑budget borrowing. The 15th FC’s “quality of expenditure” incentive links a portion of grants to outcome indicators in health, education and infrastructure, signalling a shift from input‑based to outcome‑based fiscal federalism. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) declined to interfere with the FC’s formula, holding that the Commission’s recommendations are advisory and acquire legal force only after Presidential acceptance. The 2023 Economic Survey highlighted that the 15th FC’s vertical share, combined with the GST compensation shortfall, resulted in a net transfer of 48 % of gross tax revenue to States, the highest since the 10th FC. Aspirants must differentiate statutory grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 (FC‑recommended, non‑conditional) from centrally sponsored scheme (CSS) grants (executive‑driven, output‑conditional), a frequent source of confusion in mains answer‑writing.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 12(1)(a) to inquire suo motu into violations of human rights, and under Section 12(1)(b) on receipt of a petition. The Commission’s standard operating procedure requires the concerned authority to submit a post‑mortem report, magisterial inquiry report, and action‑taken report within 30 days. Section 18 authorises the NHRC to approach the Supreme Court or High Court for enforcement of its recommendations. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009), the Commission awarded ₹10 lakh compensation for a custodial death; the Supreme Court treated the NHRC report as an amicus brief and ordered compliance. The 2019 amendment introduced Section 18A, allowing a penalty of up to ₹1 lakh per day for non‑compliance, though it has been invoked sparingly. Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21, which mandates the NHRC to monitor the functioning of SHRCs and to transfer cases where the violation spans multiple States. The 2023 NHRC Annual Report records 1,842 custodial death cases, with 1,017 resulting in compensation recommendations totalling ₹112 crore. However, the NHRC’s investigative staff of roughly 300 officers leads to an average disposal time of 18 months. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Maharashtra (2012) directed installation of CCTV cameras in all police lock‑ups, a directive later incorporated into the Model Prison Manual (2016). A critical procedural trap: a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must be completed before the NHRC can effectively intervene; many aspirants erroneously assume the NHRC can initiate prosecution directly. The NHRC’s role remains recommendatory; enforcement depends on State cooperation or judicial orders. Understanding the interplay between the NHRC’s suo motu powers, the mandatory magisterial inquiry, and the limited coercive tools is essential for accurate mains analysis.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone an entire general election; it can only order re‑poll or countermand polls for specific constituencies under Sections 58/58A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of an autonomous university covers academic decisions such as curriculum or faculty appointments; its mandate is strictly financial.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding on the government; it is advisory, and the government may differ only after recording reasons in writing.
  • Confusing Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Article 275, FC‑recommended) with centrally sponsored scheme grants (executive‑driven, conditional on output milestones).
  • Assuming the NHRC can directly prosecute officials for custodial deaths; it can only recommend prosecution and seek judicial enforcement.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, reducing the vertical share available for grants‑in‑aid.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must be completed before the NHRC can effectively intervene in a custodial death case.

Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Provisions, Judicial Scrutiny, and Operational Challenges

The Constitution vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections under Article 324. Simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies would require synchronising the five‑year terms mandated by Articles 83(2) and 172(1). The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) provides for the dissolution of Houses (Sections 14 and 15) and for the President’s or Governor’s power to dissolve the legislature before the expiry of its term. A constitutional amendment would be needed to either fix a common term or to empower the EC to curtail or extend existing terms without violating the basic structure doctrine. The 170th Law Commission Report (2018) and the NITI Aayog Discussion Paper (2022) recommended a phased approach: first aligning the Lok Sabha and a group of State Assemblies, then extending to all States. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice (2023) highlighted that any amendment must preserve federalism and the principle of periodic elections, citing the Supreme Court’s observation in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) that the dissolution power is a constitutional safeguard, not a routine executive tool. Operationally, the EC would need to manage a single electoral roll, deploy VVPAT‑enabled EVMs across 1 million polling stations, and coordinate security forces for a compressed schedule. The 2024 pilot in the Union Territory of Puducherry demonstrated logistical feasibility but also exposed challenges in voter‑awareness campaigns and the handling of simultaneous model‑code‑of‑conduct violations. Aspirants should note that the EC cannot unilaterally postpone a general election; it can only order re‑poll or countermand polls for specific constituencies under Sections 58/58A of the RPA.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State‑Owned Enterprises: Scope, Methodology, and Parliamentary Follow‑Up

Article 149 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of all Government companies and corporations in which the Union or a State holds not less than 51 % of the paid‑up capital. The audit covers financial statements, compliance with statutes, and performance‑audit parameters such as efficiency, economy and effectiveness. The CAG’s 2022 Report No. 12 on “Performance Audit of Public Sector Undertakings” examined 42 central PSUs, including Air India, Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) and Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC). The methodology combines test‑check of transactions, analytical review of financial ratios, and beneficiary‑survey techniques for service‑delivery PSUs. Findings are presented to Parliament through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), which examines the CAG’s observations, calls for executive action‑taken reports, and may recommend policy changes. In 2023, the PAC’s 73rd Report on the CAG’s audit of the Indian Railways’ freight‑loading efficiency led to a revision of the freight‑rate structure. The CAG also conducts “special audits” on request of the President or Governor under Section 19 of the DPC Act; the 2021 special audit of the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation’s phase‑IV cost overruns resulted in a recovery of ₹1,200 crore. A critical procedural point: the CAG’s audit of an autonomous university does not extend to academic decisions such as curriculum or faculty appointments; its mandate remains strictly financial and compliance‑oriented.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain the constitutional and statutory basis for the CAG’s audit of State‑Owned Enterprises and the role of the Public Accounts Committee in ensuring executive accountability.”
Start with Article 149 and the DPC Act, 1971 (Sections 13‑19). Mention the 51 % shareholding threshold. Describe the three audit streams – financial, compliance, performance – citing the 2022 CAG Report No. 12. Explain that the CAG submits reports to the President/Governor who lays them before Parliament/State Legislature. The PAC, constituted under Rule 308 of the Lok Sabha Rules, examines the reports, summons officials, and demands action‑taken notes. Illustrate with the 2023 PAC 73rd Report on Indian Railways and the 2021 special audit of Delhi Metro. Conclude that the PAC’s recommendations are not binding but carry significant political weight, and the executive must respond within a stipulated period.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes constitutional articles with statutory provisions, structure the answer in two columns: “Constitutional Basis” and “Statutory Elaboration”. Quote the exact article/section numbers; examiners award marks for precise citations. Keep a ready list of recent CAG reports (2021‑2024) and corresponding PAC reports for quick illustration.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Disciplinary Proceedings: Procedural Safeguards and Judicial Review

Article 320(3) of the Constitution requires the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union in a civil capacity. The UPSC’s advice is advisory; the President (or the Governor for State services) may differ only after recording reasons in writing, a safeguard affirmed in Union of India v. K. S. Subramanian (2010) where the Supreme Court held that non‑consultation vitiates the disciplinary order. The UPSC’s Regulations, 1969 prescribe the procedure: the disciplinary authority forwards the charge‑sheet, the employee’s representation, and the inquiry officer’s report to the Commission. The Commission examines whether the inquiry followed natural justice, whether the penalty is proportionate, and whether the evidence supports the findings. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2009) the Court quashed a dismissal where the UPSC’s advice was ignored without recorded reasons. The 2022 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations expanded the list of posts exempt from consultation, but the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2023) struck down the exemption for Group A posts as violative of Article 320. Aspirants must distinguish between the UPSC’s advisory role in recruitment (Article 320(1)) and its mandatory consultation in disciplinary matters (Article 320(3)). The Commission does not act as an appellate body; its function is to ensure procedural fairness and uniformity across services.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and the Impact of GST on Fiscal Federalism: Data‑Driven Analysis

The vertical devolution formula determines the share of the net proceeds of Union taxes (the divisible pool) that is transferred to the States. The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV) recommended a vertical share of 41 % for the 2021‑26 period, a marginal reduction from the 14th FC’s 42 %. A pivotal change was the exclusion of the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, as the cess is earmarked for compensating States for revenue loss under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017. This exclusion reduced the effective vertical envelope for States such as Kerala and Punjab, compelling them to resort to off‑budget borrowing. The 2023 Economic Survey reported that the 15th FC’s vertical share, combined with the GST compensation shortfall, resulted in a net transfer of 48 % of gross tax revenue to States, the highest since the 10th FC. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) declined to interfere with the FC’s formula, reiterating that the Commission’s recommendations are advisory and acquire legal force only after Presidential acceptance under Article 280(3). The horizontal devolution criteria (income distance, demographic performance, forest cover, tax effort) remain unchanged, but the vertical squeeze has intensified inter‑State disparities. Aspirants should differentiate statutory grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 (FC‑recommended, non‑conditional) from centrally sponsored scheme (CSS) grants (executive‑driven, output‑conditional), a frequent source of confusion in mains answer‑writing.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Police Reforms: Supreme Court Directives and Implementation Gaps

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the NHRC under Section 12(1)(a) to inquire suo motu into violations of human rights, including custodial deaths and police excesses. The Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) issued seven directives for police reforms, including the establishment of State Security Commissions, Police Establishment Boards, and a fixed tenure for the Director General of Police. The NHRC monitors compliance through its annual reports and by issuing directions under Section 18 of the PHRA. The 2023 NHRC Annual Report recorded 1,842 custodial death cases, with 1,017 resulting in compensation recommendations totalling ₹112 crore. However, the NHRC’s investigative staff of roughly 300 officers leads to an average disposal time of 18 months. In NHRC v. State of Maharashtra (2012) the Court directed installation of CCTV cameras in all police lock‑ups, a directive later incorporated into the Model Prison Manual (2016). The 2019 amendment introduced Section 18A, allowing a penalty of up to ₹1 lakh per day for non‑compliance, though it has been invoked sparingly. A critical procedural trap: a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must be completed before the NHRC can effectively intervene; many aspirants erroneously assume the NHRC can initiate prosecution directly. The NHRC’s role remains recommendatory; enforcement depends on State cooperation or judicial orders.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone an entire general election; it can only order re‑poll or countermand polls for specific constituencies under Sections 58/58A of the RPA.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of an autonomous university covers academic decisions such as curriculum or faculty appointments; its mandate is strictly financial.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding on the government; it is advisory, and the government may differ only after recording reasons in writing.
  • Confusing Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Article 275, FC‑recommended) with centrally sponsored scheme grants (executive‑driven, conditional on output milestones).
  • Assuming the NHRC can directly prosecute officials for custodial deaths; it can only recommend prosecution and seek judicial enforcement.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission excluded the GST compensation cess from the divisible pool, reducing the vertical share available for grants‑in‑aid.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC must be completed before the NHRC can effectively intervene in a custodial death case.

The Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Judicial Review

The Constitution does not explicitly provide for simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. Article 83(2) fixes the term of the Lok Sabha at five years unless dissolved earlier, while Article 172(1) provides a similar five‑year term for State Assemblies. The Election Commission derives its authority to schedule elections from Article 324 read with the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA). Section 14 of the RPA empowers the Commission to notify the election programme, but it does not grant a power to extend or curtail the term of any House.

In 2018 the Law Commission of India, in its 255th Report, recommended a phased approach to simultaneous elections, suggesting a constitutional amendment to align the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. The report highlighted that a constitutional amendment under Article 368 would be required because the existing framework treats the dissolution of each House as an independent executive act. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the President’s power to dissolve a State Assembly under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, reinforcing that any attempt to synchronise terms must respect the federal distribution of powers.

The Election Commission’s 2023 discussion paper on “One Nation, One Election” outlined operational challenges: the need for a unified electoral roll, synchronisation of the Model Code of Conduct, and the logistical deployment of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units across 28 States and 8 Union Territories. The Commission noted that a constitutional amendment would also have to address the contingency of a mid‑term dissolution — whether a “constructive vote of no confidence” mechanism (as in Germany) could be transplanted without violating the basic structure doctrine.

Judicial scrutiny would likely focus on whether a mandatory simultaneous election law infringes the autonomy of State legislatures guaranteed under Article 172 and the principle of federalism upheld in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). The Court has repeatedly struck down provisions that undermine the independent functioning of State legislatures (e.g., State of Rajasthan v. Union of India, 1977). Therefore, any legislative move toward simultaneous elections must either obtain the consent of a majority of States under Article 368(2) or be structured as a voluntary alignment through a political consensus, leaving the constitutional timetable untouched.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State‑Owned Enterprises and the Role of the Public Accounts Committee

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit Government companies from Section 19(1) of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Section 619 of the Companies Act, 2013. A “Government company” is defined in Section 2(45) of the Companies Act as any company in which not less than 51 % of the paid‑up share capital is held by the Central Government, a State Government, or both. The CAG appoints the statutory auditors of such companies under Section 139(5) of the Companies Act and has the right to conduct a supplementary audit under Section 143(6).

The audit scope covers financial statements, compliance with applicable laws, and the efficiency of resource utilisation. In 2022 the CAG’s report on “Performance Audit of Select Central Public Sector Enterprises” highlighted that 12 out of 45 sampled enterprises had not submitted their annual accounts within the statutory period, delaying the CAG’s supplementary audit. The report also flagged instances where the Board of Directors approved capital expenditure without adequate techno‑economic appraisal, a procedural lapse that the CAG classified as a “deficiency in governance”.

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament examines the CAG’s reports on Government companies. Rule 308 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha requires the PAC to call for the Ministry’s “Action Taken Notes” within six months of the report’s presentation. In practice, the PAC often summons the Chairman and Managing Director of the concerned enterprise to explain deviations. The 2021 PAC report on “Air India Asset Monetisation” recommended that the Ministry of Civil Aviation institutionalise a quarterly review mechanism for all CPSEs to ensure timely corrective action.

A recurring issue is the distinction between “commercial audit” (focused on profitability) and “propriety audit” (focused on legality and prudence). The CAG’s 2019 guidance note clarified that while commercial viability is relevant, the primary constitutional duty under Article 149 is to ensure that expenditure from the Consolidated Fund — whether direct or through a CPSE — conforms to the principles of financial propriety. This distinction becomes critical when CPSEs raise off‑budget borrowings; the CAG treats such borrowings as contingent liabilities of the Government and includes them in the “Fiscal Deficit” analysis presented to the PAC.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Can the CAG directly audit the day‑to‑day operational decisions of a Government company such as pricing of its products?”
No. The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the CAG’s DPC Act is limited to financial audit, compliance audit, and performance audit. Operational decisions like product pricing fall within the commercial judgment of the Board unless they involve a breach of statutory provisions, misuse of public funds, or violation of the principles of financial propriety. The CAG may comment on the *process* by which pricing decisions were approved (e.g., absence of Board minutes, lack of cost‑benefit analysis) but cannot substitute its own commercial judgment for that of the management.
Answer‑writing tip
When a mains question asks about CAG’s jurisdiction over CPSEs, structure the answer in three layers: (1) constitutional source (Art. 149, 150), (2) statutory framework (CAG DPC Act, Companies Act 2013), (3) institutional interface (PAC, Committee on Public Undertakings). Cite the 2022 CAG performance audit report and the 2021 PAC recommendation on quarterly reviews to demonstrate current awareness.

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes’ Advisory Role in Tribal Sub‑Plan Allocation and Monitoring

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) was constituted under Article 338A of the Constitution (inserted by the 89th Amendment Act, 2003). Its mandate under Clause (5) of Article 338A includes “to participate and advise on the planning process of socio‑economic development of the Scheduled Tribes”. The Tribal Sub‑Plan (TSP) strategy, introduced in the Fifth Five‑Year Plan (1974‑79), earmarks a proportion of the State Plan outlay at least equal to the ST population percentage in the State. The NCST’s advisory role is operationalised through the Ministry of Tribal Affairs’ “Guidelines for Implementation of Tribal Sub‑Plan” (2014), which require the State Governments to submit TSP proposals to the NCST for comments before finalisation.

In practice, the NCST reviews the “Annual Tribal Sub‑Plan” documents forwarded by the State Tribal Welfare Departments. The Commission’s 2022‑23 Annual Report noted that only 14 out of 28 States submitted TSP proposals within the prescribed timeline, and in 9 States the allocation fell short of the mandated percentage by more than 5 %. The NCST issued advisories under Section 8(1) of the NCST Act, 2004, urging the defaulting States to rectify the shortfall and to establish a dedicated TSP monitoring cell.

The Commission also monitors the utilisation of funds through the “Tribal Sub‑Plan Monitoring System” (TSPMS), a web‑based portal launched in 2018. The portal captures scheme‑wise physical and financial progress, enabling the NCST to flag delays. In 2021 the NCST directed the Government of Odisha to explain a 23 % under‑utilisation of funds under the “Vanbandhu Kalyan Yojana”, leading to a supplementary allocation of ₹312 crore in the revised estimates.

Judicial oversight reinforces the NCST’s advisory authority. In State of Maharashtra v. National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (2018), the Bombay High Court held that the State Government’s failure to consult the NCST before finalising the TSP violated the constitutional mandate of Article 338A(5). The Court directed the State to place the TSP before the NCST for comments within 30 days. This judgment clarified that the NCST’s advice, while not legally binding, carries a constitutional expectation of compliance, and non‑consultation is justiciable.

The Central Vigilance Commission’s Preventive Vigilance Framework and the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, pursuant to the Supreme Court’s direction in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997). Its preventive vigilance mandate is articulated in Section 8(1)(a) of the Act, which requires the CVC to “exercise superintendence over the vigilance administration of the various Ministries and Departments of the Central Government”. The CVC issues “Vigilance Manuals” and “Standard Operating Procedures” that prescribe periodic surprise inspections, rotation of officials in sensitive posts, and the maintenance of “Integrity Index” scores for each department.

The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (WBPA) came into force on 12 May 2014. Section 4 of the WBPA designates the CVC as the “Competent Authority” to receive protected disclosures from public servants. The Act provides for confidentiality of the complainant’s identity (Section 11) and protection against victimisation (Section 12). However, the Act excludes disclosures related to “matters of national security” and “information received in confidence from foreign governments” (Section 3). The CVC’s 2022 Annual Report recorded 1,142 disclosures received under the WBPA, of which 378 were forwarded to the concerned disciplinary authorities for action.

Operational challenges persist. The CVC’s “Preventive Vigilance” circular of 2020 mandated that each Ministry appoint a “Chief Vigilance Officer” (CVO) of the rank of Joint Secretary or above. Yet, as of March 2023, 17 out of 58 Ministries had not filled the CVO post on a regular basis, relying on ad‑hoc arrangements. The CVC has recommended to the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) that the CVO position be included in the Annual Performance Appraisal Report (APAR) of the concerned Secretary to ensure accountability.

Judicial scrutiny has shaped the CVC’s preventive role. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court directed the CVC to formulate a “Whistle Blower Protection Policy” for the Central Government within six months. The CVC complied by issuing the “Guidelines for Protection of Whistle Blowers” in 2019, which prescribe a 90‑day timeline for preliminary inquiry and a 180‑day timeline for final disposal. The Court also held that the CVC’s recommendation for disciplinary action is not binding but the competent authority must record reasons for disagreement, reinforcing the principle of institutional integrity.

The Finance Commission’s Treatment of Cess and Surcharge in the Divisible Pool: Impact on Vertical Devolution

Article 270 of the Constitution provides that all taxes and duties referred to in the Union List, except those listed in Articles 268, 269, and 269A, shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and distributed between the Union and the States. However, Article 271 permits Parliament to impose a surcharge on certain taxes for the purposes of the Union, and the proceeds of such surcharge are not part of the divisible pool. Similarly, a cess imposed under a specific statute (e.g., the GST Compensation Cess under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017) is earmarked for a defined purpose and excluded from the divisible pool unless the statute provides otherwise.

The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV), in its report for 2021‑26, noted that the share of cesses and surcharges in the Union’s gross tax revenue rose from 10.4 % in 2010‑11 to 19.8 % in 2020‑21. Because these levies are outside the divisible pool, the effective vertical share of States in the Union’s total tax receipts declined even though the nominal vertical devolution was fixed at 41 %. The Commission recommended that the Union consider “rationalising” cesses and surcharges by either subsuming them into the base tax rate or providing a compensatory transfer to States.

The GST Compensation Cess presents a distinct case. The cess is collected on luxury and sin goods and is constitutionally mandated to compensate States for revenue loss arising from GST implementation for a period of five years (2017‑22). The 15th FC excluded the cess from the divisible pool, arguing that its purpose is transitional and that including it would distort the horizontal distribution formula. However, the cessation of the compensation regime in June 2022 left a revenue gap for several States. The Union Government subsequently extended the cess collection until March 2026 to service the back‑to‑back loans taken to meet the compensation shortfall, effectively keeping the cess outside the divisible pool for an additional four years.

The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) declined to intervene in the Finance Commission’s treatment of the GST Compensation Cess, reiterating that the Commission’s recommendations are advisory and acquire legal force only after Presidential acceptance under Article 280(3). The Court observed that the constitutional scheme grants the Finance Commission wide discretion in determining the composition of the divisible pool, subject only to the requirement that the distribution be based on “the net proceeds of taxes”. This judgment underscores that any challenge to the exclusion of cesses or surcharges must be framed as a question of constitutional interpretation of “net proceeds” rather than a challenge to the Commission’s wisdom.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally extend the term of a State Assembly to align with Lok Sabha elections; it has no such power under Article 172 or the RPA.
  • Believing the CAG’s supplementary audit of a Government company replaces the statutory auditor’s report; the CAG’s audit is additional and does not absolve the statutory auditor of responsibility.
  • Thinking the NCST’s advisory comments on the Tribal Sub‑Plan are merely recommendatory with no constitutional consequence; failure to consult the NCST has been held justiciable by High Courts.
  • Confusing the CVC’s preventive vigilance guidelines with binding disciplinary rules; the guidelines are administrative directions, and non‑compliance attracts departmental action only after a reasoned order.
  • Overlooking that cesses and surcharges excluded from the divisible pool reduce the effective vertical devolution to States even when the nominal share remains unchanged.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory reading and case‑law awareness.

The Election Commission’s Delimitation Interface: Constitutional Mandate, Judicial Scrutiny, and the 2026 Freeze

Article 82 and Article 170 read with the Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002 empower the President to constitute a Delimitation Commission after each Census. The Election Commission (EC) does not draw boundaries but supplies the electoral data — polling‑station maps, elector‑population ratios, and constituency‑wise turnout — that the Delimitation Commission uses as its primary evidence base. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly seats at the 1971 Census figures until the first Census after 2026, effectively postponing the next full delimitation to 2031. However, the 87th Amendment (2003) permitted readjustment of territorial constituencies within the existing seat count using the 2001 Census, a process completed in 2008. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2002) upheld the freeze, ruling that the power to delimit is a legislative function that Parliament may regulate, and that the freeze does not violate the basic structure because it preserves the federal balance of representation. In 2020 the EC issued a directive to State Chief Electoral Officers to update the electoral rolls in anticipation of the post‑2026 exercise, highlighting the logistical challenge of aligning 1.3 billion electors with new boundaries. The Commission also flagged the need for a constitutional amendment to extend the freeze beyond 2026 if political consensus on a new formula (e.g., population‑weight‑plus‑performance) is not reached. The interplay between the EC’s data‑curation role and the Delimitation Commission’s quasi‑judicial adjudication creates a unique institutional interface: the EC’s data are treated as prima facie evidence, yet the Delimitation Commission may reject them if they are shown to be inconsistent with the “as far as practicable” principle of equal population enshrined in Section 9 of the Delimitation Act, 2002. Recent litigation in the Madras High Court (State of Tamil Nadu v. Election Commission of India, 2023) examined whether the EC’s provisional publication of draft rolls before the Delimitation Commission’s final order amounted to pre‑empting the delimitation process; the Court held that the EC’s statutory duty under Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 to maintain accurate rolls is independent and does not encroach on delimitation. This jurisprudence clarifies that the EC’s operational autonomy in roll management coexists with the Delimitation Commission’s constitutional mandate, but any attempt by the EC to alter constituency boundaries without a Delimitation Commission order would be ultra vires.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Universities: Scope, Statutory Limits, and Supreme Court Pronouncements

The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to “any body or authority substantially financed by the Union or a State”. Autonomous bodies — such as the Indian Institutes of Technology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, and central universities — receive over 90 % of their recurring expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, bringing them squarely within the CAG’s audit jurisdiction. However, the statutory framework distinguishes between “financial audit” (verification of accounts) and “performance audit” (economy, efficiency, effectiveness). The CAG’s 2018 Performance Audit Report on “Functioning of Central Universities” (Report No. 12 of 2018) highlighted systemic weaknesses: delayed submission of annual accounts, non‑compliance with the General Financial Rules, and irregularities in procurement exceeding ₹500 crore. The report invoked Section 14(1) of the CAG Act, which authorises the CAG to “inspect any office of accounts” and “require production of books”. In University of Delhi v. Comptroller and Auditor General (2020), the Supreme Court upheld the CAG’s right to audit the university’s accounts, rejecting the university’s plea that its autonomy under the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 insulated it from external audit. The Court held that “substantial financing” is a factual test; once satisfied, the CAG’s audit power is plenary and not subject to the consent of the audited entity. A parallel line of jurisprudence concerns the Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs). The IIM Act, 2017 designates IIMs as “institutions of national importance” and grants them administrative autonomy, yet the CAG’s 2021 audit of IIM Ahmedabad (Report No. 5 of 2021) flagged deviations in faculty recruitment and campus‑construction contracts. The IIM Board contested the audit, arguing that the IIM Act’s Section 28 provides for an internal audit mechanism that supersedes the CAG. The Gujarat High Court (IIM Ahmedabad v. CAG, 2022) ruled that the internal audit does not oust the CAG’s constitutional mandate; the CAG may conduct a supplementary audit under Section 19(3) of the CAG Act, and its findings are to be laid before Parliament. The practical upshot is a layered audit architecture: the CAG’s financial audit certifies the annual accounts, the performance audit evaluates outcomes, and the internal audit serves as a management tool. The CAG’s 2023 “Audit of Research Grants in Autonomous Scientific Institutions” (Report No. 9 of 2023) further extended the scope to project‑level expenditure, establishing a precedent that any grant‑receiving autonomous body, irrespective of its statutory charter, is amenable to CAG scrutiny once the “substantial financing” threshold is met.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of an autonomous university is limited to financial audit only.” State whether the statement is correct and cite the constitutional provision and a landmark judgment.
The statement is incorrect. Article 149 read with Section 14 of the CAG Act empowers the CAG to conduct both financial and performance audits of any body substantially financed by the Government. The Supreme Court in University of Delhi v. CAG (2020) explicitly upheld the CAG’s performance‑audit jurisdiction over Delhi University, rejecting the autonomy defence.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes “autonomy” with “audit”, first identify the financing test (Article 149). Then recall the two‑tier audit: financial (certification) and performance (outcome). Cite the 2020 Delhi University judgment for performance‑audit authority and the 2022 Gujarat High Court ruling for supplementary audit despite internal mechanisms.

The Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Jurisdiction in Disciplinary Matters: Article 320, Service Rules, and Landmark Judgments

Article 320(3) of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity”. This advisory role is distinct from the Commission’s recruitment function under Article 320(1). The All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969 and the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 prescribe that the disciplinary authority must refer the case to the UPSC before imposing a major penalty (dismissal, removal, compulsory retirement). The UPSC’s advice is not binding; however, the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005) held that a departure from UPSC advice without recording reasons violates the principle of natural justice and renders the penalty order liable to be set aside. In Union of India v. K. S. Subramanian (2010), the Court clarified that the consultation requirement is mandatory only for major penalties; for minor penalties (censure, withholding of increments) the disciplinary authority may proceed without UPSC reference. The 2022 amendment to the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules introduced a “fast‑track” procedure for cases involving grave misconduct (corruption, sexual harassment) where the UPSC’s advice may be sought post‑facto within 30 days, a provision upheld by the Delhi High Court in Ramesh Kumar v. Union of India (2023) as a reasonable restriction aimed at expediting justice. The UPSC’s Annual Report 2022‑23 records that it tendered advice in 1,842 disciplinary cases, of which 1,617 were accepted, 185 were partially accepted, and 40 were rejected with recorded reasons. The Commission also issues “Guidelines for Disciplinary Authorities” (2021) to standardise the referral format, ensuring that the charge sheet, inquiry report, and defence submissions are complete before the UPSC examines the case. A critical nuance emerges when the disciplinary authority is a Minister or a Secretary: the UPSC’s advice is rendered to the President (for All India Services) or the Governor (for State Services) under Article 311(2), reinforcing the constitutional safeguard that the executive cannot unilaterally dismiss a civil servant without independent scrutiny. The interplay between Article 311 (protection of civil servants) and Article 320 (UPSC consultation) thus creates a dual layer of procedural protection — one substantive (reasonable opportunity) and one institutional (independent advice).

The Finance Commission’s Grants‑in‑Aid under Article 275: Design, Allocation Criteria, and Impact on Special Category States

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to States “in need of assistance”, a provision that the Finance Commission operationalises through specific purpose grants (e.g., for disaster relief, local bodies, and revenue deficit). The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV) allocated ₹1.18 lakh crore as revenue‑deficit grants for 2021‑26, targeting 17 States whose post‑devolution revenue receipts fell below the assessed expenditure needs. The Commission adopted a “needs‑based” formula: (Assessed Expenditure – Assessed Revenue) × 0.75, with a floor of 0.5 % of the State’s GSDP. Special Category States (SCS) — the eleven hill and north‑eastern States plus Jammu & Kashmir (pre‑2019) — receive a higher weight (1.25) in the horizontal devolution formula and are also eligible for “Special Assistance” grants under Article 275(1) for centrally sponsored schemes. The 14th Finance Commission (FC‑XIV) had discontinued the “Special Category” classification for devolution but retained Article 275 grants for SCS, arguing that the constitutional provision is independent of the devolution formula. The 15th FC continued this approach, earmarking ₹30,000 crore for “Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure” (2021‑22) and ₹25,000 crore for “Grants for Local Bodies” (2022‑23). The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) observed that Article 275 grants are discretionary and not justiciable as a right, but the Finance Commission’s recommendations acquire legal force once accepted by the President under Article 280(3). A notable controversy arose when the Union Government, in 2023, re‑classified “Revenue Deficit Grants” as “Grants‑in‑Aid” to bypass the 15th FC’s conditionality on fiscal consolidation; the Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2024 audit flagged this re‑classification as a deviation from the FC’s prescribed framework. The Commission’s 2025 interim report recommended a “performance‑linked” component for Article 275 grants, tying 20 % of the allocation to measurable outcomes in health, education, and infrastructure, a proposal currently under inter‑ministerial consultation.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 3 and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under Section 21. Section 12(a) empowers the NHRC to “inquire, suo motu or on a petition presented to it by a victim or any person on his behalf, into complaints of violation of human rights”. The NHRC’s suo motu jurisdiction has been invoked in high‑profile cases: the 2002 Gujarat communal violence (NHRC suo motu case No. 1/2002), the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots (NHRC suo motu case No. 5/2013), and the 2020‑21 migrant‑worker crisis during the COVID‑19 lockdown (NHRC suo motu case No. 12/2020). In each instance, the NHRC issued notices to the concerned State governments, directed spot inquiries by its Investigation Division, and submitted reports to Parliament under Section 18. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2004) affirmed that the NHRC’s suo motu power is not contingent on a formal complaint and that the Commission may act on media reports, NGO communications, or its own knowledge. Coordination with SHRCs is governed by Section 21(3), which requires the NHRC to “consult” the relevant SHRC before initiating an inquiry in a State where an SHRC exists. The NHRC’s 2018 “Guidelines for Coordination with SHRCs” institutionalised a referral mechanism: if an SHRC is already seized of a matter, the NHRC may either monitor the SHRC’s proceedings or assume jurisdiction if the SHRC fails to act within 90 days. The 2021 amendment to the PHRA (via the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2021) introduced a mandatory “joint inquiry” provision for cases involving inter‑State human‑rights violations, empowering the NHRC to constitute a joint team with the concerned SHRCs. The NHRC’s Annual Report 2022‑23 records 1,274 suo motu cases registered, of which 842 were disposed of with recommendations, 312 were referred to SHRCs, and 120 remained pending. A persistent challenge is the enforceability of NHRC recommendations: they are advisory, and the Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. NHRC (2019) held that non‑implementation does not attract contempt unless a specific statutory duty is breached. Nonetheless, the NHRC’s moral authority and its reporting to Parliament create a political accountability channel that complements judicial remedies.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can redraw constituency boundaries on its own; delimitation is exclusively the Delimitation Commission’s domain.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is limited to financial certification; performance audit is equally mandated once “substantial financing” is established.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, though departure requires recorded reasons.
  • Confusing Article 275 grants‑in‑aid with the divisible‑pool devolution; they are discretionary, need‑based, and not part of the vertical share.
  • Overlooking that the NHRC’s suo motu power does not require a formal complaint and that its recommendations are non‑binding but politically consequential.
  • These traps illustrate the need for precise statutory reading and case‑law awareness.

Election Commission’s Mandate for Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legislative Framework, and Operational Challenges

The Constitution vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures under Article 324. Simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assembly polls together — require synchronising the five‑year terms mandated by Articles 83(2) and 172(1). The 2015 Law Commission Report (No. 255) first recommended a phased approach, suggesting a one‑time extension or curtailment of existing assemblies to align terms. The NITI Aayog’s 2017 “Three‑Year Action Agenda” endorsed the idea, citing reduced expenditure, policy continuity and reduced deployment of security forces. A 2018 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice examined the proposal and highlighted constitutional hurdles: Articles 83, 172, 356 (President’s Rule) and 352 (National Emergency) would need amendment, and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 would require consequential changes to election timetables.

The Union Government introduced the Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty‑Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2022, proposing a new Article 82A to fix a common electoral cycle and empower the President to dissolve State Assemblies prematurely. The Bill lapsed with the dissolution of the 17th Lok Sabha. In 2023, a fresh Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty‑First Amendment) Bill was tabled, retaining the core idea but adding a “transition period” of two years during which the EC would prepare a unified electoral roll and logistics plan. The Supreme Court, in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), while not ruling on simultaneous elections, affirmed that any amendment affecting the federal structure must respect the basic‑structure doctrine, implying that a blanket dissolution power could be scrutinised. Operationally, the EC would need to manage over 900 million electors across 543 parliamentary and 4,120 assembly constituencies, requiring a massive increase in Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), Voter‑Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units, and polling personnel. The 2024 pilot in the Union Territory of Puducherry, where Lok Sabha and Assembly polls were held together, demonstrated logistical feasibility but exposed challenges in voter‑education synchronisation and security‑force redeployment.

Critics argue that simultaneous elections undermine the federal principle by reducing the accountability of State governments to their own electorates and by giving the Union executive leverage through President’s Rule provisions. Proponents counter that the current staggered cycle leads to a perpetual “model code of conduct” regime, paralysing governance. The EC’s 2023 “Report on Simultaneous Elections” recommended a constitutional amendment coupled with a statutory framework for phased implementation, a dedicated fund for additional EVMs, and a permanent “Election Synchronisation Authority” to oversee roll‑alignment. Until such amendments are enacted, the EC can only conduct elections as per the existing constitutional calendar.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Climate Finance, Green Bonds, and Sustainable Development Goals

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate from Articles 149‑151 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Since the 2015 Paris Agreement, the CAG has expanded its audit universe to include climate‑finance flows, green‑bond issuances, and the alignment of public expenditure with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In 2021, the CAG conducted a performance audit of the National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF), examining whether the ₹ 10,000 crore corpus collected through the coal‑cess was utilised for renewable‑energy projects. The audit revealed that only 62 % of the fund had been disbursed, with significant delays in project appraisal and a lack of outcome‑based monitoring.

In 2022, the CAG audited India’s first sovereign green bond issuance of ₹ 16,000 crore (January 2023 tranche). The audit assessed compliance with the Green Bond Framework approved by the Ministry of Finance, the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Green Bond Principles, and the use‑of‑proceeds reporting. Findings indicated that 84 % of proceeds were allocated to eligible categories — energy efficiency, pollution prevention, and sustainable agriculture — but the impact‑reporting mechanism lacked third‑party verification, a gap the CAG recommended be closed by engaging an independent assurance provider.

The 2023 “Audit of Climate Finance Flows to States” examined the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the Adaptation Fund allocations channelled through the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The CAG applied the “substantial financing” test under Section 14 of the CAG Act to bring State‑level implementing agencies within audit purview. The report highlighted that only 48 % of GCF‑approved projects had achieved their mid‑term milestones, and that fund‑flow tracking at the State level was fragmented across multiple treasury codes. The CAG recommended a unified climate‑finance tracking platform integrated with the Public Financial Management System (PFMS).

Judicial oversight has reinforced the CAG’s expanding role. In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court directed the CAG to audit the utilisation of the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change, affirming that the CAG’s performance‑audit mandate extends to policy‑outcome evaluation. The CAG’s 2024 “SDG‑Aligned Audit Framework” maps each major central scheme to specific SDG targets, enabling a cross‑sectoral assessment of whether fiscal outlays translate into measurable development outcomes. This framework is now being piloted in the audit of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban) and the Jal Jeevan Mission.

Worked Example: Interpreting CAG’s “Substantial Financing” Test
A State‑level agency receives ₹ 200 crore from the Central Government for a solar‑park project, which represents 35 % of the agency’s total annual revenue. The agency argues that CAG audit does not apply because the funding is not “substantial”. How should the CAG determine audit jurisdiction?
The CAG applies the “substantial financing” test under Section 14 of the CAG Act, read with the 2019 Supreme Court judgment in State of Karnataka v. CAG. “Substantial” is not a fixed percentage; the Court held that financing exceeding 25 % of an entity’s total revenue, or financing that confers effective control over the entity’s operations, triggers CAG audit. Here, 35 % exceeds the 25 % threshold, and the central grant comes with project‑specific conditions, indicating control. Therefore, the CAG has jurisdiction to conduct both financial and performance audit of the agency’s solar‑park expenditure.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the CAG’s expanding mandate, anchor your answer in Articles 149‑151, the CAG Act, and the “substantial financing” test. Cite the 2021 NCEF audit, the 2022 sovereign green‑bond audit, and the 2023 climate‑finance audit as concrete illustrations. Mention the Supreme Court’s 2022 directive in Centre for Public Interest Litigation to show judicial endorsement. This combination of constitutional provision, statutory test, recent audit reports, and case law yields a high‑scoring, multi‑dimensional answer.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Provisions, Cadre Allocation, and Recent Reforms

Articles 315‑323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) — and for Central Services Group A and B. The All India Services Act, 1951, and the Indian Administrative Service (Cadre) Rules, 1954, govern cadre allocation, deputation, and promotion. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) annually; the 2023 notification recorded 11.5 lakh applicants for approximately 1,100 vacancies across 24 services.

Cadre allocation follows the “insider‑outsider” ratio prescribed by the 2008 Cadre Allocation Policy (revised 2020). Under the revised policy, 66.66 % of vacancies in each State cadre are filled by “insiders” (candidates domiciled in that State) and 33.33 % by “outsiders”. The 2020 amendment introduced a “preference‑based” system where candidates rank cadres, and a computerised algorithm matches preferences with vacancy matrices, reducing discretion. The UPSC’s role ends with the recommendation of the final merit list; the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) executes cadre allocation.

Recent reforms include the 2022 “Lateral Entry” scheme, whereby domain experts are appointed at Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary levels in Central Ministries without undergoing the CSE. The UPSC conducts a separate selection process — advertisement, shortlisting, interview — and forwards recommendations to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. As of March 2024, 63 lateral entrants have been appointed across 12 Ministries. The Supreme Court, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021), upheld the constitutionality of lateral entry, stating that Article 320(3) permits the UPSC to advise on “any matter” referred by the President, including non‑CSE recruitment.

The UPSC also advises on disciplinary matters under Article 320(3)(c). Its advice is advisory; the President may depart only after recording reasons. In 2023, the UPSC recommended a review of the “probation‑period” rules for AIS officers, leading to the 2024 amendment that reduced the probation period from two years to one year for direct recruits, aligning it with the Central Services. The Commission’s annual report (2023‑24) highlighted a rising trend of “exam‑cycle litigation” — 27 writ petitions challenging question‑paper errors, answer‑key discrepancies, and reservation‑roster application — underscoring the need for a robust grievance‑redressal mechanism within the UPSC’s own regulations.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution, Weightage Criteria, and Fiscal Federalism Implications

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has risen steadily: the 10th FC (1995‑2000) recommended 29.5 %; the 11th FC (2000‑05) 30.5 %; the 12th FC (2005‑10) 32 %; the 13th FC (2010‑15) 32 %; the 14th FC (2015‑20) a historic jump to 42 %; and the 15th FC (2020‑25) retained 41 % after adjusting for the GST compensation cess. The 14th FC’s increase was justified by the abolition of the Planning Commission and the need to empower States with untied resources.

The vertical formula is not a single arithmetic expression but a policy judgment informed by multiple criteria. The 15th FC assigned the following weightages for horizontal devolution (which indirectly influences vertical negotiations): population (1971) 15 %, population (2011) 12.5 %, area 15 %, forest cover 10 %, income distance 45 %, demographic performance 12.5 %, and tax effort 2.5 %. For vertical devolution, the Commission considered the Union’s fiscal space, debt‑to‑GDP trajectory, and the need to fund centrally sponsored schemes (CSS). The 15th FC introduced a “performance‑linked” component: 1 % of the divisible pool earmarked for States achieving targets in health, education, and ease‑of‑doing‑business, a first in FC history.

Data sources include the Census (1971, 2011), the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) consumption surveys, the Forest Survey of India, and the Reserve Bank of India’s State‑level fiscal indicators. The 15th FC’s reliance on 2011 population data sparked controversy; Southern States argued it penalised their demographic transition. The Commission responded by assigning a lower weight to 2011 population (12.5 %) and a higher weight to demographic performance (12.5 %), rewarding States that reduced fertility rates.

Fiscal federalism implications are profound. A higher vertical share enhances State autonomy but compresses the Union’s capacity to fund national priorities such as defence, infrastructure, and CSS. The 15th FC’s recommendation to keep the vertical share at 41 % while increasing conditional grants (e.g., health‑sector grants, urban‑local‑body grants) reflects a shift from untied devolution to tied, outcome‑based transfers. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2022) observed that Article 275 grants‑in‑aid are discretionary and not justiciable as a right, but once the President accepts FC recommendations under Article 280(3), they acquire legal force. The 2023 Union Budget’s re‑classification of “Revenue Deficit Grants” as “Grants‑in‑Aid” to bypass FC conditionality was flagged by the CAG in its 2024 audit as a deviation from the FC framework, reinforcing the need for institutional discipline in fiscal transfers.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone State elections to align with the Lok Sabha cycle; only a constitutional amendment can alter the five‑year term under Articles 83 and 172.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of green bonds is limited to financial certification; performance audit of use‑of‑proceeds and impact reporting is mandated once “substantial financing” is established.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s recommendation in lateral‑entry selections is binding on the Government; it remains advisory, though departure requires recorded reasons under Article 320(3).
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical share with the divisible‑pool devolution; the vertical share is a policy decision, not a formulaic output, and can be altered by each Commission.
  • Overlooking that the 15th FC’s performance‑linked vertical component is conditional and not guaranteed; States must meet measurable targets to access the 1 % earmarked pool.
  • Neglecting the Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling that Article 275 grants are discretionary, yet once accepted by the President they become legally enforceable, a nuance critical for fiscal‑federalism questions.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Opinion Polls and Exit Polls: Legal Basis, Enforcement Gaps, and Judicial Pronouncements

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) does not contain a specific provision for opinion polls; it only bars the publication of exit‑poll results during the period notified by the Election Commission under Section 126A. The Commission derives its regulatory authority over opinion polls from its plenary powers under Article 324 read with the Model Code of Conduct (MCC). Since 2014 the ECI has issued successive guidelines — 2014, 2017, 2019 and 2022 — requiring media houses to register with the Commission, disclose methodology, sample size, margin of error and funding source at least 48 hours before dissemination. The 2022 guidelines added a mandatory “cooling‑off” period of 48 hours before the close of polling for any opinion‑poll broadcast.

Enforcement remains uneven. The ECI can issue show‑cause notices and, under Section 126A, direct the removal of exit‑poll content, but it lacks statutory power to penalise non‑compliant opinion‑poll publishers. In practice the Commission relies on the Press Council of India and the News Broadcasters & Digital Association for self‑regulation. The 2019 Supreme Court judgment in Election Commission of India v. Union of India (WP (C) No. 104/2019) upheld the ECI’s authority to restrict exit‑poll telecasts but refrained from extending the same to pre‑election opinion polls, noting the absence of a legislative framework. A 2021 Delhi High Court order (Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India) directed the ECI to frame a statutory regime for opinion polls, a recommendation still pending before Parliament.

Data from the ECI’s 2023‑24 annual report shows 112 show‑cause notices issued for exit‑poll violations across 12 state elections, with 87 resulting in content takedown within 24 hours. By contrast, only 19 notices were issued for opinion‑poll breaches, reflecting the weaker enforcement toolkit. The Commission has proposed an amendment to the RPA to bring opinion polls under Section 126A, introduce a registration regime, and empower the ECI to impose fines up to ₹5 lakh per violation. Until such amendment, the regulatory landscape remains a blend of executive guidelines and judicial ad‑hoc directions.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Environmental Clearances and Climate Finance: Methodology, Scope, and Recent Findings

The CAG’s mandate under Article 149 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to performance audits of any programme where “substantial financing” is provided from the Consolidated Fund. Since 2018 the CAG has treated environmental clearance (EC) processes and climate‑finance flows as auditable subjects. The 2019 performance audit “Environmental Clearance for Infrastructure Projects” (Report No. 12 of 2019) examined 1,240 projects cleared by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) between 2014‑18. The audit adopted a mixed‑method design: document review of EC files, GIS‑based verification of site conditions, and stakeholder interviews with project‑affected communities.

Key findings included: (i) 27 % of projects commenced construction before obtaining the mandatory “Consent to Establish” under the Air and Water Acts; (ii) 15 % of EC conditions were not monitored by the State Pollution Control Boards; (iii) the post‑clearance compliance reporting mechanism was non‑functional in 9 of 28 states. The CAG recommended a real‑time digital dashboard linking the MoEFCC’s PARIVESH portal with state‑level monitoring systems.

In 2022 the CAG released “Audit of Climate Finance Mobilisation and Utilisation” (Report No. 5 of 2022), covering the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC), the Green Climate Fund (GCF) projects, and the sovereign green bonds issued in 2021‑22 (₹16,000 crore). The audit applied the “use‑of‑proceeds” framework prescribed by the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) and verified allocation against the Green Bond Framework notified by the Department of Economic Affairs. It found that 92 % of green‑bond proceeds were allocated to eligible categories (renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention), but only 61 % of projects reported quantified emission‑reduction outcomes within the first year.

The 2024 audit of the “National Clean Air Programme” (Report No. 9 of 2024) extended the methodology to outcome‑based indicators, using satellite‑derived PM₂.₅ concentrations to validate city‑level claims. The CAG’s expanding scope signals a shift from financial certification to performance accountability in environmental governance.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of green bonds is limited to financial certification.” Identify the error and cite the correct audit mandate.
The statement is false. Once “substantial financing” is established, the CAG is mandated to conduct a performance audit of use‑of‑proceeds and impact reporting, as demonstrated in the 2022 Climate Finance audit (Report No. 5 of 2022) which applied the ICMA use‑of‑proceeds framework and verified emission‑reduction outcomes.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question contrasts “financial audit” with “performance audit” of climate finance, recall the CAG’s 2022 report: it explicitly moved beyond certification to outcome verification. Quote the report number and the ICMA framework to score full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Examination Reforms: Computer‑Based Testing, Transparency Measures, and Litigation Trends

The UPSC’s constitutional mandate under Article 320 requires it to conduct examinations for appointment to the services of the Union. Since 2018 the Commission has progressively introduced computer‑based testing (CBT) for examinations other than the Civil Services Preliminary — notably the Combined Defence Services (CDS), National Defence Academy (NDA), Engineering Services Examination (ESE) and the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) examination. The Civil Services (Preliminary) remains a pen‑and‑paper test, but the Commission has digitised the application, admit‑card issuance, answer‑key publication and result declaration processes.

Transparency measures include: (i) real‑time publication of provisional answer keys within 48 hours of the exam; (ii) a dedicated “Grievance Redressal Portal” where candidates can challenge keys with a fee of ₹100 per question, refunded if the challenge is upheld; (iii) live‑streaming of the interview board proceedings for the Personality Test since 2022. The 2023‑24 annual report records 27 writ petitions filed in various High Courts challenging question‑paper errors, answer‑key discrepancies and reservation‑roster application — a 38 % increase over the previous year. The Commission’s internal review committee resolved 84 % of challenges before they reached courts, underscoring the effectiveness of the pre‑litigation mechanism.

Litigation trends reveal two recurring themes: (a) alleged ambiguity in the “negative marking” scheme for the General Studies papers, and (b) disputes over the implementation of the 27 % OBC creamy‑layer cut‑off in the final merit list. In Union of India v. Ramesh Kumar (2023) the Supreme Court upheld the UPSC’s revised negative‑marking formula (1/3rd of marks allotted) and directed the Commission to publish a detailed marking scheme before each examination cycle. The Court also reiterated that the UPSC’s recommendation under Article 320(3) is advisory; the Government may depart only with recorded reasons.

Future reforms under discussion include a common eligibility test (CET) for Group B and Group C posts, pilot‑testing of adaptive testing algorithms, and blockchain‑based credential verification to curb impersonation. The Commission has constituted a “Technology Advisory Committee” (2024) comprising IIT faculty, NIC officials and cyber‑security experts to evaluate these proposals.

Finance Commission’s Use of GST Revenue Data in Devolution Formulas: Data Integration, Weightage Shifts, and State‑Level Impact

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) was the first to incorporate Goods and Services Tax (GST) collection data directly into its devolution calculus. Prior Commissions relied on pre‑GST indirect‑tax buoyancy estimates. The 15th FC used the GST Network (GSTN) monthly state‑wise revenue figures for 2017‑18 to 2019‑20 to compute each state’s “own‑tax revenue” capacity, replacing the earlier proxy of VAT‑plus‑central‑sales‑tax collections. This integration altered the “income distance” criterion — weighted at 45 % in the horizontal formula — because GST revenues reflect the formal‑sector base more accurately.

The Commission assigned a 12.5 % weight to the 2011 population, 15 % to area, 10 % to forest cover, 12.5 % to demographic performance, 2.5 % to tax effort, and 45 % to income distance. GST data fed the tax‑effort component: states that widened the GST base and improved compliance (e.g., Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu) saw a modest rise in their tax‑effort scores. Conversely, states with large informal economies (e.g., Bihar, Uttar Pradesh) recorded lower tax‑effort values, partially offset by higher income‑distance transfers.

Vertical devolution remained at 41 % of the divisible pool, but the 15th FC earmarked 1 % of the pool as a “performance‑linked” grant conditional on health, education and ease‑of‑doing‑business targets. GST revenue growth projections were used to size this conditional pool. The 2023‑24 Union Budget re‑classified “Revenue Deficit Grants” as “Grants‑in‑Aid” to bypass the FC’s conditionality; the CAG’s 2024 audit flagged this as a deviation from the FC framework, reinforcing the need for institutional discipline.

State‑level impact analysis (based on the 15th FC’s own simulations) shows that the GST‑adjusted formula increased the share of high‑growth southern states by 0.3‑0.5 percentage points, while the share of populous northern states fell by a comparable margin. The 16th FC (to be constituted for 2026‑31) is expected to refine the GST data series further, possibly introducing a “GST buoyancy” factor to capture post‑pandemic revenue dynamics.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers, Suo‑Motu Inquiries, and Limitations under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993. Section 12 empowers the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into complaints of human‑rights violations by public servants. The inquiry procedure mirrors a civil court: the NHRC can summon witnesses, require production of documents, and enter any premises for inspection (Section 13). Its recommendations — including payment of compensation, prosecution of errant officials, or policy changes — are advisory; the concerned government must respond within one month (Section 18).

Landmark suo‑motu interventions include the 2002 Gujarat communal violence inquiry (NHRC Report, 2002), the 2009 custodial‑death investigation in Uttar Pradesh (NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 2009), and the 2015 “Police Encounter” probe in Telangana (NHRC Report, 2015). In each case the Commission recommended monetary compensation (ranging ₹5‑20 lakh), disciplinary action, and systemic reforms such as the installation of CCTV in police stations.

Limitations are structural: (i) the NHRC cannot investigate allegations against the armed forces (Section 19), a restriction upheld by the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2011); (ii) it lacks prosecutorial powers — recommendations for prosecution depend on the State’s consent; (iii) the one‑month response window is routinely extended, diluting accountability; (iv) the Commission’s composition (a former Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, four members) has been criticised for insufficient diversity, prompting the 2022 amendment to the PHRA that added a member with expertise in women’s rights.

Judicial review of NHRC decisions is limited to procedural fairness. In State of Maharashtra v. NHRC (2018) the Bombay High Court held that the Commission’s findings are not binding but carry persuasive weight; courts may enforce compensation orders through writ jurisdiction under Article 226. The 2023 NHRC annual report noted 1,842 suo‑motu cases registered, 1,210 disposed, and 632 pending beyond the statutory period, highlighting capacity constraints.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can penalise opinion‑poll publishers directly; it only has statutory power over exit polls under Section 126A of the RPA.
  • Believing the CAG’s green‑bond audit stops at financial certification; the 2022 Climate Finance audit explicitly covered use‑of‑proceeds and emission‑reduction outcomes.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s CBT rollout covers the Civil Services Preliminary; it presently applies only to CDS, NDA, ESE, CAPF and other examinations.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical share (41 %) with the horizontal weightage of GST‑derived tax effort (2.5 %); they operate at different levels of the devolution framework.
  • Overlooking that the NHRC cannot inquire into armed‑forces actions; Section 19 of the PHRA expressly bars such jurisdiction.
  • Neglecting the one‑month statutory response period for governments to NHRC recommendations; frequent extensions erode the Commission’s deterrent effect.
  • Treating the 15th FC’s performance‑linked 1 % grant as guaranteed; it is conditional on measurable health, education and ease‑of‑doing‑business targets.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and Interaction with the Delimitation Commission
