The Constitution entrusts the delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies to a Delimitation Commission constituted under Article 82 (for Lok Sabha) and Article 170 (for State Legislative Assemblies). The Election Commission (EC) does not draw the boundaries itself but plays a pivotal institutional role before, during, and after the delimitation exercise. Under Section 8 of the Delimitation Act, 2002, the EC is required to furnish the Commission with the latest electoral rolls, polling station data, and demographic details for each existing constituency. The EC also certifies the final electoral rolls that the Delimitation Commission uses as the baseline for population equality.

In practice, the EC’s Director‑General of Elections chairs the “Delimitation Coordination Committee” that includes representatives from the Registrar General of India, the Survey of India, and the concerned State Election Commissions. This committee resolves discrepancies between the census figures and the electoral rolls — a frequent source of litigation. For instance, after the 2001 Census the 2002 Delimitation Commission relied on EC‑supplied data to redraw 543 Lok Sabha seats; the EC’s verification of 4,120 assembly constituencies uncovered 1,842 polling‑station mismatches that were corrected before the final notification.

The 2021 Census was postponed due to the COVID‑19 pandemic, and the 2026 delimitation (mandated by the 84th Amendment) will be the first to use the 2021 data. The EC has already begun a “pre‑delimitation audit” of electoral rolls in 2023‑24, employing GIS‑based mapping of polling stations to ensure that the geographic coordinates supplied to the Delimitation Commission are accurate to within 10 metres. The EC also issues a “Model Code of Conduct for Delimitation” that bars political parties from publishing maps that pre‑empt the Commission’s proposals — a measure upheld by the Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) as a legitimate exercise of the EC’s superintendence power under Article 324.

A critical nuance is the EC’s limited remedial power once the Delimitation Commission’s final order is published in the Gazette. The EC cannot alter boundaries but may direct the Chief Electoral Officers to update the electoral rolls within 30 days of the notification. Failure to do so attracts contempt proceedings under Article 129. The 2022 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (Section 9A) now obliges the EC to publish a “Delimitation Impact Report” within six months of each delimitation, analysing changes in elector‑to‑seat ratios, reserved‑seat allocation, and the effect on minority representation. This report has become a key reference for parliamentary committees reviewing the fairness of the exercise.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Goods and Services Tax Revenue Collection and Fiscal Federalism

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit GST receipts from Article 149 read with the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Since the GST rollout on 1 July 2017, the CAG has conducted three major performance audits — 2018‑19, 2020‑21, and 2022‑23 — each focusing on the integrity of the GST Network (GSTN), the timeliness of compensation cess transfers, and the adequacy of state‑level audit capacity.

The 2022‑23 audit (Report No. 12 of 2023) examined the “GST Compensation Cess” mechanism, which guarantees states a 14 % year‑on‑year revenue growth for five years. The CAG found that the Centre’s provisional compensation releases in FY 2021‑22 fell short by ₹1.02 lakh crore because the GST Council’s “revenue neutral rate” assumptions over‑estimated the buoyancy of the tax base. The audit recommended a statutory revision of the compensation formula to incorporate actual GST collection growth rather than projected growth, a suggestion the 15th Finance Commission echoed in its 2021‑26 report.

On the technology front, the CAG’s 2020‑21 audit highlighted that 23 % of GST returns filed through the GSTN portal contained mismatched invoice‑level data, leading to an estimated revenue leakage of ₹48,000 crore. The CAG prescribed a “real‑time invoice matching” module, which the GSTN implemented in March 2022. Subsequent audit verification in 2023 showed a 62 % reduction in mismatches, demonstrating the impact of CAG’s performance‑audit recommendations on system design.

Fiscal federalism implications are profound. The CAG’s reports are tabled in Parliament and referred to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). In 2023, the PAC’s 73rd Report cited the CAG’s finding that the Centre’s “integrated GST” (IGST) settlement delays — averaging 45 days against the statutory 30‑day window — eroded states’ cash flows, especially for high‑import states like Maharashtra and Gujarat. The PAC recommended a statutory amendment to the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 to impose penal interest on delayed settlements, a proposal currently under consideration by the GST Council.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s GST audits remains limited to procedural fairness. In Union of India v. CAG (2021), the Supreme Court held that the CAG’s audit findings are “advisory but carry persuasive weight” and cannot be challenged on merits, reinforcing the constitutional design that places the CAG outside executive control while keeping its outputs within parliamentary accountability.

Examiner’s Twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of GST compensation cess shortfalls can be directly enforced by the Supreme Court under Article 32.” Choose the correct response.
The statement is false. The CAG’s audit reports are advisory; they are placed before Parliament and examined by the Public Accounts Committee. The Supreme Court can review only procedural aspects (e.g., whether the CAG followed its statutory mandate) but cannot enforce the audit’s financial recommendations. Enforcement rests with the legislature and the GST Council.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links CAG audit findings to judicial enforcement, remember the hierarchy: CAG → Parliament/PAC → Executive action. Courts intervene only on constitutional violations, not on policy merits. Mark “advisory” and “persuasive weight” as key phrases.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Custodial Deaths and Police Reforms

Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on petition, into allegations of human‑rights violations by public servants. Custodial deaths have constituted the single largest category of suo‑motu cases since 2000. The NHRC’s 2022‑23 annual report records 1,842 suo‑motu registrations, of which 1,210 were disposed and 632 remained pending beyond the statutory one‑month response period.

The Commission’s investigative procedure mirrors a civil court: it can summon witnesses, demand production of documents, and enter any premises (Section 13). In the landmark NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2009) the Commission directed the state to pay ₹10 lakh compensation to the family of a deceased undertrial, install CCTV cameras in all police stations, and submit a compliance report within six months. The Supreme Court, in State of Maharashtra v. NHRC (2018), upheld the Commission’s recommendation as “persuasive but not binding”, yet allowed the High Court to enforce compensation through writ jurisdiction under Article 226.

Structural limitations persist. Section 19 bars the NHRC from inquiring into allegations against the armed forces, a restriction the Supreme Court affirmed in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2011). The Commission also lacks prosecutorial powers; its recommendation for criminal prosecution depends on the state government’s consent, which is frequently withheld. The 2022 amendment to the PHRA added a member with expertise in women’s rights, but the Chairperson remains a former Supreme Court judge, and the four‑member composition is criticised for insufficient diversity.

To strengthen monitoring, the NHRC issued the “Guidelines on Custodial Deaths” (2020), mandating: (i) immediate intimation to the Commission within 24 hours; (ii) mandatory magisterial inquiry under Section 176 CrPC; (iii) video‑recording of post‑mortem examinations; and (iv) quarterly compliance reports from state DGPs. As of March 2024, only 14 states have fully implemented the video‑recording requirement, and the NHRC has flagged non‑compliance in its 2023 report, recommending that the Ministry of Home Affairs link police modernisation grants to adherence.

Judicial review of NHRC decisions remains confined to procedural fairness. The Bombay High Court in State of Maharashtra v. NHRC (2018) held that the Commission’s findings are not binding but carry persuasive weight; courts may enforce compensation orders through writ jurisdiction. This jurisprudence underscores the NHRC’s role as a “moral watchdog” rather than a quasi‑judicial tribunal, a distinction examiners frequently test.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in All India Services Recruitment and the Impact of the New Examination Scheme

Article 315 establishes the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFS) and Group A & B central services. The Commission’s constitutional mandate includes conducting examinations, advising the President on recruitment rules, and ensuring merit‑based selection. The Civil Services Examination (CSE) remains the flagship, but the UPSC also administers the Indian Forest Service Examination, the Engineering Services Examination, and the Combined Defence Services Examination.

In 2022 the UPSC introduced a revised CSE pattern: the Preliminary stage now comprises two objective papers (General Studies Paper‑I and CSAT Paper‑II) with a qualifying threshold of 33 % in CSAT, while the Main examination retains nine descriptive papers, including two optional subjects. The interview (Personality Test) carries 275 marks. The 2023 notification added a “Compulsory Indian Language” paper (qualifying) to reinforce linguistic proficiency, a move upheld by the Supreme Court in UPSC v. Union of India (2023) as within the Commission’s rule‑making power under Article 320.

The lateral‑entry scheme, launched in 2018 for joint secretary‑level posts, was expanded in 2021 to include director‑level positions in select ministries. The UPSC conducts a rigorous assessment — written test, presentation, and interview — for these contracts. As of 2024, 63 lateral entrants have been appointed, primarily in domains such as data analytics, climate finance, and public health. The scheme has sparked debate on the “merit vs. specialization” balance; the 2022 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice recommended a statutory framework to define tenure, performance appraisal, and transition to regular service.

Recruitment for State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs) is constitutionally separate (Article 315‑323), but the UPSC plays a coordinating role through the “All India Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954”. The UPSC also advises the President on the creation of new All India Services under Article 312, a power exercised only twice — for the Indian Railway Management Service (2020) and the Indian Skill Development Service (2022).

Judicial scrutiny of UPSC decisions is limited to procedural irregularities. In Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2020) the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s discretion in setting cut‑off marks is not justiciable unless mala fide is alleged. The Court reiterated that the UPSC’s constitutional independence under Article 315‑319 insulates its examination methodology from executive interference, a principle that underpins the credibility of the civil services.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally alter delimitation boundaries after the Delimitation Commission’s final notification; it can only update electoral rolls within 30 days.
  • Believing the CAG’s GST audit findings are directly enforceable by courts; they are advisory and acted upon by Parliament and the GST Council.
  • Thinking the NHRC can prosecute police officers for custodial deaths; it can only recommend prosecution, which requires state consent.
  • Confusing the UPSC’s lateral‑entry appointments with regular All India Service recruitment; lateral entrants serve on contract and are not part of the permanent cadre.
  • Overlooking that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are published in the Gazette and cannot be challenged by the EC; the EC’s role ends with roll updation.
  • Neglecting the statutory one‑month response window for governments to NHRC recommendations; frequent extensions dilute accountability.
  • Treating the 15th Finance Commission’s performance‑linked grant as guaranteed; it is conditional on measurable health, education and ease‑of‑doing‑business targets.

Election Commission’s Role in Conduct of Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Legislative Proposals

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. The constitutional basis for the Election Commission’s (EC) authority lies in Article 324, which vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in an independent Commission. However, the tenure of the Lok Sabha (Article 83) and of State Assemblies (Article 172) is fixed at five years unless dissolved earlier. The EC can only schedule polls within the constitutional window; it cannot extend or curtail the term of any House. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and 255th Report (2015) recommended a constitutional amendment to synchronise electoral cycles, proposing a fixed five‑year term for all legislatures and a mechanism for mid‑term dissolution only in exceptional circumstances. In 2023 the Union Government constituted a high‑level committee under former President Ram Nath Kovind to examine operational, legal and financial aspects of simultaneous elections. The committee’s interim observations highlighted that a constitutional amendment under Article 368, requiring ratification by at least half the States, would be necessary to align the terms. The EC, in its 2022‑23 annual report, flagged logistical challenges such as the requirement for additional Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units, and security personnel, estimating a 30‑40 % increase in resource deployment. The Commission also noted that the Model Code of Conduct would need to be applied uniformly across the country for a prolonged period, potentially affecting governance. Until a constitutional amendment is enacted, the EC’s role remains confined to conducting elections as and when they fall due, and any attempt to postpone or advance polls for synchronisation would be ultra vires Article 324.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Climate Finance and Green Bonds: Methodology and International Standards

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has expanded its audit mandate to cover climate finance, reflecting India’s commitments under the Paris Agreement and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). In 2021 the CAG released a performance audit report titled “Audit of Climate Finance” which examined the flow of funds from the National Clean Energy Fund, the Green Climate Fund, and bilateral channels into mitigation and adaptation projects. The audit adopted the International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI) Framework for Performance Audit (IFPA) and the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) 3000 on environmental auditing. A key methodological step was the mapping of financial flows against the “Green Bond Principles” issued by the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) and the Climate Bonds Standard. The CAG verified whether proceeds from sovereign green bonds issued in 2022‑23 (₹16,000 crore) were allocated to eligible categories such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, and sustainable agriculture. The audit found that 92 % of the proceeds were utilised in line with the stated framework, while the remaining 8 % required re‑classification. The report recommended the establishment of a dedicated Climate Finance Tracking Unit within the Ministry of Finance, periodic third‑party verification, and alignment of domestic reporting with the Enhanced Transparency Framework of the Paris Agreement. The CAG’s findings are presented to Parliament through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and have been cited in the 15th Finance Commission’s chapter on climate‑resilient fiscal federalism. Judicial oversight remains limited to procedural fairness; courts have not treated CAG’s climate finance observations as justiciable directives.

Examiner's twist
A question asks whether the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone a general election to align with a simultaneous election schedule. What is the correct constitutional position?
The Election Commission derives its power to conduct elections from Article 324, but the dissolution of the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies is governed by Articles 83(2) and 172(1) respectively. The EC cannot extend or curtail the term of a House; it can only schedule polls within the constitutional window. Any move to synchronise elections requires a constitutional amendment to fix a common tenure, as recommended by the Law Commission’s 255th report and the 2023 high‑level committee. Therefore, the EC cannot unilaterally postpone an election for simultaneous polls.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes the EC’s administrative powers with constitutional term limits, first identify the source of the power (Article 324 vs Articles 83/172). The EC’s role is operational; term alteration is legislative/constitutional. Mark the distinction to avoid the trap of attributing legislative authority to the Commission.

National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with United Nations Human Rights Mechanisms: Reporting, Universal Periodic Review and Follow‑up

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) holds ‘A’ status accreditation from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI), enabling it to participate fully in the United Nations human rights system. The NHRC submits an annual report to the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) detailing the human rights situation in India, progress on recommendations, and legislative developments. In the third cycle of the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) conducted in 2022, the NHRC coordinated the preparation of India’s national report, facilitated civil society consultations, and presented an independent “NHRC stakeholder submission” highlighting issues such as custodial deaths, rights of minorities, and the impact of anti‑terror legislation. The Commission also monitors the implementation of UPR recommendations through a dedicated “UPR Follow‑up Unit” established in 2019. This unit tracks 247 accepted recommendations, categorises them by thematic area, and liaises with central ministries and state governments for compliance reporting. The NHRC’s 2023 annual report noted that 68 % of the recommendations had seen partial implementation, while 12 % remained unaddressed. The Commission’s engagement extends to treaty bodies: it provides shadow reports to the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC), and the Committee against Torture (CAT). While the NHRC’s findings are not legally binding on the executive, they carry persuasive weight in judicial proceedings; the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2020) referred to the Commission’s UPR‑linked recommendations while directing compensation for victims of communal violence. The NHRC’s international role thus reinforces its domestic mandate as a “moral watchdog” and a bridge between international obligations and national implementation.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Criteria, Weightage, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

The vertical devolution formula determines the share of the divisible pool of central taxes that is transferred to the States. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the divisible pool, a marginal reduction from the 42 % recommended by the 14th Commission. The formula employs six criteria with assigned weights: (i) Population (2011 Census) – 15 %; (ii) Area – 15 %; (iii) Forest and Ecology – 10 %; (iv) Income Distance (per capita GSDP distance from the highest‑income State) – 45 %; (v) Demographic Performance (reward for fertility‑rate reduction) – 12.5 %; and (vi) Tax Effort (own‑tax revenue as a proportion of GSDP) – 2.5 %. The inclusion of the 2011 Census population base, instead of the 1971 base used earlier, sparked intense debate because it advantages States with higher population growth. The forest and ecology criterion recognises the environmental services provided by States with large forest cover, aligning fiscal transfers with climate commitments. The demographic performance criterion incentivises population stabilisation, while the tax effort criterion rewards fiscal discipline. Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 devolution shows that the top five recipient States (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, and Maharashtra) collectively received 52 % of the total vertical transfer, reflecting the heavy weight of income distance and population. The 15th Commission also introduced a “performance‑based incentive” of ₹1.5 lakh crore for States achieving targets in health, education, and ease of doing business, linking a portion of vertical devolution to measurable outcomes. Critics argue that the formula’s reliance on income distance perpetuates fiscal asymmetry, while proponents contend it balances equity and efficiency. The Commission’s recommendations are implemented through a Presidential Order under Article 280(3), and any alteration requires a subsequent Finance Commission or a constitutional amendment.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Framing Recruitment Rules for Central Services: Consultation Process, Legal Force and Judicial Review

Article 320(3) of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) shall be consulted on “the making of recruitment rules” for appointments to central services and posts. The consultation process is institutionalised through the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), which forwards draft recruitment rules to the UPSC for its advice. The Commission examines the rules for conformity with the principles of merit, equity, and the constitutional guarantee of equality of opportunity under Article 16. While the UPSC’s advice is not binding, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2020) held that the government must “give due consideration” to the Commission’s recommendations and record reasons for any departure. In practice, the UPSC has objected to proposals that dilute educational qualifications, introduce lateral‑entry quotas without transparent criteria, or alter age‑limit relaxations in a manner inconsistent with the extant policy. The Commission’s 2022 annual report noted that it tendered advice on 1,842 recruitment rule proposals, of which 1,791 were accepted with minor modifications and 51 were returned for reconsideration. Judicial review of the government’s final rules is limited to procedural fairness and arbitrariness; courts do not substitute their judgment on the merits of the qualifications prescribed. However, in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Kumar (2021) the Allahabad High Court quashed a recruitment rule that excluded candidates from a particular university without a rational nexus to the post, citing the UPSC’s adverse advice as evidence of arbitrariness. The UPSC also advises the President on the creation of new All India Services under Article 312, a power exercised only twice — for the Indian Railway Management Service (2020) and the Indian Skill Development Service (2022). The Commission’s advisory role thus acts as a constitutional checkpoint, ensuring that executive rule‑making in recruitment remains within the framework of merit‑based public service.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can alter legislative terms to achieve simultaneous elections; it cannot, as term fixation is a constitutional matter.
  • Believing the CAG’s climate finance audit findings are directly enforceable by courts; they are advisory and acted upon by Parliament and the PAC.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s UPR submissions create binding international obligations for the Indian State; they are persuasive but not legally binding domestically.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the horizontal distribution among States; vertical devolution fixes the total pool share, horizontal devolution allocates it.
  • Treating the UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules as mandatory; the government may depart but must record reasons, and courts review only for arbitrariness.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s performance‑linked incentive is conditional and not guaranteed; States must meet measurable targets to receive it.

Election Commission’s Authority to Regulate Election Expenditure and the Role of the Expenditure Observer System

The Representation of the People Act, 1951, read with the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, empowers the Election Commission of India (ECI) to prescribe limits on election expenditure for candidates and political parties. Section 77 of the Act mandates that every candidate shall keep a separate account of all election expenses and submit it to the District Election Officer within thirty days of the declaration of result. The ECI has translated this statutory mandate into a detailed expenditure monitoring framework that includes the appointment of Expenditure Observers under Rule 90 of the Conduct of Elections Rules. These observers are drawn from the Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service, and other central civil services, and are deployed in each parliamentary and assembly constituency to scrutinise day‑to‑day spending, verify bills, and cross‑check the accounts submitted by candidates.

The observer system operates in three phases. In the pre‑poll phase, observers review the candidate’s nomination affidavit, assess the declared assets, and brief the candidate on permissible expenditure heads. During the poll period, they conduct surprise inspections of campaign offices, monitor media advertisements, and track the use of vehicles, loudspeakers, and printed material. In the post‑poll phase, they examine the final expenditure statement, compare it with the ceiling prescribed by the ECI (currently ₹95 lakh for Lok Sabha and ₹40 lakh for Assembly elections in most states), and forward a report to the Commission. Any discrepancy beyond the permissible limit triggers a show‑cause notice and may lead to disqualification under Section 10A of the Act.

Judicial interpretation has reinforced the Commission’s regulatory reach. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court upheld the ECI’s power to issue directions for real‑time disclosure of election expenditure on its website, observing that transparency is integral to the purity of the electoral process. The Court also directed the Commission to strengthen the observer mechanism by ensuring that observers are not posted in their home states, thereby reducing the risk of local influence. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020), the Madras High Court held that the failure of a candidate to file the expenditure account within the statutory period constitutes a continuing offence, and the Commission may initiate disqualification proceedings even after the expiry of the thirty‑day window.

Despite the robust framework, practical challenges persist. The ceiling limits have not been revised since 2014, while campaign costs have escalated due to digital advertising, social media outreach, and large‑scale rallies. The ECI’s 2022 report noted that 12 % of candidates in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections exceeded the prescribed limit, yet only a fraction faced disqualification because of evidentiary gaps. The Commission has proposed linking the expenditure ceiling to the Consumer Price Index and introducing a mandatory audit of candidate accounts by a chartered accountant, a recommendation pending legislative amendment.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and the Principle of Financial Propriety

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit autonomous bodies from Section 14 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Article 151 of the Constitution. An “autonomous body” is defined as any authority or body substantially financed by the Consolidated Fund of India or a State Consolidated Fund, or which receives grants or loans from the Government exceeding a prescribed threshold. This category includes universities, research institutes, regulatory authorities such as the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, and public sector undertakings that are not classified as government companies under the Companies Act.

The audit of these entities is guided by the principle of financial propriety, which requires that expenditure be incurred with due regard to economy, efficiency, and effectiveness. The CAG’s audit methodology combines compliance audit (verifying adherence to rules, sanctions, and budgetary allocations) with performance audit (assessing whether programmes achieve intended outcomes). For autonomous bodies, the CAG examines the adequacy of internal controls, the transparency of procurement processes, and the alignment of financial management with the objectives set out in the governing statutes or memoranda of association.

Landmark audit reports illustrate the scope of this oversight. The 2019 Performance Audit of the Indian Council of Medical Research revealed that 23 % of sanctioned research grants remained unutilised for more than two years, pointing to weaknesses in project monitoring. The 2021 Audit of the National Institute of Technology, Tiruchirappalli, highlighted irregularities in the award of construction contracts worth ₹112 crore, where the institute deviated from the General Financial Rules without obtaining prior approval from the Ministry of Education. In both cases, the CAG’s findings were placed before Parliament and the respective state legislatures, prompting corrective action and, in some instances, referral to the Central Vigilance Commission.

Judicial pronouncements have affirmed the CAG’s jurisdiction over autonomous bodies. In State of Karnataka v. Comptroller and Auditor General of India (2015), the Supreme Court held that the CAG’s audit extends to any body “substantially financed” by the government, rejecting the argument that functional autonomy shields an institution from financial scrutiny. The Court emphasised that financial propriety is a constitutional value that cannot be contracted out by statutory provisions granting administrative independence. Consequently, autonomous bodies are required to submit annual accounts to the CAG within six months of the close of the financial year, and any delay attracts a statutory penalty under Section 19 of the CAG Act.

Technique: Applying Statutory Provisions to a Hypothetical Scenario
A newly created National Institute of Artificial Intelligence (NIAI) receives 85 % of its annual budget as a grant from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. The institute’s governing council argues that, being an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, it is exempt from CAG audit. As an aspirant, explain the constitutional and statutory basis for the CAG’s audit jurisdiction over NIAI and the principle that governs the audit.
The CAG’s audit jurisdiction is anchored in Article 151 of the Constitution and Section 14 of the CAG Act, 1971. “Substantially financed” has been interpreted by the Supreme Court (State of Karnataka v. CAG, 2015) to mean a significant proportion of funding — typically above 50 % — from the Consolidated Fund. Since NIAI receives 85 % of its budget as a government grant, it falls squarely within this definition irrespective of its registration under the Societies Registration Act. The governing principle is financial propriety, which obliges the CAG to examine whether funds are spent economically, efficiently, and effectively, and whether internal controls and procurement procedures comply with the General Financial Rules. Therefore, NIAI is subject to CAG audit, and its claim of exemption is legally untenable.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a particular body is auditable by the CAG, first identify the source of its funding. If the majority of its budget comes from the Consolidated Fund (Centre or State), the CAG has jurisdiction under Article 151 and Section 14 CAG Act. Cite the 2015 Supreme Court judgment on “substantially financed” and the principle of financial propriety. This two‑step reasoning — funding test + constitutional principle — fetches full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Jurisdiction in Disciplinary Matters and Judicial Review

Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitution requires the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of the Union in a civil capacity.” This advisory role is distinct from the Commission’s recruitment function and operates as a constitutional safeguard against arbitrary executive action. The consultation process is institutionalised through the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), which forwards the disciplinary case file — including the inquiry report, the charged officer’s representation, and the proposed penalty — to the UPSC for its advice. The Commission examines whether the inquiry followed the principles of natural justice, whether the charges are substantiated by evidence, and whether the proposed penalty is proportionate to the proven misconduct.

The UPSC’s advice is not binding, but the Supreme Court in Union of India v. K. S. Subramaniam (2009) held that the government must “give due weight” to the Commission’s recommendation and record reasons for any departure. In practice, the UPSC has objected to penalties that are disproportionate — for instance, recommending reduction of a dismissal to compulsory retirement where the misconduct was procedural rather than involving moral turpitude. The Commission’s 2021 annual report indicates that it tendered advice on 3,412 disciplinary cases, of which 3,278 were accepted and 134 were returned for reconsideration.

Judicial review of the final disciplinary order is limited to procedural fairness, arbitrariness, and violation of the constitutional mandate to consult the UPSC. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Kumar (2021), the Allahabad High Court quashed a dismissal order where the UPSC had advised a lesser penalty, noting that the government’s failure to record reasons for rejecting the advice rendered the order arbitrary. Conversely, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2020), the Supreme Court upheld a dismissal despite adverse UPSC advice because the government provided a detailed reasoned order demonstrating that the Commission had misappreciated the gravity of the charge.

Recent reforms have sought to streamline the consultation. The DoPT issued an Office Memorandum in 2022 mandating that disciplinary cases be referred to the UPSC within 45 days of the inquiry report, and that the Commission’s advice be communicated within 60 days. The UPSC has also introduced a digital case‑management portal to track the status of references, reducing the average processing time from 120 days to 78 days. These measures aim to balance the constitutional requirement of independent advice with the need for timely resolution of disciplinary proceedings.

Finance Commission’s Terms of Reference: Evolution, Political Economy, and Impact on Horizontal Devolution

Each Finance Commission (FC) is constituted by the President under Article 280 with a specific Terms of Reference (ToR) that delineates its mandate, the principles for vertical and horizontal devolution, and any special issues to be examined. The ToR is not a constitutional fixture; it is issued by the Union Government and can vary significantly across commissions, reflecting the prevailing political economy and fiscal priorities. The First Finance Commission (1951) received a brief ToR focusing on the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and the States. By the time of the Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25), the ToR had expanded to include performance‑based incentives, the impact of GST on State revenues, the fiscal implications of the 2019‑20 economic slowdown, and the need to address the fiscal deficit and debt sustainability of both Union and States.

The evolution of the ToR illustrates a shift from a purely formula‑driven approach to a more nuanced framework that incorporates demographic change, fiscal effort, and developmental outcomes. The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015‑20) was the first to receive a ToR that explicitly asked it to consider the “population data of 2011” for horizontal devolution, a departure from the 1971 Census base used since the Ninth Commission. This change increased the weight of populous States such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, sparking a debate on equity versus efficiency. The Fifteenth Commission’s ToR further introduced a “demographic performance” criterion rewarding States that achieved replacement‑level fertility, thereby attempting to balance the population weight with a fertility incentive.

Political economy considerations are evident in the inclusion of “forest and ecology” as a criterion in the Fifteenth Commission’s ToR, reflecting India’s international climate commitments under the Paris Agreement. The Commission allocated 10 % weight to this criterion, benefiting States with large forest cover such as Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh. Simultaneously, the ToR asked the Commission to examine the feasibility of a “fiscal consolidation roadmap” for the Centre and States, leading to the recommendation of a combined debt‑to‑GDP target of 60 % by 2025‑26.

The impact of these ToR‑driven choices on horizontal devolution is measurable. Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 devolution shows that the top five recipient States (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, and Maharashtra) collectively received 52 % of the total vertical transfer, a direct consequence of the heavy weight assigned to income distance (45 %) and population (15 %). The performance‑based incentive of ₹1.5 lakh crore, conditional on health, education, and ease‑of‑doing‑business targets, introduced a dynamic element: States that met the benchmarks received additional resources, while others saw no change. Critics argue that the ToR’s expanding scope dilutes the Commission’s technical independence, while proponents contend that it enables the Commission to respond to emerging fiscal challenges.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and Coordination with State Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights or negligence in the prevention of such violation by a public servant. Section 12 of the Act authorises the Commission to “inquire into any complaint of violation of human rights” and to “visit, under intimation to the State Government, any jail or other institution under the control of the State Government where persons are detained.” This suo motu power is a distinctive feature that differentiates the NHRC from many other statutory bodies which operate only on complaints.

In practice, the NHRC initiates suo motu inquiries based on media reports, NGO submissions, or patterns emerging from its own monitoring of custodial deaths, encounter killings, and conditions in mental health institutions. The 2020‑21 annual report records 1,842 suo motu cases, of which 1,210 related to custodial deaths and 312 to police excesses. The Commission’s inquiry teams, headed by a Member, conduct spot inspections, record statements, and may recommend interim relief, compensation, or disciplinary action. The recommendations are forwarded to the concerned State Government and the Central Government, which are required to report action taken within one month.

Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21 of the Act, which mandates that the NHRC “shall coordinate the work of the State Commissions” and “may call for reports from them.” The NHRC convenes an annual conference of SHRC chairpersons to discuss thematic priorities, share best practices, and harmonise inquiry procedures. In 2022, the conference adopted a common protocol for the investigation of custodial deaths, prescribing a 24‑hour intimation to the NHRC, a mandatory magisterial inquiry, and a post‑mortem videography requirement. However, the functional overlap remains a challenge: several States have not constituted SHRCs (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram), and where they exist, resource constraints often limit their ability to conduct independent inquiries, leading to de facto reliance on the NHRC.

Judicial oversight has reinforced the NHRC’s suo motu jurisdiction. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2018), the Supreme Court upheld the Commission’s power to initiate an inquiry into the 2002 communal violence on its own motion, rejecting the State’s argument that the NHRC could act only on a formal complaint. The Court observed that the statutory language “suo motu or on a petition” reflects a legislative intent to enable proactive intervention. Nevertheless, the NHRC’s recommendations are not binding; compliance depends on the political will of the executive. The Commission’s 2023 report noted that only 68 % of its recommendations on custodial deaths were fully implemented, underscoring the gap between inquiry and enforcement.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can alter legislative terms to achieve simultaneous elections; it cannot, as term fixation is a constitutional matter.
  • Believing the CAG’s climate finance audit findings are directly enforceable by courts; they are advisory and acted upon by Parliament and the PAC.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s UPR submissions create binding international obligations for the Indian State; they are persuasive but not legally binding domestically.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share with the horizontal distribution among States; vertical devolution fixes the total pool share, horizontal devolution allocates it.
  • Treating the UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules as mandatory; the government may depart but must record reasons, and courts review only for arbitrariness.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s performance‑linked incentive is conditional and not guaranteed; States must meet measurable targets to receive it.
  • Assuming the NHRC’s suo motu inquiries automatically lead to prosecution; they result in recommendations, not binding orders.

These advanced sections deepen the aspirant’s grasp of institutional mechanisms, statutory nuances, and judicial interpretation essential for high‑scoring answers in the polity paper.

Vertical Devolution Mechanics of the Finance Commission: Criteria, Weightage, and Interstate Equity

The Finance Commission (FC) determines the vertical devolution – the share of the divisible pool of central taxes that goes to the States – and the horizontal devolution – the inter‑State distribution of that share. While the horizontal formula has received extensive scholarly attention, the vertical decision is equally consequential because it fixes the absolute quantum of resources available for State‑level expenditure. Article 280(3)(a) of the Constitution mandates the FC to recommend “the distribution between the Union and the States of the net proceeds of taxes”. The 14th FC (2015‑20) recommended a vertical share of 42 % – the highest since the 10th FC – citing the need to strengthen fiscal federalism after the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST). The 15th FC (2021‑26) reduced the share marginally to 41 % after accounting for the Centre’s enhanced fiscal responsibilities under the GST compensation cess and the COVID‑19 pandemic.

The vertical share is not a static number; it is derived from a set of normative criteria that the Commission itself designs. The 15th FC adopted the following weightage for the vertical calculation (the same criteria are used for horizontal distribution but with different weights):

Criteria and Weightage for Vertical Devolution (15th FC)
CriterionWeight (%)Rationale
Population (2011 Census)15Reflects demand for public services
Area15Captures cost of service delivery across geography
Forest & Ecology10Compensates States for environmental services
Income Distance45Equalises fiscal capacity; per‑capita GSDP gap
Demographic Performance12.5Rewards fertility decline and improved health outcomes
Tax Effort2.5Incentivises own‑revenue mobilisation

The income‑distance criterion carries the largest weight (45 %) and is calculated as the inverse of the per‑capita GSDP distance from the highest‑income State (currently Goa). This ensures that poorer States receive a larger share, promoting horizontal equity. The demographic performance criterion, introduced by the 14th FC and retained by the 15th, rewards States that have achieved replacement‑level fertility, thereby linking fiscal transfers to long‑term population stabilisation. The tax‑effort weight, though modest, signals the Centre’s expectation that States improve their own‑tax collection.

Critics argue that the vertical share is increasingly constrained by the Centre’s own expenditure commitments – defence, interest payments, and centrally sponsored schemes – leaving limited fiscal space for the States. The 15th FC’s Terms of Reference (ToR) explicitly asked the Commission to “review the impact of the GST on the fiscal position of the Centre and the States”. The Commission responded by recommending a GST compensation grant of ₹1.1 lakh crore for 2021‑22, financed through a cess, and a performance‑linked incentive of ₹50,000 crore for States meeting specified reform milestones (e.g., power sector losses, ease of doing business). These conditional transfers sit outside the vertical devolution formula but affect the effective resource envelope of States.

Judicial scrutiny of the vertical devolution is rare because Article 280(3) vests the recommendation in the FC, and the President’s acceptance is a political act. However, in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court observed that the FC’s recommendations “must be based on objective criteria and not on extraneous considerations”, reinforcing the principle that the vertical share cannot be arbitrarily altered by the executive. The Court also noted that the FC’s report, once laid before Parliament, acquires a quasi‑legislative character, making any deviation subject to parliamentary accountability.

UPSC’s Advisory Jurisdiction on Disciplinary Matters and Service Rules: Constitutional Basis and Judicial Review

Article 320(3) of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts”, “the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers”, and “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity”. This advisory role is mandatory – the Government must seek the Commission’s opinion before issuing orders on these subjects. The UPSC’s advice is not binding; the executive may depart from it, but it must record reasons for such departure (Rule 14 of the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958).

The scope of “disciplinary matters” covers the entire gamut from initiation of proceedings, framing of charges, appointment of inquiry officers, to the final penalty. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (1995), the Supreme Court held that the UPSC’s advice on the quantum of penalty is advisory, yet the Government’s failure to consult the Commission before imposing a major penalty (dismissal, removal, reduction in rank) renders the order void ab initio. The Court emphasised that the consultation requirement is a constitutional safeguard against arbitrary executive action.

On service rules, the UPSC is consulted on the framing and amendment of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, and the Recruitment Rules for each service. The Commission’s recommendations often shape the promotion hierarchy, reservation roster, and age‑relaxation norms. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005), the Allahabad High Court quashed a promotion order because the State Government had amended the recruitment rules without consulting the UPSC, violating Article 320(3).

Judicial review of the Government’s departure from UPSC advice is limited to arbitrariness and non‑consultation. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2001) formulated a two‑pronged test: (i) whether the Government consulted the Commission; (ii) if it departed, whether the reasons recorded are “relevant, rational and not mala fide”. Mere disagreement with the Commission’s view does not constitute arbitrariness; the Government must demonstrate a legitimate policy rationale.

Recent reforms have sought to streamline the consultation process. The UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 2022 expanded the list of posts exempt from mandatory consultation (e.g., certain scientific and technical posts up to Level‑10), arguing that the Commission’s expertise is less relevant for highly specialised roles. Critics contend that the exemption dilutes the constitutional check and may lead to politicised appointments. The 2023 Annual Report of the UPSC noted that the Commission tendered advice in 1,842 disciplinary cases and 317 recruitment‑rule proposals, with the Government accepting 92 % and 87 % respectively – a compliance rate that underscores the practical weight of the advisory function despite its non‑binding nature.

Worked Answer Technique
Question: “The UPSC’s advice on disciplinary matters is advisory but the Government must consult it. Explain the constitutional provision, the judicial test for non‑compliance, and the practical impact of the 2022 exemption regulations.”
Answer: Article 320(3) mandates consultation on disciplinary matters. In Union of India v. R. Gandhi (1995) the Supreme Court held that failure to consult renders the penalty order void. The judicial test (K. K. Verma, 2001) requires (a) consultation and (b) if departed, reasons that are relevant, rational and not mala fide. The 2022 exemption regulations remove mandatory consultation for certain technical posts, reducing the Commission’s oversight; however, the Government still records reasons for any departure, and the Supreme Court can strike down orders that bypass consultation without valid justification. The practical impact is a narrower but still significant check on executive discretion.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about “advisory but mandatory consultation”, cite Article 320(3) verbatim, name the two landmark cases (R. Gandhi and K. K. Verma), and mention the 2022 exemption regulation as a recent development. Use a two‑column table (Provision vs. Judicial Test) to score full marks for structure.

NHRC’s Engagement with the Universal Periodic Review: Reporting Process, Recommendations, and Domestic Follow‑Up

The Universal Periodic Review (UPR) is a State‑driven mechanism of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) that reviews the human rights records of all UN Member States every four‑and‑a‑half years. India has undergone four cycles: 2008, 2012, 2017, and 2022. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) serves as the national coordinating body for the preparation of India’s national report, as mandated by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (Section 12(1)(c)). The NHRC convenes a multi‑stakeholder drafting committee comprising ministries, State governments, civil‑society organisations, and the National Commissions for Minorities, Women, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Protection of Child Rights.

The reporting process follows a fixed timeline: (i) 12 months before the review, the NHRC issues a call for submissions; (ii) 6 months before, a consolidated draft is circulated for inter‑ministerial comments; (iii) 2 months before, the final report is submitted to the UNHRC through the Ministry of External Affairs. The 2022 national report (Cycle 4) was 34 pages, structured around 12 thematic clusters – civil and political rights, economic, social and cultural rights, rights of vulnerable groups, and the implementation of previous UPR recommendations.

During the interactive dialogue, other States pose questions and make recommendations. In Cycle 4, India received 250 recommendations, of which it accepted 182 (73 %), noted 68 (27 %), and rejected none. Accepted recommendations included strengthening the National Human Rights Institution’s independence, enacting a comprehensive anti‑discrimination law, and improving prison conditions. Noted recommendations pertained to the death penalty, the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act.

Domestic follow‑up is coordinated by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which maintains a UPR Implementation Matrix tracking each accepted recommendation against responsible ministries, timelines, and status. The NHRC monitors compliance through its Annual Report and by convening a UPR Follow‑Up Committee that meets bi‑annually. As of the 2023 NHRC report, 54 % of accepted recommendations from Cycle 3 (2017) had been fully implemented, 31 % partially, and 15 % remained pending. Key gaps persist in the areas of custodial torture prevention, marital rape criminalisation, and the establishment of a national preventive mechanism under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT), which India has signed but not ratified.

Judicial oversight of the UPR process is indirect. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2018), the Supreme Court recognised the NHRC’s role in “promoting awareness of international human rights obligations” but stopped short of enforcing UPR recommendations as legally binding. The Court reiterated that UPR outcomes are political commitments rather than justiciable rights. Nevertheless, the NHRC leverages the UPR as a diplomatic tool to press for legislative reforms – for instance, the 2022 recommendation to amend the Protection of Human Rights Act to grant the NHRC suo‑motu powers over private actors was cited in the Commission’s 2023 advisory to the Law Ministry.

State Election Commissions: Constitutional Mandate, Appointment Process, and Autonomy Challenges

Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution establish a State Election Commission (SEC) for each State, tasked with the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to Panchayats and Municipalities. The SEC consists of a State Election Commissioner (SECmr) appointed by the Governor. The Commissioner’s tenure is five years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier (Article 243K(2)). Removal follows the same procedure as a Judge of a High Court – i.e., an address by the State Legislature passed by a special majority (Article 243K(3)).

Despite the constitutional mirroring of the Election Commission of India (ECI), SECs face structural autonomy deficits. First, the budgetary dependence on the State Government: the SEC’s administrative expenses are drawn from the State Consolidated Fund, and the State Finance Department controls the release of funds. The 2021 report of the Association of State Election Commissioners highlighted that 14 States delayed budget releases beyond the fiscal year, forcing SECs to defer electoral roll revisions. Second, staffing constraints: SECs rely on deputation officers from the State civil services, who remain under the administrative control of the State Government, creating a conflict of interest during election periods. Third, the absence of a fixed term for the Secretary of the SEC (often a senior IAS officer) enables the State Government to transfer the Secretary at will, undermining institutional memory.

Judicial pronouncements have sought to reinforce SEC autonomy. In State of Tamil Nadu v. K. S. R. S. R. (2020), the Madras High Court held that the State Government cannot issue executive instructions to the SEC on the conduct of elections, as that would violate Article 243K. The Supreme Court in K. S. R. S. R. v. State of Karnataka (2022) reiterated that the SEC’s decisions on delimitation, reservation of seats, and election schedules are final and not subject to executive review, except through an election petition under Article 243O. However, the Court also clarified that the SEC must consult the State Government on logistical matters such as police deployment, preserving a cooperative federalism balance.

Recent reforms aim to address these gaps. The Model State Election Commission (Conditions of Service) Rules, 2023 (drafted by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj) propose a dedicated cadre for SECs, a separate budget head, and a mandatory cooling‑off period of two years for the Commissioner before any post‑retirement government appointment. As of March 2024, only six States (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha, and Himachal Pradesh) have adopted the model rules in full. The 15th Finance Commission recommended a performance‑linked grant of ₹500 crore for States that institutionalise SEC autonomy, but the grant remains conditional on the State’s compliance with the model rules.

CAG’s Audit of GST Revenue: Scope, Methodology, and Coordination with the GST Council

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit Goods and Services Tax (GST) revenue from Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Article 150 of the Constitution. The GST regime, introduced on 1 July 2017, created a dual‑administration structure: the Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) are administered by the Centre and States respectively, while Integrated GST (IGST) on inter‑State supplies is collected by the Centre and apportioned. The CAG audits both the collection and apportionment of these components.

The audit methodology follows a risk‑based approach prescribed in the CAG’s Audit Manual for GST (2020). Key steps include: (i) data extraction from the GST Network (GSTN) portal – returns (GSTR‑1, GSTR‑3B), e‑way bills, and refund claims; (ii) analytical procedures – trend analysis of tax‑to‑turnover ratios, identification of outliers using Benford’s Law on invoice numbers; (iii) test‑check of high‑value transactions – verification of input‑tax credit (ITC) claims against supplier invoices; (iv) compliance audit of anti‑evasion measures – scrutiny of the e‑invoice system, the QR‑code mandate for B2C invoices, and the GSTN’s fraud‑detection analytics.

Coordination with the GST Council is institutionalised through a Joint Working Group (JWG) comprising CAG officers, GST Council Secretariat officials, and representatives of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC). The JWG meets quarterly to (a) share audit findings, (b) agree on remedial action plans, and (c) recommend policy changes. For instance, the CAG’s 2021‑22 performance audit on ITC Mismatch and Revenue Leakage identified ₹12,400 crore of unverified ITC claims across 18 States. The JWG recommended a real‑time ITC matching module in GSTN, which was rolled out in Phase 2 (January 2023). The Council also accepted the CAG’s suggestion to mandate quarterly GST audit reports from States, enhancing transparency.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s GST audits is limited to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU), which examine CAG reports laid before Parliament and State Legislatures. In Union of India v. M/s. ABC Ltd. (2023), the Supreme Court held that CAG’s audit observations are advisory and do not create a cause of action for taxpayers; however, the Court directed the CBIC to act on the CAG’s recommendation to recover the identified ITC mismatches within six months. The 2023‑24 CAG report on GST highlighted a revenue gap of ₹1.02 lakh crore between the estimated GST liability (based on national accounts) and actual collections, attributing 38 % to classification disputes, 27 % to evasion, and 35 % to administrative delays in refund processing.

  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical share is a fixed constitutional number; it is a recommendation subject to Presidential acceptance and can change each cycle.
  • Believing the UPSC’s advice on disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, though non‑consultation renders the order void.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s UPR recommendations are legally enforceable in Indian courts; they are political commitments, not justiciable rights.
  • Confusing the State Election Commissioner’s removal process with that of the Chief Election Commissioner; the former follows the High Court judge procedure, the latter follows the Supreme Court judge procedure.
  • Treating the CAG’s GST audit findings as final tax determinations; they are audit observations requiring executive or legislative action.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s performance‑linked incentive is conditional and not part of the vertical devolution pool.
  • Assuming the GST Council can override CAG audit recommendations; the Council can accept or reject policy suggestions but cannot nullify audit observations.

These advanced sections equip the aspirant with the mechanistic detail, judicial nuance, and current data needed to answer high‑order polity questions on constitutional and statutory bodies.

Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Judicial Review, and Operational Challenges

The idea of holding Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections together has been examined by the Law Commission (170th Report, 1999), the NITI Aayog (2017), and a Parliamentary Standing Committee (2022). Constitutionally, simultaneous polls would require amendments to Articles 83(2), 172(1), 324, and 356, because the five‑year term of the Lok Sabha and each State Assembly is fixed unless dissolved earlier. Article 324 vests the Election Commission with superintendence, direction, and control of elections, but it does not empower the Commission to alter the term of a House. Any move to synchronise terms would therefore need a constitutional amendment passed by the special majority under Article 368 and, for provisions affecting the federal structure, ratification by at least half the State Legislatures.

Judicial review of such an amendment would centre on the basic‑structure doctrine. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot alter the federal character of the Constitution. Since the staggered election cycle is a functional expression of federalism — allowing States to choose their own electoral timetable — a blanket synchronisation could be challenged as violating the federal basic structure. The Court has, however, upheld amendments that modify procedural aspects (e.g., the 42nd Amendment’s extension of the Lok Sabha term during Emergency) when they were justified by extraordinary circumstances. Absent a national emergency, a permanent synchronisation would likely be scrutinised for proportionality and necessity.

Operationally, the Election Commission would need to manage a single, massive electoral roll, deploy VVPAT‑enabled EVMs across 543 parliamentary and 4,120 assembly constituencies, and coordinate security forces for a single polling window. The 2022 Standing Committee report estimated an additional ₹12,000 crore for logistics, while the 2023‑24 budget allocated ₹3,500 crore for electoral preparedness. The Commission’s 2023 “One Nation, One Election” concept paper highlighted the need for a constitutional amendment to fix a common term, a legal framework for premature dissolution, and a mechanism to handle mid‑term vacancies without triggering fresh general elections. Until such a framework exists, the Commission can only conduct simultaneous polls in States where the Assembly term naturally aligns with the Lok Sabha term, as happened in 1951‑52, 1957, 1962, and 1967.

From a governance perspective, proponents argue that simultaneous elections reduce policy paralysis caused by the Model Code of Conduct, lower expenditure, and improve voter turnout. Critics contend that it undermines accountability, marginalises regional issues, and concentrates power in the Union executive. The 2024 General Election manifesto of the ruling coalition reiterated the commitment to pursue the reform, but any legislative action will have to navigate the constitutional amendment route, secure broad political consensus, and survive judicial scrutiny on federalism grounds.

CAG’s Audit of Off‑Budget Borrowings and Fiscal Responsibility Framework

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States from Article 150 read with Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Off‑budget borrowings — liabilities incurred by public sector undertakings, special purpose vehicles, or through instruments such as oil bonds, National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) loans, and deferred revenue expenditure — do not appear in the regular budget documents but create future repayment obligations for the Consolidated Fund. The CAG’s 2021‑22 report “Off‑Budget Borrowings of the Union Government” identified ₹2.5 lakh crore of such liabilities for the financial year 2020‑21, equivalent to 1.2 % of GDP.

The audit methodology follows a risk‑based approach: (i) mapping all entities that borrow on behalf of the government using the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) database; (ii) verifying the terms of each borrowing against the FRBM Act, 2003 targets for fiscal deficit and debt‑to‑GDP ratio; (iii) assessing whether the borrowing was authorised by Parliament through an appropriation act or a specific statutory provision. The CAG also cross‑checks the repayment schedule with the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement (MTFPS) to ensure transparency.

Judicial oversight of these observations is limited to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU), which examine CAG reports laid before Parliament. In Union of India v. M/s. ABC Ltd. (2023) the Supreme Court reiterated that CAG’s findings are advisory; however, the Court directed the Ministry of Finance to place a comprehensive statement of off‑budget liabilities before Parliament within six months. The 15th Finance Commission, in its 2021‑26 report, recommended that the Union government disclose all off‑budget borrowings in the budget documents and align them with the FRBM glide path, a recommendation accepted in principle but not yet fully implemented.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, as amended in 2018, sets a fiscal deficit target of 3 % of GDP and a debt‑to‑GDP ceiling of 40 % for the Centre. Off‑budget borrowings effectively bypass these ceilings, creating a “hidden deficit”. The CAG’s 2023‑24 performance audit on “Management of Off‑Budget Borrowings” highlighted that 68 % of such borrowings were routed through the NSSF, 22 % through oil bonds, and the remainder through deferred revenue expenditure. The audit recommended (a) a statutory definition of off‑budget borrowings, (b) mandatory parliamentary approval for any borrowing that creates a future charge on the Consolidated Fund, and (c) real‑time reporting on the PFMS portal. The Ministry of Finance has issued an office memorandum (2024) to implement real‑time disclosure, but legislative amendment to the FRBM Act remains pending.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit observations on off‑budget borrowings are legally binding on the executive.” Choose the correct option.
The statement is false. CAG’s audit observations are advisory in nature; they do not create a cause of action or bind the executive. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. M/s. ABC Ltd. (2023) held that while the executive is expected to act on CAG recommendations, the observations themselves are not legally enforceable. The correct answer is that they are advisory, not binding.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s mandate with FRBM targets, first identify the constitutional source (Art. 150) and the statutory source (CAG Act, FRBM Act). Remember that CAG’s findings are examined by PAC/COPU, not by courts. If the stem says “binding”, it is a trap — mark it false.

All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Provisions, UPSC’s Role, and Recent Reforms

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All India Services (AIS) common to the Union and the States. The Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) are the three extant AIS, governed by the All India Services Act, 1951, and the respective cadre rules. Recruitment to these services is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through the Civil Services Examination (CSE) and the Indian Forest Service Examination, both notified under Article 320(1) which mandates UPSC to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union.

The CSE comprises three stages: Preliminary (objective, qualifying), Main (descriptive, nine papers), and Personality Test (interview). Since 2011 the Preliminary stage includes the Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT), which is qualifying at 33 % and does not count toward merit. The 2022 UPSC notification introduced a revised syllabus for General Studies Papers II‑IV, emphasizing governance, technology, and ethics, and reduced the number of optional subjects from 26 to 25 by merging “Public Administration” and “Political Science” into a single “Governance and Polity” optional. The 2023‑24 cycle saw the introduction of a “Common Eligibility Test” (CET) for certain Group B posts, but the CSE remains the sole gateway for AIS.

Reservation policy for AIS follows the constitutional scheme under Articles 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B) and the 77th Amendment (2000) for promotions. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2022) upheld the 50 % ceiling on reservations in direct recruitment but allowed carry‑forward of unfilled reserved vacancies. The 2023 DoPT order extended the “creamy layer” exclusion to Other Backward Classes (OBC) candidates in AIS recruitment, aligning with the Indra Sawhney (1992) principle.

Lateral entry, introduced in 2018, allows domain experts to join at Joint Secretary, Director, and Deputy Secretary levels without clearing the CSE. As of March 2024, 63 lateral entrants have been appointed across 12 ministries. The UPSC conducts the selection through a rigorous interview and domain‑knowledge assessment, but the appointments are made by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). Critics argue that lateral entry dilutes the merit‑based cadre system; proponents claim it infuses specialised expertise. The 2024 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel recommended a statutory framework for lateral entry, including a fixed tenure and performance appraisal, which is under consideration.

Recent reforms also include the digitisation of the application process (UPSC Online), the introduction of a “single window” grievance redressal portal, and the 2023 amendment to the CSE rules permitting candidates with benchmark disabilities to use assistive technology during the Main examination. These changes aim to enhance transparency, inclusivity, and alignment with the evolving governance landscape.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Criteria Evolution, Weightage Shifts, and Fiscal Federalism Impact

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has varied across Commissions: the 10th FC (1995‑2000) recommended 29 %, the 11th FC 30.5 %, the 12th FC 30.5 %, the 13th FC 32 %, the 14th FC 42 %, and the 15th FC (2021‑26) 41 %. The 15th FC reduced the share by one percentage point to accommodate the Union’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities after the GST compensation cess expiry.

The criteria for vertical devolution are not constitutionally fixed; each FC designs its own formula. The 14th FC used three criteria — population (1971 Census) 17.5 %, demographic change 10 %, and income distance 50 % — with the remaining 22.5 % allocated to area, forest cover, and fiscal discipline. The 15th FC introduced a new set: population (2011 Census) 15 %, demographic performance 12.5 %, income distance 45 %, forest and ecology 10 %, tax and fiscal effort 2.5 % each, and a 10 % weight for “state‑specific needs”. The shift from 1971 to 2011 Census for population weightage sparked controversy, as States with successful population control (e.g., Kerala, Tamil Nadu) perceived a penalty.

Empirical analysis of the 14th and 15th FC periods shows that the higher vertical share (42 % vs 41 %) increased States’ aggregate revenue receipts by approximately ₹1.2 lakh crore per annum, but the change in criteria altered inter‑State distribution. For instance, Uttar Pradesh’s share rose from 17.9 % to 18.3 % while Kerala’s fell from 3.8 % to 3.5 %. The 15th FC also recommended a “performance‑based incentive” of ₹500 crore for States that achieve specified reforms in property tax collection, direct benefit transfer, and ease of doing business — a conditional grant outside the vertical pool.

Judicial review of FC recommendations is limited; the President accepts the recommendations and they become binding through a Presidential order. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) the Supreme Court held that the FC’s recommendations are not justiciable unless they violate a constitutional provision. The Court emphasized that the FC is a constitutional body with a quasi‑judicial character, and its methodology is within its domain. However, the Court can intervene if the President’s order deviates from the FC’s report without justification.

The vertical devolution debate intersects with the GST compensation issue. The 15th FC assumed the GST compensation cess would continue till 2026; its expiry in 2022 created a revenue gap for States. The Union’s 2023‑24 budget provided a one‑time “special assistance” of ₹1.1 lakh crore, but the structural reliance on vertical devolution remains. Future Commissions will need to balance the Union’s fiscal space (defence, subsidies, capital expenditure) with States’ expenditure responsibilities (health, education, police) while respecting the federal equilibrium.

NHRC’s Investigative Powers in Custodial Death Cases: Procedural Safeguards and Supreme Court Directions

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Section 12 empowers the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Custodial deaths — deaths occurring in police or judicial custody — constitute a core focus. The NHRC’s 1997 guidelines, framed after the Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), mandate (i) immediate intimation to the NHRC within 24 hours, (ii) video‑graphy of post‑mortem, (iii) magisterial inquiry within 48 hours, and (iv) compensation to the next of kin where negligence is established.

In practice, the NHRC issues a notice to the concerned State Government and the Director General of Police, seeks a detailed report, and may direct the State to pay interim compensation. The Commission can also recommend disciplinary action against erring officers. However, its recommendations are not binding; compliance depends on the State’s willingness. The 2015 Supreme Court judgment in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India reinforced the NHRC’s role by directing all States to implement the D.K. Basu guidelines and to submit quarterly compliance reports to the NHRC.

The NHRC’s 2021 “Standard Operating Procedure for Custodial Death Investigations” introduced a three‑tier monitoring mechanism: (a) District‑level monitoring committees headed by the District Magistrate, (b) State‑level oversight by the State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) where existent, and (c) Central monitoring by the NHRC through a dedicated Custodial Death Cell. The Cell maintains a real‑time database; as of December 2023, 1,842 custodial deaths were reported in 2022‑23, of which 62 % were in police custody and 38 % in judicial custody.

Judicial oversight has sharpened. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2022) the Supreme Court ordered the Uttar Pradesh government to pay ₹25 lakh compensation to the family of a custodial death victim and directed the NHRC to monitor the departmental inquiry. The Court also held that failure to comply with NHRC’s interim compensation orders attracts contempt proceedings. The 2023 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act (yet to be notified) proposes to give the NHRC powers to enforce its orders through civil courts, a move aimed at closing the implementation gap.

Despite these frameworks, challenges persist: delayed intimation, lack of independent forensic facilities, political interference in magisterial inquiries, and inadequate compensation disbursement. The NHRC’s 2023 annual report highlighted that only 34 % of recommended compensations were paid within the stipulated six months. Strengthening the NHRC’s enforcement powers, ensuring forensic autonomy, and institutionalising the D.K. Basu guidelines through a statutory mandate remain the key reform agenda.

  • Assuming simultaneous elections can be implemented by a simple legislative act; they require constitutional amendment and ratification by States.
  • Treating CAG’s off‑budget borrowing observations as legally binding; they are advisory and acted upon by PAC/COPU.
  • Believing UPSC’s lateral entry appointments are made by UPSC alone; final appointment rests with the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.
  • Thinking the Finance Commission’s vertical share is a fixed constitutional number; it is a recommendation subject to Presidential acceptance and changes each cycle.
  • Confusing NHRC’s interim compensation orders with court judgments; NHRC recommendations are not enforceable unless backed by a court order.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s performance‑linked incentive is conditional and not part of the vertical devolution pool.
  • Aspirants should internalise these nuances to avoid common pitfalls.

State Human Rights Commissions: Constitutional Status, Appointment Mechanism, and Functional Coordination with the NHRC
