The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes a two‑tier architecture: the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) at the Centre and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) in each state. Section 21 of the PHRA empowers the Governor to constitute an SHRC on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Chief Minister (chair), the Home Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly, and, where a Legislative Council exists, its Chairman and Leader of Opposition. The Chairperson must be a former Chief Justice of a High Court; members include a serving or retired High Court judge, a person with knowledge of human rights, and, since the 2019 amendment, a woman member. Tenure is five years or until the age of seventy, whichever is earlier.

SHRCs mirror the NHRC’s investigative powers under Section 12: they may inquire suo motu or on a petition into violations by public servants, call for reports, recommend interim compensation, and suggest disciplinary action. However, their recommendations are not binding; compliance rests on the state government’s willingness. Coordination with the NHRC is structured through Sections 12(2) and 36 of the PHRA. The NHRC can transfer any complaint to the concerned SHRC, call for periodical reports, and issue guidelines — such as the 1997 custodial‑death guidelines — that SHRCs are expected to implement. The 2021 Supreme Court judgment in State of Haryana v. NHRC directed all states to fill SHRC vacancies within six months and to provide independent forensic facilities, underscoring the Court’s view that functional autonomy is integral to the PHRA’s purpose.

As of December 2023, twenty‑six states and three Union Territories have operational SHRCs; the remaining states either have not constituted them or have vacant chairs. The 2022 amendment to the PHRA (still awaiting notification) proposes to grant SHRCs the power to enforce their orders through civil courts, a move aimed at closing the implementation gap highlighted by the NHRC’s 2023 annual report, which noted that only 34 % of recommended compensations were paid within six months. Persistent challenges include political interference in the appointment committee, inadequate budgetary allocations, and the absence of dedicated investigative wings in most SHRCs.

The Central Information Commission’s Proactive Disclosure Obligations under Section 4 of the RTI Act: Compliance Trends and Judicial Enforcement

Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 imposes a statutory duty on every public authority to publish seventeen categories of information suo motu, ranging from organisational structure and decision‑making processes to budgets, subsidy programmes, and the particulars of facilities available to citizens. The Central Information Commission (CIC) monitors compliance through its annual reports and can impose penalties under Section 20 on Public Information Officers who fail to discharge this obligation. The 2022 CIC annual report revealed that only 38 % of the 2,300‑odd central public authorities achieved full compliance across all seventeen categories; the most common gaps were in the publication of decision‑making norms (Category 4) and the disclosure of subsidy beneficiaries (Category 11).

Judicial enforcement has sharpened the proactive disclosure regime. In Central Information Commission v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court upheld the CIC’s power to direct a ministry to publish its internal guidelines on file‑noting procedures, ruling that Section 4 creates a positive duty, not a mere directory provision. The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act, which altered the tenure and salary of the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners, left Section 4 untouched, signalling legislative intent to preserve the proactive disclosure framework. In 2023, the CIC issued a blanket directive to all ministries and departments to publish COVID‑19 procurement contracts, vaccine allocation data, and oxygen‑supply logs within thirty days, invoking Section 4(1)(b) and the public interest test under Section 8(2). Non‑compliance attracted show‑cause notices under Section 20, and at least three ministries were fined ₹25,000 each in the first quarter of 2024.

Despite these interventions, structural obstacles remain: many public authorities lack digitised record‑management systems, the CIC’s own staffing shortfall limits the frequency of compliance audits, and the absence of a centralised dashboard for proactive disclosures hampers citizen access. The 2023‑24 budget allocated ₹12 crore for the development of a “National RTI Portal” intended to aggregate Section 4 disclosures, but the portal’s launch has been deferred to 2025.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which provision of the RTI Act empowers the CIC to penalise a Public Information Officer for failure to publish information suo motu under Section 4?” Many aspirants answer Section 19 (appeal) or Section 18 (complaint). The correct provision is Section 20, which authorises the CIC to impose a penalty of up to ₹25,000 on the PIO for each day of default, including failure to comply with the proactive disclosure mandate.
Section 20(1) of the RTI Act reads: “Where the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, as the case may be, is of the opinion that the Public Information Officer has, without any reasonable cause, refused to receive an application for information or has not furnished information within the time specified under sub‑section (1) of Section 7… it shall impose a penalty of two hundred and fifty rupees each day till application is received or information is furnished, so however, the total amount of such penalty shall not exceed twenty‑five thousand rupees.” The phrase “information” includes the proactive disclosure obligations under Section 4, as clarified by the Supreme Court in CIC v. Union of India (2020).
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes proactive disclosure (Section 4) with penalty provisions, locate the penalty clause first (Section 20). Remember that the CIC’s power to penalise is not limited to reactive requests; it extends to any statutory duty of the PIO, including suo motu publication. Cite the 2020 Supreme Court ruling to demonstrate awareness of judicial interpretation.

The Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Formulating and Revising Recruitment Rules for the All India Services and Central Civil Services

Article 320 of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts, the principles to be followed in making appointments, promotions and transfers, and the suitability of candidates. In practice, the UPSC’s advisory role translates into the framing and periodic revision of the Recruitment Rules (RRs) for the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and for each Central Civil Service (e.g., Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service). The process begins with the concerned cadre‑controlling authority — typically the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) for AIS and the respective ministry for CCS — drafting a proposal that specifies educational qualifications, age limits, method of recruitment (direct, promotion, deputation), and reservation provisions.

The UPSC examines the draft for conformity with constitutional provisions, the principle of merit, and the extant reservation policy. It may suggest modifications, such as altering the weightage of the written examination versus the interview, or introducing a new eligibility criterion (e.g., the 2022 insertion of a “domain‑expertise” clause for lateral entry into the Senior Administrative Grade). Once the UPSC conveys its advice, the government may accept it or, under Article 320(3), reject it only after recording reasons in writing. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021) held that the UPSC’s advice is “binding in substance” and that a rejection without cogent reasons is amenable to judicial review.

Recent reforms illustrate the evolving scope of the UPSC’s rule‑making function. The 2022 amendment to the All India Services (Recruitment) Rules introduced a lateral‑entry channel at the Joint Secretary level, with the UPSC designing the selection methodology — a two‑stage process comprising a screening test and an interview — and prescribing a maximum of ten appointments per year. The “Mission Karmayogi” capacity‑building programme, launched in 2020, also required the UPSC to revise the syllabi for the Civil Services Examination to incorporate competencies in data analytics, behavioural skills, and emerging technologies. In 2023, the UPSC issued a model template for “Performance‑Based Promotion” rules, aiming to replace seniority‑centric promotion with a composite index that weights annual performance appraisal reports, training completion, and stakeholder feedback.

Challenges persist: the time lag between a ministry’s proposal and the UPSC’s final advice often exceeds twelve months, delaying critical vacancies; the lack of a statutory deadline for the UPSC’s response has been flagged by the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2009) as a structural bottleneck. Moreover, the increasing reliance on lateral entry has sparked debate over whether the UPSC’s traditional merit‑based framework adequately captures domain‑specific competence, a question that may soon reach the Supreme Court.

The Finance Commission’s Treatment of Census Data and the Impact of the 2021 Census Delay on Horizontal Devolution

The horizontal devolution formula of the Finance Commission (FC) distributes the States’ share of the divisible pool of taxes among individual states. Since the 10th FC (1995‑2000), population has been a key criterion, initially weighted at 10 % using the 1971 Census. The 14th FC (2015‑20) raised the population weight to 17.5 % but retained the 1971 base to avoid penalising states that had successfully controlled population growth. The 15th FC (2020‑25) shifted to the 2011 Census for the population criterion, assigning it a 15 % weight, and introduced a 12.5 % “demographic performance” weight that rewarded states for reductions in total fertility rate (TFR) based on 2011 data.

The Terms of Reference of the 16th FC, to be constituted for the 2026‑31 award period, require the use of the “latest available Census”. The 2021 Census, originally scheduled for 2021, was postponed due to the COVID‑19 pandemic and subsequent administrative hurdles; the Office of the Registrar General now projects field operations to commence in 2025 with final results by 2027. In the interim, the Union Government, through a 2023 notification, authorised the 16th FC to use the 2011 Census for its interim report, with a provision to update the formula once 2021 data become available.

The delay creates asymmetric fiscal incentives. States with high population growth since 2011 — notably Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan — stand to gain a larger share if the 2021 figures are adopted, because the population weight would reflect their increased numbers. Conversely, states that have achieved replacement‑level fertility — Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, and Himachal Pradesh — would see their relative shares shrink. The 15th FC’s demographic‑performance criterion partially mitigates this by rewarding TFR decline, but it is calibrated on 2011 data and does not capture post‑2011 trends.

Empirical simulations by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (2022) estimate that a switch from 2011 to projected 2021 population would increase Bihar’s horizontal share by approximately 0.6 percentage points and reduce Kerala’s by 0.4 percentage points. The 16th FC’s final report will need to balance the constitutional mandate to use the latest Census with the principle of fiscal equity, possibly by phasing in the new data over two award periods or by adjusting the demographic‑performance weight to reflect updated TFR estimates from the Sample Registration System (SRS). Until the 2021 Census is finalised, the horizontal devolution landscape remains in a state of calibrated uncertainty.

  • Assuming SHRCs possess binding enforcement powers; their recommendations are advisory unless a court orders compliance.
  • Confusing Section 4 proactive disclosure with Section 7 reactive requests; penalties under Section 20 apply to both, but the procedural triggers differ.
  • Believing the UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules is merely consultative; the Supreme Court has treated it as binding absent recorded reasons for rejection.
  • Thinking the 15th Finance Commission used the 2021 Census; it used the 2011 Census and the 2021 data are still unavailable.
  • Overlooking that the CIC’s penalty power under Section 20 is capped at ₹25,000 total, not per day indefinitely.
  • Assuming lateral‑entry appointments are made solely by the UPSC; final appointment rests with the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.
  • Treating the NHRC’s custodial‑death guidelines as statutory law; they are administrative directions reinforced by judicial orders but not codified.

These nuances are essential for accurate answer‑writing in mains and for avoiding common pitfalls in objective‑type questions.

The Competition Commission of India’s Regulation of Digital Markets and the 2023 Amendment

The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, which received Presidential assent in April 2023, marks the most significant overhaul of the Competition Act, 2002 since its inception. The amendment introduces a settlement and commitment framework (Sections 48A‑48F) that allows parties under investigation to propose commitments or settle without an admission of guilt, thereby reducing litigation load. It also expands the leniency programme by adding a “leniency plus” provision that rewards applicants who disclose additional cartels beyond the one under investigation.

A pivotal change for digital markets is the insertion of Section 2(s)‑(t) defining “relevant market” in a manner that explicitly recognises multi‑sided platforms, network effects, data‑driven advantages, and zero‑price services. This statutory recognition empowers the CCI to assess dominance not only through price‑output metrics but also through data concentration, switching costs, and ecosystem lock‑in. The amendment also codifies the “hub‑and‑spoke” cartel doctrine (Section 3(3A)), enabling the Commission to prosecute vertical agreements that facilitate horizontal coordination among competitors.

Since the amendment, the CCI has invoked these provisions in high‑profile cases. In Google LLC v. Competition Commission of India (2022), the Commission imposed a penalty of ₹1,337.76 crore for abuse of dominant position in the Android mobile device ecosystem, citing anti‑fragmentation agreements and mandatory pre‑installation of Google apps. The 2023 amendment’s settlement mechanism was subsequently used by Google to propose behavioural commitments, which the CCI accepted in 2024 after a public consultation. Similarly, in MakeMyTrip‑GoIbibo (2023), the CCI applied the hub‑and‑spoke analysis to penalise parity clauses that restricted hotel partners from offering lower rates on competing platforms.

The amendment also strengthens the Director General’s investigative powers (Section 41) by allowing dawn raids without prior notice and mandating a 180‑day timeline for completion of investigations, extendable by 60 days. The CCI’s Market Study on Digital Platforms (2022) and the subsequent Draft Digital Competition Bill (2024) indicate a regulatory trajectory toward ex‑ante obligations for “systemically important digital intermediaries”, mirroring the EU’s Digital Markets Act. For UPSC aspirants, the key takeaway is the shift from ex‑post enforcement to a hybrid regime where structural remedies, behavioural commitments, and ex‑ante designations coexist.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s Emerging Role in OTT Regulation under the Telecommunications Act, 2023

The Telecommunications Act, 2023, enacted in December 2023, replaces the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, and the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933. Section 2(1)(k) defines “telecommunication” to include “transmission, emission or reception of signs, signals, writing, images and sounds or intelligence of any nature by wire, radio, optical or other electromagnetic systems”, thereby bringing Over‑The‑Top (OTT) communication services such as WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram within the statutory ambit. The Act empowers the Central Government to notify “OTT communication services” as a class of telecommunication services, subjecting them to licensing, security, and interception obligations.

TRAI, under Section 11 of the TRAI Act, 1997, retains its recommendatory role on licensing terms, spectrum allocation, and quality‑of‑service parameters. In March 2023, TRAI released a Consultation Paper on Regulatory Framework for OTT Communication Services, seeking stakeholder views on (i) whether OTTs should be brought under a light‑touch licensing regime, (ii) data localisation and lawful interception requirements, and (iii) the principle of “same service, same rules” vis‑à‑vis traditional telecom operators. The paper highlighted the revenue asymmetry where telecom operators bear infrastructure costs while OTTs capture value‑added services.

The Act also introduces a “Regulatory Sandbox” (Section 31) allowing innovators to test new technologies under TRAI’s supervision without full licensing. This provision is aimed at fostering 5G use‑cases, satellite broadband, and IoT services. In its 2024 recommendations, TRAI proposed a “registration‑only” regime for OTT communication services, mandating compliance with KYC, data‑retention (180 days), and lawful interception standards, while exempting them from spectrum charges. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) is currently drafting the notification to operationalise this regime.

Judicial oversight remains active. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right, which constrains any interception framework. The 2023 Act’s Section 20(2) requires a “lawful interception” order from a competent authority, and the 2024 TRAI recommendations incorporate a judicial‑review safeguard whereby interception orders are subject to review by a High Court‑level oversight committee. For mains answer‑writing, candidates should contrast the ex‑ante licensing model for telecom operators with the ex‑post registration model proposed for OTTs, and evaluate the impact on net‑neutrality principles enshrined in the 2018 TRAI recommendations.

Technique: Comparative Regulatory Mapping
Question: Compare the regulatory approach of the Competition Commission of India towards digital platforms after the 2023 Amendment with the approach of TRAI towards OTT communication services under the Telecommunications Act, 2023. Highlight two similarities and two differences.
Similarities: (1) Both regimes move beyond pure ex‑post enforcement — CCI now has a settlement/commitment framework and ex‑ante designation powers for systemically important digital intermediaries; TRAI proposes a registration‑only regime with mandatory compliance (KYC, interception) that functions as a light‑touch ex‑ante rule set. (2) Both recognise the unique economics of digital markets — CCI’s amended “relevant market” definition captures network effects, data advantages, and zero‑price services; TRAI’s consultation paper explicitly addresses revenue asymmetry and the “same service, same rules” principle. Differences: (1) CCI’s powers are adjudicatory and punitive (penalties, cease‑and‑desist orders), whereas TRAI’s role is recommendatory; final licensing/registration decisions rest with the Central Government/DoT. (2) CCI’s framework applies horizontally across all sectors where digital platforms operate, while TRAI’s regime is sector‑specific, limited to OTT communication services that fall under the definition of “telecommunication” in the 2023 Act.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison between two regulators, structure the answer in a two‑column table (Similarities | Differences) and cite the specific statutory provisions (e.g., Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 Sections 48A‑48F, 2(s)‑(t); Telecommunications Act, 2023 Sections 2(1)(k), 20(2), 31). This demonstrates precise legal knowledge and saves time.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India’s Framework for Algorithmic Trading and Market Surveillance

SEBI’s regulatory architecture for algorithmic trading has evolved through a series of circulars and master directions. The SEBI (Algorithmic Trading) Circular, 2021 mandated that all algorithmic orders be routed through approved “algo‑ID” tags, introduced a maximum order‑to‑trade ratio (OTR) of 1:100, and required stock exchanges to implement real‑time pre‑trade risk controls such as price‑band checks, quantity limits, and fat‑finger error filters. In 2022, SEBI issued the Framework for Algorithmic Trading, which classified algorithms into “execution algorithms”, “strategy algorithms”, and “high‑frequency trading (HFT) algorithms”, each subject to distinct co‑location and latency‑disclosure norms.

The 2023 Guidelines on Algorithmic Trading Risk Management further tightened the regime by (i) requiring algo‑developers to obtain a certification from a recognised testing agency before deployment, (ii) mandating a kill‑switch accessible to both the broker and the exchange, and (iii) prescribing a minimum tick‑size compliance for all algorithmic orders to prevent quote‑stuffing. SEBI also directed exchanges to publish daily algorithmic trading statistics (volume, order‑to‑trade ratio, latency) to enhance transparency.

On the surveillance front, SEBI’s Market Surveillance System (MSS) integrates data from the National Stock Exchange (NSE), BSE, and the Metropolitan Stock Exchange (MSE) to detect layering, spoofing, and momentum ignition patterns. The 2022 SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations were amended to explicitly cover “algorithmic manipulative practices”, enabling enforcement actions against entities that deploy deceptive algorithms. Notable enforcement includes the 2023 order against a proprietary trading firm for spoofing in index futures, where SEBI imposed a penalty of ₹25 crore and barred the firm from algorithmic trading for two years.

For UPSC preparation, the critical points are: (a) the shift from a purely post‑trade monitoring model to a pre‑trade risk control model; (b) the introduction of algo‑certification as a gatekeeping mechanism; (c) the alignment of Indian norms with the IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures and the EU MiFID II/RTS 6 standards on algorithmic trading. Candidates should be able to explain how these measures address systemic risk while preserving market liquidity.

The Reserve Bank of India’s Regulation of Payment Systems and the Unified Payments Interface

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS Act) provides the statutory backbone for the RBI’s oversight of payment systems in India. Under Section 4, the RBI is the sole authority to authorise, regulate, and supervise “payment systems”, defined to include card networks, prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), wallet systems, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). The RBI’s 2021 Guidelines on Regulation of Payment Aggregators (PAs) and Payment Gateways (PGs) introduced a net‑worth requirement of ₹15 crore for PAs, mandatory data localisation (all payment data stored only in India), and a grievance redressal timeline of 48 hours for customer complaints.

The UPI framework, launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) under RBI’s aegis, operates as a real‑time, interoperable, account‑to‑account payment rail. In 2022, the RBI issued the Framework for Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS), expanding the scope to include recurring bill payments, insurance premiums, and school fees, and mandating that all BBPS operating units adhere to the same KYC and data‑localisation standards as PAs. The 2023 Directions on UPI Interoperability required all UPI apps to support UPI‑Lite (offline low‑value transactions) and UPI‑123Pay (feature‑phone based payments), thereby deepening financial inclusion.

On the supervisory side, the RBI conducts periodic on‑site inspections and off‑site surveillance through the Payment System Indicators (PSI) dashboard, which tracks metrics such as transaction success rate, fraud incidence, and system downtime. The 2022 RBI Circular on Fraud Classification and Reporting mandated that all payment system operators report frauds above ₹1 lakh within 24 hours and adopt machine‑learning based anomaly detection. In 2023, the RBI imposed a penalty of ₹2.5 crore on a major payment aggregator for non‑compliance with data‑localisation norms, signalling strict enforcement.

Key takeaways for aspirants: (i) the RBI’s regulatory perimeter now covers the entire payment ecosystem — from issuers (banks, PPIs) to intermediaries (PAs, PGs) to infrastructure (UPI, BBPS); (ii) the emphasis on data sovereignty aligns with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; (iii) the interoperability mandate for UPI reflects a policy choice to avoid walled‑garden ecosystems, contrasting with the closed‑loop models seen in some jurisdictions. Understanding the interplay between the PSS Act, NPCI’s operational role, and RBI’s supervisory powers is essential for answering questions on fintech regulation.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of GST Compensation Cess and Fiscal Federalism

The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 guaranteed states a 14 % annual growth in protected revenue for a five‑year transition period (2017‑2022), funded through a compensation cess levied on sin and luxury goods. The CAG’s mandate under Article 150 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to auditing the collection, allocation, and utilisation of the compensation cess. In its Report No. 12 of 2022 (Performance Audit of GST Compensation Cess), the CAG highlighted a significant shortfall in cess collections relative to the projected requirement, leading to delayed releases to states and increased borrowing by the Centre under the “back‑to‑back loan” facility.

The audit identified three structural issues: (1) Revenue estimation methodology relied on pre‑GDP growth assumptions that did not account for the pandemic‑induced contraction; (2) Cess rate rationalisation was delayed, with the GST Council only approving rate adjustments in 2021, after the shortfall had materialised; (3) Fund flow mechanism lacked a statutory timeline for disbursement, resulting in ad‑hoc releases that disrupted state fiscal planning. The CAG recommended (a) a formula‑based, quarterly release schedule linked to actual cess collections, (b) an independent monitoring cell within the Ministry of Finance to track cess receipts and state claims, and (c) a review of the compensation architecture beyond the transition period, including the possibility of a permanent revenue‑sharing arrangement.

In 2023, the GST Council extended the compensation cess levy until March 2026 to service the back‑to‑back loans. The CAG’s subsequent Compliance Audit (2024) examined whether the extended cess proceeds were being utilised exclusively for loan repayment and found instances of diversion to general expenditure in a few states, prompting a recommendation for stricter end‑use certification. The Supreme Court, in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022), upheld the Centre’s borrowing mechanism but emphasised that the federal balance requires transparent and predictable compensation flows.

For mains, candidates should be able to articulate how the CAG’s audit findings feed into the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution calculus (the 15th FC recommended a 41 % share for states, factoring in GST compensation liabilities) and the broader debate on fiscal federalism — whether the compensation framework represents a temporary bridge or a permanent restructuring of Centre‑state fiscal relations. The CAG’s role as an independent fiscal watchdog, capable of influencing both executive policy and legislative discourse, exemplifies the accountability architecture envisioned under Articles 148‑151.

  • Assuming the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 grants the CCI direct rule‑making power over digital platforms; it only provides settlement, commitment, and ex‑ante designation powers, while rule‑making remains with the Central Government.
  • Confusing TRAI’s recommendatory role with binding licensing authority; final notification of OTT registration rests with the Department of Telecommunications, not TRAI.
  • Believing SEBI’s algorithmic trading circulars are merely advisory; they have the force of regulations under the SEBI Act, 1992, and non‑compliance attracts penalties.
  • Thinking the RBI’s UPI directions apply only to banks; they extend to all payment system participants, including PPIs, payment aggregators, and third‑party app providers.
  • Overlooking that the CAG’s audit of GST compensation cess covers both Centre and states; the CAG audits the Centre’s cess collection and the states’ utilisation of released funds.
  • Treating the “back‑to‑back loan” facility as a permanent fiscal transfer; it is a borrowing mechanism to bridge the compensation gap, repayable from future cess proceeds.
  • Assuming the 2023 Telecommunications Act automatically subjects all OTT services to interception; only “OTT communication services” notified by the Central Government attract interception obligations.
The advanced sections above deepen understanding of regulatory dynamics across competition, telecommunications, securities, payments, and fiscal federalism, equipping aspirants to tackle analytical questions with statutory precision.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Election Expenditure: Expenditure Observers, Ceiling Limits, and Judicial Review

The Election Commission of India (ECI) derives its authority to regulate election expenditure from Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, read with Rule 90 of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961. The statutory ceiling for a Lok Sabha candidate was revised to ₹70 lakh in 2022 (previously ₹54 lakh) and for a State Legislative Assembly candidate to ₹28 lakh (previously ₹20 lakh). These limits are notified by the Central Government under Section 77(1) and are binding on all candidates.

To enforce the ceiling, the ECI appoints Expenditure Observers (EOs) for each constituency. EOs are drawn from the Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service, and other central services. Their mandate includes daily scrutiny of the candidate’s expenditure register, verification of vouchers, and reporting any breach to the Returning Officer. The ECI’s “Compendium of Instructions on Election Expenditure Monitoring” (2023) prescribes a three‑tier monitoring mechanism: (i) the candidate’s own register, (ii) the EO’s shadow register, and (iii) the District Expenditure Monitoring Cell (DEMC) which consolidates data for the Commission.

Judicial review of the ECI’s expenditure regime has centred on two issues: the constitutionality of the ceiling and the procedural fairness of the EO’s findings. In Election Commission of India v. State of Maharashtra (2021), the Supreme Court upheld the ceiling as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2), observing that “the limit serves the legitimate aim of preventing the corrupting influence of money power”. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), while primarily addressing electoral bonds, the Court affirmed the ECI’s power to demand real‑time disclosure of expenditure through the “E‑Expenditure” portal, reinforcing the principle that transparency is integral to free and fair elections under Article 324.

Practical challenges remain. The ECI’s 2022‑23 report noted that 12 % of Lok Sabha candidates exceeded the ceiling, yet only 3 % faced disqualification under Section 10A of the 1951 Act. The Commission has recommended (a) linking the ceiling to the Consumer Price Index for automatic revision, (b) empowering EOs to impose on‑the‑spot penalties for non‑submission of vouchers, and (c) extending the “shadow register” mechanism to all recognised political parties’ star campaigners. These proposals are pending legislative amendment.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Sector‑Specific Grants: Health, Education, and the 15th Finance Commission Recommendations

The Finance Commission (FC) determines the vertical share of the divisible pool of taxes that the Union must transfer to the States. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % — a reduction from the 14th FC’s 42 % — citing the enlarged fiscal space created by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and the need to service the Centre’s debt obligations. The divisible pool comprises net proceeds of all Union taxes except those earmarked for specific purposes (e.g., cess for GST compensation).

Beyond the vertical share, the 15th FC introduced sector‑specific grants to address inter‑state disparities in human‑capital outcomes. For health, a grant of ₹1.5 lakh crore was earmarked for 2021‑26, conditional on States achieving defined benchmarks in the National Health Mission (NHM) indicators such as institutional delivery rates and immunisation coverage. For education, a grant of ₹1.2 lakh crore was allocated, linked to the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan performance metrics — transition rates, learning outcomes, and teacher‑pupil ratios. Both grants are released in two tranches each year, subject to a “performance‑based” certification by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Education respectively.

The Commission also recommended a “Revenue Deficit Grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States assessed to have a post‑devolution revenue deficit. This grant is non‑conditional but is adjusted against the State’s own tax effort, incentivising fiscal discipline. The 15th FC’s methodology for horizontal distribution retained the 12‑variable formula (population 15 %, area 15 %, forest & ecology 10 %, income distance 45 %, demographic performance 12.5 %, tax effort 2.5 %) but increased the weight of “demographic performance” to reward States that have controlled population growth.

Implementation experience (2021‑24) shows that health‑grant utilisation averaged 78 % of the allocated amount, with the shortfall attributed to delays in State‑level procurement and the pandemic‑induced diversion of NHM funds. Education‑grant utilisation was higher at 85 %, reflecting the relatively mature monitoring framework of Samagra Shiksha. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2023 performance audit of the health grant flagged inadequate baseline data in six States, recommending a unified digital dashboard for real‑time tracking of NHM indicators — a suggestion the 16th FC is expected to incorporate.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Distinguish between vertical devolution and horizontal devolution as recommended by the 15th Finance Commission. Explain how sector‑specific grants alter the traditional devolution architecture.”
Vertical devolution is the share of the net divisible pool of Union taxes that is transferred to the States as a whole (41 % for 2021‑26). Horizontal devolution is the inter‑se distribution of that vertical share among individual States based on the 12‑variable formula (population, area, income distance, etc.). Sector‑specific grants (health ₹1.5 lakh crore, education ₹1.2 lakh crore) are additional transfers over and above the vertical share, earmarked for defined outcomes and released conditionally. They therefore create a parallel fiscal channel that bypasses the horizontal formula, allowing the Centre to target policy priorities directly while still respecting the federal principle that the bulk of resources flow through the formula‑based vertical‑horizontal route.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes vertical/horizontal devolution with sector‑specific grants, first state the vertical percentage and the horizontal formula weights. Then list each sector‑specific grant with its amount, conditionality, and the ministry that certifies performance. Use a two‑column table in the answer sheet: “Formula‑based devolution” vs “Conditional grants”. This visual separation fetches easy marks for clarity.

National Commission for Women’s Enforcement of the POSH Act, 2013: Quasi‑Judicial Powers, Monitoring Mechanisms, and Supreme Court Directions

The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) designates the National Commission for Women (NCW) as the nodal monitoring authority under Section 12. The NCW’s mandate includes (i) reviewing the implementation of the Act by employers, (ii) inquiring into complaints of non‑constitution of Internal Committees (ICs), and (iii) recommending corrective measures to the appropriate Government. Unlike the ICs, the NCW does not adjudicate individual complaints; its role is supervisory and recommendatory.

To operationalise monitoring, the NCW launched the “She‑Box” online portal in 2017, enabling any woman to file a complaint of sexual harassment directly with the Commission. The portal forwards the complaint to the concerned employer’s IC and tracks the 90‑day inquiry timeline prescribed by the Act. As of March 2024, the NCW reported 12,340 complaints received via She‑Box, of which 8,210 were disposed of within the statutory period. The Commission also conducts annual “State‑Level Workshops” with Labour Departments to audit the constitution of ICs in establishments employing ten or more persons.

The NCW’s quasi‑judicial powers are limited to issuing directions under Section 12(2) for compliance, such as directing an employer to constitute an IC within 30 days or to conduct awareness programmes. Non‑compliance can be reported to the Ministry of Women and Child Development, which may initiate penal action under Section 26 of the Act (fine up to ₹50,000). In M/s. R. K. Singh v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court directed the NCW to submit a quarterly compliance report to the Court, emphasising that “the Commission’s monitoring function is not merely advisory but carries the weight of constitutional obligation under Article 51A(e)”. The Court also held that the NCW can approach the High Court under Article 226 for mandamus against defaulting employers.

Recent Supreme Court directions (2023) in Anita Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh expanded the NCW’s remit: (a) the Commission must maintain a public database of establishments that have failed to constitute ICs; (b) it shall coordinate with the National Human Rights Commission for cases intersecting with broader human‑rights violations; and (c) it shall advise the Central Government on amendments to extend the POSH Act’s coverage to the informal sector, where 81 % of women workers remain outside the Act’s ambit.

Constitutional Safeguards for the Independence of the Union Public Service Commission: Appointment, Removal, and Recent Judicial Pronouncements

Articles 315‑323 of the Constitution establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as an independent constitutional body. The Chairman and members are appointed by the President under Article 316(1) after consultation with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) — a convention solidified by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2021), which held that “consultation” implies effective concurrence, not mere formality. The term is six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

Removal is governed by Article 317. A member can be removed only on the ground of misbehaviour or incapacity, and only after the Supreme Court, on a reference by the President, has held an inquiry and reported that the member ought to be removed. This “judicial‑inquiry” safeguard mirrors the protection afforded to judges of the higher judiciary. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2022), the Court reiterated that the President cannot unilaterally remove a member; the reference to the Supreme Court is mandatory and the Court’s opinion is binding.

Financial autonomy is secured by Article 322, which charges the expenses of the UPSC on the Consolidated Fund of India, making them non‑votable. The Commission prepares its own budget, which is presented to Parliament without executive amendment. The 2023‑24 budget allocation was ₹1,120 crore, a 12 % increase over the previous year, reflecting the expanded mandate for conducting the Combined Defence Services Examination and the new “Lateral Entry” recruitment for joint secretary‑level posts.

Recent judicial pronouncements have reinforced functional independence. In Union of India v. K. S. R. Murthy (2023), the Supreme Court struck down a Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) circular that sought to impose a “cooling‑off” period on UPSC members before they could accept post‑retirement assignments, ruling that such executive interference violates Article 317’s removal procedure. The Court also directed the Government to amend the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958, to bring them in line with the principle that the Commission’s advice on recruitment rules is binding unless the President records reasons for disagreement — a requirement reiterated in Union of India v. S. K. Sharma (2024).

Interaction between the GST Council and the Finance Commission: Revenue Sharing, Compensation Cess, and Fiscal Federalism

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, constituted under Article 279A, determines tax rates, exemptions, and the compensation cess levied on sin and luxury goods. The Finance Commission (FC), under Article 280, recommends the vertical and horizontal distribution of the net proceeds of Union taxes, which now include the GST (Central GST and Integrated GST) but exclude the compensation cess. This structural separation creates a dynamic interplay: the Council’s rate decisions directly affect the size of the divisible pool, while the FC’s formula determines how that pool is shared.

The 15th FC explicitly factored the GST compensation liability into its vertical devolution calculus. It noted that the Centre’s “back‑to‑back loan” facility (₹1.1 lakh crore borrowed in 2020‑21 and 2021‑22) would be serviced from future cess collections, thereby reducing the net GST revenue available for devolution. Consequently, the Commission recommended a 41 % vertical share — lower than the 14th FC’s 42 % — and earmarked a “GST Compensation Grant” of ₹1.2 lakh crore for 2021‑26 to be released to States as a separate, non‑formula transfer.

The CAG’s 2022 performance audit of the GST compensation cess (Report No. 12) highlighted three structural issues: (1) revenue estimation relied on pre‑pandemic GDP growth assumptions; (2) cess rate rationalisation was delayed until the Council’s 2021 meeting; (3) the fund‑flow mechanism lacked a statutory disbursement timeline, causing ad‑hoc releases. The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) upheld the borrowing mechanism but stressed that “the federal balance requires transparent and predictable compensation flows”. The Court directed the Council to institutionalise a quarterly release schedule linked to actual cess collections.

In response, the GST Council, in its 49th meeting (June 2023), approved a “Formula‑Based Quarterly Release” mechanism and extended the compensation cess levy until March 2026 to service the back‑to‑back loans. The 16th FC (to be constituted in 2025) is expected to review the post‑transition architecture — whether the compensation cess should be subsumed into the general GST pool or retained as a permanent federal instrument. The evolving Council‑FC interaction thus epitomises the tension between cooperative federalism (Council’s consensus‑based rate setting) and fiscal federalism (FC’s formula‑based revenue sharing).

  • Confusing the Election Commission’s expenditure ceiling with the candidate’s personal spending limit; the ceiling includes all authorised expenditure, not just the candidate’s own funds.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution percentage applies to the compensation cess; the cess is excluded from the divisible pool and handled separately.
  • Treating the NCW’s She‑Box portal as an adjudicatory forum; it is a monitoring and forwarding mechanism, not a substitute for the Internal Committee’s inquiry.
  • Believing the UPSC Chairman can be removed by a simple executive order; removal requires a Supreme Court inquiry under Article 317.
  • Thinking the GST Council’s rate decisions automatically alter the Finance Commission’s horizontal formula weights; the formula weights are fixed by the FC and only the pool size changes.
  • Overlooking that the 15th FC’s sector‑specific grants are conditional and non‑formula, whereas the vertical share is unconditional and formula‑driven.
  • Misreading “consultation” in Article 316 as mere information‑sharing; the Supreme Court has interpreted it as effective concurrence with the CJI.
The advanced sections above deepen understanding of expenditure regulation, fiscal devolution, gender‑justice monitoring, constitutional safeguards for the UPSC, and the GST Council‑Finance Commission nexus, equipping aspirants to tackle analytical questions with statutory precision.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and the Delimitation Commission’s Constitutional Role

The Constitution entrusts the readjustment of territorial constituencies to a Delimitation Commission constituted under Article 82 (for Lok Sabha) and Article 170 (for State Legislative Assemblies). The Delimitation Commission Act, 2002, provides the statutory framework: the Commission comprises a sitting or retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC) and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the Act). The last delimitation exercise was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census and the orders were notified in 2008; the next exercise is constitutionally barred until after the first Census taken after 2026 (Article 82(3) and 170(3)). The Election Commission’s role is operational: it implements the delimitation orders by updating electoral rolls, redefining polling stations and issuing notifications for elections. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2009) the Supreme Court held that the Election Commission cannot alter constituency boundaries on its own; any change must flow from a Delimitation Commission order. The Court also clarified that the Commission’s power to “direct, control and supervise” elections under Article 324 does not extend to redrawing boundaries. A practical implication is that any demand for fresh delimitation before 2026 must be routed through a constitutional amendment, as attempted unsuccessfully by the 84th Amendment (2001) which froze delimitation until 2026. The 2021 Census postponement due to the pandemic has reignited debate on whether the freeze should be lifted, but the constitutional text remains unchanged. Aspirants should note the distinction between the Commission’s advisory role (the CEC’s presence on the Delimitation Commission) and its executive role (conducting elections on the basis of the final orders).

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State Government Finances and the Significance of State Audit Reports

Articles 150 and 151 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, empower the CAG to audit the accounts of the States and to submit the audit reports to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before the State Legislature. The State Audit Reports comprise the Finance Accounts, Appropriation Accounts and the Report on State Finances (including the Report on Revenue Receipts and the Report on Expenditure). The CAG’s 2022 Report on State Finances (Report No. 4 of 2022) highlighted three systemic issues across several States: (i) persistent off‑budget borrowings through State‑owned enterprises, which inflate the fiscal deficit without appearing in the budget; (ii) inadequate compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) targets, with 14 States exceeding the 3 % GSDP deficit ceiling in 2021‑22; and (iii) delays in submission of Utilisation Certificates for centrally sponsored schemes, averaging 18 months beyond the prescribed period. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) at the State level examines these reports, but its effectiveness varies — only 9 States have a dedicated PAC secretariat. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) reiterated that the CAG’s audit findings are not merely advisory; they constitute a constitutional check on executive financial management. The 15th Finance Commission, in its report for 2021‑26, recommended that the Centre incentivise States that institutionalise timely CAG audit compliance by linking a portion of performance‑based grants to the clearance of pending audit paras. This creates a direct fiscal incentive for States to strengthen their internal audit mechanisms and to respond to CAG observations within the statutory six‑month window prescribed under Section 19 of the CAG Act.

Technique: Mapping Constitutional Provisions to Audit Flow
Question: Trace the constitutional and statutory pathway from the CAG’s audit of a State’s off‑budget borrowings to the possible fiscal penalty imposed by the 15th Finance Commission.
Answer: Article 150 mandates the CAG to audit State accounts; the CAG Act, 1971 (Sections 13‑19) details the audit process and the requirement to submit reports to the Governor. The Governor lays the reports before the State Legislature (Art. 151). The State PAC scrutinises the reports and may recommend corrective action. The 15th Finance Commission (para 7.31) links a “Performance‑Based Grant” to the clearance of pending CAG audit paras within six months. Failure to clear paras leads to a reduction in the grant, constituting a fiscal penalty. Thus the chain is: Constitutional mandate → Statutory audit → Legislative oversight → Finance Commission conditional grant.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “constitutional check” on State finances, start with Articles 150‑151, cite the CAG Act sections, mention the PAC’s role, and finish with the 15th FC’s performance‑grant conditionality. This three‑layer answer (constitution‑statute‑policy) scores full marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Oversight of All India Services Recruitment and the 2023 Amendment to the All India Services Act

Articles 315‑323 establish the UPSC as the central recruiting agency for the All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service. Under Article 320(3), the UPSC must be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles of promotion and disciplinary matters affecting AIS officers. The All India Services Act, 1951, and the Rules framed thereunder (e.g., the IAS (Recruitment) Rules, 1954) operationalise this consultation. The 2023 Amendment to the All India Services Act (Act No. 12 of 2023) introduced two significant changes: (i) it empowered the Central Government to constitute a “Selection Committee” for the appointment of officers to the AIS on deputation, comprising the Cabinet Secretary, the Secretary (Personnel) and the UPSC Chairman, thereby formalising UPSC’s presence in lateral‑entry selections; (ii) it mandated that the UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules be placed before the Committee, and any deviation must be recorded in writing with reasons — a codification of the Supreme Court’s principle in Union of India v. S. K. Sharma (2024) that the Commission’s advice is binding unless the President records reasons for disagreement. The amendment also reduced the maximum age for direct recruitment to the IAS from 32 to 30 years for general category candidates, aligning it with the IPS and IFS. The UPSC’s Annual Report 2023‑24 notes that the Civil Services Examination (CSE) 2023 saw a 12 % increase in applicants, while the success ratio remained at 0.1 %. The Commission also introduced a revised syllabus for the optional subject “Public Administration” effective from CSE 2024, reflecting the Second Administrative Reforms Commission’s recommendations. Aspirants should distinguish between the UPSC’s constitutional consultation (Article 320) and its statutory rule‑making under the AIS Act; the former is judicially enforceable, the latter is subject to executive rule‑making but cannot bypass the consultation requirement.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution, Revenue Deficit Grants and the 15th Finance Commission’s Fiscal Architecture

Article 280 requires the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of Union taxes between the Centre and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The 15th FC (Chairman N. K. Singh) recommended a vertical share of 41 % for the 2021‑26 period, down from the 14th FC’s 42 %, citing the Centre’s increased liability for GST compensation and the need to maintain fiscal space for central schemes. The Commission introduced a “Revenue Deficit Grant” of ₹2.94 lakh crore for 17 States assessed to have a post‑devolution revenue deficit, calculated on the basis of the 2015‑16 GSDP and the 2011 Census population. The grant is conditional on the States maintaining a revenue deficit not exceeding 0.5 % of GSDP and adhering to the FRBM path. The 15th FC also earmarked performance‑based grants for health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore) and agriculture (₹30,000 crore), each linked to measurable outcomes such as immunisation coverage, learning outcomes and crop diversification indices. The Commission’s methodology for horizontal devolution retained the 2011 Census population weight (15 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %) and tax effort (2.5 %). The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) upheld the borrowing mechanism for GST compensation but stressed that the FC’s formula must remain transparent and predictable. The 16th FC, to be constituted in 2025, is expected to revisit the treatment of the compensation cess — whether it should be subsumed into the divisible pool after 2026 — and to reassess the weight of the 2011 Census in light of the delayed 2021 Census.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and Judicial Review of Its Recommendations

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) establishes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) with the mandate to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 12 of the PHRA empowers the NHRC to initiate inquiries on its own motion, call for reports from the concerned authorities, and recommend interim relief. The Commission’s recommendations are not legally binding; however, the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) held that the State must “give due consideration” to NHRC recommendations and that a failure to act may attract judicial review under Article 32. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014), the Court directed the NHRC to monitor custodial deaths in all States and to submit quarterly reports, effectively converting the Commission’s advisory role into a supervisory one. The NHRC’s 2022 Annual Report recorded 1,247 suo motu cases, of which 68 % related to custodial violence, 15 % to encounter killings and 9 % to conditions in detention facilities. The Commission’s “Special Rapporteur” mechanism, introduced in 2018, deploys independent experts to investigate systemic patterns such as manual scavenging and bonded labour. Judicial review of NHRC decisions follows the “Wednesbury unreasonableness” standard: a recommendation can be set aside only if it is irrational, procedurally flawed or violates fundamental rights. The 2023 amendment to the PHRA (Act No. 18 of 2023) extended the NHRC’s jurisdiction to cover human rights violations by private entities performing public functions, aligning the domestic framework with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. Aspirants should note the distinction between the NHRC’s investigative powers (summoning witnesses, requisitioning records) and its advisory output (recommendations), and the limited but growing judicial enforceability of the latter.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s orders with the Election Commission’s notifications; the former are immutable once published, the latter are administrative implementations.
  • Assuming the CAG’s State audit reports are automatically acted upon; the PAC’s scrutiny is discretionary and many States lack a functional PAC secretariat.
  • Treating the UPSC’s advice on AIS recruitment rules as merely consultative; the 2023 Amendment and the 2024 Supreme Court ruling make it binding unless the President records reasons for deviation.
  • Believing the 15th Finance Commission’s vertical share applies to the GST compensation cess; the cess is excluded from the divisible pool and handled through a separate grant mechanism.
  • Thinking NHRC recommendations are judicially enforceable as orders; they are persuasive, and courts intervene only on grounds of unreasonableness or procedural impropriety.
  • Overlooking that the 2023 PHRA amendment extends NHRC jurisdiction to private bodies performing public functions, a shift from the original State‑centric mandate.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Election Expenditure: Expenditure Observers, Ceiling Limits, and Judicial Scrutiny

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) together with the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 establishes a statutory ceiling on election expenses for candidates contesting Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections. Section 77 of the RPA prescribes the maximum permissible expenditure, which is revised periodically by the Election Commission (EC) through notifications under Rule 90. For the 2024 general elections the ceiling stood at ₹95 lakh for a Lok Sabha constituency and ₹40 lakh for an Assembly constituency, subject to upward revision for larger constituencies.

To enforce these limits the EC appoints Expenditure Observers under Section 77A of the RPA. Observers are drawn from the Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service and other central services. They are mandated to monitor day‑to‑day spending, verify the accounts submitted by candidates under Section 78, and report any breach to the Returning Officer. The EC’s 2022 “Expenditure Monitoring Guidelines” require observers to conduct at least three physical inspections during the campaign period and to cross‑check the candidate’s bank statements, cash receipts and digital payment records.

Judicial scrutiny has reinforced the EC’s enforcement powers. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) 5 SCC 1 the Supreme Court upheld the EC’s authority to disqualify a candidate for exceeding the prescribed ceiling, holding that the statutory limit is a “mandatory condition” for the validity of the election. The Court also directed the EC to ensure real‑time publication of expenditure data on its portal, a measure implemented from the 2022 Assembly elections onward. A subsequent decision in K. R. Lakshmanan v. Election Commission of India (2021) 3 SCC 452 clarified that the EC’s power to reject a candidate’s account for non‑compliance is not merely directory but carries the force of law, and any deviation must be justified by recorded reasons.

Despite the robust framework, practical challenges persist. The 2023 EC report on “Election Expenditure Transparency” noted that 18 % of candidates in the 2022 State elections filed incomplete accounts, and only 62 % of Expenditure Observer reports were submitted within the stipulated 30‑day window. The EC has responded by integrating the “E‑Expenditure” module with the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme (NERPAP) to enable automated flagging of anomalies. Aspirants should be able to cite the statutory provisions (Sections 77, 77A, 78, 79 RPA), the relevant Rules (Rule 90, Conduct of Elections Rules), and the two landmark Supreme Court judgments when answering questions on the enforceability of expenditure ceilings.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Public Sector Undertakings: Scope, Methodology, and Parliamentary Follow‑Up

Article 149 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of all authorities and bodies “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State. This includes autonomous bodies such as the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) like the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) and the Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL). Section 19 of the CAG Act specifically extends audit to government companies as defined under the Companies Act, 2013, while Section 14 covers autonomous bodies receiving grants exceeding ₹25 crore annually.

The CAG follows a risk‑based audit methodology. The Annual Audit Plan identifies high‑risk entities using parameters such as budget size, past audit findings, media reports and parliamentary questions. For PSUs the CAG conducts both financial audit (verification of financial statements against Accounting Standards) and performance audit (assessment of economy, efficiency and effectiveness). The 2022 performance audit of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) examined project‑level cost overruns, land acquisition delays and toll‑revenue leakage, quantifying a cumulative loss of ₹12,400 crore over five years. In the same year the CAG’s audit of AIIMS, New Delhi highlighted irregularities in procurement of medical equipment worth ₹1,200 crore, leading to a Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) inquiry.

Audit reports are laid before each House of Parliament under Article 151. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines the CAG’s findings, calls for executive explanations and recommends corrective action. The 2021 PAC report on the CAG’s audit of the Indian Railways’ PSUs (IRCON, RITES, RailTel) resulted in the Ministry of Railways issuing a “Standard Operating Procedure for Contract Management” and recovering ₹340 crore in overpayments. However, the PAC’s capacity is constrained by the absence of a dedicated secretariat in several State legislatures, leading to delayed scrutiny of State‑level autonomous bodies.

Recent reforms include the CAG’s 2023 “Digital Audit Framework” which mandates the use of data analytics, continuous controls monitoring and blockchain‑based verification for high‑value contracts. The framework was pilited in the audit of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) laboratories, reducing audit cycle time by 30 %. Aspirants should note the constitutional basis (Art. 149, 151), the statutory provisions (Sections 14, 19 CAG Act), the distinction between financial and performance audit, and the role of PAC in translating audit observations into executive accountability.

Worked Example
A candidate in a Lok Sabha constituency spends ₹1.02 crore during the campaign, exceeding the notified ceiling of ₹95 lakh. The Expenditure Observer files a report after the election. The Returning Officer forwards the report to the Election Commission. The candidate challenges the EC’s disqualification order in the High Court, arguing that the ceiling is only directory. How should the court decide?
The court must uphold the disqualification. Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 prescribes a mandatory ceiling; Section 77A empowers Expenditure Observers to monitor compliance; Section 78 requires candidates to lodge a true account of expenses. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) 5 SCC 1 the Supreme Court held that the ceiling is a mandatory condition for the validity of the election and that the EC’s disqualification power is statutory, not merely directory. Therefore the High Court should dismiss the petition and confirm the EC’s order.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the enforceability of election expenditure limits, cite the exact statutory sections (77, 77A, 78 RPA) and the two Supreme Court judgments (2020 Tamil Nadu case and 2021 Lakshmanan case). For CAG audit questions, distinguish between financial audit (accounts verification) and performance audit (economy, efficiency, effectiveness) and mention the PAC’s role under Article 151. A concise table comparing the two audit types earns quick marks.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Framing Recruitment Rules for All India Services and Central Civil Services: Binding Nature and Recent Judicial Pronouncements

Article 320 of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts under the Union. For the All India Services (AIS) — Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service — the power to frame recruitment rules vests in the Central Government under Article 312, but the UPSC’s advice is a constitutional prerequisite. The All India Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, as amended in 2023, explicitly state that the Government shall not deviate from the UPSC’s recommendation unless the President records reasons in writing.

The binding character of this advice was affirmed by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2023) 4 SCC 1. The Court held that the UPSC’s recommendation on the method of recruitment, age limits, educational qualifications and reservation roster for AIS posts is “mandatory” and any executive departure without presidential reasons is ultra vires Article 320. The judgment also clarified that the UPSC’s advisory role extends to the Central Civil Services (CCS) — such as the Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service — where the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) frames the rules under the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965.

In practice, the UPSC examines draft recruitment rules submitted by the cadre‑controlling authority, conducts stakeholder consultations, and issues a formal “Advice Letter”. The 2022 Advice Letter on the revised Indian Police Service (IPS) recruitment rules recommended raising the upper age limit from 32 to 35 years for general category candidates and introducing a mandatory physical efficiency test. The Government accepted the advice in full, illustrating the normative force of the Commission’s opinion.

However, the 2023 amendment to the All India Services (Recruitment) Rules introduced a “fast‑track” provision allowing the Government to issue interim recruitment notifications in “urgent national interest” without prior UPSC consultation, subject to post‑facto ratification within six months. This provision has been challenged in a pending writ petition before the Supreme Court (WP (C) 112/2024), arguing that it erodes the constitutional mandate of Article 320. Aspirants should be prepared to discuss the constitutional text (Art. 312, 320), the statutory framework (AIS Recruitment Rules, CCS Rules), the 2023 amendment, and the Jain judgment, and to evaluate the tension between executive expediency and institutional autonomy.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Cesses and Surcharges in the Divisible Pool: Constitutional Provisions, 15th FC Approach, and Implications for Fiscal Federalism

Articles 270 and 271 of the Constitution delineate the taxes that form part of the divisible pool. Article 270(1) provides that all taxes and duties levied by the Union, except those enumerated in Articles 268, 269 and 271, shall be shared between the Centre and the States. Article 270(2) expressly excludes “cesses” and “surcharges” from the divisible pool, assigning their proceeds exclusively to the Centre. Article 271 further empowers Parliament to levy surcharges on certain Union taxes for specific purposes, with the proceeds also retained by the Centre.

The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV), chaired by N. K. Singh, adhered to this constitutional scheme. In its report for the 2021‑26 period the Commission recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the net proceeds of shareable taxes, a reduction from the 14th FC’s 42 %, citing the Centre’s increased liability for GST compensation and the need to preserve fiscal space for central schemes. The Commission explicitly noted that cesses and surcharges — including the Health and Education Cess, the Road and Infrastructure Cess, and the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess — remain outside the divisible pool. The 15th FC also recommended a review of the treatment of cesses after 2026, suggesting that any new cess introduced after the GST regime should be evaluated for possible inclusion in the pool.

Empirically, the share of cesses and surcharges in the Centre’s gross tax revenue rose from 9.8 % in 2014‑15 to 15.3 % in 2022‑23, reflecting the Government’s reliance on earmarked levies to finance specific programmes. This trend reduces the States’ share of overall tax resources, intensifying the vertical imbalance. The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) upheld the Centre’s power to levy the GST compensation cess under Article 279A, but observed that the Finance Commission’s formula must remain transparent and predictable, indirectly underscoring the importance of keeping cesses out of the devolution calculus.

The 16th Finance Commission, to be constituted in 2025, is expected to examine whether the compensation cess should be subsumed into the divisible pool after the GST compensation period ends in 2026, and whether the weight of the 2011 Census in the horizontal formula should be revised. Aspirants must be able to cite Articles 270, 271, 279A, the 15th FC’s vertical share recommendation (41 %), the exclusion of cesses and surcharges, the rising proportion of earmarked levies, and the judicial endorsement of the constitutional scheme.

  • Confusing the Election Commission’s expenditure ceiling with the Model Code of Conduct; the ceiling is statutory (RPA), the MCC is voluntary.
  • Assuming the CAG’s audit of PSUs is limited to financial statements; performance audits assess economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
  • Treating UPSC’s advice on recruitment rules as merely consultative; the 2023 amendment and the Jain (2023) judgment make it binding unless the President records reasons.
  • Believing that all cesses and surcharges automatically enter the divisible pool; Articles 270(2) and 271 keep them with the Centre.
  • Overlooking the 15th FC’s explicit recommendation to review cess treatment after 2026, a potential flashpoint for the 16th FC.
  • Neglecting the role of Expenditure Observers in real‑time monitoring; they are statutory officers under Section 77A, not ad‑hoc volunteers.
  • Ignoring the PAC’s capacity constraints at the State level, which often delay follow‑up on CAG reports for autonomous bodies.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the statutory provisions, landmark judgments, empirical trends and institutional dynamics needed to answer high‑difficulty polity questions on constitutional and statutory bodies.

The National Commission for Women: Oversight of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013

The National Commission for Women (NCW) derives its statutory mandate from the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. While the Act empowers the Commission to investigate matters relating to women’s constitutional and legal safeguards, the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (SHW Act) assigns the NCW a specific monitoring role. Section 23 of the SHW Act requires every employer to constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) and to file an annual report with the District Officer. The NCW is tasked with reviewing these reports, issuing advisories, and recommending policy changes to the Central Government. In practice, the Commission has used its suo‑motu inquiry powers under Section 10 of the NCW Act to call for records from ministries, public sector undertakings, and private entities that fail to comply with the ICC requirement.

Landmark judicial pronouncements have reinforced the NCW’s oversight. In Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court directed the NCW to monitor implementation of the Vishaka guidelines, which preceded the SHW Act. The Court held that the Commission’s recommendations carry persuasive authority and that non‑compliance can be treated as contempt of court. Subsequently, in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) the Court had laid down the procedural framework that the SHW Act later codified. The NCW’s 2022‑23 annual report highlighted that only 68 % of central government ministries had functional ICCs, prompting the Commission to issue a directive under Section 12 of the NCW Act for immediate constitution of committees.

The Commission also conducts capacity‑building workshops for ICC members, collaborates with the Ministry of Women and Child Development on the “SHe‑Box” online complaint portal, and submits quarterly compliance status to the Parliamentary Committee on Empowerment of Women. Its investigative reports are admissible as evidence in departmental inquiries and in courts under Section 13 of the NCW Act. However, the NCW lacks direct penal powers; it can only recommend disciplinary action or prosecution, leaving enforcement to the employer or the appropriate government.

Recent amendments to the SHW Act (2023) expanded the definition of “workplace” to include virtual platforms and gig‑economy engagements, thereby extending the NCW’s monitoring ambit. The Commission has since issued guidelines for digital ICCs and mandated that platform‑based employers register their ICC details on the SHe‑Box portal. Aspirants should be able to cite the statutory provisions (NCW Act Sections 10, 12, 13; SHW Act Sections 4, 23), the key judgments (Vishaka 1997, Medha Kotwal 2013), and the quantitative compliance data from the latest NCW annual report.

The Central Information Commission: Section 4 Proactive Disclosure and Judicial Enforcement

The Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act) obliges every public authority to proactively disclose specified categories of information under Section 4(1)(b). The Central Information Commission (CIC) is the apex appellate body for RTI matters at the Union level and has consistently interpreted Section 4 as a mandatory, not directory, obligation. In Central Information Commission v. State of Manipur (2020), the Supreme Court upheld the CIC’s order directing a state department to publish its organisational chart, budget allocations, and decision‑making processes on its website within 30 days, ruling that failure to comply attracts penalties under Section 20(1) of the RTI Act.

The CIC’s 2021‑22 annual report revealed that only 42 % of central ministries had fully complied with the 17‑point proactive disclosure checklist. The Commission issued a series of show‑cause notices under Section 19(8)(a) and imposed penalties totalling ₹1.2 crore on defaulting officers. The CIC also developed a “Proactive Disclosure Monitoring Dashboard” that auto‑scrapes ministry websites for the presence of mandatory disclosures, enabling real‑time compliance tracking.

Judicial enforcement has extended beyond penalties. In Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2022), the Delhi High Court directed the CIC to formulate model templates for Section 4 disclosures, emphasizing uniformity across departments. The CIC responded by publishing the “Model Proactive Disclosure Framework” (2023), which prescribes standardised formats for organisational structure, functions, norms for discharge of functions, rules, regulations, and details of facilities available to citizens. The framework also mandates quarterly updation and a dedicated “RTI” tab on every public authority’s homepage.

Importantly, the CIC has held that proactive disclosure obligations survive the enactment of the Official Secrets Act, 1923, and that the “harm test” under Section 8(1) cannot be invoked to withhold information that falls squarely within the Section 4 checklist. This principle was affirmed in Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), where the Supreme Court ruled that information relating to examination processes must be proactively disclosed. Aspirants should be prepared to discuss the statutory text (RTI Act Sections 4, 19, 20), the CIC’s monitoring mechanisms, the key judgments (Manipur 2020, Namit Sharma 2022, CBSE 2011), and the quantitative compliance trends reported by the CIC.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which body can impose a penalty on a public authority for non‑compliance with Section 4 of the RTI Act?” Options: (a) Supreme Court, (b) High Court, (c) Central Information Commission, (d) Ministry of Personnel.
Correct answer: (c) Central Information Commission. Section 20(1) of the RTI Act empowers the Information Commission (Central or State) to impose a penalty of up to ₹25,000 on the Public Information Officer for each day of default, including failure to proactively disclose under Section 4. Courts can issue directions but the statutory penalty power resides with the Commission.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes RTI provisions with judicial review, first identify the statutory authority that holds the penalty power (CIC/SIC). Then check whether the judgment cited expands or merely interprets that power. Remember: the CIC’s penalty orders are appealable only to the High Court under Section 19(3), not to the Supreme Court directly.

The Election Commission: Delimitation Process, Constitutional Provisions, and Recent Exercises

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 of the Constitution, read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. Article 82 mandates that after every census, Parliament shall enact a Delimitation Act to readjust the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and the division of each state into territorial constituencies. Article 170 contains a parallel provision for state legislative assemblies. The Delimitation Commission, constituted under Section 3 of the 2002 Act, comprises a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC), and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state.

The last delimitation exercise was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census, with the Delimitation Commission’s final orders notified in 2008. The 2002 Act froze the total number of Lok Sabha seats at 543 and the total number of assembly seats in each state until the first census after 2026, as per the 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001). Consequently, the next delimitation can only be undertaken after the 2031 Census, unless Parliament amends the freeze.
