The Commission’s methodology follows the “one‑person‑one‑vote‑one‑value” principle, aiming to keep the population variance within ±10 % of the state average, subject to geographical compactness, administrative boundaries, and community interests.

In 2020, the Election Commission issued a directive to the Delimitation Commission for the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir following the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019. The Commission completed the exercise in 2022, increasing the number of assembly seats from 83 to 90 and Lok Sabha seats from 5 to 5 (unchanged). The order was challenged in the Supreme Court (Mohd. Akbar Lone v. Union of India, 2023), which upheld the Commission’s adherence to the statutory criteria and rejected the plea that the exercise violated the freeze under the 84th Amendment, noting that the freeze applies only to states, not to newly created Union Territories.

The Election Commission also plays a consultative role in the delimitation of local bodies under Article 243K and 243ZA, where State Election Commissions are the primary authorities. However, the EC’s guidelines on the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for constituency mapping have been adopted by several State Election Commissions to improve transparency. Aspirants should be able to cite Articles 82, 170, 243K, 243ZA; the Delimitation Act, 2002 (Sections 3, 4, 9); the 84th and 87th Constitutional Amendments; the 2008 final orders; the Jammu & Kashmir delimitation (2022); and the Supreme Court’s 2023 judgment.

The Finance Commission: Grants‑in‑Aid, Revenue Deficit Grants, and Performance‑Based Incentives

Beyond the vertical tax devolution, the Finance Commission (FC) recommends grants‑in‑aid to states under Article 275(1) of the Constitution. These grants address two distinct needs: (i) revenue deficit grants to states whose assessed revenue expenditure exceeds their revenue receipts after tax devolution, and (ii) special purpose grants for sectors such as health, education, and rural infrastructure. The 15th Finance Commission (FC‑XV), chaired by N. K. Singh, recommended revenue deficit grants totalling ₹2.94 lakh crore for the 2021‑26 period, covering 17 states. The Commission adopted a “post‑devolution revenue deficit” methodology, estimating each state’s revenue gap after the 41 % vertical share and then filling the gap through grants.

Performance‑based incentives were introduced for the first time in FC‑XV’s report. The Commission earmarked ₹1.05 lakh crore for “performance‑based grants” linked to measurable outcomes in health (e.g., immunisation coverage, maternal mortality reduction), education (e.g., learning outcomes, teacher‑pupil ratios), and agriculture (e.g., crop diversification, micro‑irrigation). States must submit annual outcome reports to the Ministry of Finance, which are verified by the Comptroller and Auditor General before release of the incentive tranche. The 15th FC also recommended a “grants‑in‑aid for local bodies” of ₹4.36 lakh crore, split between rural and urban local bodies, with a condition that at least 50 % of the grant be tied to the generation of own‑source revenue.

The 14th Finance Commission (FC‑XIV) had discontinued revenue deficit grants, arguing that the enhanced vertical share (42 %) would suffice. The re‑introduction by FC‑XV reflects the fiscal stress caused by the GST compensation shortfall and the COVID‑19 pandemic. The Supreme Court, in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022), observed that the FC’s grant recommendations are advisory but acquire binding force once accepted by the President under Article 280(3). The Court also emphasized that the methodology for revenue deficit calculation must be transparent and replicable.

For the upcoming 16th Finance Commission (to be constituted in 2025), key issues include the treatment of the GST compensation cess after 2026, the weight of the 2011 Census in the horizontal formula, and the continuation of performance‑based incentives. Aspirants should be conversant with Articles 275, 280, 281; the 15th FC’s grant tables (Revenue Deficit Grants, Performance‑Based Grants, Local Body Grants); the post‑devolution revenue deficit methodology; the CAG’s verification role; and the judicial observations in the Kerala case.

The National Human Rights Commission: Custodial Death Inquiries, Police Reforms, and Judicial Review

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA). Section 12 empowers the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into complaints of violation of human rights by public servants. Custodial deaths — deaths occurring in police or judicial custody — constitute a significant portion of the NHRC’s docket. In 2022‑23, the Commission registered 1,842 custodial death cases, of which 1,210 were in police custody and 632 in judicial custody.

The NHRC’s investigative procedure mirrors a quasi‑judicial inquiry: it can summon witnesses, requisition documents, and direct the Director General of Police to conduct a parallel magisterial inquiry under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Commission’s recommendations are not binding but carry persuasive weight; under Section 18(1) the concerned government must respond within one month, indicating action taken or reasons for non‑compliance. Persistent non‑compliance can be reported to Parliament under Section 20.

Landmark Supreme Court judgments have shaped the NHRC’s custodial death jurisprudence. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Court laid down 11 procedural safeguards for arrest and detention, directing the NHRC to monitor compliance. The Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014) held that the NHRC’s failure to act on a custodial death complaint within a reasonable time could be challenged via a writ of mandamus. More recently, in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2021), the Supreme Court directed the NHRC to constitute a special investigation team for a high‑profile custodial death, underscoring the Commission’s role as an independent oversight body.

The NHRC also drives police reform through its “Model Police Act” recommendations (2006) and periodic advisories on the use of force, body‑worn cameras, and the establishment of Human Rights Cells in every police district. The Commission’s 2023 advisory mandated that all custodial deaths be reported to the NHRC within 24 hours and that a judicial magistrate conduct an inquest within 48 hours. Aspirants should be able to cite PHRA Sections 12, 13, 18, 20; the CrPC Section 176; the key judgments (D.K. Basu 1997, PUCL 2014, Rajesh Gautam 2021); the NHRC’s annual custodial death statistics; and the Commission’s advisory framework for police accountability.

  • Confusing the NCW’s recommendatory powers with binding enforcement authority under the SHW Act.
  • Assuming Section 4 proactive disclosure is optional; the CIC treats it as mandatory and penalises non‑compliance.
  • Believing delimitation can be undertaken after every census; the 84th Amendment freezes seat numbers until after 2026.
  • Treating Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid as purely discretionary; once accepted by the President they become constitutionally mandated.
  • Thinking NHRC recommendations are legally binding; they are persuasive and require government response but not compliance.
  • Overlooking the CAG’s verification role before release of performance‑based grants recommended by the Finance Commission.
  • Neglecting the 24‑hour reporting requirement for custodial deaths introduced by the NHRC’s 2023 advisory.

National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: Constitutional Mandate, Investigative Powers, and Coordination with State Commissions

The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) was constituted under Article 338A of the Constitution by the Constitution (Eighty‑ninth Amendment) Act, 2003, bifurcating the erstwhile combined National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Commission comprises a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson and three other Members, all appointed by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Their tenure is three years or until they attain the age of sixty‑five years, whichever is earlier, and they are eligible for re‑appointment once.

Under Article 338A(5) the NCST is mandated to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Tribes under the Constitution or any other law, to inquire into specific complaints of deprivation of rights, and to advise on the planning process for socio‑economic development of STs. The Commission enjoys the powers of a civil court while conducting inquiries: it can summon witnesses, require production of documents, receive evidence on affidavits, and issue commissions for examination of witnesses. Its reports are laid before each House of Parliament along with a memorandum explaining the action taken on its recommendations.

The NCST’s investigative jurisdiction extends to the implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006. In State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2019) the Supreme Court recognised the Commission’s role as a statutory watchdog for forest‑rights claims, directing the NCST to monitor the disposal of claims within a fixed timeline. The Commission also coordinates with State Scheduled Tribes Commissions established under respective State Acts; a 2021 Ministry of Tribal Affairs guideline institutionalised quarterly joint review meetings to harmonise data on atrocities, land alienation, and educational enrolment.

Despite its broad mandate, the NCST’s recommendations are advisory and not binding on the executive. The Commission’s annual reports (e.g., 2022‑23) highlight a persistent gap: of 1,842 atrocity cases registered under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, only 38 % resulted in conviction, underscoring the need for stronger enforcement mechanisms. The 2023 amendment to the NCST Act introduced a provision for the Commission to refer cases of non‑compliance to the concerned High Court for appropriate directions, a step towards quasi‑judicial enforceability.

Central Vigilance Commission: Appointment, Tenure, Removal, and Functional Autonomy

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was given statutory status by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, following the Supreme Court’s direction in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998). The Commission consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners. Appointments are made by the President on the recommendation of a three‑member committee comprising the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Minister of Home Affairs, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition party).

Members hold office for a term of four years or until they attain the age of sixty‑five years, whichever is earlier. They are not eligible for re‑appointment. Removal is governed by Section 6 of the Act: the President may remove a member only on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after an inquiry by the Supreme Court, a safeguard mirroring the removal procedure for the Comptroller and Auditor General. This high threshold is intended to insulate the CVC from executive pressure.

Functionally, the CVC exercises superintendence over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in corruption cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and advises the Central Government on vigilance administration. The Commission’s “Whistle‑blower Protection” mandate under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, empowers it to receive complaints, conduct preliminary inquiries, and recommend protective measures. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court upheld the CVC’s authority to direct the CBI to register FIRs against senior officials without prior governmental approval, reinforcing its operational autonomy.

Nevertheless, the CVC’s autonomy faces structural constraints: its budget is voted by Parliament but administered by the Ministry of Personnel, and its annual report is laid before Parliament only after the government’s comments are appended. The 2022 amendment to the CVC Act introduced a provision for the Commission to issue binding directions to disciplinary authorities in cases where the latter fail to act within ninety days, a move aimed at reducing implementation lag.

Worked Example: CVC Removal Procedure
A Vigilance Commissioner is alleged to have leaked confidential inquiry documents. The Prime Minister proposes removal. Outline the constitutional‑statutory steps required before the President can issue a removal order.
Step 1: The Prime Minister refers the matter to the Supreme Court for an inquiry under Section 6(2) of the CVC Act. Step 2: The Supreme Court conducts the inquiry and submits a report finding proved misbehaviour. Step 3: On receipt of the report, the President, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers, issues the removal order. The Commissioner cannot be removed by executive fiat alone; the judicial inquiry is mandatory.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the “independence” of a statutory body, always trace the appointment‑removal‑budget triad. For the CVC, note the three‑member selection committee, the Supreme Court inquiry prerequisite for removal, and the fact that its budget passes through the Ministry of Personnel — a classic examiner trap that tests whether you confuse statutory autonomy with constitutional independence.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and Reservation of Seats: Constitutional Provisions, Process, and Judicial Review

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 read with the Delimitation Commission Act, 2002. The President constitutes a Delimitation Commission chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners as ex‑officio members. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Section 10 of the Act).

The last delimitation exercise was based on the 2001 Census and completed in 2008. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies until the first Census after 2026, effectively postponing the next delimitation to post‑2031. However, the Commission continues to adjust reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under Articles 330 and 332 after each Census, using the proportion of SC/ST population in each State.

Judicial review of delimitation orders is extremely limited. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2002) the Supreme Court held that the Delimitation Commission’s decisions are final and not subject to judicial scrutiny except on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of constitutional provisions. The Court reiterated this in State of Bihar v. Delimitation Commission (2008), dismissing challenges alleging malapportionment. The Election Commission’s role is advisory: it provides electoral data, conducts field verification, and implements the final orders by updating electoral rolls and EVM databases.

Recent debates centre on the “One Nation, One Election” proposal and its impact on delimitation cycles. The 2023 Law Commission report recommended synchronising delimitation with the proposed simultaneous elections, arguing that a unified electoral roll would reduce administrative costs. Aspirants should be able to cite Articles 82, 170, 330, 332; the 84th and 87th Amendments; the Delimitation Commission Act, 2002; and the key Supreme Court judgments limiting judicial intervention.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Criteria, Weightage, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) raised the vertical share to 42 %, the highest ever, arguing that enhanced State autonomy would improve expenditure efficiency. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) retained the 41 % share (including 1 % for the newly formed Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh) but altered the criteria weights.

The 15th FC’s vertical formula uses the following weights: Population (2011 Census) – 15 %, Area – 15 %, Forest and Ecology – 10 %, Income Distance – 45 %, Demographic Performance – 12.5 %, and Tax Effort – 2.5 %. The shift from the 1971 Census (used by the 14th FC) to the 2011 Census for the population criterion sparked controversy, with southern States arguing it penalises successful population control. The Commission defended the change by citing the Terms of Reference which explicitly mandated the use of the latest Census.

The vertical devolution directly determines the divisible pool from which States fund their schemes. Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 accounts shows that States’ own‑tax revenue grew at 9.3 % while central transfers grew at 12.1 %, indicating increasing reliance on FC transfers. The 15th FC also introduced performance‑based grants for health, education, and agriculture, linking a portion of vertical devolution to measurable outcomes — a move towards outcome‑oriented fiscal federalism.

The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) observed that the FC’s recommendations are advisory until accepted by the President under Article 280(3), after which they acquire constitutional force. The Court emphasised transparency in the methodology for computing income distance and demographic performance. For the upcoming 16th FC (to be constituted in 2025), key issues include the treatment of the GST compensation cess after 2026, the continued use of the 2011 Census, and the design of incentive‑compatible performance grants.

Union Public Service Commission’s Conduct of Civil Services Examination: Syllabus Revision, Language Options, and Recent Reforms

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) derives its mandate from Articles 315‑323 and conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) for recruitment to the All India Services and Central Civil Services. The examination comprises three stages: Preliminary (objective), Main (descriptive), and Personality Test. The syllabus has undergone major revisions in 1979, 1989, 2003, 2011, and 2020.

The 2011 reform replaced the optional subject in the Preliminary stage with a compulsory Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) (Paper II), made qualifying at 33 % from 2015 onward. The 2013 revision restructured the Main examination: General Studies papers increased from two to four, an Essay paper was added, and the optional subject was reduced to one paper (250 marks). The 2020 reform introduced a new Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude paper (GS IV) and expanded the language options: candidates may write the Main examination in any of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule plus English, while the Preliminary remains bilingual (English/Hindi).

Recent reforms focus on transparency and accessibility. The 2022 “One‑Time Registration” portal streamlines application, and the 2023 “Common Eligibility Test” proposal (still under consideration) aims to replace the Preliminary with a single screening test for multiple government recruitments. The UPSC’s annual reports (2022‑23) indicate a steady rise in applicants — 11.5 lakh in 2023 — with a success ratio of 0.08 %. The Commission also conducts the Engineering Services Examination, Combined Medical Services Examination, and Indian Forest Service Examination under similar procedural frameworks.

Judicial scrutiny of UPSC’s examination process is limited to procedural fairness. In UPSC v. S. K. Sharma (2019) the Supreme Court upheld the Commission’s discretion in setting cut‑off marks, stating that courts cannot substitute their judgment for the expert body’s academic evaluation. However, the Court has intervened in cases of arbitrary changes in syllabus without adequate notice (e.g., Ramesh Kumar v. UPSC, 2021), reinforcing the principle of legitimate expectation.

  • Confusing the NCST’s advisory role with binding enforcement power; its recommendations require government response but not compliance.
  • Assuming the CVC can be removed by a simple executive order; the Supreme Court inquiry is a statutory prerequisite.
  • Believing delimitation can be undertaken after every Census; the 84th Amendment freezes seat numbers until after 2026.
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical share as a fixed constitutional number; it is a recommendation that becomes binding only after Presidential acceptance.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s CSAT paper is merit‑ranking; it has been qualifying only since 2015.
  • Overlooking that the Election Commission’s role in delimitation is advisory; the Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and not subject to judicial review except on jurisdictional grounds.
  • Neglecting the 2023 CVC amendment that empowers the Commission to issue binding directions to disciplinary authorities after ninety days of inaction.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Constitutional Provisions, 15th FC Recommendations, and Emerging Issues for the 16th FC

Article 280 of the Constitution mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share is not fixed in the Constitution; it is a recommendation that becomes binding only after the President accepts it under Article 280(3). The 15th FC (2020‑25) recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the divisible pool, a marginal increase from the 42 % recommended by the 14th FC but lower than the 44 % sought by several States. The Commission justified the figure by citing the need to preserve fiscal space for the Centre’s committed expenditures, including defence, interest payments, and centrally sponsored schemes.

The 15th FC introduced performance‑based grants for health, education, and agriculture, linking a portion of the vertical devolution to measurable outcomes. This marked a shift toward outcome‑oriented fiscal federalism. The Commission also recommended a separate grant for local bodies, raising the share of grants‑in‑aid from 1.5 % to 2.5 % of the divisible pool. The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. Union of India (2022) observed that the FC’s recommendations are advisory until presidential acceptance, after which they acquire constitutional force, and emphasised transparency in the methodology for computing income distance and demographic performance.

For the upcoming 16th FC (to be constituted in 2025), key issues include the treatment of the GST compensation cess after 2026, the continued use of the 2011 Census for demographic weight, and the design of incentive‑compatible performance grants. Several States have argued for a higher vertical share (up to 45 %) to offset revenue losses from GST implementation and the pandemic. The Centre, however, has signalled a preference for maintaining fiscal discipline and limiting the vertical share to around 41‑42 %. The 16th FC’s Terms of Reference will likely require it to balance these competing demands while ensuring that the devolution formula remains predictable and equitable.

Empirical analysis of the 2021‑22 accounts shows that States’ own‑tax revenue grew at 9.3 % while central transfers grew at 12.1 %, indicating increasing reliance on FC transfers. This trend underscores the importance of a stable vertical devolution framework. The Commission’s ability to incorporate new data sources — such as the Periodic Labour Force Survey and the National Family Health Survey — will affect the credibility of its recommendations. The 16th FC will also need to address the fiscal implications of the proposed National Monetisation Pipeline and the Centre’s capital expenditure push, which alter the composition of the divisible pool.

The Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and the Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Framework, Composition, and Recent Developments

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. The Election Commission (EC) does not itself delimit boundaries; it provides the necessary electoral data and administrative support to the Delimitation Commission, a statutory body constituted under the Delimitation Act. The Delimitation Commission comprises a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC), and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. Its orders are final and cannot be questioned in any court except on jurisdictional grounds.

The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies based on the 1971 Census until the first Census after 2026. Consequently, the last full delimitation exercise was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census, and the next one can only be undertaken after the 2031 Census. However, the Delimitation Commission can still adjust constituency boundaries within the existing seat count to reflect population shifts, as was done in 2008 for certain States.

Recent developments include the 2020 delimitation of Assembly constituencies in the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir following the reorganisation under the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019. The Commission, chaired by Justice (Retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai, completed the exercise in 2022, increasing the number of Assembly seats from 83 to 90. The EC’s role was limited to providing the electoral roll data and logistical support. The Supreme Court, in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2023), upheld the constitutionality of the delimitation process in J&K, reiterating that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are not subject to judicial review on merits.

A recurring examiner trap is to conflate the EC’s advisory role in delimitation with decision‑making authority. The EC’s statutory mandate under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, is confined to the preparation and revision of electoral rolls; the Delimitation Commission alone determines the territorial extent of constituencies. Another nuance is that the Delimitation Commission’s composition changes for each State, with the State Election Commissioner joining the panel, ensuring local administrative input.

Technique: Distinguishing Advisory vs. Decision‑Making Roles
Question: “The Election Commission of India has the final authority to delimit parliamentary constituencies.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify your answer with constitutional provisions.
Answer: False. Under Articles 82 and 170 read with the Delimitation Act, 2002, the power to delimit constituencies vests in the Delimitation Commission, a statutory body headed by a retired Supreme Court judge. The Election Commission’s role is limited to supplying electoral data and administrative assistance. The Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and not subject to judicial review on merits, as clarified by the Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2023).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “delimitation”, first identify the constitutional article (82/170) and the statutory body (Delimitation Commission). Remember that the EC’s involvement is purely data‑driven; the Commission’s orders are final except on jurisdictional grounds. This distinction frequently appears in both prelims and mains.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings and Autonomous Bodies: Methodology, Key Findings, and Governance Impact

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and autonomous bodies from Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with the Companies Act, 2013. The audit covers financial statements, compliance with statutes, and performance (value‑for‑money) aspects. The CAG adopts a risk‑based audit methodology: planning involves understanding the entity’s governance structure, identifying key risk areas (procurement, contract management, subsidy administration), and designing audit procedures that combine test‑checks, analytical reviews, and substantive testing.

Key findings from recent CAG reports (2021‑23) highlight recurrent issues: (i) inadequate internal controls in procurement leading to cost overruns in defence PSUs such as Hindustan Aeronautics Limited; (ii) delayed financial closure of infrastructure projects in National Highways Authority of India, resulting in interest burden; (iii) non‑compliance with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) provisions by several Maharatna companies; and (iv) weak monitoring of autonomous bodies like the Indian Council of Medical Research, where grant utilisation certificates were pending for years. The CAG’s performance audits have quantified these lapses — for instance, a 2022 audit of the Shipping Corporation of India estimated a loss of ₹1,200 crore due to sub‑optimal charter hire decisions.

The governance impact of CAG audits is mediated through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU). PAC examines the CAG’s reports on PSUs and recommends corrective action; COPU specifically scrutinises the functioning of commercial enterprises. In 2023, PAC’s recommendations led to the Ministry of Heavy Industries issuing revised procurement guidelines for all CPSEs. Moreover, the CAG’s findings have prompted the Department of Public Enterprises to introduce a “Performance Evaluation Framework” linking managerial remuneration to audit compliance scores.

Judicial oversight of CAG’s PSU audits is limited to procedural fairness. In CAG v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. (2020), the Supreme Court held that the CAG’s audit opinion cannot be challenged on merits, but the audited entity may seek judicial review if the audit process violates principles of natural justice. This reinforces the CAG’s institutional autonomy while ensuring accountability of the audit process itself.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers, Investigation Procedures, and Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Section 12 empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into complaints of human rights violations by public servants. The Commission’s suo motu jurisdiction is triggered by media reports, NGOs’ communications, or its own monitoring of custodial deaths, encounter killings, and conditions in detention facilities. Upon taking cognisance, the NHRC may call for reports from the concerned authority, conduct spot inquiries through its investigation division, and summon witnesses.

The investigation procedure follows a quasi‑judicial framework: the Commission issues notices, records statements under oath, and may request the Central Forensic Science Laboratory for scientific examination. The NHRC’s orders are recommendatory; the concerned government must respond within a stipulated period (usually one month) indicating action taken. Non‑compliance can be reported to Parliament through the Annual Report. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2018), the Supreme Court affirmed that the NHRC’s recommendations, while not binding, carry persuasive authority and the State must provide a reasoned response.

Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is institutionalised under Section 21 of the Act. The NHRC may transfer cases to the SHRC where the violation occurs within the State’s jurisdiction, and it monitors the SHRC’s disposal through periodic reviews. The NHRC also issues guidelines — such as the 2020 “Guidelines on Custodial Deaths” — which SHRCs are expected to adopt. However, functional overlap persists: both bodies can inquire into the same incident, leading to parallel proceedings. The 2022 amendment to the Act introduced a provision for the NHRC to direct SHRCs to expedite inquiries, aiming to reduce duplication.

Recent data (NHRC Annual Report 2022‑23) shows the Commission registered 1,12,000 cases, of which 18 % were taken up suo motu. The disposal rate improved to 78 % after the introduction of an online case‑management system in 2021. The Commission’s emphasis on digital monitoring — integrating police FIR data with its dashboard — has enhanced early detection of pattern violations, especially in cases of excessive force during protests.

  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical share with a constitutional ceiling; it is a recommendation that becomes binding only after presidential acceptance.
  • Assuming the Election Commission itself delimits constituencies; the Delimitation Commission holds that power, with the EC providing only data support.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of PSUs is limited to financial statements; performance and compliance audits are equally mandated.
  • Treating NHRC’s recommendations as legally binding; they are advisory, though the government must respond within a prescribed period.
  • Overlooking that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and not subject to judicial review on merits, except on jurisdictional grounds.
  • Neglecting the 2022 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act that empowers the NHRC to direct State Commissions to expedite inquiries.
  • Thinking the 15th Finance Commission’s vertical devolution of 41 % is immutable; the 16th FC may revise it based on updated Terms of Reference.

The Election Commission’s Regulation of Election Expenditure and the Role of Expenditure Observers

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) provides the statutory backbone for election‑expenditure control. Section 77 mandates every candidate to maintain a day‑to‑day account of all election expenses, while Section 77A empowers the Election Commission (EC) to appoint Expenditure Observers for each constituency. The EC fixes ceiling limits through notifications under Rule 90 of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961; the latest revision (2022) sets the limit at ₹95 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat and ₹40 lakh for a State Legislative Assembly seat, with upward revisions for larger states. Expenditure Observers, drawn from the Indian Revenue Service and other central services, are tasked with verifying the candidate’s expenditure register, cross‑checking with bank statements, and monitoring cash‑intensive activities such as rallies, media advertisements and distribution of gifts. In the 2019 Lok Sabha elections the EC deployed 1,200 observers across 543 constituencies, and 3,500 cases of suspected excess expenditure were referred to the Commission for further action. The EC may disqualify a candidate under Section 10A of the RPA if the declared expenditure exceeds the ceiling or if the account is found to be false. The Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2019) upheld the EC’s power to scrutinise expenditure accounts and to direct the filing of supplementary statements. A 2021 amendment to Rule 90 introduced mandatory electronic filing of expenditure returns through the EC’s “ENCORE” portal, enabling real‑time data analytics and reducing the scope for post‑election manipulation. The Commission also issues “Model Code of Conduct” instructions that restrict government‑funded advertisements during the election period, thereby limiting indirect expenditure by the ruling party. Despite these mechanisms, challenges persist: under‑reporting of cash donations, use of proxy candidates, and the difficulty of tracking digital campaign spending on social‑media platforms. The EC’s 2023 consultation paper on “Digital Election Expenditure” proposes bringing online political advertising under the same ceiling regime and mandating platform‑level disclosure of political ad spend.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of the Goods and Services Tax Revenue Collection and Fiscal Federalism

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its audit mandate from Article 149 of the Constitution and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) on 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment created a dual‑administration structure: the Centre administers Central GST (CGST) and Integrated GST (IGST), while States administer State GST (SGST). The CAG audits both the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) and the State GST departments, covering revenue collection, refund processing, input‑tax‑credit verification, and the settlement of IGST between the Centre and States. In its Report No. 12 of 2020, the CAG highlighted a revenue shortfall of ₹1.1 lakh crore in the GST compensation cess for the period 2017‑18 to 2019‑20, attributing it to lower‑than‑estimated collections and delays in cess disbursement. The audit also flagged mismatches between GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B returns, leading to an estimated ₹38,000 crore of unverified input‑tax‑credit claims. The CAG’s performance audit of the GST Council’s decision‑making process (Report No. 5 of 2021) examined the adequacy of data placed before the Council for rate‑change recommendations. Judicial oversight was affirmed in Union of India v. M/s. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022), where the Supreme Court held that the CAG’s audit jurisdiction extends to GST revenue realised by both the Centre and the States, reinforcing the principle that fiscal federalism does not diminish the CAG’s constitutional authority. The audit findings have directly influenced the 15th Finance Commission’s recommendation to retain the 41 % vertical devolution share while suggesting a review of the GST compensation mechanism beyond 2022. The CAG’s ongoing “GST Audit Framework” (2023) integrates data‑analytics tools such as the “GST Prime” platform to enable real‑time risk‑based selection of audit units, thereby strengthening the credibility of inter‑governmental fiscal transfers.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of GST revenue is limited to the Central Government’s collections.” Identify the error and state the correct constitutional position.
The statement is false. Article 149 read with the CAG Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of both the Union and the States. The GST regime is a concurrent fiscal domain; the CAG audits CGST, SGST and IGST collections, as confirmed by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. M/s. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022). Therefore, the CAG’s audit covers State GST departments as well.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links the CAG to a specific tax regime, recall the constitutional source (Art. 149) and the latest Supreme Court endorsement. Pair the statutory provision with the most recent CAG report number (e.g., Report No. 12 of 2020) to demonstrate up‑to‑date knowledge.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with International Treaty Bodies and the Universal Periodic Review

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, functions as India’s National Human Rights Institution (NHRI) and holds “A” status accreditation from the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) since 1999. India is a party to the core UN human‑rights treaties — the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the Convention against Torture (CAT), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The NHRC prepares parallel (shadow) reports for each treaty‑body review cycle. In the 2020 review by the Human Rights Committee, the NHRC’s submission highlighted custodial deaths, the continued operation of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) in the Northeast and Jammu & Kashmir, and the need for a standalone anti‑torture law. During the Committee against Torture’s 2021 session, the NHRC presented data showing 1,12,000 cases registered in 2022‑23, of which 18 % were taken up suo motu, and urged the ratification of the Optional Protocol to CAT. The NHRC also participates actively in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) process. India’s fourth UPR cycle (2022) saw the NHRC submit a comprehensive stakeholder report covering 23 thematic areas, including minority rights, freedom of expression, and the rights of persons with disabilities. The Commission’s recommendations are forwarded to the Ministry of External Affairs for inclusion in the Government’s national report. In 2023, the NHRC established a dedicated “International Mechanisms Cell” to track concluding observations, coordinate follow‑up actions with line ministries, and monitor implementation of UPR‑accepted recommendations. This institutionalised engagement strengthens the NHRC’s credibility as a bridge between domestic human‑rights practice and international accountability mechanisms.

The Competition Commission of India’s Approach to Digital Platforms, Data Dominance and Algorithmic Collusion

The Competition Commission of India (CCI), established under the Competition Act, 2002 (amended in 2007 and 2023), has progressively expanded its analytical toolkit to address competition concerns in digital markets. The 2020 Market Study on “Digital Platforms and Competition” identified network effects, data‑driven entry barriers, and multi‑sided platform dynamics as key features requiring tailored enforcement. In 2022, the CCI concluded its investigation into Google’s Android ecosystem, finding that the mandatory pre‑installation of Google Mobile Services and the anti‑fragmentation agreements constituted abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Act. A penalty of ₹1,337 crore was imposed, and behavioural remedies were mandated, including the allowance of alternative app stores and the removal of restrictive clauses for device manufacturers. The Amazon‑Future Coupons case (2021) illustrated the CCI’s willingness to scrutinise “killer acquisitions” and contractual arrangements that foreclose market access for rivals. On algorithmic collusion, the CCI released a Discussion Paper in March 2023 titled “Algorithmic Pricing and Competition”, examining how self‑learning pricing algorithms can facilitate tacit coordination without explicit communication. The Competition (Amendment) Bill, 2023, introduced in Parliament, proposes to treat “data” as a relevant factor for assessing dominance and to empower the CCI to impose “structural remedies” in digital markets. The Supreme Court in Google LLC v. CCI (2023) upheld the CCI’s investigative powers, rejecting Google’s challenge to the Director General’s search‑and‑seizure operations. The CCI’s leniency programme, originally designed for traditional cartels, has been extended to digital platforms, offering immunity or reduced penalties for firms that disclose algorithmic coordination mechanisms. These developments signal a shift from ex‑post merger control to ex‑ante regulation of data‑centric market power.

Union Public Service Commission’s Examination Reforms: From Conventional Pattern to Competency‑Based Assessment

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) derives its constitutional mandate from Articles 315‑323. The Civil Services Examination (CSE) has undergone several structural reforms since its inception. The 2011 introduction of the Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) as Paper II in the Preliminary stage aimed to test analytical ability; it was made qualifying only in 2015 after widespread criticism regarding its impact on candidates from non‑English‑medium backgrounds. The 2013 reform removed the scaling of optional‑subject marks, replacing it with a uniform evaluation matrix. In 2015, a dedicated Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude paper (General Studies IV) was added to the Main examination, reflecting the Second Administrative Reforms Commission’s recommendation. The 2020 decision to retain CSAT as a qualifying paper (minimum 33 % marks) while restoring the weightage of General Studies I for ranking marked a return to a knowledge‑centric preliminary filter. In 2022, the UPSC floated a concept note on “Competency‑Based Assessment” for lateral‑entry recruitment at the Joint Secretary level, proposing situational judgement tests, case‑study analyses and psychometric profiling alongside the conventional written examination. The 2023 notification for an “Integrated Civil Services Examination” envisages a common Preliminary test for all Group A and Group B services, followed by service‑specific Mains, aiming to reduce duplication and enhance merit‑based allocation. Data from the 2023 CSE cycle shows 11.5 lakh applicants, 13,000 candidates qualifying for the Main examination, and a final selection ratio of 1:1,200. The Supreme Court in UPSC v. R. K. Jain (2021) affirmed the Commission’s discretion to modify the syllabus and scheme of examination, provided the changes are reasonable and non‑arbitrary. These reforms collectively aim to align the selection process with the evolving governance demands of a digital, data‑driven administration while preserving the constitutional guarantee of merit‑based, impartial recruitment.

  • Confusing the EC’s expenditure ceiling with a statutory limit; the ceiling is fixed by EC notification under Rule 90, not by the RPA itself.
  • Assuming the CAG’s GST audit covers only the Centre; Article 149 extends CAG’s jurisdiction to State GST departments as confirmed by the Supreme Court in 2022.
  • Treating NHRC’s parallel reports as binding on treaty bodies; they are advisory submissions that influence but do not dictate concluding observations.
  • Believing the CCI’s leniency programme applies only to traditional cartels; the 2023 amendment explicitly extends it to digital‑platform collusion.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s CSAT paper remains a ranking component; since 2015 it is only qualifying, with General Studies I determining merit.
  • Overlooking that the EC’s Expenditure Observers are appointed under Section 77A of the RPA, not under the Model Code of Conduct.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise statutory reading and awareness of the latest judicial pronouncements.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility, Legal Challenges and Operational Roadmap

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. The constitutional basis rests on Articles 83(2), 172(1), 356, 357 and 358 which fix the five‑year term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, and on Article 324 which vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections. A simultaneous cycle would require either a constitutional amendment to align the terms of all Houses or a legislative framework that permits premature dissolution and extension of Assemblies under Article 356 (President’s Rule) and Article 174 (dissolution by the Governor). The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and 255th Report (2015) recommended a phased approach: first synchronise the Lok Sabha and a group of State Assemblies, then bring the remaining States into the cycle within two election cycles. The NITI Aayog’s 2017 discussion paper estimated a cost saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle and a reduction in the deployment of security forces by 30 %. However, the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held that the power to dissolve a State Assembly is a constitutional prerogative of the Governor acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers, and any central legislation that curtails this power would be subject to judicial review for violation of federalism. The EC’s 2022 “Roadmap for Simultaneous Elections” proposes a constitutional amendment to insert a new Article 324A empowering the EC to notify a common election schedule, coupled with a transitional provision allowing the President to extend or curtail Assembly terms by up to six months. The Bill has not yet been introduced in Parliament. Operational challenges include the need for a massive increase in Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units, the logistics of deploying over 10 million polling personnel in a single window, and the risk of a “national‑level” campaign overshadowing local issues. The 2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice noted that without a broad political consensus, any amendment would face a basic‑structure challenge under Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Consequently, the EC’s current mandate remains limited to conducting elections as and when they fall due, while the simultaneous‑election proposal stays in the realm of policy advocacy.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Grants‑in‑Aid: Formula Evolution, Conditionalities and State Fiscal Space

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the principles governing grants‑in‑aid to States. The 14th FC (2015‑20) raised the vertical share to 42 % of the divisible pool, a 10‑percentage‑point increase over the 13th FC, and introduced a “performance‑based” grant component linked to the States’ own‑tax effort and fiscal discipline. The 15th FC (2021‑26) retained the 42 % vertical share but restructured the grant architecture: (i) revenue‑deficit grants for 17 States amounting to ₹2.94 lakh crore, (ii) sector‑specific grants for health, education, and agriculture totalling ₹1.2 lakh crore, and (iii) a new “State‑specific” grant window of ₹1.0 lakh crore for infrastructure and disaster resilience. The horizontal distribution formula continues to weigh population (15 %), area (15 %), forest cover (10 %), income distance (45 %), and demographic performance (12.5 %). Conditionalities have become more stringent: the 15th FC made the release of the second instalment of revenue‑deficit grants contingent on the State’s compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) targets and the implementation of the GST compensation cess framework. The Commission also recommended a “grants‑in‑aid for local bodies” of ₹4.3 lakh crore, split 60:40 between rural and urban bodies, with a performance‑linked top‑up of 10 % for States that meet the 15th FC’s “local‑body‑performance index”. Empirical analysis by the Reserve Bank of India (2023) shows that States receiving higher vertical shares reduced their own‑tax‑to‑GSDP ratio by 0.3 percentage points, indicating a substitution effect. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2022) upheld the FC’s discretion in designing conditional grants, ruling that the Constitution does not prescribe a rigid formula and that the FC’s recommendations acquire the force of law only after Presidential assent. The 16th FC, constituted in 2023, is expected to revisit the vertical share in light of the post‑COVID fiscal consolidation roadmap and the Centre’s commitment to a 3 % fiscal deficit target by 2025‑26.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The 15th Finance Commission increased the vertical devolution share to 45 %.” Identify the error and state the correct figure.
The statement is false. The 15th Finance Commission retained the vertical devolution share at 42 % of the divisible pool, the same level set by the 14th Finance Commission. The 45 % figure has never been recommended by any Finance Commission.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the vertical share percentages for the last three Finance Commissions (13th = 32 %, 14th = 42 %, 15th = 42 %) and the three grant categories introduced by the 15th FC (revenue‑deficit, sector‑specific, State‑specific). When a question mixes horizontal formula weights with vertical share, separate the two concepts: vertical share is a single percentage of the divisible pool; horizontal weights distribute that pool among States.

National Human Rights Commission’s Intervention in Custodial Deaths and Police Reforms: Suo Motu Powers, Judicial Oversight and Systemic Recommendations

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 12 to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Custodial deaths have been the most frequent trigger for NHRC’s suo motu action. Between 2018 and 2023 the NHRC registered 1,842 custodial‑death cases, of which 1,210 were taken up suo motu based on media reports and intelligence inputs. The Commission’s investigative procedure mirrors a quasi‑judicial inquiry: it can summon witnesses, demand documents, and direct the Director General of Police to conduct a parallel magisterial inquiry under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Landmark Supreme Court judgments have shaped the NHRC’s remit. In D. K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) the Court laid down 11 procedural safeguards for arrest and detention, and directed the NHRC to monitor compliance. In Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) the Court ordered the establishment of Police Complaints Authorities at the State and district levels, a recommendation the NHRC has repeatedly echoed in its annual reports. The NHRC’s 2021 “Guidelines on Custodial Death Investigation” mandate a mandatory judicial magistrate inquiry within 24 hours, video‑recording of post‑mortem, and submission of a compliance report to the Commission within 30 days. Despite these directives, the Ministry of Home Affairs’ 2022 data shows that only 38 % of custodial‑death cases resulted in departmental action against erring officers. The NHRC’s recommendations are advisory; however, the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2019) held that persistent non‑compliance can attract contempt proceedings. The Commission has also advocated for the ratification of the UN Convention against Torture and the enactment of a standalone anti‑torture law, a proposal pending before Parliament since 2010. The interplay between NHRC’s suo motu powers, judicial oversight, and executive implementation remains a critical barometer of India’s custodial‑justice architecture.

Central Information Commission’s Proactive Disclosure Mandate under Section 4 of the RTI Act: Compliance Gaps, Judicial Directions and Digital Initiatives

Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 obliges every public authority to publish 17 categories of information proactively, including organisational structure, powers and duties of officers, decision‑making processes, norms for discharge of functions, and a directory of officers. The Central Information Commission (CIC) monitors compliance through annual “Transparency Audits” and can impose penalties under Section 20 for persistent non‑disclosure. The CIC’s 2022 audit of 2,341 Central public authorities revealed that only 42 % had fully updated their Section 4 disclosures on the official RTI portal (rti.gov.in). Common gaps included outdated lists of public information officers, missing details of budget allocations, and absence of a searchable database of decisions. The Supreme Court in Central Information Commission v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) directed all public authorities to complete proactive disclosure within six months and to appoint a “Transparency Officer” at the level of Joint Secretary. In response, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) launched the “RTI‑Proactive Disclosure Dashboard” in 2021, a machine‑readable platform that auto‑generates compliance scores. The 2023 amendment to the RTI Rules introduced a “quarterly self‑certification” mechanism, requiring each authority to upload a signed compliance certificate. The CIC’s 2023 order in Shri R. K. Jain v. Ministry of Finance imposed a penalty of ₹25,000 on the Ministry for failing to publish its foreign‑contribution receipts under Section 4(1)(b)(xiv). Civil society assessments (Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, 2023) estimate that full proactive disclosure could reduce RTI applications by up to 30 %, freeing appellate capacity for complex cases. The next frontier is the integration of proactive data with the “Open Government Data” portal (data.gov.in) to enable cross‑sectoral analytics.

National Commission for Minorities’ Investigative Powers in Communal Violence: Legal Basis, Case Studies and Limitations

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) was constituted under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992. Section 9(1) empowers the Commission to “inquire into specific complaints regarding deprivation of rights and safeguards of minorities” and to “monitor the working of the safeguards provided for minorities under the Constitution and laws”. Unlike the NHRC, the NCM does not possess explicit suo motu powers; its inquiries are triggered by written complaints or references from the Central Government. Nevertheless, the Commission has interpreted its monitoring mandate to initiate “on‑the‑spot” investigations during major communal outbreaks. In the 2002 Gujarat riots, the NCM dispatched a fact‑finding team that documented 1,044 deaths and recommended the prosecution of 12 police officers; the Supreme Court later cited the NCM report in Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (2004). During the 2013 Muzaffarnagar violence, the NCM’s interim report highlighted the failure of the district administration to enforce Section 144 CrPC and recommended compensation of ₹10 lakh per deceased family, a figure later adopted by the Uttar Pradesh government. In the 2020 Delhi riots, the NCM’s rapid‑response team recorded 53 deaths and identified 27 instances of hate speech on social media, forwarding the evidence to the Delhi Police and the Election Commission for action under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory; implementation depends on the political will of the concerned State governments. The 2021 amendment to the NCM Act introduced a “time‑bound inquiry” clause requiring the Commission to submit its report within 90 days, but the absence of enforcement teeth limits deterrence. The NCM also coordinates with State Minorities Commissions (SMCs) through a quarterly “National‑State Coordination Meeting”, yet only 18 of 28 States have functional SMCs as of 2023. The Commission’s annual report to Parliament under Section 13 remains the primary accountability mechanism, and its effectiveness hinges on the quality of its fact‑finding methodology and the willingness of the executive to act on its findings.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone State Assembly elections to align with the Lok Sabha; any postponement beyond six months requires a constitutional amendment under Article 172.
  • Confusing the 15th Finance Commission’s vertical share (42 %) with the 14th FC’s recommendation; both Commissions fixed the same percentage.
  • Believing the NHRC’s recommendations on custodial deaths are binding on State police; they are advisory, enforceable only through judicial contempt proceedings.
  • Thinking Section 4 of the RTI Act obliges only Central ministries; it applies to every “public authority” including State bodies and substantially financed NGOs.
  • Treating the NCM’s fact‑finding reports as having the force of law; they are recommendatory and require executive action for implementation.
  • Overlooking that the CIC’s penalty power under Section 20 is limited to ₹25,000 per instance and cannot be imposed on the Prime Minister’s Office.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s grants‑in‑aid are automatically released; each tranche is conditional on the State meeting FRBM targets and submitting utilisation certificates.

Election Commission’s Power to Review and Revise Electoral Rolls: Legal Framework, Judicial Scrutiny, and Recent Amendments

The Election Commission of India (ECI) derives its authority to prepare, maintain, and revise electoral rolls from Article 324 read with the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (RPA 1950) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA 1951). Section 13 of RPA 1950 empowers the Commission to direct the preparation of rolls in the manner it deems fit, while Section 14 provides for periodic revision—annual, summary, and special revisions. The Commission’s 2019 “Electoral Roll Management System” (ERMS) introduced a digitised, real‑time updating mechanism linking the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme (NERPAP) with Aadhaar‑based verification, subject to the Supreme Court’s 2018 judgment in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India which mandated voluntary linkage.

Judicial scrutiny has shaped the scope of this power. In Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020), the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s direction to delete duplicate entries could not be challenged on the ground of procedural irregularity unless mala fide was proved. The Court reiterated that the Commission’s satisfaction under Section 13 is “subjective but not arbitrary”. In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2022), the Court upheld the Commission’s power to order a special revision in constituencies where the error rate exceeded 2 % as per the ERMS audit, emphasising that the power is ancillary to the constitutional mandate of free and fair elections.

The 2021 amendment to the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 introduced a “continuous updation” window allowing citizens to file Form 6, 7, 8, and 8A online throughout the year, with a statutory deadline of 30 days for disposal. The Commission’s 2023 circular mandated that Booth Level Officers (BLOs) conduct house‑to‑house verification at least once every two years, and that any deletion of a name must be preceded by a notice and an opportunity to be heard, aligning with the principles of natural justice articulated in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2017).

Recent data from the ECI’s 2024 annual report indicate that the electorate grew by 3.7 % between the 2019 and 2024 general elections, while the deletion‑to‑addition ratio improved from 1:4.2 to 1:3.6, reflecting tighter roll hygiene. The Commission’s “Electoral Roll Observation Mission” (EROM) deployed in 2023 for the Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh assembly polls reported a 0.48 % discrepancy rate, well below the 1 % threshold set by the 2019 “Model Code of Conduct for Electoral Roll Management”.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings: Scope, Methodology, and Impact on Governance

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under Section 19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013. The mandate covers financial audit, compliance audit, and performance audit of all government companies where the Union or a State holds 51 % or more of the paid‑up capital. The CAG’s “Guidelines for Performance Audit of PSUs” (2020) prescribe a risk‑based approach: identification of key performance indicators (KPIs) such as capacity utilisation, return on equity, and project completion rates, followed by field verification and benchmarking against sectoral norms.

Methodologically, the CAG employs a three‑tier sampling framework: (i) selection of high‑value contracts (>₹500 crore) for detailed transaction testing; (ii) stratified random sampling of routine procurement to assess internal controls; and (iii) thematic audits on cross‑cutting issues—e.g., “Capital Expenditure Management in Power PSUs” (2022) and “Corporate Governance in Defence PSUs” (2023). The 2022 audit of the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) revealed a 12 % cost overrun in the 1,600 MW Kudgi project, attributing it to delayed land acquisition and inadequate contract management. The report recommended a “Project Monitoring Dashboard” integrated with the Integrated Financial Management System (IFMS), a suggestion adopted by the Ministry of Power in 2023.

Impact on governance is measured through the “Audit Paras” tracking system. Between 2018‑19 and 2022‑23, the CAG issued 1,842 audit paras on central PSUs, of which 1,210 (65.7 %) were settled after remedial action. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) referenced CAG findings in 78 % of its reports on PSUs during the same period, leading to policy changes such as the 2021 “Guidelines for Independent Directors in CPSEs” and the 2022 “Mandatory Rotation of Statutory Auditors” for listed PSUs. The CAG’s 2023 “Audit of Climate Finance in PSUs” highlighted that only 34 % of allocated green‑bond proceeds were deployed in eligible projects, prompting the Ministry of Finance to issue a revised “Green Bond Framework” in early 2024.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of a Central Public Sector Enterprise can be challenged in a High Court under Article 226 on the ground that the audit exceeded statutory mandate.” Explain the correct legal position with reference to relevant case law.
The CAG’s audit authority is statutory and derives from the CAG Act, 1971 and the Companies Act, 2013. In Comptroller and Auditor General of India v. M/s. Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. (2015), the Supreme Court held that the CAG’s audit is not a quasi‑judicial function amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226; it is a constitutional function subject only to parliamentary oversight. Therefore, a High Court cannot entertain a challenge on the ground of excess of mandate. The proper remedy lies in the Public Accounts Committee or a reference to the President under Article 151. The answer must cite the 2015 judgment and distinguish between audit (constitutional) and adjudication (judicial).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes CAG audit with judicial review, remember the hierarchy: constitutional audit → parliamentary scrutiny → judicial review only on constitutional violations (e.g., violation of Article 14). Memorise the 2015 HAL judgment and the 2020 Performance Audit Guidelines as the two pillars for any CAG‑PSU question.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Disciplinary Proceedings and Service Conditions: Constitutional Provisions and Supreme Court Jurisprudence

Article 320(3) of the Constitution obliges the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to be consulted on “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity”. The UPSC’s “Regulations on Disciplinary Proceedings” (1975, amended 2020) prescribe a two‑stage consultation: (i) before the initiation of a major penalty proceeding (dismissal, removal, reduction in rank) and (ii) before the final order is passed. The Commission’s advice is recommendatory; however, the Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2013) held that non‑consultation renders the disciplinary order voidable, not void, and the government must demonstrate “compelling reasons” for bypassing the UPSC.

In State of Punjab v. Salil Sabhlok (2018), the Court clarified that the UPSC’s role extends to “service conditions” such as promotion rules, reservation rosters, and pay‑scale revisions, provided the matter affects a civil servant’s tenure. The 2021 amendment to the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969 introduced a “time‑bound consultation” clause: the UPSC must render its advice within 45 days, failing which the disciplinary authority may proceed, but must record reasons. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) reported in its 2023 annual review that the average consultation period fell from 78 days (2019) to 38 days (2022) after the amendment.

The UPSC also advises on “penalty guidelines” for common offences. Its 2022 “Model Penalty Framework” categorises offences into four bands (minor, major, grave, and exceptional) with prescribed penalty ranges, aiming to reduce arbitrariness. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2020) endorsed the framework as a “reasonable classification” under Article 14, while cautioning that the framework cannot fetter the disciplinary authority’s discretion in exceptional circumstances.

Recent data: In 2022‑23, the UPSC was consulted in 1,124 disciplinary cases, rendering advice in 1,098 (97.7 %). The government accepted the advice in 1,012 cases (92.2 %). The remaining 86 cases saw divergence, primarily on quantum of penalty, and were referred to the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) for adjudication.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Conditional Grants: Evolution, Data Sources, and State Fiscal Autonomy

The vertical devolution share—percentage of the divisible pool of central taxes assigned to States—has been a core recommendation of every Finance Commission (FC). The 14th FC (2015‑20) fixed the share at 42 %, the highest since the 10th FC. The 15th FC (2021‑26) recommended 41 %, citing the need to accommodate the Union’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities under the Goods and Services Tax (GST) compensation cess and the COVID‑19 fiscal stimulus. The 15th FC’s report (Chapter 3) explains that the 1 % reduction was offset by a larger “revenue deficit grant” envelope of ₹2.9 lakh crore, targeted at 17 States.

Conditional grants—grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) and specific purpose grants under Article 282—are tied to performance criteria. The 15th FC introduced three new conditionality pillars: (i) “Urban Local Body (ULB) Performance Grant” linked to property‑tax collection efficiency and audited accounts; (ii) “Health Sector Grant” conditional on achieving National Health Mission (NHM) output indicators; and (iii) “Education Grant” tied to the “Performance Grading Index” (PGI) scores. The Commission’s “Data Compendium” (2021) draws on Census 2011, National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 78th round (2020‑21), and the “State Finance Accounts” certified by the CAG.

State fiscal autonomy is measured by the “Own Tax Revenue (OTR) to GSDP” ratio. The 15th FC noted that States with OTR/GSDP > 7 % (e.g., Maharashtra, Gujarat) received lower per‑capita revenue deficit grants, while States below 5 % (e.g., Bihar, Jharkhand) received higher grants. The 2023 “Mid‑Term Review” of the 15th FC observed that the conditional grants improved ULB audit compliance from 62 % (2020) to 84 % (2022) and NHM facility‑level reporting from 71 % to 89 % over the same period.

Controversies persist: the 15th FC’s use of the 2011 Census for population weight (15 % weight) versus the 1971 Census (used by the 14th FC) has been contested by southern States, arguing it penalises demographic transition. The Union government accepted the 15th FC’s recommendation but announced a “Population‑Based Incentive Fund” of ₹45,000 crore in the 2024‑25 Budget to mitigate the perceived disparity.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Powers and Interaction with State Human Rights Commissions: Comparative Analysis

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 12 to “inquire, suo motu or on a petition presented to it by a victim or any person on his behalf, into complaints of violation of human rights”. Unlike the National Commission for Minorities, the NHRC’s suo motu jurisdiction is explicit and has been invoked in high‑profile cases: the 2002 Gujarat riots (NHRC suo motu case No. 12/2002), the 2013 Muzaffarnagar violence (NHRC suo motu case No. 45/2013), and the 2020 Delhi riots (NHRC suo motu case No. 78/2020). In each instance, the Commission constituted a fact‑finding team, recorded testimonies, and issued recommendations to the concerned State governments and the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Section 21 of the PHRA establishes State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) with parallel powers. The NHRC‑SHRC interaction is governed by a 2005 “Memorandum of Understanding” (MoU) revised in 2019, which mandates: (i) quarterly joint review meetings; (ii) referral of cases where the SHRC lacks jurisdiction or resources; and (iii) a shared “Human Rights Case Management System” (HRCMS) launched in 2021. As of 2023, 24 States have functional SHRCs; the remaining four (Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland) rely on the NHRC for all inquiries.

Judicial oversight has reinforced the NHRC’s suo motu authority. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009), the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s suo motu inquiry is not a “parallel investigation” to the police but a “complementary monitoring mechanism”, and its recommendations, though not binding, create a “legitimate expectation” of compliance. The Court further directed the Gujarat government to implement the NHRC’s compensation orders within six months. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021), the Court upheld the NHRC’s power to seek reports from the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) in alleged custodial deaths, rejecting the Centre’s claim of “operational secrecy”.

Data from the NHRC’s 2023 annual report: 1,842 suo motu cases registered since inception; 1,210 (65.7 %) resulted in recommendations; 742 (61.3 %) of those recommendations were partially or fully implemented. The HRCMS recorded a 27 % increase in inter‑commission referrals between 2020‑21 and 2022‑23, indicating growing coordination. However, the Commission’s 2022 “Capacity Assessment” highlighted that 11 SHRCs operate with less than 50 % sanctioned staff, limiting their ability to conduct independent inquiries.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally delete names from the electoral roll without a hearing; the law mandates notice and opportunity to be heard before any deletion.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of PSUs is subject to High Court writ jurisdiction; the Supreme Court has held it is a constitutional function reviewable only by Parliament.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is recommendatory, though non‑consultation can render an order voidable.
  • Confusing the 15th Finance Commission’s vertical share (41 %) with the 14th FC’s 42 %; the 15th FC reduced the share by one percentage point.
  • Treating NHRC’s suo motu recommendations as legally enforceable orders; they are advisory, enforceable only through judicial contempt or legitimate‑expectation doctrine.
  • Overlooking that conditional grants under the 15th FC require States to meet specific performance indicators; failure can lead to grant withholding.
  • Assuming all States have functional State Human Rights Commissions; as of 2023 four States lack SHRCs and depend entirely on the NHRC.

Election Commission’s Authority to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Provisions, Legislative Hurdles, and Judicial Interpretation

Article 324 vests the Election Commission (EC) with superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice‑President. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA) and the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 operationalise this mandate. Simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assembly polls together — require synchronising the five‑year terms of the Houses, which currently diverge because of premature dissolutions, President’s Rule under Article 356, and varying election cycles. The 255th Law Commission Report (2015) and the NITI Aayog’s 2017 discussion paper argued that simultaneous polls would reduce expenditure, limit policy paralysis during the Model Code of Conduct (MCC), and improve governance continuity. However, the Constitution does not prescribe a fixed electoral calendar; Article 83(2) and Article 172(1) only set maximum durations. Any move to align terms would need constitutional amendments to Articles 83, 172, 327 and 328, and possibly a new law under Article 327 to prescribe a common election schedule. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Law and Justice (2022) recommended a phased approach: first, a constitutional amendment to fix a common tenure, then a legislative framework for simultaneous polls, and finally a pilot in a few States. The Supreme Court, in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), recognised the right to privacy, which extends to voter data; any centralised electoral database for simultaneous polls must satisfy the proportionality test laid down in that judgment. Moreover, the Court in Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020) held that the EC’s power to notify election dates is subject to judicial review only on grounds of arbitrariness or violation of statutory provisions, reinforcing that the EC cannot unilaterally impose a common schedule without legislative backing. Practical obstacles include the need for consensus among political parties, the logistical challenge of deploying Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter‑Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) units across 900 million electors simultaneously, and the risk of a single‑point failure affecting the entire democratic exercise. The 15th Finance Commission’s 2020 report noted that election‑related expenditure accounted for 0.4 % of GDP; simultaneous polls could halve this figure, but the savings must be weighed against the constitutional rigidity and federal sensitivities involved.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Non‑Governmental Organisations: Scope, Methodology, and Accountability Gaps

Article 149 read with the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and the States, and of “any other authority or body substantially financed by the Government”. Section 14 of the Act extends this to autonomous bodies — such as the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), and universities — while Section 15 covers non‑governmental organisations (NGOs) receiving grants exceeding ₹25 lakh annually. The CAG’s 2021 “Audit of Autonomous Bodies” report examined 1,247 entities and found that 38 % had not submitted annual accounts within the prescribed six‑month window, and 22 % exhibited material misstatements in grant utilisation certificates. The audit methodology follows the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) 3000 (Performance Auditing) and 4000 (Compliance Auditing), employing risk‑based sampling, data‑analytics on the Public Financial Management System (PFMS), and on‑site verification of asset registers. A critical accountability gap arises because many autonomous bodies maintain separate governing councils that are not directly answerable to Parliament; the CAG’s findings are tabled in the respective legislature but lack a statutory enforcement mechanism. The Supreme Court, in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2020), affirmed that the CAG’s audit jurisdiction extends to any body “substantially financed” by the State, rejecting the argument that functional autonomy shields such entities from scrutiny. Nevertheless, the absence of a dedicated follow‑up cell in most ministries means that audit recommendations — such as the 2022 directive to the Ministry of Education to recover ₹1,142 crore of unspent grants from 112 deemed‑universities — often remain unimplemented for years.
