The 2023 CAG “Performance Audit of NGO Grants” highlighted that only 41 % of NGOs complied with the mandatory social audit under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and that the Ministry of Home Affairs’ online portal captured merely 68 % of mandated disclosures. Strengthening the CAG’s institutional capacity — through a statutory “Audit Follow‑Up Authority” and mandatory quarterly reporting by autonomous bodies to the Public Accounts Committee — has been recommended by the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2009) and reiterated in the 15th Finance Commission’s chapter on fiscal transparency.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The CAG can audit an NGO only if the NGO is registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860.” Identify the error and state the correct legal position.
The statement is false. Under Section 15 of the CAG’s DPC Act, 1971, the CAG’s audit jurisdiction covers any NGO or body “substantially financed” by the Government, irrespective of its registration statute. The threshold is financial — grants exceeding ₹25 lakh per annum — not the legal form of registration. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2020) confirmed that functional autonomy does not oust CAG audit where substantial public funding exists.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links CAG audit to “autonomous bodies” or “NGOs”, first locate the statutory trigger: “substantially financed” (Section 14/15, DPC Act). Then check whether the entity receives recurring government grants above the prescribed monetary limit. Remember that the CAG’s report is advisory; enforcement depends on PAC/Parliament. Cite the 2020 Supreme Court ruling to demonstrate awareness of judicial endorsement.

Union Public Service Commission’s Coordination with State Public Service Commissions in All India Services Recruitment: Constitutional Framework and Operational Challenges

Articles 315‑323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs) as independent constitutional bodies. The All India Services Act, 1951 (AIS Act) and the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS) Rules, 1954 provide that recruitment to the All India Services (AIS) shall be made through a competitive examination conducted by the UPSC, while the SPSCs conduct separate examinations for State Civil Services. The UPSC’s role is not merely examinational; under Article 320(3) it must be consulted on “all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts”. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. S. K. Sharma (2020) reiterated that non‑consultation with the UPSC renders an appointment voidable, underscoring the mandatory nature of the consultative clause. Operationally, the UPSC designs the Civil Services Examination (CSE) syllabus, sets the preliminary and main examination papers, and conducts the personality test. The SPSCs, however, frame their own syllabi for State Services, leading to divergence in assessment standards. The 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2009) recommended a “Common Recruitment Framework” whereby the UPSC would develop a model syllabus and question bank for State Services, allowing SPSCs to adopt or adapt it, thereby ensuring parity and reducing duplication. In practice, only a few States — notably Maharashtra and Karnataka — have signed MoUs with the UPSC for sharing question‑paper design expertise. A further challenge is the cadre allocation policy: after the CSE, the UPSC recommends candidates to the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), which allocates cadres based on merit‑cum‑preference. The SPSCs have no role in this allocation, yet they are responsible for the subsequent training and career management of officers allotted to their States. The 2022 “Lateral Entry” scheme, whereby domain experts are appointed at Joint Secretary level on contract, bypasses both UPSC and SPSC processes, raising questions about the constitutional mandate of Article 320. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice (2023) urged the DoPT to institutionalise a joint UPSC‑SPSC committee to harmonise recruitment rules, share best practices in examination security (including biometric verification and AI‑based proctoring), and develop a unified grievance redressal portal for candidates across the Union and States.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and the GST Council’s Fiscal Architecture: Inter‑Linkages, Data Dependencies, and Reform Proposals

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the principles governing grants‑in‑aid. The 15th FC (2020‑25) fixed the vertical share at 41 % of the divisible pool, a one‑percentage‑point reduction from the 14th FC’s 42 %. Simultaneously, Article 279A created the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, a constitutional body that decides tax rates, exemptions, and the compensation cess. The GST Council’s decisions directly affect the size of the divisible pool because the Union’s share of Central GST (CGST) and the States’ share of State GST (SGST) flow into it, while the Integrated GST (IGST) settlement mechanism determines inter‑State revenue flows. The 15th FC’s report noted that the GST Council’s rate rationalisation in 2021‑22 — merging the 12 % and 18 % slabs into a single 15 % slab for a basket of goods — expanded the tax base by an estimated 3.2 % and increased the divisible pool by ₹0.9 lakh crore. However, the Council’s compensation cess, designed to guarantee States a 14 % annual revenue growth for five years (2017‑22), created a fiscal overhang: the cess collection fell short by ₹1.1 lakh crore in 2021‑22, prompting the Union to borrow on behalf of States under the “back‑to‑back loan” arrangement. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. State of Kerala (2022) upheld the GST Council’s decision‑making process, ruling that the Council’s recommendations acquire the force of law only after presidential assent, and that the Union’s borrowing to meet compensation obligations does not violate Article 293. Data dependencies are acute: the FC relies on the GST Network (GSTN) for real‑time revenue data, while the Council depends on the FC’s devolution formula to assess States’ fiscal capacity. The 15th FC recommended a “GST‑linked performance grant” of ₹1.5 lakh crore, conditional on States achieving a 90 % filing compliance rate on GSTN and maintaining a revenue‑neutral rate structure. The 2023‑24 Union Budget accepted this recommendation but deferred the compliance benchmark to 2025‑26, citing technical glitches in GSTN’s new return‑filing system. Reform proposals from the 2nd ARC (2009) and the 15th FC converge on three points: (i) institutionalising a joint FC‑GST Council data‑sharing protocol; (ii) moving from a fixed vertical share to a dynamic formula that incorporates GST buoyancy; and (iii) establishing an independent “Fiscal Council” to monitor the interplay between devolution and GST policy, thereby reducing ad‑hoc borrowing and enhancing predictability for State budgets.

National Commission for Scheduled Tribes’ Implementation of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996: Mandate, Monitoring Mechanisms, and Judicial Oversight

The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution to the Fifth Schedule Areas, empowering Gram Sabhas with ownership of minor forest produce, management of village markets, control over local water bodies, and the power to prevent land alienation. Article 338A establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) with the duty to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for STs under the Constitution, including PESA. The NCST’s 2022 annual report recorded that only 12 of the 10 States with Fifth Schedule Areas (Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana) had enacted conforming State PESA Rules, and that 43 % of Gram Sabhas lacked functional Forest Rights Committees (FRCs) required under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA). The Commission’s monitoring mechanism comprises (i) quarterly “PESA Implementation Review Meetings” with State Tribal Welfare Departments; (ii) a web‑based “PESA Dashboard” launched in 2021 that tracks Gram Sabha resolutions, FRC constitution, and minor forest produce revenue; and (iii) suo‑motu inquiries triggered by media reports or petitions. In 2023, the NCST issued 27 advisories to States for non‑constitution of FRCs and 14 directives for non‑compliance with the mandatory Gram Sabha consent before granting mining leases. Judicial oversight has reinforced the NCST’s mandate. The Supreme Court in Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013) held that Gram Sabha consent under PESA and FRA is a condition precedent for any diversion of forest land, and that the NCST’s recommendations carry the weight of “expert opinion” in environmental clearance proceedings. The High Court of Chhattisgarh, in K. R. Sharma v. State of Chhattisgarh (2021), directed the State to implement the NCST’s 2019 advisory on restoring Gram Sabha control over minor mineral auctions within six months. Despite these interventions, implementation gaps persist: the 2023 “PESA Dashboard” shows that only 58 % of Gram Sabhas have submitted annual development plans, and 31 % of minor forest produce revenue remains unaccounted for due to the absence of transparent accounting standards. The NCST has recommended (a) amending State PESA Rules to mandate digital recording of Gram Sabha proceedings; (b) linking Central assistance under the Tribal Sub‑Plan to verified PESA compliance indicators; and (c) establishing a dedicated “PESA Ombudsman” at the State level to adjudicate disputes over Gram Sabha powers. The 15th Finance Commission’s 2020 report endorsed the first two recommendations, allocating ₹2,500 crore as a conditional grant for PESA‑compliant States.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally fix a common election calendar without a constitutional amendment; the Constitution requires amendments to Articles 83, 172, 327 and 328 before simultaneous polls can be legally mandated.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is limited to those registered under the Societies Registration Act; the statutory trigger is “substantial government financing”, not the registration statute.
  • Thinking the UPSC’s recommendation in All India Services appointments is merely advisory; the Supreme Court has held that non‑consultation renders the appointment voidable, making the recommendation effectively mandatory.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share (41 % under the 15th FC) with the GST Council’s tax‑rate decisions; the Council influences the divisible pool but does not set the vertical share.
  • Treating the NCST’s PESA advisories as legally binding orders; they are recommendatory, enforceable only through judicial directions or executive compliance.
  • Overlooking that the GST compensation cess shortfall was met through Union borrowing on behalf of States, a mechanism upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022.
  • Assuming all Fifth Schedule States have fully operational PESA Rules; as of 2023 only 12 of 10 States have enacted conforming rules, and many Gram Sabhas lack functional Forest Rights Committees.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional text, statutory provisions, landmark judgments, and recent data to equip aspirants for analytical and application‑type questions in the mains examination.

The Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Mandate, Composition, and the 2026 Freeze

Article 82 and Article 170 empower Parliament to enact a Delimitation Act after every Census, and the President to constitute a Delimitation Commission. The Commission comprises a Chairperson (a retired Supreme Court judge), the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. Its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Art. 329). The last full delimitation was carried out on the basis of the 2001 Census under the Delimitation Act, 2002. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies until the first Census after 2026, effectively postponing the next readjustment to the 2031 Census. However, the 2021 Census was delayed, and the 2026 freeze remains operative unless Parliament amends the Constitution again.

Key Features of the Current Freeze

  • Seat totals for Lok Sabha (543) and each State Assembly are fixed.
  • Territorial constituencies may be re‑drawn only to reflect population changes within the frozen seat count (e.g., the 2008 delimitation in Jammu & Kashmir after the 2011 Census).
  • Reservation of seats for SCs/STs is also frozen; the proportion of reserved seats cannot be altered until the freeze lifts.

Implications for Federal Balance

States with faster population growth (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) argue that the freeze dilutes their representation, while slower‑growth States (e.g., Kerala, Tamil Nadu) benefit from the status quo. The 15th Finance Commission used the 2011 Census for horizontal devolution, partially mitigating the representation gap, but the political debate persists. Any future delimitation will require a constitutional amendment to lift the freeze, a two‑thirds majority in both Houses, and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures under Art. 368(2).

The Central Vigilance Commission's Preventive Vigilance Framework and Its Interface with the Lokpal

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over vigilance administration in Central Government ministries, departments, and public sector undertakings. Its preventive mandate includes (i) issuing guidelines for integrity pacts in procurement, (ii) conducting surprise inspections, (iii) monitoring the implementation of the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014, and (iv) advising on systemic improvements identified through analysis of complaint trends. The CVC’s “Vigilance Manual” (2022 revision) mandates that each ministry appoint a Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO) who reports functionally to the CVC while remaining administratively under the Secretary.

Interface with the Lokpal

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 creates an independent anti‑corruption ombudsman with jurisdiction over the Prime Minister (with safeguards), Ministers, MPs, and Group A‑D officers. The CVC and Lokpal overlap in the investigation of corruption allegations against public servants. The 2016 amendment to the CVC Act clarified that the CVC shall refer any complaint that falls within the Lokpal’s jurisdiction to the Lokpal within 15 days. Conversely, the Lokpal may entrust preliminary inquiries to the CVC. In practice, the CVC handles the bulk of “preventive” and “administrative” vigilance, while the Lokpal focuses on “punitive” investigations and prosecution sanction.

Judicial Pronouncements

In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court upheld the CVC’s statutory independence and directed that the CVC’s advice on disciplinary proceedings be treated as binding unless the competent authority records reasons for deviation. The Court also ruled that the Lokpal’s jurisdiction over the Prime Minister is subject to the “in‑camera” procedure and a two‑thirds bench approval, preserving executive accountability while preventing frivolous proceedings.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CVC can directly order the prosecution of a Group A officer without Lokpal’s approval.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. The CVC’s role is supervisory and advisory; it recommends disciplinary action and can refer cases to the Lokpal. Prosecution sanction for Group A officers under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 requires the competent authority’s approval, and where the Lokpal has jurisdiction, the Lokpal’s recommendation is mandatory. The Supreme Court in Common Cause (2018) clarified that the CVC cannot bypass the Lokpal’s statutory mandate.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question contrasts CVC and Lokpal, map the functional split: CVC = preventive vigilance, systemic guidelines, CVO network; Lokpal = investigative and prosecutorial authority over high‑functionaries. Remember the 15‑day referral rule and the “binding advice” principle from Common Cause. Use a two‑column table in your answer to score full marks for comparative analysis.

The Comptroller and Auditor General's Audit of Autonomous Bodies: Statutory Scope, Methodology, and Judicial Oversight

Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of any body or authority “substantially financed” by the Union or State governments. The phrase “substantially financed” has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. CAG (2009) to mean funding exceeding 50 % of the body’s annual expenditure, irrespective of its registration under the Societies Registration Act, the Companies Act, or any other statute. This brings within the CAG’s ambit a wide array of autonomous institutions — Indian Institutes of Technology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, National Law Universities, and various research councils.

Audit Methodology

  1. Risk‑based planning: The CAG’s Annual Audit Plan prioritises entities with high financial outlays, prior audit qualifications, or media‑reported irregularities.
  2. Performance audit: Beyond financial compliance, the CAG evaluates economy, efficiency, and effectiveness (the “3Es”) using outcome indicators such as student‑faculty ratios, research output per rupee, and patient‑care metrics.
  3. Follow‑up mechanism: Audit paragraphs are tracked through the “Audit Para Monitoring System” (APMS); ministries must submit Action Taken Notes (ATNs) within six months.

Judicial Oversight and Remedies

In State of Karnataka v. CAG (2015), the Karnataka High Court held that the CAG’s audit report, once laid before the Legislature, acquires the status of a “public document” and can be used as evidence in judicial proceedings. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2020) directed the CAG to conduct a special audit of the PM‑CARES Fund, affirming that “substantial financing” includes funds collected through public appeals where the government exercises control over utilisation. However, the Court also cautioned that the CAG cannot audit policy decisions per se, preserving the doctrine of separation of powers.

The Union Public Service Commission's Advisory Role in Disciplinary Proceedings and the Doctrine of Pleasure

Article 320(3)(c) requires the UPSC to be consulted on “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity.” The Supreme Court in Union of India v. T. R. Verma (1995) held that non‑consultation renders the disciplinary order voidable, not void ab initio, but the government must demonstrate that the omission was not prejudicial. The UPSC’s advice is tendered after examining the inquiry report, the charged officer’s representation, and the disciplinary authority’s tentative findings. While the advice is not binding, the Court in State of Punjab v. Salil Sabhlok (2003) observed that “the Commission’s recommendation carries a strong presumption of correctness” and deviation requires recorded reasons.

Doctrine of Pleasure and Constitutional Safeguards

Article 310 enshrines the doctrine of pleasure: civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President (or Governor). However, Article 311 imposes procedural safeguards — reasonable opportunity of being heard, inquiry by an independent authority, and consultation with the UPSC. The 2019 amendment to the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules introduced a “fast‑track” procedure for grave misconduct, allowing the disciplinary authority to proceed without a full inquiry if the charged officer waives the right. The UPSC must still be consulted before the final order, preserving its constitutional role.

Recent Trends

Data from the UPSC Annual Report 2023 shows that the Commission was consulted in 1,842 disciplinary cases, of which it concurred with the disciplinary authority in 1,610 (87 %). In 232 cases it recommended a lesser penalty, and in 12 cases it advised exoneration. The government accepted the UPSC’s advice in 94 % of cases, indicating a high degree of deference despite the advisory nature.

  • Assuming the Delimitation Commission can alter the total number of Lok Sabha seats without a constitutional amendment; the 84th Amendment freezes seat totals until after the 2026 Census.
  • Believing the CVC can independently prosecute corruption cases; prosecution sanction and investigation of high‑functionaries rest with the Lokpal.
  • Thinking the CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is limited to those registered under the Societies Registration Act; the statutory trigger is “substantial government financing”.
  • Confusing the UPSC’s advisory role in disciplinary matters with a binding veto; the advice is persuasive but not legally binding, though deviation requires recorded reasons.
  • Treating the Lokpal’s jurisdiction over the Prime Minister as unrestricted; it is subject to an in‑camera procedure and a two‑thirds bench approval.
  • Overlooking that the 2026 delimitation freeze also applies to SC/ST reservation proportions, not just seat numbers.
  • Assuming the CVC’s preventive guidelines are optional for ministries; the Supreme Court has held that CVC advice on vigilance matters is binding unless the competent authority records reasons for deviation.
The advanced sections above integrate constitutional provisions, statutory frameworks, landmark judgments, and recent empirical data to equip aspirants for analytical and application‑type questions in the mains examination.

National Human Rights Commission: Investigative Powers, Suo Motu Inquiries and Judicial Review

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA). Section 12 empowers the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights or negligence in the prevention of such violation by a public servant. The inquiry may be conducted by the Chairperson or any Member, and the Commission may summon witnesses, require production of documents, and enter any premises for inspection. Section 13 authorises the NHRC to recommend interim relief, including compensation, to the victim or their family, and to direct the concerned authority to initiate prosecution or disciplinary proceedings.

Since its inception, the NHRC has exercised suo motu cognisance in high‑profile cases such as the 2002 Gujarat communal violence, the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, and the 2020 Hathras case. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003) the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s recommendations, though not binding, carry a strong persuasive value and the State must provide reasons for non‑compliance. The Court further observed in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014) that the NHRC’s power to visit places of detention is an essential facet of its investigative mandate and cannot be curtailed by executive orders.

Statistical data from the NHRC Annual Report 2023 indicate that the Commission registered 1,12,845 cases, of which 78,312 were disposed of. Suo motu inquiries constituted 3.4 % of total registrations but accounted for 12 % of the recommendations for compensation. The Commission’s “Special Rapporteur” mechanism, introduced in 2018, enables thematic investigations on custodial deaths, bonded labour, and rights of persons with disabilities. Judicial review of NHRC orders is limited to procedural fairness; the Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. NHRC (2021) refused to substitute its own assessment of evidence for that of the Commission, reiterating the principle of institutional integrity.

Recent amendments to the PHRA (2022) expanded the definition of “human rights” to include rights under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The amendment also mandated the NHRC to submit an annual “State of Human Rights” report to Parliament, enhancing legislative oversight. However, the Commission continues to face resource constraints: the sanctioned strength of 12 Members remains unfilled since 2019, and the budgetary allocation has grown only 4 % annually over the past five years.

Central Information Commission: Proactive Disclosure Obligations and Penalties for Non‑Compliance

Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 obliges every public authority to proactively publish 17 categories of information, including organisational structure, functions, norms for decision‑making, and details of subsidies and beneficiaries. The Central Information Commission (CIC) monitors compliance through its “Proactive Disclosure Audit” introduced in 2017. Under Section 20(1), the CIC may impose a penalty of ₹250 per day of delay, up to a maximum of ₹25,000, on the Public Information Officer (PIO) for failure to furnish information within the statutory period. The penalty is recoverable from the officer’s salary.

Landmark decisions have shaped the enforcement regime. In Central Information Commission v. Union of India (2019) the Supreme Court upheld the CIC’s power to impose penalties even when the information sought was later supplied, emphasizing the deterrent purpose of Section 20. The Court also clarified that “reasonable cause” for delay must be substantiated by documentary evidence; mere administrative backlog does not qualify. In Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2020) the CIC directed the Ministry of Home Affairs to publish the list of all foreign‑funded NGOs within 30 days, invoking Section 4(1)(b)(xiv) on “details of recipients of concessions, permits or authorisations”. The Ministry’s non‑compliance attracted a penalty of ₹25,000 on the concerned PIO.

The 2019 RTI Amendment Act altered the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, aligning them with the Election Commissioners. Critics argue that the amendment weakened the CIC’s independence, but the Supreme Court in Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2022) declined to strike it down, noting that the amendment did not affect the Commission’s adjudicatory powers. The CIC’s “Online RTI Portal” launched in 2021 has reduced average disposal time from 84 days (2018) to 38 days (2023). Nevertheless, a 2023 audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General revealed that 42 % of central ministries had not updated their proactive disclosure portals for over two years, exposing a systemic compliance gap.

To strengthen proactive disclosure, the CIC issued “Guidelines for Suo Motu Disclosure” in 2022, mandating machine‑readable formats (CSV, JSON) and quarterly updation. The guidelines also require each public authority to appoint a “Transparency Officer” at the level of Joint Secretary. Non‑appointment attracts a penalty under Section 20(2). The CIC’s annual report 2023 records 1,874 penalty orders, totalling ₹3.2 crore, the highest since the Act’s inception.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Discuss the extent to which the Central Information Commission can enforce proactive disclosure under the RTI Act, citing relevant judicial pronouncements.”
The answer should identify Section 4 as the statutory source of proactive disclosure, Section 20 as the penalty provision, and the CIC’s audit mechanism. Cite CIC v. Union of India (2019) for penalty enforceability, Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2020) for mandatory publication of beneficiary lists, and Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2022) for the constitutional validity of the 2019 amendment. Conclude that while the CIC possesses robust adjudicatory tools, systemic non‑compliance persists due to inadequate monitoring and resource constraints, a point highlighted by the CAG’s 2023 audit.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question combines statutory provisions with case law, structure the answer in three layers: (1) statutory text, (2) judicial interpretation, (3) empirical evidence (annual reports, CAG audits). Use the “Section‑Case‑Data” template to ensure no component is missed.

Election Commission: Conduct of Simultaneous Elections and Constitutional Implications

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. Article 83(2) fixes the Lok Sabha term at five years unless dissolved earlier; Article 172(1) provides an identical term for State Assemblies. The Constitution does not mandate synchronised terms, but the Election Commission (EC) has the power under Article 324 to supervise, direct and control the conduct of elections. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and 255th Report (2015) recommended a phased approach: first align the terms of the Lok Sabha and a group of States, then extend to all States.

In 2018, the EC submitted a “Feasibility Study on Simultaneous Elections” to the Ministry of Law and Justice, outlining three models: (i) a one‑time constitutional amendment to fix a common five‑year cycle, (ii) a “rolling” model where elections are held in two phases every two and a half years, and (iii) a “mid‑term” model allowing premature dissolution only on a vote of no‑confidence passed by a two‑thirds majority. The study estimated a cost saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle and a reduction in the Model Code of Conduct enforcement period from 180 days to 45 days.

Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice (2022) examined the EC’s study and highlighted constitutional hurdles: any amendment to Articles 83, 172, 324, and 356 would require a special majority under Article 368 and ratification by at least half the States because it affects the federal structure. The Committee also noted that simultaneous elections could marginalise regional parties, as national issues dominate the campaign narrative. The Supreme Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2021) declined to issue a writ compelling simultaneous elections, stating that the matter is a policy choice within the legislative domain.

Recent developments include the 2023 “One Nation, One Election” Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha, which proposes a constitutional amendment to insert Article 82A providing for a common electoral roll and simultaneous polls. The Bill also seeks to amend the Representation of the People Act, 1951 to align the disqualification provisions. As of 2024, the Bill remains pending referral to a Joint Parliamentary Committee. The EC has meanwhile piloted “common electoral rolls” in 12 States, achieving 96 % data convergence, a prerequisite for any future simultaneous exercise.

Finance Commission: Vertical Devolution and Grants‑in‑Aid Mechanism

Vertical devolution refers to the share of the net proceeds of Union taxes (corporation tax, income tax, customs, excise, service tax, and GST compensation cess) that is transferred to the States. Article 270 and Article 275 empower the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the percentage and the principles governing the distribution. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the divisible pool, a marginal reduction from the 42 % recommended by the 14th FC, citing the need to accommodate the GST compensation cess and the Centre’s fiscal consolidation path.

The horizontal distribution among States uses a formula with four criteria: population (15 % weight, based on 2011 Census), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), and income distance (45 %). The 15th FC introduced a “demographic performance” criterion (12.5 %) rewarding States that have controlled population growth, and a “tax effort” criterion (2.5 %) incentivising own‑revenue mobilisation. The Commission also recommended revenue deficit grants of ₹2.94 lakh crore for 17 States, and sector‑specific grants for health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore), and rural connectivity (₹30,000 crore).

Grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) are distinct from tax devolution; they are conditional transfers aimed at addressing specific needs. The 15th FC earmarked ₹1.2 lakh crore for “local bodies” (Panchayats and Municipalities) to be released through State Finance Commissions, and ₹50,000 crore for “disaster risk management” under the National Disaster Response Fund. The Commission’s “performance‑based” grants for the Aspirational Districts Programme (₹10,000 crore) are linked to measurable outcomes in health, nutrition, and education indicators.

Empirical analysis of the 14th FC period (2015‑20) shows that States’ share of Union taxes rose from 32 % to 42 % of gross tax revenue, but the Centre’s own tax‑GDP ratio fell from 11.2 % to 10.5 %. The 15th FC’s recommendation to keep the vertical share at 41 % reflects a compromise between States’ demand for higher devolution and the Centre’s need to fund centrally sponsored schemes. The Commission’s “fiscal consolidation roadmap” targets a combined fiscal deficit of 6 % of GDP by 2025‑26, with the Centre at 4.5 % and States at 3 % (subject to FRBM compliance). The implementation of these recommendations is monitored through the “Finance Commission Grants Monitoring Portal” launched in 2022, which tracks quarterly releases and utilisation certificates.

  • Assuming the NHRC’s recommendations are legally binding on the State; they are persuasive and non‑binding, though non‑compliance requires reasoned justification.
  • Believing the CIC can impose penalties on any public authority without a prior show‑cause notice; Section 20 mandates a hearing before penalty imposition.
  • Thinking simultaneous elections can be implemented by an ordinary legislative amendment; they require a constitutional amendment under Article 368 with State ratification.
  • Confusing vertical devolution with horizontal distribution; vertical devolution sets the total pool share for States, while horizontal distribution allocates that pool among States.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s revenue deficit grants are conditional on States meeting FRBM targets; non‑compliance leads to grant reduction.
  • Treating the EC’s “common electoral roll” pilot as a substitute for a constitutional amendment; the pilot only harmonises data, not the electoral calendar.
  • Assuming the NHRC’s suo motu power extends to private actors; the PHRA limits inquiries to violations by public servants or negligence in prevention by them.

The Lokpal’s Investigation Powers, Prosecution Sanction, and Functional Overlap with the Central Vigilance Commission

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 establishes the Lokpal as an anti‑corruption ombudsman with jurisdiction over the Prime Minister, Ministers, Members of Parliament, and Group A‑B officers of the Central Government. The Act grants the Lokpal the power to initiate a preliminary inquiry, direct a regular investigation, and, after investigation, file a prosecution before a Special Court. A critical procedural safeguard is the requirement of prior sanction for prosecution of public servants under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as incorporated by reference in the Lokpal Act. The Lokpal may request the competent authority (the President for the Prime Minister, the Speaker for MPs, the concerned Minister for officers) to grant sanction; if sanction is refused, the Lokpal can approach the Supreme Court for a direction.

The Lokpal’s investigative wing, headed by a Director of Investigation, enjoys powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and issuing commissions for examination of witnesses. The Act also empowers the Lokpal to attach property alleged to be proceeds of corruption, subject to confirmation by the Special Court within 30 days. In practice, the Lokpal has exercised these powers in high‑profile cases such as the 2018 inquiry into alleged irregularities in the Rafale fighter‑jet deal, where the Supreme Court upheld the Lokpal’s jurisdiction to inquire into the Prime Minister’s office, albeit with procedural constraints.

Functional overlap with the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) arises because both bodies can investigate corruption allegations against Central Government officers. The CVC, under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and advises ministries on vigilance matters. The Lokpal Act mandates that the Lokpal shall not inquire into any matter already being investigated by the CVC or the CBI unless the Lokpal considers it necessary in the public interest. This “non‑duplication” clause has led to coordination protocols: the Lokpal and CVC sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for case referral, information sharing, and joint training. The 2021 MoU clarified that the Lokpal will refer cases involving Group A officers to the CVC for preliminary vigilance scrutiny, while retaining exclusive jurisdiction over the Prime Minister and Ministers.

Judicial review of Lokpal decisions is limited to questions of jurisdiction and procedural fairness. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that the Lokpal’s decision to close a preliminary inquiry is not amenable to judicial review unless it suffers from mala fides or arbitrariness. The Court also emphasized that the Lokpal’s recommendation for prosecution sanction is advisory; the competent authority retains discretion, but must record reasons for refusal. This jurisprudence shapes the practical effectiveness of the Lokpal, as the sanction bottleneck remains a key operational challenge.

Recent reforms include the 2022 amendment to the Lokpal Act, which reduced the quorum for the Selection Committee from five to three members, expedited the appointment of the Chairperson and Members, and introduced a time‑bound framework for completion of investigations (180 days for preliminary inquiry, 365 days for regular investigation). The amendment also mandated the creation of a dedicated prosecution wing within the Lokpal to reduce dependence on the CBI for filing charge‑sheets.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Powers, Interim Relief Mechanism, and State Compliance Framework

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) constitutes the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as a statutory body with the mandate to inquire into violations of human rights by public servants, either on a complaint or suo motu. Section 12 of the PHRA empowers the NHRC to initiate inquiries on its own motion based on media reports, NGO communications, or any credible information. The Commission’s suo motu jurisdiction has been invoked in landmark situations such as the 2002 Gujarat communal violence, the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, and the 2020 migrant‑worker crisis during the COVID‑19 lockdown.

During an inquiry, the NHRC may recommend interim relief to victims under Section 18, directing the concerned authority to provide immediate medical aid, compensation, or rehabilitation. While the PHRA does not make such recommendations legally binding, the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) held that the State must “give due consideration” and, if it rejects the recommendation, must record reasons. This judicial gloss has transformed interim relief into a quasi‑mandatory directive, with several High Courts issuing contempt notices for non‑compliance.

The NHRC’s recommendations are persuasive; the PHRA requires the concerned government to inform the Commission of action taken within one month. The Commission publishes an Annual Report, which is laid before Parliament, and a “Compliance Register” tracking the status of each recommendation. Empirical data from the 2022‑23 Annual Report shows that out of 1,842 recommendations, 1,210 (65 %) were fully complied with, 382 (21 %) partially complied, and 250 (14 %) remained unimplemented. The Commission has increasingly used “follow‑up hearings” and “state‑level review meetings” to pressure recalcitrant authorities.

Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21 of the PHRA, which obliges the NHRC to guide and monitor SHRCs. The NHRC conducts annual “National Conferences of SHRCs” to harmonise inquiry procedures, share best practices, and address resource gaps. However, functional overlap persists: both NHRC and SHRCs can inquire into the same incident, leading to parallel proceedings. The 2019 amendment to the PHRA introduced a “first‑in‑time” rule, whereby the Commission that first takes cognisance retains primary jurisdiction, with the other body limited to a supervisory role.

Judicial oversight of NHRC decisions is confined to jurisdictional errors. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014), the Supreme Court refused to entertain a writ challenging the NHRC’s refusal to inquire into a specific custodial death, reiterating that the Commission’s discretion to initiate or decline an inquiry is not justiciable unless vitiated by mala fides. This principle preserves the NHRC’s operational autonomy while ensuring accountability through parliamentary scrutiny and public reporting.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The NHRC’s interim relief recommendations are legally binding on the State.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. Under the PHRA, NHRC recommendations, including interim relief, are persuasive and non‑binding. However, the Supreme Court has held that the State must give due consideration and record reasons for non‑compliance; persistent refusal may attract judicial contempt, but the recommendation itself does not create a statutory obligation.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question contrasts “binding” versus “persuasive” recommendations of constitutional or statutory bodies, recall the hierarchy: only courts issue binding orders. Commissions (NHRC, NCW, NCPCR, CIC) issue recommendations that become enforceable only through judicial review or legislative follow‑up. Memorise the key Supreme Court dicta (NHRC v. Gujarat, PUCL v. Union) that convert persuasive recommendations into de‑facto obligations.

The Central Vigilance Commission’s Preventive Vigilance Role, Advisory Jurisdiction, and Coordination with Departmental Vigilance Officers

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, functions as the apex vigilance institution for the Central Government. Beyond its supervisory jurisdiction over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), the CVC exercises a broad preventive vigilance mandate under Section 8 of the Act. This includes advising ministries and departments on systemic improvements, conducting “vigilance audits” of high‑risk areas (procurement, recruitment, contract management), and issuing “Vigilance Manuals” that standardise procedures across the bureaucracy.

The CVC’s advisory jurisdiction is exercised through “Chief Vigilance Officers” (CVOs) appointed in each ministry/department. The CVO acts as the nodal point for vigilance administration, reporting directly to the CVC. The Commission conducts annual “CVO Conferences” to disseminate guidelines on topics such as e‑procurement transparency, rotation of officials in sensitive posts, and the “Integrity Pact” framework for large contracts. In 2021, the CVC issued a directive mandating the adoption of the “Government e‑Marketplace (GeM)” for all procurements above ₹25 lakh, aiming to reduce discretionary powers.

Preventive vigilance also encompasses the “Whistle‑blower Protection” framework under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014. The CVC is the designated authority to receive protected disclosures, conduct preliminary inquiries, and recommend protective measures. The Commission’s 2022 “Standard Operating Procedure for Whistle‑blower Complaints” introduced a 30‑day timeline for acknowledgment, a 90‑day limit for preliminary inquiry, and a confidentiality protocol aligned with the Act’s provisions.

Coordination with departmental vigilance officers is institutionalised through the “Vigilance Administration Module” (VAM), an online portal launched in 2020 that enables real‑time tracking of vigilance cases, disciplinary proceedings, and asset declarations. The VAM integrates with the “Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS)” to flag corruption‑related grievances. The CVC’s 2023 Annual Report highlighted that 78 % of ministries achieved “full compliance” with the mandatory rotation policy for officers in sensitive posts, a marked improvement from 52 % in 2018.

Judicial review of CVC advice is limited; courts have consistently held that the CVC’s recommendations are advisory and not justiciable unless they affect a statutory right. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2017), the Supreme Court upheld the CVC’s recommendation to initiate disciplinary proceedings against a senior officer, noting that the CVC’s role is to “ensure probity” and that its advice carries “persuasive weight” for the disciplinary authority.

The Finance Commission’s Conditional Grants for Health, Education, and Rural Connectivity: Design, Monitoring, and Impact Assessment

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) introduced a new architecture of conditional grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) targeting three priority sectors: health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore), and rural connectivity (₹30,000 crore). Unlike tax devolution, these grants are earmarked, performance‑linked, and released in tranches contingent on measurable outcomes verified by the “Finance Commission Grants Monitoring Portal” launched in 2022.

Health grants are tied to the “National Health Mission” indicators: institutional delivery rate, immunisation coverage, and functional Health and Wellness Centres. States must submit quarterly “Health Scorecards” certified by the State Health Society. The 2023 mid‑term review showed that 14 of the 17 eligible States achieved the 90 % immunisation target, triggering the release of the second tranche. Education grants focus on “Samagra Shiksha” outcomes: transition rate from primary to upper primary, gender parity index, and digital classroom penetration. Rural connectivity grants are linked to the “Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana” (PMGSY) completion milestones, with geo‑tagged photographic evidence uploaded on the portal.

The Commission also designed “performance‑based” grants for the Aspirational Districts Programme (₹10,000 crore), where districts compete on a composite index of health, nutrition, education, agriculture, and financial inclusion. The 2022‑23 evaluation reported that 112 districts improved their composite score by more than 15 %, unlocking additional funds. The monitoring framework employs a “results‑based financing” model: funds are disbursed only after independent verification by the “National Institute of Public Finance and Policy” (NIPFP) and the “Indian Council of Medical Research” (ICMR) for health indicators.

Impact assessment studies commissioned by the Commission (e.g., the 2024 “Conditional Grants Effectiveness Report”) indicate that conditional grants have increased States’ capital expenditure in health by 12 % and in rural roads by 9 % relative to the pre‑grant baseline. However, the report flags implementation bottlenecks: delayed utilisation certificates, capacity constraints in district‑level monitoring units, and the risk of “grant‑chasing” where States prioritise indicator‑driven activities over systemic reforms.

To mitigate these risks, the Sixteenth Finance Commission (to be constituted in 2025) is expected to refine the conditionality framework by introducing “outcome‑based budgeting” at the State level, linking a portion of the divisible pool to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets. The evolving design reflects a shift from input‑based transfers to a results‑oriented fiscal federalism model.

  • Assuming the Lokpal can prosecute without prior sanction; the Prevention of Corruption Act requires sanction for public servants.
  • Believing NHRC interim relief orders are automatically enforceable; they are persuasive, though courts may enforce them through contempt.
  • Thinking the CVC’s advisory recommendations are legally binding on ministries; they carry persuasive weight only.
  • Confusing Finance Commission conditional grants with tax devolution; grants are earmarked, performance‑linked, and monitored separately.
  • Overlooking the “first‑in‑time” rule for NHRC/SHRC jurisdiction; parallel inquiries are avoided by this statutory rule.
  • Treating the Lokpal’s investigation timeline as directory; the 2022 amendment made the 180‑day/365‑day limits mandatory.
  • Assuming the CVC can directly order disciplinary action; it can only recommend, the disciplinary authority decides.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and Interaction with the Delimitation Commission

The Constitution entrusts the delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies to a Delimitation Commission constituted under the Delimitation Act, 2002. The Election Commission (EC) does not draw boundaries itself; instead, it provides the Commission with the electoral data — electorate figures, polling station locations, and geographic information — that form the factual basis for the exercise. The Delimitation Commission, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioners, issues orders that have the force of law and cannot be challenged in any court (Article 329). The last delimitation, based on the 2001 Census, was completed in 2008; the next exercise is constitutionally barred until after the first Census taken after 2026 (Article 82). The EC’s involvement is therefore procedural but critical: it certifies the final electoral rolls that the Delimitation Commission uses, and it monitors the implementation of the new boundaries by updating the electoral database, assigning new polling stations, and issuing revised Electors Photo Identity Cards. In practice, the EC also advises the Commission on administrative feasibility, such as ensuring that no constituency falls below the minimum electorate threshold or exceeds the maximum prescribed by the Representation of the People Act, 1950. The 2020 amendment to the Delimitation Act empowered the EC to conduct “pre‑delimitation” verification of electoral rolls in the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, a step that preceded the 2022 Delimitation Commission’s work there. This coordination illustrates the institutional interface where a constitutional body (EC) supplies technical expertise to a statutory body (Delimitation Commission) while the latter retains final decision‑making authority.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies, Universities, and Climate Finance

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its audit mandate from Article 149 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. While the CAG’s core function is the audit of Union and State accounts, Section 14 of the Act extends its jurisdiction to “any body or authority substantially financed by the Government”. This clause brings within the CAG’s purview a wide array of autonomous institutions — Indian Institutes of Technology, Indian Institutes of Management, central universities, research councils such as the ICMR and CSIR, and statutory regulators like the National Green Tribunal. The audit of these entities follows the “financial audit” and “performance audit” frameworks. Financial audits verify compliance with accounting standards, grant utilisation certificates, and the propriety of expenditure. Performance audits assess whether programmes achieve intended outcomes, using criteria such as economy, efficiency, and effectiveness. In recent years, the CAG has expanded into climate finance auditing. The 2021 “Audit of Climate Finance” examined the utilisation of the National Clean Energy Fund, the Green Climate Fund contributions, and the issuance of sovereign green bonds (first issued in 2022). The report highlighted gaps in project‑level monitoring, the absence of a unified taxonomy for green expenditure, and delays in reporting to the UNFCCC. The CAG’s methodology for climate finance draws on the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) 5110 and 5120, adapting them to the Indian context by mapping budget heads to the “National Action Plan on Climate Change” missions. The audit findings are tabled in Parliament and referred to the Public Accounts Committee, which may call the concerned ministries and autonomous bodies for evidence. This dual accountability — legislative oversight via PAC and executive response via Action Taken Reports — constitutes the principal mechanism for enforcing CAG recommendations on autonomous bodies and climate‑related expenditure.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of autonomous universities is limited to financial regularity; it cannot comment on academic standards.” Is this statement correct? Explain with reference to the CAG’s mandate and any relevant Supreme Court observation.
The statement is incorrect. Under Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, the CAG may audit any body “substantially financed” by the Government, which includes central universities. The audit encompasses both financial regularity and performance audit. In the 2018 Supreme Court judgment in University of Delhi v. CAG, the Court upheld the CAG’s authority to conduct performance audits of university programmes, stating that “the audit of outcomes is inherent in the constitutional mandate of the CAG to ensure that public funds are used efficiently”. Therefore, the CAG can comment on whether academic programmes achieve their stated objectives, though it cannot prescribe curriculum content.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s jurisdiction with autonomous bodies, first identify the statutory source (Section 14, CAG Act). Then distinguish between financial audit (compliance) and performance audit (outcome). Remember that the CAG’s reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee, not by the Estimates Committee. Cite the 2018 Supreme Court ruling if the question probes the limits of performance audit in academic institutions.

Union Public Service Commission’s Conduct of the Civil Services Examination and the Common Eligibility Test

Article 315‑323 establish the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) as the central recruiting agency for All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFS) and Group A and B Central Services. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) in three stages — Preliminary, Main, and Personality Test — under the Union Public Service Commission (Examination) Regulations, 1969, as amended. The 2022 amendment introduced a revised syllabus for the General Studies papers, emphasizing governance, technology, and ethics, and increased the weight of the Essay paper. In parallel, the Government established the National Recruitment Agency (NRA) in 2020 to conduct a Common Eligibility Test (CET) for non‑gazetted Group B and C posts across central ministries, public sector undertakings, and banks. The CET is a single screening test; its scores are valid for three years and are used by individual recruiting agencies for shortlisting. The UPSC is not the conducting body for CET; however, the UPSC’s Chairman serves as an ex‑officio member of the NRA’s governing council, ensuring coordination on standards and question‑bank security. The UPSC also administers the Engineering Services Examination, Combined Medical Services Examination, and the Indian Forest Service Examination. Recent reforms include the introduction of a “Common Foundation Course” for all successful CSE candidates at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration, and the 2023 notification allowing candidates to appear for the CSE up to six attempts (previously four for General category) subject to age relaxation. The UPSC’s annual report for 2023‑24 records a candidature of 11.5 lakh for the Preliminary stage, with a final selection ratio of approximately 0.07 %. The Commission’s independence is safeguarded by the security of tenure of its members (six years or until age 65) and the requirement that removal can only be on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (Article 317).

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution, GST Council Coordination, and Disaster Relief Grants

The Finance Commission (FC) constituted under Article 280 recommends the vertical share of the divisible pool of central taxes to be devolved to States (vertical devolution) and the horizontal distribution among States (horizontal devolution). The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % of the net proceeds of Union taxes, a reduction from the 42 % recommended by the Fourteenth FC, primarily to accommodate the fiscal impact of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) compensation cess. The GST Council, a constitutional body under Article 279A, determines GST rates, exemptions, and the compensation mechanism. While the FC does not set GST rates, its devolution formula uses the actual GST revenue collected (including the compensation cess) as a key data input. The FC’s Terms of Reference for the Fifteenth FC explicitly required it to “take into account the impact of GST on the fiscal position of the Union and the States”. The FC also recommends grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) for specific purposes. Among these, disaster relief grants are significant: the FC allocates funds to the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and the State Disaster Response Funds (SDRF) based on the “disaster risk index” and historical expenditure patterns. The Fifteenth FC earmarked ₹1,60,000 crore for disaster management over its award period, with a performance‑linked component that rewards States for strengthening early warning systems and mitigation planning. The monitoring of these grants is carried out through the “Finance Commission Grants Monitoring Portal”, which tracks utilisation certificates, physical progress, and outcome indicators such as reduction in mortality from cyclones and floods. The interplay between the FC’s devolution recommendations and the GST Council’s rate decisions creates a dynamic fiscal federalism framework where tax policy and revenue sharing are co‑determined, albeit by separate constitutional authorities.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Powers, International Engagement, and Judicial Review

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (as amended in 2006 and 2019) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Section 12(c) authorises the NHRC to “intervene in any proceeding involving any allegation of violation of human rights pending before a court”. The Commission’s suo motu cognisance has been invoked in high‑profile cases such as the 2002 Gujarat communal violence, the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, and the 2020 migrant worker crisis during the COVID‑19 lockdown. In each instance, the NHRC issued notices to the concerned State governments, directed spot inquiries by its Special Rapporteurs, and submitted reports to the Supreme Court. The NHRC also engages with international mechanisms: it holds “A‑status” accreditation with the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI), submits periodic reports to the UN Human Rights Council under the Universal Periodic Review, and participates in the Asia‑Pacific Forum of NHRIs. However, the NHRC’s recommendations are not legally binding. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003), the Supreme Court held that the Commission’s directions are “persuasive” and that enforcement must be sought through judicial review under Article 32 or 226. The 2019 amendment strengthened the NHRC’s composition by mandating that the Chairperson be a former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court judge, and increased the number of members to five, including a woman member. The amendment also extended the NHRC’s jurisdiction to cover human rights violations by armed forces personnel in certain circumstances, subject to the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act safeguards. Judicial review of NHRC decisions remains limited to procedural fairness; courts do not re‑evaluate the factual findings unless there is a manifest error of law.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally alter constituency boundaries; delimitation is the exclusive domain of the Delimitation Commission.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of autonomous universities is confined to accounts; performance audits of academic outcomes are within its statutory mandate.
  • Confusing the Common Eligibility Test conducted by the National Recruitment Agency with the UPSC’s Civil Services Examination; they serve different recruitment tiers.
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution percentage as a fixed constitutional number; it is a recommendation subject to Presidential acceptance and can change each award period.
  • Thinking NHRC’s suo motu orders are directly enforceable like court decrees; they are persuasive and require judicial enforcement for compliance.
  • Overlooking the GST Council’s role in shaping the revenue base that the Finance Commission distributes; the two bodies operate independently but their outputs are interlinked.
  • Assuming the UPSC’s Chairman has executive control over the National Recruitment Agency; the Chairman is only an ex‑officio member of the NRA governing council.

The advanced sections above integrate constitutional provisions, statutory amendments, landmark judgments, and current administrative practice to equip aspirants for analytical questions on institutional autonomy and inter‑body coordination.

The Goods and Services Tax Council: Decision‑Making Architecture, Voting Weights, and Federal Implications

The GST Council, constituted under Article 279A inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, is the apex federal body that determines tax rates, exemptions, threshold limits, and the model GST law. Its composition reflects the asymmetric federal design: the Union Finance Minister chairs the Council, the Union Minister of State (Finance) is a member, and each State nominates a Minister in charge of finance or taxation. The Council decides by a three‑fourths majority of the weighted votes cast, where the Centre holds one‑third of the total voting weight and the States collectively hold two‑thirds. Each State’s vote weight is proportional to its share of the total GST revenue base, ensuring that larger economies do not dominate smaller ones.

The Council’s mandate extends beyond rate‑setting. It recommends the principles of levy, the model GST legislation, the place of supply rules, and the mechanism for dispute resolution between the Centre and States. The Council also decides on the compensation cess and the methodology for the five‑year compensation guarantee to States, a provision that expired in June 2022 but continues to influence fiscal negotiations. Since its first meeting in September 2016, the Council has held over 50 meetings, with major decisions including the rationalisation of the 28% slab, the introduction of the composition scheme for small taxpayers, and the recent move to bring petroleum products and electricity under GST in a phased manner.

Judicial scrutiny of Council decisions remains limited but significant. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Council’s recommendations acquire the force of law only after they are notified by the Centre under Section 9 of the Central GST Act, and that the Council’s deliberative process is not subject to judicial review on merits. However, the Court affirmed that any recommendation violating the constitutional distribution of legislative competence can be struck down. The Council’s voting record is not publicly disclosed in full, but the minutes released after each meeting reveal the consensus‑building dynamics and occasional dissent, notably on the inclusion of real estate and the rate on lottery tickets.

The Council’s operation illustrates a cooperative federalism model where fiscal policy is co‑determined. Its decisions directly affect the revenue pool that the Finance Commission later distributes, creating a feedback loop between tax policy and revenue sharing. The 2023‑24 budget introduced a “GST Council Secretariat” to institutionalise research support, signalling a move toward evidence‑based rate calibration. Aspirants should note the interplay between Article 279A, the GST Acts, and the Finance Commission’s devolution formula, as examiners often frame questions around the “dual federalism” of tax legislation and revenue allocation.

State Election Commissions: Constitutional Mandate, Appointment Procedure, and Autonomy Challenges

Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution vest the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Panchayats and Municipalities in the State Election Commission (SEC). The SEC consists of a State Election Commissioner (SEC) appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Commissioner holds office for a term of five years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds prescribed for a Judge of a High Court — a safeguard intended to insulate the office from executive pressure.

Despite constitutional protection, the functional autonomy of SECs has been contested. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Kumar (2020), the Supreme Court held that the Governor’s pleasure doctrine does not apply to the removal of the SEC; the procedure under Article 243K(2) read with Article 311 must be followed. The Court also directed that the SEC’s conditions of service cannot be altered to the disadvantage of the incumbent after appointment. Several States, however, have enacted legislation that empowers the State Government to appoint the SEC on a part‑time basis or to designate a serving bureaucrat, diluting independence.

The SEC’s powers include delimitation of wards, preparation of electoral rolls, notification of election schedules, and the authority to disqualify candidates for corrupt practices under the respective State Panchayat Raj Acts. The Commission also enforces the Model Code of Conduct for local body elections, a power that mirrors the Election Commission of India’s role at the national level. Recent reforms in States such as Kerala and Karnataka have introduced online nomination filing and real‑time voter turnout dashboards, enhancing transparency.

A persistent challenge is the lack of a dedicated, independent secretariat. In many States, the SEC operates with staff on deputation from the State Government, creating a conflict of interest during election periods. The 2019 amendment to the Karnataka Panchayat Raj Act mandated a permanent secretariat headed by a Secretary‑level officer, a model cited by the Law Commission in its 255th Report as a best practice. Aspirants should be able to contrast the SEC’s constitutional design with that of the Election Commission of India, especially regarding appointment (President vs Governor), removal (impeachment vs High Court judge procedure), and the scope of judicial review.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The State Election Commissioner can be removed by the Governor at pleasure.” Identify the error and cite the constitutional provision that governs removal.
The statement is false. Article 243K(2) read with Article 311 provides that the State Election Commissioner shall not be removed except in the manner and on the grounds prescribed for a Judge of a High Court. The Governor’s pleasure doctrine does not apply; removal requires a proven misbehaviour or incapacity established through an inquiry, mirroring the safeguards for higher judiciary.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question compares the Election Commission of India and State Election Commissions, structure the answer in a three‑column table: Constitutional Article, Appointment Authority, Removal Procedure. This visual cue earns full marks for “compare and contrast” prompts and prevents omission of the High Court judge removal standard for SECs.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution, Criteria, and Inter‑State Equity

Article 280 mandates the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has risen steadily: the Tenth FC (1995‑2000) recommended 29.5 %, the Eleventh 30.5 %, the Twelfth 32 %, the Thirteenth 32 %, the Fourteenth 42 %, and the Fifteenth (2021‑26) 41 %. The jump to 42 % in the Fourteenth FC reflected the inclusion of the States’ share in the newly introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) and the abolition of the Planning Commission, which shifted plan‑grant resources to the FC.

The vertical formula is not a single arithmetic expression but a weighted composite of criteria. The Fifteenth FC assigned the following weights for vertical devolution: 15 % to population (2011 Census), 45 % to income distance (per capita GSDP gap), 10 % to forest and ecology, 12.5 % to demographic performance (fertility rate), and 17.5 % to tax effort. The use of the 2011 Census for population weight sparked controversy because several States argued it penalised those that had successfully controlled population growth. The Commission defended the choice by citing data availability and the need for a uniform base across all criteria.

Vertical devolution directly determines the size of the divisible pool. For 2023‑24, the Centre’s gross tax revenue was estimated at ₹33.6 lakh crore; after deducting collection costs and the GST compensation cess, the net proceeds available for sharing were approximately ₹27.8 lakh crore. Applying the 41 % vertical share yields roughly ₹11.4 lakh crore for States, which is then split horizontally. The FC also recommends grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) for revenue deficit, local bodies, and disaster relief, which are over and above the vertical share.

Judicial intervention in vertical devolution is rare. In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2019), the Supreme Court declined to entertain a challenge to the Fourteenth FC’s 42 % recommendation, holding that the FC’s recommendations are advisory and become binding only after Presidential acceptance. The Court emphasised that the FC’s methodology, provided it is rational and non‑arbitrary, falls within its constitutional domain. Aspirants should be prepared to discuss how the vertical share interacts with the GST Council’s rate decisions, as both bodies influence the revenue base that the FC distributes.

The Central Bureau of Investigation: Statutory Framework, Supreme Court Directives, and Reform Proposals

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) derives its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946. Section 3 empowers the Central Government to constitute a special police force for investigation of offences notified under Section 2, while Section 4(1) places the superintendence of the CBI with the Central Government. This executive superintendence has been the focal point of autonomy debates. The Supreme Court in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998) issued a series of directions — collectively known as the “Vineet Narain guidelines” — mandating a fixed two‑year tenure for the Director, selection by a high‑powered committee (Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, Chief Justice of India), and insulation from transfer without the committee’s consent.

The 2014 amendment to the DSPE Act institutionalised the selection committee and introduced a two‑year minimum tenure, but retained the Central Government’s power to extend or curtail tenure in “public interest”. In Alok Verma v. Union of India (2019), the Court quashed the Government’s midnight removal of the Director, reiterating that any premature removal must be approved by the selection committee. The judgment reinforced the principle that the CBI’s functional independence is a facet of the rule of law and the basic structure.

Despite these safeguards, structural issues persist. The CBI remains dependent on the Ministry of Personnel for budgetary allocations, infrastructure, and personnel on deputation. The absence of a dedicated, independent prosecution wing means that the agency often relies on the Central Government’s law officers, creating a perception of conflict of interest in politically sensitive cases. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, envisages the Lokpal’s supervisory role over the CBI for cases referred by it, but operationalisation has been slow.

Reform proposals by the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2007) and the Law Commission’s 243rd Report (2012) advocate a statutory CBI Act that would: (i) replace the DSPE Act, (ii) vest superintendence in an independent board comprising the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, Chief Justice, and two eminent jurists, (iii) guarantee a five‑year non‑renewable term for the Director, and (iv) create a separate prosecution directorate under the CBI. The 2021 “CBI (Amendment) Bill” introduced in Parliament incorporated some of these elements but lapsed. Aspirants should track the legislative trajectory and be able to articulate the tension between executive accountability and investigative autonomy, a recurring theme in GS‑II polity questions.

  • Assuming the GST Council’s decisions are immune from judicial review; the Supreme Court can strike down recommendations that exceed constitutional competence.
  • Believing the State Election Commissioner serves at the pleasure of the Governor; removal follows the High Court judge procedure under Article 243K(2).
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical share as a fixed constitutional percentage; it is a recommendation that changes each award period.
  • Thinking the CBI Director can be removed unilaterally by the Government; the Vineet Narain guidelines and the 2014 amendment require selection‑committee approval.
  • Overlooking the GST Council’s voting weight formula; the Centre holds one‑third and States two‑thirds, not equal votes.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution with horizontal devolution; vertical divides Union‑State pool, horizontal distributes among States.
  • Assuming the CBI’s budget is independently sanctioned; it is routed through the Ministry of Personnel, affecting functional autonomy.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and the Simultaneous Elections Debate

The Election Commission of India (ECI) derives its delimitation mandate from Articles 82 and 170 read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. After each Census the President constitutes a Delimitation Commission, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioners. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court except on grounds of mala fide or lack of jurisdiction. The last delimitation exercise, based on the 2001 Census, was completed in 2008; the next will follow the 2026 Census as mandated by the 84th Constitutional Amendment which froze the total number of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly seats until 2026.

Simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Assembly polls together — have been examined by the Law Commission (170th Report, 1999) and the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice (2015). The ECI has consistently highlighted operational advantages: reduced expenditure, minimised deployment of security forces, and continuity in governance. However, constitutional hurdles remain. Article 83(2) and Article 172(1) fix the five‑year term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies unless dissolved earlier. Synchronising terms would require either a constitutional amendment to allow premature dissolution or a political consensus to align election cycles, both of which raise federal‑balance concerns. The 2018 “One Nation, One Election” draft bill proposed a fixed five‑year cycle with a provision for mid‑term elections only on a vote of no‑confidence, but it lapsed with the dissolution of the 16th Lok Sabha.

Judicial pronouncements have reinforced the ECI’s autonomy in delimitation. The Supreme Court has held that the Delimitation Commission’s orders are final and binding, and that any challenge must demonstrate a clear violation of constitutional provisions. In practice, the ECI’s technical expertise in GIS‑based mapping and voter‑data analytics has become decisive in drawing constituency boundaries that satisfy the “as far as practicable” equality principle under Article 81(2)(b). Aspirants should be able to articulate the interplay between the freeze on seat numbers, the upcoming 2026 delimitation, and the political feasibility of simultaneous polls, as these themes frequently appear in GS‑II essay and case‑study questions.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Universities

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) exercises audit jurisdiction over “any body or authority substantially financed by the Union or a State” under Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. This provision extends CAG’s reach to autonomous institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology, Indian Institutes of Management, central universities, and a host of registered societies receiving recurring grants. The audit covers both financial regularity — verification of receipts, expenditure, and compliance with grant conditions — and performance audit, assessing whether objectives are achieved economically, efficiently, and effectively.

In the higher‑education sector, the University Grants Commission (UGC) Act, 1956, and the Central Universities Act, 2009, explicitly subject central universities to CAG audit. State universities, while primarily audited by State Accountants General, also fall under CAG’s purview when they receive central assistance under schemes like the Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (RUSA). The CAG’s 2021 performance audit of the “Implementation of the National Education Policy 2020 in Central Universities” highlighted gaps in faculty recruitment, infrastructure utilisation, and research output, prompting the Ministry of Education to issue revised monitoring guidelines.

A recurring legal issue is the scope of “substantial financing”. The Supreme Court, in a series of decisions, has held that receipt of more than 50 % of recurring expenditure from government sources constitutes substantial financing, thereby attracting CAG audit.
