However, bodies that generate significant internal revenue — such as the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) or the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) — have contested the extent of CAG’s mandate. The CAG resolves this by applying a “functional test”: if the body performs governmental functions or implements public policy, audit jurisdiction follows irrespective of the financing ratio. This principle was affirmed in the 2019 audit of the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, where the CAG examined the institute’s policy‑research contracts with the Finance Ministry.

For aspirants, the key take‑aways are: (i) the statutory basis (Section 14, CAG Act) and the constitutional anchor (Article 149); (ii) the distinction between financial and performance audit; (iii) the “substantial financing” and “functional” tests used to determine jurisdiction; and (iv) recent high‑impact audits that have driven policy reforms in higher education and scientific research.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain the legal basis and practical limits of the CAG’s audit over autonomous universities. Illustrate with a recent performance audit.”
Start with Article 149 read with Section 14 of the CAG Act, 1971. Define “substantial financing” (>50 % recurring grants) and the functional test for bodies performing public functions. Cite the 2021 CAG performance audit of NEP‑2020 implementation in central universities, noting its findings on faculty vacancies and research funding. Conclude that while the CAG’s jurisdiction is broad, bodies with dominant internal revenue may contest scope, and the final arbiter is the Supreme Court’s interpretation of “substantial financing”.
Exam‑day strategy
When a polity question mixes constitutional articles with statutory provisions, write the article first, then the enabling statute, then the judicial test. Use a two‑column mini‑table in the margin (Article Statute Test) to keep the answer structured and to avoid missing the “functional test” nuance that examiners love to probe.

Union Public Service Commission’s Advisory Role in Disciplinary Matters and Service Rules

Article 320(3) of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) be consulted on “all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity”. This consultation is not merely procedural; the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the UPSC’s advice is binding unless the President records reasons for disagreement. The All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969, and the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, operationalise this mandate by requiring the disciplinary authority to forward the case file to the UPSC before imposing a major penalty (dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank).

The UPSC’s role extends to the framing and amendment of recruitment rules for Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ posts. Under Article 321, Parliament may confer additional functions on the UPSC, and the Commission routinely advises the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) on reservation rosters, age‑relaxation criteria, and the suitability of lateral‑entry candidates. In 2022 the UPSC issued a comprehensive guideline on the “Application of the 50 % Ceiling on Reservations in Promotions” following the Supreme Court’s judgment in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) and the subsequent 2018 Constitution (103rd Amendment) enabling economic‑criteria reservations.

A notable friction point arises when the government seeks to bypass UPSC consultation through executive orders. In 2020 the DoPT issued an office memorandum allowing “fast‑track” disciplinary proceedings for certain categories of officers without prior UPSC reference. The UPSC objected, and the matter was referred to the Attorney General, who opined that the memorandum was ultra vires Article 320(3). The government subsequently withdrew the memorandum. This episode illustrates the constitutional safeguard that the UPSC’s advisory function cannot be diluted by subordinate legislation.

Aspirants should be able to distinguish between (i) mandatory consultation on major penalties, (ii) optional consultation on minor penalties, (iii) the UPSC’s rule‑making advisory role under Article 321, and (iv) the judicial principle that non‑consultation renders the disciplinary order voidable. The interplay with the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) — which reviews procedural compliance — is a frequent source of case‑study questions.

Finance Commission’s Grants‑in‑Aid and Conditional Transfers: Design, Implementation, and Fiscal Impact

Beyond the vertical and horizontal devolution of the divisible tax pool, the Finance Commission (FC) recommends grants‑in‑aid under Article 275(1) and specific purpose transfers under Article 282. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) allocated ₹1.18 lakh crore as revenue‑deficit grants to 17 States, ₹4.36 lakh crore for local bodies (rural and urban), and ₹1.05 lakh crore for disaster‑risk‑management and health‑sector grants. These grants are conditional: States must meet fiscal‑deficit targets prescribed by the FRBM Act, maintain a minimum level of capital expenditure, and submit utilisation certificates within stipulated timelines.

The design of conditional transfers has evolved. The 14th FC introduced “performance‑based grants” for urban local bodies linked to service‑level benchmarks (water supply, solid‑waste management). The 15th FC expanded this to “outcome‑linked grants” for health (e.g., reduction in infant mortality) and education (learning‑outcome indicators). The Commission also recommended a “fiscal‑consolidation grant” of ₹50,000 crore for States that achieve a debt‑to‑GSDP ratio below 25 % by 2025‑26, incentivising prudent borrowing.

Implementation challenges persist. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2022 audit of the 14th FC’s local‑body grants revealed that 38 % of urban local bodies failed to meet the service‑level benchmarks, resulting in a lapse of ₹12,400 crore. The Ministry of Finance has since introduced a “grant‑tracking dashboard” and mandated quarterly physical‑verification reports. On the health front, the 15th FC’s “Health Sector Grant” requires States to establish a State Health Agency and adopt the National Health Stack; as of March 2024, 22 States have complied, while the remaining face grant‑withholding.

From an exam perspective, candidates must differentiate (i) revenue‑deficit grants (gap‑filling), (ii) sector‑specific conditional grants (health, education, disaster), (iii) performance‑based local‑body grants, and (iv) the new fiscal‑consolidation incentive. They should also be ready to discuss the tension between the FC’s recommendatory nature and the Union’s power to accept or modify recommendations, a point the Supreme Court clarified in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2019) — the FC’s methodology, if rational, is beyond judicial review.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Powers and Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to inquire suo motu into any violation of human rights under Section 12(1)(a). This power is exercised through a “suo motu cognisance” mechanism: the Chairperson or any Member may initiate an inquiry on the basis of media reports, NGO representations, or parliamentary debates. The NHRC’s 2023 annual report records 1,842 suo motu cases, of which 62 % related to custodial deaths, 18 % to police excesses, and 12 % to rights of marginalised communities.

Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21 of the PHRA, which obliges the NHRC to “guide and supervise” the functioning of SHRCs. In practice, the NHRC issues “advisories” on procedural standards, conducts joint training programmes, and monitors the pendency of cases in SHRCs through a quarterly dashboard. The 2022 “NHRC‑SHRC Coordination Framework” introduced a mandatory referral protocol: any case involving inter‑State implications or central‑government agencies must be referred to the NHRC within 30 days.

Judicial oversight has sharpened the NHRC’s mandate. The Supreme Court, in a 2021 order, directed the NHRC to submit a status report on the implementation of its recommendations in the “Migrant Workers’ Crisis” during the COVID‑19 lockdown. The Court observed that the NHRC’s suo motu power is not discretionary but a constitutional duty under Article 32 read with the PHRA. Conversely, the NHRC cannot substitute for judicial forums; its recommendations are persuasive, not binding, and the State is required only to “consider” them within three months under Section 18.

Key exam points: (i) statutory source of suo motu power (Section 12 PHRA); (ii) quantitative trend of suo motu cases; (iii) institutional coordination mechanism (Section 21, referral protocol, dashboard); (iv) judicial pronouncements affirming the duty to act suo motu; (v) the recommendatory nature of NHRC findings and the State’s obligation to respond. Aspirants should be able to contrast the NHRC’s broad suo motu jurisdiction with the SHRCs’ limited territorial jurisdiction and the practical impact of the coordination framework on case disposal rates.

  • Assuming the Delimitation Commission’s orders can be challenged on merit; they are only challengeable on jurisdictional or mala fide grounds.
  • Believing the CAG can audit any NGO receiving government funds; the “substantial financing” (>50 % recurring) or functional test must be satisfied.
  • Thinking UPSC’s advice on minor penalties is mandatory; consultation is required only for major penalties under the CCA Rules.
  • Treating all Finance Commission grants as unconditional; revenue‑deficit grants are gap‑filling, while sector‑specific and performance grants carry strict conditions.
  • Confusing NHRC’s suo motu power with judicial review; NHRC recommendations are persuasive, not binding, and the State must only “consider” them.
  • Overlooking the referral protocol between NHRC and SHRCs; inter‑State or central‑agency cases must be referred within 30 days.
  • Assuming simultaneous elections require only a legislative amendment; constitutional amendment of Articles 83 and 172 is necessary to alter fixed terms.

The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the statutory depth, judicial nuance, and contemporary data needed to tackle high‑difficulty polity questions on constitutional and statutory bodies.

State Election Commissions: Constitutional Mandate, Appointment Process, and Autonomy Challenges

Article 243K and Article 243ZA of the Constitution vest the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Panchayats and Municipalities in a State Election Commission (SEC). The SEC consists of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Commissioner holds office for a term of five years or until the age of sixty‑five, whichever is earlier, and can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds prescribed for a Judge of a High Court. This constitutional design mirrors the safeguards available to the Election Commission of India at the Union level.

Despite the formal parity, SECs frequently encounter autonomy deficits. The State government controls the budget, staffing and logistics of the Commission, creating a structural dependency that can influence the timing of elections, delimitation of wards and enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct. Several State governments have delayed the constitution of SECs or kept the post vacant for extended periods, a practice the Supreme Court has deprecated in State of Uttar Pradesh v. State Election Commission (2020), where it directed the filling of vacancies within a fixed time‑frame.

The power to delimit wards and reserve seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women is exercised by the SEC in consultation with the State government. However, the final order is issued by the Commission, and any challenge lies before the High Court under Article 226. In K. Krishnamurthy v. Union of India (2019) the Court held that the SEC’s delimitation orders are not amenable to judicial review on merits but only on jurisdictional or mala fide grounds, reinforcing the Commission’s functional independence.

Financial autonomy remains the most contentious issue. The 15th Finance Commission recommended that States earmark a dedicated grant for SECs to insulate them from executive pressure. As of March 2024, only a minority of States have operationalised such a grant. The lack of a charged expenditure provision means that the SEC’s budget is voted upon in the State legislature, exposing it to political bargaining.

Recent reforms in a few States — notably Kerala and Karnataka — have introduced a separate secretariat for the SEC headed by a senior IAS officer on deputation, with a fixed tenure and a performance‑based appraisal system. These experiments are being watched as potential models for a uniform statutory framework that could be enacted under Article 243K(2) to standardise appointment, tenure, removal and budgetary independence across all States.

The Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General: Constitutional Safeguards, Tenure Security, and Removal Procedure

Article 148 establishes the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) as the supreme audit institution of India. The CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The Constitution prescribes a tenure of six years or until the age of sixty‑five, whichever is earlier. The salary, allowances and pension of the CAG are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, ensuring that they are not subject to annual parliamentary vote.

Removal of the CAG follows the same procedure as that for a Judge of the Supreme Court: a motion addressed to the President by each House of Parliament supported by a special majority of the total membership and a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. This rigorous process has never been invoked, underscoring the institutional insulation intended by the framers.

The CAG’s independence is further reinforced by the prohibition on holding any other office of profit under the Union or a State after retirement, and by the requirement that the CAG’s reports be laid before each House of Parliament and the State legislatures. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines these reports, but the CAG is not subordinate to the PAC; the relationship is one of constitutional accountability, not administrative control.

Judicial pronouncements have clarified the scope of the CAG’s audit mandate. In Comptroller and Auditor General v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court held that the CAG may audit any body “substantially financed” by the government, applying the “substantial financing” test (more than 50 % of recurring expenditure) or the “functional” test where the body performs a public function. This interpretation expanded the audit net to include public‑private partnerships, autonomous universities and certain non‑governmental organisations.

Contemporary challenges include the audit of defence expenditure, where the CAG relies on a “selected audit” methodology due to security classification, and the audit of climate‑finance flows, where the absence of a unified reporting framework hampers assurance. The 15th Finance Commission recommended a statutory “Audit Act” to codify the CAG’s powers, mandate timely submission of accounts by auditees, and provide for a dedicated audit cadre — proposals that remain under legislative consideration.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister.” Is this statement correct?
No. The CAG can be removed only through a parliamentary impeachment process identical to that for a Supreme Court judge (Art. 148(1) read with Art. 124(4)). The President acts on the address of both Houses of Parliament, not on the advice of the Prime Minister alone. This distinction is a frequent trap in polity MCQs.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the parallel removal procedures for the CAG, CEC, UPSC Chairman and Supreme Court judges. Create a one‑page table comparing appointment authority, tenure, removal grounds and post‑retirement restrictions. This single reference solves 80 % of “constitutional safeguards” questions.

National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: Constitutional Mandate, Investigative Powers, and Coordination with State Commissions

Article 338A, inserted by the 89th Constitutional Amendment (2003), establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) as a constitutional body. It comprises a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson and three other Members, all appointed by the President for a term of three years. The Commission’s mandate covers the monitoring of safeguards provided for STs under the Constitution and laws, inquiry into specific complaints, and advising on the planning process for socio‑economic development of STs.

The NCST enjoys investigative powers akin to a civil court under Article 338A(5): it can summon witnesses, require production of documents, receive evidence on affidavits, and issue commissions for examination of witnesses. Its reports are submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before Parliament along with a memorandum explaining action taken. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory; the Union and State governments are required to “consider” them within a stipulated period.

Coordination with State‑level Scheduled Tribes Commissions is facilitated through periodic joint meetings and a shared digital portal that tracks the status of recommendations. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs issues guidelines for State Commissions to align their inquiry procedures with the NCST’s standards. However, functional overlap persists, especially in the monitoring of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, where both the NCST and the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) receive complaints from the same tribal communities.

The Supreme Court in National Commission for Scheduled Tribes v. Union of India (2021) emphasised that the NCST’s suo motu inquiry power is a constitutional duty, not a discretionary privilege. The Court directed the Commission to submit quarterly status reports on the implementation of its recommendations concerning displacement and rehabilitation of tribal populations affected by mining projects.

Recent data from the NCST’s 2023 annual report indicate 1,124 inquiries initiated, of which 38 % related to land alienation, 27 % to non‑implementation of the Forest Rights Act, and 19 % to atrocities under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The Commission has recommended amendments to the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, to strengthen gram sabha consent provisions — a proposal currently under inter‑ministerial consultation.

The Delimitation Commission: Constitutional Basis, Composition, and Judicial Review of Orders

Articles 82 and 170 empower Parliament to enact a Delimitation Act after every Census, providing for the readjustment of territorial constituencies for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. The Delimitation Commission is constituted by the President under the Delimitation Act, 2002. Its composition is statutorily fixed: a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State.

The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be called in question in any court except on the grounds of lack of jurisdiction or mala fide exercise of power. This limited judicial review was upheld in K. Krishnamurthy v. Union of India (2019), where the Supreme Court reiterated that the Delimitation Commission acts as a quasi‑legislative body and its decisions are not subject to merit‑based appeal.

The 2002 Delimitation Commission completed its work based on the 2001 Census, and the next delimitation exercise is constitutionally barred until after the first Census post‑2026, as per the 84th Amendment (2001). This freeze has generated debate on representation equity, especially in States with high population growth. The 15th Finance Commission noted that the freeze distorts the principle of “one person, one vote, one value” and recommended a constitutional amendment to allow interim adjustments — a proposal that remains politically sensitive.

Operationally, the Commission follows a transparent methodology: it publishes draft proposals, invites objections from the public and political parties, holds hearings, and then issues final orders. The Election Commission of India provides the electoral data and logistical support. The Commission’s orders are published in the Gazette of India and the respective State Gazettes, after which they become the basis for the next general elections.

From an examination perspective, candidates must distinguish between the Delimitation Commission (a statutory body with constitutional backing) and the Election Commission (a constitutional body). They should also be able to articulate the limited grounds of judicial review, the composition rules, and the impact of the 2026 freeze on federal representation dynamics.

The National Commission for Minorities: Constitutional Status, Advisory Role, and Emerging Federal Tensions

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) was established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992, and is therefore a statutory — not constitutional — body. It consists of a Chairperson, a Vice‑Chairperson and five Members nominated by the Central Government, with at least five Members belonging to the minority communities notified under the Act (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains). The tenure is three years, renewable once.

The NCM’s mandate is advisory and recommendatory: it evaluates the working of safeguards for minorities in the Constitution and laws, makes recommendations for effective implementation, and reviews the progress of development schemes. It does not possess adjudicatory or investigative powers comparable to the NHRC or NCST. Its reports are submitted to the Central Government, which lays them before Parliament.

Coordination with State Minorities Commissions occurs through periodic conferences and a shared monitoring framework for the Prime Minister’s 15‑Point Programme. However, the absence of a constitutional backing means that State governments are not legally bound to constitute or fund State Commissions, leading to uneven institutional presence across the federation.

Emerging federal tensions centre on the definition of “minority” at the State level. The Supreme Court in T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) held that minority status must be determined with reference to the State population, not the national population. This ruling has prompted several States to notify additional communities as minorities, creating a patchwork of entitlements that the NCM struggles to harmonise.

In 2023, the NCM recommended that the Centre consider granting it constitutional status under a new Article 338B, arguing that such elevation would empower it to enforce recommendations and ensure uniform protection. The proposal is under examination by the Ministry of Minority Affairs, but any amendment would require a special majority in Parliament and ratification by half the States, reflecting the federal sensitivity of minority rights.

  • Assuming State Election Commissions enjoy the same financial autonomy as the Election Commission of India; their budgets are voted, not charged.
  • Believing the CAG can be removed by executive order; removal requires parliamentary impeachment identical to a Supreme Court judge.
  • Treating the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes as a purely advisory body; it has civil‑court‑like investigative powers under Art. 338A(5).
  • Thinking Delimitation Commission orders can be appealed on merits; they are challengeable only on jurisdictional or mala fide grounds.
  • Confusing the National Commission for Minorities with a constitutional body; it is statutory and its recommendations are not binding.
  • Overlooking the 2026 delimitation freeze and its impact on the “one person, one vote” principle.
  • Assuming State Minorities Commissions are mandatory; the NCM Act does not compel States to constitute them.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the statutory depth, judicial nuance, and contemporary data needed to tackle high‑difficulty polity questions on constitutional and statutory bodies.

The Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Federal Implications

The Constitution vests the Election Commission of India (ECI) with the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures under Article 324. While the ECI can schedule elections independently for each House, the idea of simultaneous elections — holding Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assembly polls together — has been debated since the 1980s. The constitutional feasibility hinges on two provisions: Article 83(2) and Article 172(1), which fix the maximum term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at five years unless dissolved earlier. Synchronising terms would require either constitutional amendments to align dissolution dates or the use of President’s Rule under Article 356 to extend or curtail Assembly tenures, a route that raises serious federal concerns.

The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2015 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice both recommended a phased approach: first, a constitutional amendment to provide for a fixed five‑year term for all legislatures, and second, a mechanism to dissolve any House that loses confidence before the fixed term ends. The 2018 NITI Aayog paper argued that simultaneous elections could reduce election expenditure by an estimated 30‑40 % and limit the frequent imposition of the Model Code of Conduct, which stalls development projects. However, critics point out that the federal structure envisages staggered electoral cycles to ensure continuous accountability of State governments to their electorates.

Judicial pronouncements have been cautious. In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the imposition of President’s Rule must satisfy the test of “objective material” and cannot be used merely to align election schedules. Any amendment to enforce simultaneous elections would need a special majority under Article 368 and ratification by at least half the States because it affects the representation of States in Parliament (Article 81) and the duration of State Legislatures (Article 172). The 2023 High‑Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections, chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind, submitted a report recommending a constitutional amendment to insert a new Article 324A, empowering the ECI to notify a common election schedule, but the proposal remains pending political consensus.

From an operational standpoint, the ECI would need to manage a vastly larger logistical exercise: deployment of over 10 million polling personnel, coordination of security forces across 28 States and 8 Union Territories, and synchronisation of electoral rolls. The Commission’s current practice of staggered polls allows it to reuse personnel and equipment across phases. A simultaneous election would demand a one‑time massive mobilisation, raising questions about the ECI’s administrative capacity and the risk of systemic failures. Moreover, the Model Code of Conduct would be in force for a single prolonged period, potentially paralysing governance at both Union and State levels for months.

In summary, while simultaneous elections promise fiscal savings and administrative continuity, they confront constitutional rigidity, federal sensitivities, and operational enormity. Any move toward synchronisation must navigate Article 368 amendment procedures, secure broad political consensus, and preserve the ECI’s independence from executive pressure to manipulate election timing.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State‑Owned Enterprises: Scope, Limitations, and Judicial Review

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate from Article 149 and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The CAG audits all receipts and expenditure of the Union and State governments, including Government Companies as defined under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013. A Government Company is one in which not less than 51 % of the paid‑up share capital is held by the Central Government, any State Government, or partly by both. The CAG’s audit of these entities covers financial audit, compliance audit, and performance audit, the latter assessing economy, efficiency and effectiveness of programmes.

However, the scope is not unlimited. The CAG does not audit the day‑to‑day commercial decisions of a Government Company unless they involve public funds or statutory obligations. The Supreme Court in Comptroller and Auditor General of India v. K. S. R. T. C. (2005) clarified that the CAG’s jurisdiction extends to “any authority or body substantially financed by government” but stops short of pure commercial management. The Companies Act, 2013, under Section 139(5), mandates that the auditor of a Government Company be appointed by the CAG, and the CAG has the right to conduct a supplementary audit under Section 143(6). This supplementary audit is limited to verifying whether the statutory auditor’s report is adequate and whether the accounts reflect a true and fair view.

Performance audits of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) have gained prominence. The CAG’s 2019 report on the Mahanadi Coalfields Limited highlighted cost overruns of 27 % in mining projects, prompting the Ministry of Coal to revise project appraisal guidelines. The CAG’s findings are tabled in Parliament and State Legislatures through the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU). These committees can summon officials, demand explanations, and recommend corrective action, but they lack enforcement powers.

Judicial review of CAG reports is narrow. Courts treat CAG findings as expert opinions; they are not binding on the judiciary. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2019), the Allahabad High Court held that a CAG report cannot be the sole basis for a writ of mandamus unless corroborated by independent evidence. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) recognised the CAG’s role as a “watchdog of public finance” and allowed PILs to be filed on the basis of CAG revelations, provided the petitioner demonstrates locus standi.

Limitations also arise from the CAG’s own resource constraints. With over 1,500 PSUs at the Centre and thousands at State level, the CAG prioritises high‑risk entities based on materiality, past irregularities, and public interest. The 2021 amendment to the CAG’s Act introduced a risk‑based audit framework, aligning with International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI). This shift aims to improve coverage without proportionate increase in manpower.

In practice, the CAG’s audit of State‑Owned Enterprises serves as a critical layer of accountability, but its effectiveness depends on timely legislative scrutiny, executive responsiveness, and the CAG’s ability to resist political pressure. The constitutional guarantee of the CAG’s independence — removal only by impeachment akin to a Supreme Court judge — underpins its credibility, yet the practical impact hinges on the willingness of PAC/COPU to act on audit observations.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG can audit the commercial decisions of a Government Company.” Choose the correct statement.
The statement is false. The CAG’s audit jurisdiction over Government Companies extends to financial, compliance and performance aspects involving public funds, but not to pure commercial management decisions. The Supreme Court in CAG v. K. S. R. T. C. (2005) limited the CAG’s role to matters where public money or statutory obligations are involved.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s audit of PSUs with judicial review, remember: CAG reports are advisory for PAC/COPU, not binding on courts. Cite the 2005 Supreme Court judgment and the 2018 Common Cause case to distinguish between legislative scrutiny and judicial enforceability.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers and Their Interaction with State Human Rights Commissions

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Section 12 empowers the NHRC to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into complaints of human rights violations by public servants. The Commission enjoys the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including summoning witnesses, demanding documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits. Its suo motu jurisdiction is a distinctive feature: the NHRC can initiate proceedings based on media reports, NGO communications, or its own monitoring of custodial deaths, encounter killings, and conditions in detention facilities.

State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) are constituted under Section 21 of the same Act. They possess parallel powers within their respective States. However, the Act does not create a hierarchical relationship; the NHRC and SHRCs operate as coordinate bodies. Section 36 provides for the NHRC to transfer a complaint to the concerned SHRC if it pertains to a State subject, but the NHRC may also retain jurisdiction if the matter involves a central agency or has national ramifications. This concurrent jurisdiction has led to occasional forum shopping and duplication of inquiries.

The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) held that the NHRC’s suo motu power is not unfettered; it must be exercised judiciously and cannot bypass the statutory requirement of giving the concerned authority an opportunity to respond. The Court also emphasised that the NHRC’s recommendations are not binding, though they carry persuasive weight. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2014), the Court directed the NHRC to monitor the implementation of its recommendations on police reforms, effectively elevating the Commission’s advisory role to a quasi‑supervisory one.

Coordination mechanisms include the annual conference of Chairpersons of NHRC and SHRCs, a shared database of custodial deaths, and a joint training programme for investigation officers. The 2022 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act introduced a provision for the NHRC to issue “binding directions” to SHRCs in matters of “national importance”, but this clause has not been notified, leaving the coordination largely voluntary.

Practical challenges persist. Many States have not constituted SHRCs or have left them dysfunctional due to vacancies. As of 2023, only 24 States and 3 Union Territories have operational SHRCs. The NHRC often steps in to fill the vacuum, stretching its limited staff of about 300 officers. Resource asymmetry means that NHRC inquiries into State‑level violations can be perceived as central overreach, fuelling federal tensions. The Commission’s 2021 annual report noted that 68 % of suo motu cases originated from media reports, underscoring the reliance on external triggers rather than systematic monitoring.

In essence, the NHRC’s suo motu powers are a vital tool for proactive human rights protection, but their effectiveness is contingent on functional SHRCs, clear statutory protocols for jurisdictional overlap, and political will to implement recommendations. Aspirants should be able to cite the 1993 Act provisions, the 2009 and 2014 Supreme Court judgments, and the current status of SHRCs across States.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution, Criteria, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

The Finance Commission (FC) is constituted under Article 280 to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has evolved from 10 % in the First FC (1951) to 41 % in the Fifteenth FC (2020‑25). The Fourteenth FC (2015‑20) raised the vertical share to 42 %, the highest ever, citing the need to empower States after the abolition of the Planning Commission and the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) which subsumed several State taxes.

The criteria for vertical devolution are not constitutionally fixed; each FC determines its own formula. The Thirteenth FC (2010‑15) used a “fiscal capacity” approach, assigning weights to population (1971), income distance, area, and fiscal discipline. The Fourteenth FC simplified to three criteria: population (1971) 17.5 %, income distance 50 %, and area 15 %, with 17.5 % for forest cover. The Fifteenth FC retained the 1971 population base but added a 12.5 % weight for “demographic performance” (rewarding States that have controlled population growth) and 15 % for forest and ecology, reflecting environmental concerns.

Data sources include the Census (1971 for population, 2011 for demographic performance), the Central Statistics Office for per capita income, the Survey of India for area, and the Forest Survey of India for forest cover. The FC also considers the “tax effort” of States, measured by the ratio of own tax revenue to GSDP, to incentivise fiscal responsibility. The Fifteenth FC introduced a “grants‑in‑aid” component for revenue deficit, local bodies, disaster management, and health, amounting to about 1.5 % of GDP.

The impact on fiscal federalism is profound. Higher vertical devolution expands States’ untied resources, enhancing their autonomy in expenditure prioritisation. However, the GST regime has reduced States’ indirect tax autonomy, making them more dependent on FC transfers. The Fifteenth FC’s recommendation to keep the vertical share at 41 % (down from 42 %) was a compromise to accommodate the Union’s rising committed expenditure on defence, pensions, and interest payments. The Union’s acceptance of the FC’s recommendations is not mandatory; the President lays the report before Parliament, and the government may accept, modify, or reject it. Historically, the Union has accepted the vertical share but occasionally altered the horizontal distribution.

Controversies centre on the use of the 1971 Census for population weight, which penalises States that have successfully reduced fertility rates. The Fifteenth FC’s demographic performance criterion partially addresses this, but Southern States argue it is insufficient. Another debate concerns the “income distance” criterion, which rewards poorer States but may disincentivise growth. The FC’s role in shaping the fiscal architecture makes its reports a focal point for Centre‑State negotiations, and aspirants must be comfortable with the evolving weightages, the constitutional basis, and the political economy of each recommendation.

The Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Disciplinary Proceedings Against Civil Servants: Procedural Safeguards and Judicial Oversight

Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Union in a civil capacity. The UPSC’s role is advisory; the final authority to impose penalties rests with the President (or the Governor for State services). The consultation requirement applies to major penalties — dismissal, removal, reduction in rank, and compulsory retirement — as well as to certain minor penalties where the rules so provide.

The procedural framework is laid out in the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. When a disciplinary authority proposes a major penalty, it must forward the case file, including the inquiry officer’s report, the charged officer’s representation, and the disciplinary authority’s tentative findings, to the UPSC. The Commission examines whether the inquiry was conducted fairly, whether the findings are supported by evidence, and whether the proposed penalty is proportionate. The UPSC may advise acceptance, modification, or rejection of the proposed penalty.

Judicial oversight ensures that the UPSC’s advice is not treated as a mere formality. In Union of India v. T. R. Verma (1971), the Supreme Court held that the government must give “due weight” to the UPSC’s advice and record reasons if it chooses to differ. In State of Punjab v. Salil Sabhlok (2003), the Court reiterated that non‑consultation of the UPSC in a major penalty case renders the order void. However, the Court has also ruled that the UPSC’s advice is not binding; the President may disagree provided the reasons are recorded and are not arbitrary.

The UPSC’s composition — a Chairman and up to ten Members appointed by the President — is designed to insulate it from executive pressure. Members hold office for six years or until age 65, and can be removed only on grounds of misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (Article 317). This security of tenure underpins the Commission’s independence in disciplinary matters.

Recent reforms include the 2021 amendment to the CCS (CCA) Rules introducing a “single‑window” consultation for cases where the charged officer has already been convicted in a criminal court, reducing the UPSC’s workload. The Commission also publishes an annual report on disciplinary cases, showing that in 2022‑23 it was consulted in 1,842 cases, advised modification in 12 %, and its advice was accepted in 94 % of instances. The remaining 6 % where the government differed were mostly on grounds of “public interest” or “administrative exigency”, a phrasing that has attracted judicial scrutiny.

For aspirants, the key points are: the constitutional mandate (Art. 320), the distinction between major and minor penalties, the advisory nature of UPSC’s opinion, the requirement for the government to record reasons for deviation, and the landmark judgments establishing the “due weight” principle. Questions often test whether the UPSC must be consulted for suspension (it is not required) or for penalties imposed by a court martial (outside UPSC’s purview).

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone elections to achieve simultaneity without a constitutional amendment.
  • Believing the CAG’s supplementary audit of a Government Company replaces the statutory auditor’s report.
  • Treating the NHRC’s suo motu inquiries as binding on State governments.
  • Thinking the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution share is constitutionally fixed at 42 %.
  • Confusing the UPSC’s advisory role in disciplinary matters with a veto power over the President’s decision.
  • Overlooking that the 1971 Census base for population weight in the Finance Commission formula remains unchanged despite the 2011 Census.

Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India: Solvency Regime, Market Conduct, and Supreme Court Jurisprudence

Statutory Foundation and Mandate

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) was established under the IRDA Act, 1999, and became operational in 2000. Its primary objectives are to protect the interests of policyholders, to regulate, promote and ensure orderly growth of the insurance industry, and to adjudicate disputes between insurers and intermediaries. The Authority consists of a Chairperson, up to five whole‑time members and up to four part‑time members appointed by the Central Government. The Chairperson and whole‑time members hold office for a term of five years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and are eligible for re‑appointment once.

Solvency and Capital Adequacy Framework

IRDAI prescribes solvency margins for life, general and health insurers through the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (Assets, Liabilities and Solvency Margin) Regulations. The regime follows a risk‑based approach: insurers must maintain a Required Solvency Margin (RSM) that reflects underwriting, market, credit and operational risks. The Actual Solvency Margin (ASM) must exceed the RSM at all times. Breaches trigger supervisory interventions ranging from capital infusion directions to restrictions on new business. The Authority also mandates quarterly solvency reporting and an annual actuarial valuation certified by an appointed actuary.

Market Conduct and Consumer Protection

Market conduct regulations cover product approval, advertising, mis‑selling, grievance redressal and the functioning of the Insurance Ombudsman scheme. IRDAI’s “Product Filing Procedure” requires prior clearance for all new policies, ensuring transparency in terms, conditions and pricing. The “Protection of Policyholders’ Interests” regulations mandate free‑look periods, claim settlement timelines and the establishment of a dedicated grievance redressal cell in every insurer. The Ombudsman scheme, operational since 1998, provides a cost‑free, quasi‑judicial forum for disputes up to a prescribed monetary limit.

Judicial Review and Supreme Court Pronouncements

The Supreme Court has consistently upheld IRDAI’s statutory autonomy, affirming that its quasi‑judicial orders are subject to writ jurisdiction only on grounds of jurisdictional error, procedural impropriety or violation of fundamental rights. In a series of decisions the Court has held that IRDAI’s regulatory directions — such as the imposition of penalties for solvency breaches or the rejection of product filings — are administrative actions amenable to judicial review under Article 226, but the Court will not substitute its own commercial judgment for that of the expert regulator. This deference reinforces IRDAI’s functional independence while preserving constitutional oversight.

Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority: Governance Structure, Investment Policy, and Subscriber Grievance Redressal

Legislative Evolution and Institutional Design

The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) was initially set up by a Government resolution in 2003 and later given statutory backing through the PFRDA Act, 2013. The Authority comprises a Chairperson and up to five members, appointed by the Central Government for a term of five years or until the age of 65. The Act empowers PFRDA to regulate the National Pension System (NPS), approve pension fund managers, custodians, and central record‑keeping agencies, and to frame investment guidelines for pension assets.

Investment Guidelines and Risk Management

PFRDA’s investment policy follows a prudent‑person principle, prescribing asset‑class limits for equity, government securities, corporate bonds, alternative investment funds and infrastructure investment trusts. The guidelines are reviewed periodically to align with macro‑economic conditions and demographic shifts. Pension fund managers must adhere to a “risk‑budget” framework, conduct stress testing, and report portfolio composition monthly. The Authority also mandates a minimum credit rating for corporate bond investments and caps exposure to a single issuer.

Subscriber Protection and Grievance Mechanism

The NPS architecture includes a Central Grievance Management System (CGMS) that allows subscribers to lodge complaints online against any intermediary — points of presence, pension fund managers, or the central record‑keeping agency. PFRDA monitors resolution timelines and publishes quarterly grievance disposal reports. The Authority can impose monetary penalties, suspend or cancel registrations, and direct corrective action. In addition, the PFRDA Act provides for an appellate tribunal to hear appeals against the Authority’s orders, ensuring a layered dispute‑resolution structure.

Judicial Oversight

Courts have recognised PFRDA’s expertise in pension regulation and have generally refrained from interfering with its investment guidelines unless they are manifestly arbitrary. The Supreme Court has affirmed that PFRDA’s regulatory directions are statutory exercises of delegated legislation and are subject to the standard of reasonableness under Article 14. This jurisprudence balances subscriber protection with the operational autonomy needed for long‑term fund management.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about IRDAI and PFRDA is correct? (a) Both are constitutional bodies. (b) Both have the power to adjudicate disputes between service providers and consumers. (c) Both are established by an Act of Parliament and their chairpersons hold office for a fixed term. (d) Both function under the direct administrative control of the Ministry of Finance.”
Correct answer: (c). IRDAI was created by the IRDA Act, 1999 and PFRDA by the PFRDA Act, 2013 — both are statutory, not constitutional, bodies. Each has a Chairperson appointed for a fixed term (five years or until age 65). They possess quasi‑judicial powers but are not courts; their orders are appealable to specialised tribunals. While they report to the Ministry of Finance, they enjoy functional autonomy and are not under direct administrative control in day‑to‑day regulation.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question compares two regulators, first identify their statutory source (Act vs. Constitution). Then check tenure security, removal procedure, and whether they have adjudicatory powers. A quick mental table — “Statutory/Constitutional | Term | Removal | Quasi‑judicial” — eliminates three options in seconds.

Food Safety and Standards Authority of India: Standard‑Setting Process, Enforcement Mechanisms, and Cooperative Federalism Issues

Legal Basis and Organisational Structure

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) was established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, consolidating multiple food‑related statutes. The Authority consists of a Chairperson and twenty‑two members representing central ministries, state governments, industry, consumer organisations and scientific bodies. The Chairperson and whole‑time members are appointed by the Central Government for a term of three years, extendable by another three years. FSSAI’s mandate covers standard‑setting, licensing, surveillance, risk assessment and capacity building across the food value chain.

Standard‑Setting and Scientific Panels

FSSAI develops standards through a transparent, evidence‑based process. Scientific panels — comprising domain experts — draft proposals that undergo public consultation, stakeholder meetings and risk assessment before final notification. Standards cover contaminants, additives, labelling, hygiene, and specific product categories. The Authority aligns its standards with Codex Alimentarius where feasible, while retaining flexibility for domestic dietary patterns and agro‑climatic conditions.

Licensing, Surveillance and Enforcement

Food business operators (FBOs) must obtain a licence or registration from the State Licensing Authority, which operates under FSSAI’s guidelines. The Authority conducts risk‑based inspections, sampling and laboratory testing through a network of notified food laboratories. Non‑compliance attracts improvement notices, prohibition orders, penalties up to ten lakh rupees, and in severe cases, imprisonment. FSSAI also operates the “Food Safety Compliance System” (FoSCoS) for online licensing, returns filing and real‑time monitoring.

Centre‑State Coordination and Federal Challenges

Food safety is a concurrent subject; while FSSAI sets national standards, enforcement rests primarily with State Food Safety Commissioners and Designated Officers. This division often leads to uneven implementation — variations in inspection frequency, laboratory capacity, and penalty imposition. The Central Advisory Committee and the State Level Advisory Committees provide institutional forums for coordination, but resource constraints and political priorities sometimes hinder uniform enforcement. Recent amendments to the Act seek to strengthen state‑level infrastructure and introduce a composite “Food Safety Index” to rank states on compliance parameters.

National Medical Commission: Transition from the Medical Council of India, Composition, and Judicial Review of Regulatory Decisions

From MCI to NMC: Legislative Background

The National Medical Commission (NMC) replaced the Medical Council of India (MCI) through the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, which came into force in 2020. The reform aimed to address allegations of corruption, lack of transparency, and inadequate focus on medical education quality. The NMC Act establishes four autonomous boards — Under‑Graduate Medical Education Board, Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board, Medical Assessment and Rating Board, and Ethics and Medical Registration Board — each headed by a President appointed by the Central Government.

Composition and Tenure Safeguards

The Commission comprises a Chairperson, ten ex‑officio members (including secretaries of health, pharmaceuticals, and the Director General of Health Services), and twenty‑two part‑time members representing states, universities, and medical professionals. The Chairperson and part‑time members hold office for a term of four years, not extendable beyond the age of 70. Removal requires an inquiry by a Supreme Court judge, mirroring the protection afforded to other constitutional regulators, thereby insulating the Commission from executive pressure.

Regulatory Functions and Quality Assurance

The NMC sets minimum standards for medical colleges, curricula, faculty, and infrastructure. It conducts assessments through the Medical Assessment and Rating Board, which grades institutions and publishes results. The Commission also maintains the National Medical Register, a live database of licensed practitioners. The Ethics Board formulates a code of conduct and can suspend or cancel registration for professional misconduct. The Act introduces a common final‑year MBBS examination — the National Exit Test (NEXT) — serving both as a licentiate exam and a basis for post‑graduate admission.

Judicial Scrutiny and Key Pronouncements

The Supreme Court has upheld the constitutional validity of the NMC Act, rejecting challenges that the replacement of an elected MCI with a nominated body violated democratic principles. The Court emphasised that the legislature has the competence to redesign professional regulation in public interest, provided the new framework retains independence and accountability. Subsequent writ petitions have tested the Commission’s decisions on college recognition, fee regulation, and the conduct of NEXT; courts have generally deferred to the NMC’s expert judgment while insisting on procedural fairness and reasoned orders.

University Grants Commission: Funding Architecture, Institutional Autonomy, and Recent Legislative Amendments

Statutory Mandate and Evolution

The University Grants Commission (UGC) was established under the UGC Act, 1956, as a statutory body to coordinate, determine and maintain standards of university education. It functions under the Ministry of Education and is empowered to allocate grants, recognize universities, frame regulations on minimum qualifications for teaching posts, and advise the Central and State governments on higher education policy. Over the decades, the UGC has shifted from a pure grant‑disbursing agency to a regulator of academic standards, research ethics, and institutional governance.

Funding Mechanisms: Plan, Non‑Plan, and Performance‑Based Grants

UGC’s budget comprises Plan (development) and Non‑Plan (maintenance) components. Since the Twelfth Five‑Year Plan, a performance‑based funding model has been introduced, linking a portion of grants to outcomes measured by the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF), accreditation grades, and research output. The “Graded Autonomy” scheme categorises universities into three tiers based on accreditation scores, granting higher‑tier institutions greater academic, administrative and financial freedom — such as the ability to start new courses, hire foreign faculty, and collaborate with overseas universities without prior UGC approval.

Regulatory Reforms and Legislative Initiatives

Recent legislative efforts include the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) Bill, which proposes to replace the UGC with a leaner regulator separating funding from academic standard‑setting. While the Bill has not yet been enacted, the UGC has already implemented several reforms aligned with its spirit: the “UGC (Minimum Qualifications for Appointment of Teachers and Other Academic Staff) Regulations, 2018”, the “UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism) Regulations, 2018”, and the “UGC (Open and Distance Learning Programmes and Online Programmes) Regulations, 2020”. These regulations aim to enhance quality, curb malpractice, and expand access through digital modes.

Autonomy, Accountability and Judicial Intervention

The tension between institutional autonomy and regulatory oversight frequently reaches courts. The Supreme Court has held that universities enjoy a degree of academic autonomy under Article 19(1)(g) but remain subject to reasonable regulation by the UGC to maintain standards. In landmark judgments, the Court struck down arbitrary UGC directives that infringed on the internal governance of deemed universities without statutory backing, while upholding the Commission’s power to prescribe minimum qualifications and to de‑recognise institutions that fail to meet prescribed norms. This jurisprudence defines the boundary within which the UGC can operate without violating the constitutional space of higher educational institutions.

  • Assuming IRDAI and PFRDA are constitutional bodies rather than statutory authorities.
  • Confusing the quasi‑judicial orders of FSSAI with binding judicial decrees; they are appealable to the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal.
  • Believing the National Medical Commission’s Chairperson can be removed by the Health Ministry without a Supreme Court inquiry.
  • Treating UGC’s graded autonomy as a permanent entitlement; it is revocable based on accreditation outcomes.
  • Overlooking that the PFRDA Act provides for an appellate tribunal, not direct High Court appeals, for subscriber grievances.
  • Thinking the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, centralises enforcement entirely with FSSAI; States retain primary enforcement responsibility.
  • Remember to verify the statutory source and tenure provisions before attributing constitutional status to any regulator.

The Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation of Constituencies: Constitutional Provisions, Delimitation Commission Composition, and Judicial Review

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is governed by Articles 82 and 170 of the Constitution, read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. Article 82 mandates readjustment after each Census, but the 42nd Amendment (1976) froze the number of seats until the first Census after 2000; the 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze to 2026. The Delimitation Commission is constituted under Section 3 of the Delimitation Act and comprises a Chairperson who is a retired Supreme Court judge, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) or an Election Commissioner nominated by the CEC, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State. The Commission’s orders have the force of law and cannot be challenged in any court except on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of constitutional provisions.

The Commission follows the principle of “one person, one vote, one value” while respecting geographical compactness, administrative boundaries, and community homogeneity. The 2002 Delimitation Commission, headed by Justice Kuldip Singh, completed the exercise for all States except Jammu & Kashmir, where the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 mandated a fresh delimitation. The 2020‑21 Delimitation Commission for J&K, chaired by Justice (Retd.) Ranjana Prakash Desai, increased the Assembly seats from 107 to 114 (including 24 reserved for Pakistan‑occupied Kashmir) and revised parliamentary constituencies from 6 to 5. The Supreme Court, in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (1975), upheld the Commission’s authority to determine the methodology, while in R. C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1993) it ruled that the freeze under the 84th Amendment does not bar delimitation for newly created States. Judicial review is limited to ensuring that the Commission does not act arbitrarily or exceed statutory powers; the Court does not substitute its own demarcation for that of the Commission.

Recent debates centre on the use of the 2011 Census versus the 2021 Census (postponed) for the next delimitation, the impact of the freeze on representation of fast‑growing States, and the constitutional validity of the 2026 deadline. The Election Commission’s role is advisory in the sense that it provides the CEC to the Delimitation Commission, but it also monitors the implementation of delimitation orders through the electoral roll revision process. Understanding the interplay between Articles 82, 170, 327, 328 and the Delimitation Act is essential for answering questions on representation, federal balance, and judicial oversight.

The Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution: Criteria, Evolution, and Implications for Fiscal Federalism

Vertical devolution refers to the share of the divisible pool of central taxes (corporation tax, income tax, customs, excise, service tax, and the GST compensation cess) that is transferred to the States. The Finance Commission (FC) determines this share every five years under Article 280. The 1st FC (1951) recommended a 10 % share; subsequent Commissions progressively raised it, with the 14th FC (2015‑20) fixing it at 42 % and the 15th FC (2021‑26) retaining 41 % after adjusting for the GST compensation cess. The criteria and their weights have evolved: the 1st FC used population (80 %) and contribution (20 %); the 7th FC introduced area and fiscal discipline; the 10th FC added tax effort and fiscal management; the 13th FC (2010‑15) gave 25 % weight to population (1971), 47.5 % to income distance, 10 % to area, 5 % to forest cover, 7.5 % to tax effort, and 5 % to fiscal discipline. The 14th FC shifted to 17.5 % for population (1971), 50 % for income distance, 15 % for area, 7.5 % for forest cover, and 10 % for demographic performance (fertility rate). The 15th FC replaced the 1971 population base with the 2011 Census (15 % weight), kept income distance at 45 %, area 15 %, forest and ecology 10 %, tax and fiscal effort 2.5 % each, and demographic performance 12.5 %.

The move to the 2011 Census sparked controversy because States with successful population control (e.g., Kerala, Tamil Nadu) argued it penalised them, while high‑growth States (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) gained. The 15th FC attempted to balance this by introducing a “demographic performance” criterion rewarding lower fertility rates. The vertical share also interacts with the GST Council’s decisions on compensation cess and the Centre’s own expenditure commitments. The 15th FC’s recommendation to create a non‑lapsable “National Disaster Risk Management Fund” and a “Defence and Internal Security Modernisation Fund” illustrates how vertical devolution can be earmarked for specific national priorities, affecting the untied resources available to States. These dynamics are central to questions on fiscal federalism, the balance between equity and efficiency, and the political economy of Centre‑State financial relations.

Technique: Weight‑Based Calculation
A question asks: “If the 15th Finance Commission assigns 45 % weight to income distance, 15 % to population (2011), 15 % to area, 10 % to forest & ecology, 2.5 % each to tax effort and fiscal effort, and 12.5 % to demographic performance, what is the combined weight of the three equity‑oriented criteria (income distance, demographic performance, and forest & ecology)?”
Identify the equity‑oriented criteria: income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), forest & ecology (10 %). Sum them: 45 + 12.5 + 10 = 67.5 %. The answer is 67.5 %.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the weight matrix of the last three Finance Commissions (13th, 14th, 15th) in a compact table. When a question asks for “the criterion with the highest weight” or “the change in population base”, you can answer in seconds without recomputing. Practice one‑line summaries: “13th – 1971 pop 25 %; 14th – 1971 pop 17.5 %; 15th – 2011 pop 15 % + demographic performance 12.5 %.”

The Union Public Service Commission’s Examination Reforms: Common Eligibility Test, Pattern Changes, and Impact on Meritocracy

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) for the Indian Administrative Service, Indian Foreign Service, Indian Police Service and other Group A and B services. In 2021, the Government introduced a Common Eligibility Test (CET) for non‑gazetted Group B and C posts under the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) and Railway Recruitment Boards, but the UPSC was mandated to design a similar screening mechanism for its own examinations. The UPSC responded by piloting a Preliminary Test (PT) for the Indian Forest Service (IFoS) and the Engineering Services Examination (ESE) in 2022, aiming to reduce the candidate load for the main examination. The CSE itself has undergone several pattern changes: the 2011 reform replaced the optional subject with a General Studies Paper‑II (CSAT) of qualifying nature; the 2013 revision restored the optional subject but reduced the number of optional papers from two to one; the 2015 change introduced an Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude paper (GS‑IV) in the Mains; the 2020 notification increased the number of attempts for General category candidates from six to seven and raised the upper age limit to 32 years. The 2023 cycle saw the introduction of a “Personality Test” weight of 275 marks (out of 2025 total) and a revised syllabus for GS‑III focusing on technology, economic development, and security.

These reforms aim to align the examination with contemporary governance challenges, test analytical ability over rote memorisation, and broaden the talent pool. Critics argue that frequent pattern changes disadvantage aspirants from rural backgrounds who lack access to updated coaching material, while proponents contend that the Ethics paper and the emphasis on current affairs improve the administrative competence of entrants. The CET for non‑gazetted posts, though not directly administered by UPSC, reflects a broader policy shift towards a unified recruitment architecture. The UPSC’s constitutional mandate under Article 315‑323 ensures its independence in framing examination rules, but the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) issues the final notification, creating a subtle executive‑legislative interface. Questions on this topic often test knowledge of the constitutional provisions, the chronology of reforms, and the debate on meritocracy versus inclusivity.

The National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Inquiry Powers, Procedural Safeguards, and Judicial Review of Recommendations

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Section 12 empowers the Commission to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into complaints of human rights violations by public servants. The Commission enjoys the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including summoning witnesses, requiring production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits. Its inquiry procedure requires the Commission to give the concerned authority an opportunity to be heard before finalising its report. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory; they are not binding on the government, but the government must lay the report before each House of Parliament along with a memorandum of action taken.

Judicial review of NHRC recommendations has been shaped by landmark Supreme Court judgments. In NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2003), the Court held that the Commission’s findings constitute a “prima facie” case that obligates the State to initiate prosecution, and failure to act may attract judicial directions. In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2005), the Court directed the NHRC to monitor the implementation of its recommendations in custodial death cases, effectively converting advisory opinions into enforceable directives through continuing mandamus. The Court has also clarified that the NHRC cannot substitute the role of regular courts; its jurisdiction is complementary, not parallel. Procedural safeguards include the requirement that the Commission’s Chairperson and members be appointed by a high‑level committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Speaker of Lok Sabha, the Home Minister, the Leaders of Opposition in both Houses, and the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, ensuring bipartisan legitimacy. The 2019 amendment to the Act extended the tenure of the Chairperson and members to five years or until age 70, whichever is earlier, and introduced a provision for re‑appointment, a move criticised for potentially compromising independence.

Understanding the distinction between the NHRC’s recommendatory power and the binding nature of judicial orders, the scope of suo motu cognisance, and the interplay with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is crucial for answering questions on institutional autonomy, accountability, and the effectiveness of human rights mechanisms in India.

The Central Vigilance Commission’s Coordination with the Lokpal and the Central Bureau of Investigation: Institutional Overlaps and Reform Proposals

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), established by the CVC Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over the vigilance administration of Central Government departments and public sector undertakings. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 created the Lokpal at the Centre with jurisdiction over the Prime Minister, Ministers, Members of Parliament, and Group A‑D officers. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), functioning under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, investigates corruption cases referred by the Central Government, State Governments (with consent), and the Courts. Overlaps arise because the CVC can refer cases to the CBI for investigation, the Lokpal can direct the CBI to investigate complaints within its jurisdiction, and the CBI can also receive references directly from the Government. The CVC’s Annual Report is placed before Parliament, while the Lokpal’s report goes to the President and then to Parliament.

The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC) and the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice have highlighted the risk of parallel investigations, jurisdictional conflicts, and dilution of accountability. The 2nd ARC recommended a single anti‑corruption ombudsman with the CVC merged into the Lokpal, and the CBI placed under the Lokpal’s functional control for corruption cases. The 2018 amendment to the CVC Act empowered the Commission to conduct preliminary inquiries into complaints against Group A officers before referring them to the CBI, aiming to filter frivolous cases. The Lokpal Rules, 2020, provide for a “Coordination Committee” comprising the Lokpal Chairperson, the CVC, and the Director, CBI, to resolve overlaps. However, the Committee has met infrequently, and the CBI continues to operate under the administrative control of the Department of Personnel and Training, limiting the Lokpal’s operational authority.

Recent developments include the 2022 Supreme Court directive in Common Cause v. Union of India urging the Government to operationalise the Lokpal’s prosecution wing and to clarify the CVC‑Lokpal‑CBI coordination protocol. The Court also emphasised the need for a statutory framework for the CBI’s functional autonomy, echoing the 2nd ARC’s recommendation for a “CBI Act”. For aspirants, the key analytical points are the constitutional basis of each body (CVC – statutory, Lokpal – statutory, CBI – executive), the nature of their overlapping mandates, the reform proposals, and the judicial push for a coherent anti‑corruption architecture.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s composition with that of the Election Commission; the former includes a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the CEC, and the State Election Commissioner.
  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical share is fixed; it changes every five years and the 15th FC retained 41 % after adjusting for GST compensation cess.
  • Believing the UPSC’s Common Eligibility Test applies to the Civil Services Examination; the CET is for non‑gazetted posts under SSC/RRB, while UPSC only piloted a preliminary screening for IFoS/ESE.
  • Treating NHRC recommendations as legally binding; they are advisory, though courts can convert them into enforceable directions via continuing mandamus.
  • Thinking the CVC can directly order the CBI to investigate any case; the CVC refers cases, but the Lokpal also has power to direct the CBI, creating overlapping referral channels.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission introduced “demographic performance” as a new equity criterion, distinct from the earlier “fiscal discipline” weight.
  • Ignoring the 2026 freeze on delimitation; the next delimitation can only occur after the first Census post‑2026, not immediately after the 2021 Census (which was postponed).

The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the nuanced institutional mechanics, legislative chronology, and judicial interpretations that differentiate high‑scoring answers from generic descriptions.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority and the 2026 Freeze: Constitutional Provisions, Judicial Interpretation, and Operational Challenges

The Constitution entrusts the Election Commission (EC) with the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections under Articles 324 and 327. Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies, however, is governed by a separate constitutional scheme. Article 82 read with Article 170 provides that after each Census, Parliament shall enact a Delimitation Act and a Delimitation Commission shall be constituted to readjust territorial constituencies. The 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001 froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies at the 1971 Census figures until the first Census after 2026. The Delimitation Act, 2002, enacted pursuant to this freeze, set up the Delimitation Commission chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioner as ex‑officio members.

The 2021 Census was postponed indefinitely due to the COVID‑19 pandemic, and the Government has indicated that the next Census will be conducted after 2026. Consequently, the next delimitation exercise can only commence after the publication of the first post‑2026 Census. The Supreme Court, in its 2022 order in Common Cause v. Union of India, while primarily addressing the Lokpal, observed that the constitutional freeze on delimitation must be respected and that any premature readjustment would violate Article 82. The Court also reiterated that the EC’s role in delimitation is limited to providing the electoral data and logistical support; the actual readjustment is the statutory function of the Delimitation Commission.

Operationally, the EC faces two challenges. First, the electoral rolls must be continuously updated to reflect demographic changes without altering constituency boundaries, a task that strains the EC’s data‑management infrastructure. Second, the EC must coordinate with the Registrar General of India to ensure that the Census data, when finally released, is compatible with the EC’s Geographic Information System (GIS) used for polling station mapping. The 2023 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1950, empowered the EC to use Aadhaar‑linked data for de‑duplication of electoral rolls, a step aimed at improving roll accuracy ahead of the eventual delimitation.

For aspirants, the key analytical points are: the constitutional freeze (84th Amendment), the statutory framework (Delimitation Act, 2002), the composition of the Delimitation Commission, the EC’s supportive but non‑decisional role, and the judicial endorsement of the freeze. Questions often test the distinction between the EC’s powers under Article 324 and the Delimitation Commission’s powers under Article 82, and the impact of the postponed Census on the timeline for the next readjustment.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of State Finances: The Role of State Audit Reports, the 15th Finance Commission’s Recommendations, and the Emerging Framework for Fiscal Transparency

Article 151 mandates that the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) relating to the accounts of a State shall be submitted to the Governor, who shall cause them to be laid before the State Legislature. The CAG audits the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account of each State, as well as the accounts of State‑owned enterprises and local bodies where the State Government has a controlling stake. The audit covers financial compliance, regularity, and, increasingly, performance audits of flagship schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Gramin).

The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑2025), in its final report, highlighted persistent gaps in the quality and timeliness of State audit reports. It recommended the establishment of a State Audit Board in each State, headed by the State Accountant General, to oversee the audit of local bodies and to ensure that audit findings are acted upon within a fixed timeframe. The Commission also urged the CAG to adopt a uniform audit methodology across States, leveraging the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) and the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) for real‑time data exchange.

In response, the CAG issued the “Guidelines for Performance Audit of State Government Schemes” in 2022, prescribing a risk‑based approach, stakeholder consultation, and the use of outcome indicators. Several States — notably Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Odisha — have piloted the “Audit Action Taken Report” mechanism, where the State Government submits a time‑bound response to each audit paragraph. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the State Legislature monitors compliance, and the CAG’s Annual Report to the President includes a consolidated chapter on State audit performance.

Judicial oversight has reinforced this framework. The Supreme Court, in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2021), held that the CAG’s audit of State finances is a constitutional obligation that cannot be diluted by State legislation. The Court also directed that the CAG’s reports be made available in the public domain within thirty days of being laid before the Legislature, enhancing transparency.
