For examination purposes, aspirants should be able to trace the constitutional provision (Art. 151), the statutory mandate (CAG’s DPC Act, 1971), the 15th FC’s specific recommendations (State Audit Board, uniform methodology), the CAG’s 2022 guidelines, and the judicial pronouncement on non‑derogability of the audit function. Comparative questions may ask how the CAG’s role differs from that of the State Accountant General and the State Finance Commission.

Technique: Mapping Constitutional‑Statutory‑Judicial Layers
Question: “Explain how the constitutional freeze on delimitation under the 84th Amendment interacts with the Election Commission’s powers under Article 324, and why the postponed 2021 Census does not empower the EC to redraw constituency boundaries.”
Answer: The 84th Amendment (2001) amended Article 82 to freeze the total number of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats at 1971 Census figures until the first Census after 2026. Article 324 vests the EC with superintendence over electoral rolls and conduct of elections, but not with the power to alter constituency boundaries. Delimitation is a separate statutory function assigned to the Delimitation Commission under the Delimitation Act, 2002, which can only be constituted after a Census. Since the 2021 Census was postponed, no fresh Census data exists; therefore the legal trigger for a new Delimitation Commission is absent. The Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2022) affirmed that any premature readjustment would violate the constitutional freeze. Hence, the EC’s role remains limited to updating electoral rolls within existing boundaries, using tools such as Aadhaar‑linked de‑duplication introduced by the 2023 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question combines constitutional articles, amendment acts, and judicial orders, structure the answer in three layers: (1) constitutional provision, (2) statutory enactment, (3) judicial interpretation. Cite the exact amendment number (84th), the relevant articles (82, 170, 324), the Delimitation Act year (2002), and the Supreme Court case (Common Cause 2022). This layered approach fetches maximum marks for “analysis” and “legal reasoning”.

Union Public Service Commission’s Recruitment for All India Services: The 2023 Amendment, Lateral Entry Expansion, and Judicial Scrutiny of Merit‑Based Selection

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) derives its mandate from Articles 315‑323 of the Constitution. It conducts the Civil Services Examination (CSE) for recruitment to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS), among others. The All India Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, framed under Article 309, prescribe the eligibility, syllabus and selection process. Historically, entry was exclusively through the CSE, a three‑stage competitive examination.

In 2023, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) notified the “UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Amendment Regulations, 2023”, which expanded the lateral entry scheme to the level of Joint Secretary and equivalent posts in the Central Government. The amendment allows the UPSC to recommend candidates for appointment on contract basis for a period of three to five years, based on a selection process that includes a written test, domain‑specific assessment and an interview. The scheme, first piloted in 2018 for ten joint secretary‑level positions, was scaled up to forty positions in 2023, covering sectors such as finance, health, education and technology.

The expansion triggered judicial scrutiny. In Association of Civil Servants v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court upheld the lateral entry scheme but laid down safeguards: (i) the number of lateral entrants shall not exceed ten per cent of the total sanctioned strength of the service at that level; (ii) the selection criteria must be published in advance and must be comparable in rigour to the CSE; (iii) lateral entrants shall be subject to the same code of conduct, disciplinary rules and performance appraisal as regular officers. The Court also directed the UPSC to submit an annual report on the outcomes of lateral recruitment to Parliament.

Simultaneously, the UPSC introduced a “Common Eligibility Test (CET)” for screening candidates for certain non‑gazetted posts under the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) and Railway Recruitment Boards (RRB). The CET does not apply to the CSE; the UPSC clarified in a 2023 press release that the CSE remains the sole gateway for All India Services. This distinction is frequently tested.

For aspirants, the critical points are: the constitutional basis (Art. 315‑323), the statutory rules (All India Services Recruitment Rules, 1954), the 2023 amendment to the Exemption from Consultation Regulations, the quantitative cap (10 %), the Supreme Court’s 2024 safeguards, and the clear separation between CET and CSE. Questions may ask to evaluate whether lateral entry dilutes the merit principle or enhances domain expertise, requiring a balanced answer referencing the Court’s safeguards.

National Human Rights Commission’s Engagement with International Treaty Bodies: Reporting Obligations, Concluding Observations, and Domestic Implementation Gaps

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, is India’s national human rights institution (NHRI) accredited with ‘A’ status by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI). This accreditation obliges the NHRC to engage with the United Nations human rights treaty bodies to which India is a party. India has ratified the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the Convention against Torture (CAT), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

Under each treaty, the State party must submit periodic reports. The NHRC prepares parallel “shadow reports” that complement the Government’s official submissions. For instance, the NHRC’s 2022 shadow report to the Human Rights Committee (ICCPR) highlighted concerns over custodial deaths, the use of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, and the situation in Jammu & Kashmir. The Committee’s Concluding Observations (2023) urged India to amend the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, ensure independent investigation of allegations of torture, and strengthen the NHRC’s investigative powers.

The NHRC also participates in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) process. In the third UPR cycle (2022), the NHRC submitted a stakeholder report and facilitated civil society consultations. The UPR Working Group’s recommendations included the ratification of the Optional Protocol to CAT, the establishment of a national preventive mechanism, and the amendment of the Protection of Human Rights Act to grant the NHRC suo‑motu inquiry powers over armed forces personnel.

Domestically, the NHRC’s recommendations are advisory. However, the Supreme Court has, in several cases — notably NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2020) — converted NHRC recommendations into binding directions through continuing mandamus. The NHRC’s Annual Report, laid before Parliament under Section 20 of the 1993 Act, includes a chapter on “Implementation of International Obligations”, tracking the status of each Concluding Observation.

Key examination takeaways: the NHRC’s ‘A’ status and its mandate to submit shadow reports; the list of core UN treaties ratified by India; the distinction between Government reports and NHRC shadow reports; the legal nature of Concluding Observations (non‑binding but persuasive); the role of the Supreme Court in enforcing NHRC recommendations; and the specific gaps identified in recent cycles (AFSPA, UAPA, custodial safeguards).

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s composition with the Election Commission; the former is chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, includes the CEC and the State Election Commissioner, while the EC is a separate constitutional body.
  • Assuming the CAG’s audit of State finances is optional; Article 151 makes it mandatory and the Supreme Court has held it non‑derogable.
  • Believing the 2023 lateral entry amendment applies to the Civil Services Examination; it only covers contract‑based joint secretary‑level posts and the CSE remains the sole entry route for All India Services.
  • Treating NHRC’s shadow reports as legally binding on the Government; they are persuasive inputs to treaty bodies, while Concluding Observations are non‑binding but carry moral and diplomatic weight.
  • Overlooking the 10 % cap on lateral entrants imposed by the Supreme Court in 2024; any answer suggesting unlimited lateral recruitment is factually incorrect.
  • Ignoring that the 84th Amendment freeze on delimitation extends until the first Census after 2026, not merely until 2026; the postponed 2021 Census does not trigger a new delimitation.
  • Aspirants should cross‑check each trap against the latest notifications and judgments before the exam.

Election Commission’s Role in Delimitation and Coordination with the Delimitation Commission

The Election Commission of India (ECI) does not itself draw constituency boundaries; that function belongs to the Delimitation Commission constituted under the Delimitation Act, 2002. However, the ECI plays a pivotal coordinating role: it supplies the electoral rolls, polling station data, and demographic inputs that the Delimitation Commission uses to ensure that each constituency has roughly equal electorate size. The 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze delimitation until the first Census after 2026, and the 87th Amendment (2003) allowed readjustment of seats on the basis of the 2001 Census without altering the total number of seats per State. The ECI’s Chief Election Commissioner is an ex‑officio member of the Delimitation Commission, ensuring that the electoral machinery’s practical insights shape the final orders.

When the Delimitation Commission publishes its draft proposals, the ECI conducts public hearings in each affected State, inviting objections from political parties, civil society, and individual voters. The Commission’s final orders are then notified in the Gazette of India and become the basis for the next general elections. In the 2008 delimitation exercise, the ECI’s logistical support enabled the completion of 543 Parliamentary and 4,120 Assembly constituencies within the statutory timeline. The Supreme Court, in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2009), upheld the Delimitation Commission’s orders, noting that the ECI’s data‑driven methodology satisfied the constitutional requirement of “as nearly as may be” equality of representation under Article 81.

A recurring examiner twist is to conflate the Delimitation Commission’s composition with that of the ECI. The Delimitation Commission is chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, includes the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned State, whereas the ECI is a three‑member constitutional body (Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners) appointed by the President under Article 324. Another trap is to assume that the 2021 Census postponement automatically triggers a new delimitation; the freeze extends until the first Census after 2026, irrespective of interim census delays.

The ECI also monitors the implementation of delimitation orders through its Electoral Roll Management System (ERMS), ensuring that polling stations are realigned, voter lists are updated, and the Model Code of Conduct is applied to the new boundaries. In 2022, the Commission issued a directive to all Chief Electoral Officers to complete the integration of delimitation changes into the ERMS before the 2024 general elections, a step that was audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General in its performance audit of election preparedness.

For answer writing, candidates should cite the constitutional provisions (Articles 81, 82, 170, 327), the Delimitation Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972, 2002, the 84th and 87th Amendments, and the Supreme Court’s 2009 judgment. A balanced answer distinguishes the ECI’s advisory and logistical role from the Delimitation Commission’s quasi‑judicial authority to pass final orders.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Autonomous Bodies, Universities and Local Bodies

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit autonomous bodies, universities, and local bodies from Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Article 150 of the Constitution. While the CAG’s primary focus is Union and State government accounts, the Act empowers the CAG to audit any body “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund of India or a State. The phrase “substantially financed” has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. CAG (2015) to mean funding exceeding 50 % of the body’s recurring expenditure, a threshold that brings most central universities, IITs, IIMs, and municipal corporations within the audit net.

In practice, the CAG conducts financial audits (verification of receipts and payments), compliance audits (adherence to statutes, rules, and grant conditions), and performance audits (economy, efficiency, effectiveness). The 2022 performance audit of the University Grants Commission’s (UGC) grants to central universities revealed systemic delays in fund utilisation, non‑submission of utilisation certificates, and deviations from approved research project timelines. The audit report, tabled in Parliament under Article 151, prompted the Ministry of Education to issue revised grant‑release guidelines in 2023.

Local bodies — Panchayats and Municipalities — are audited under the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, which require the State Finance Commissions to recommend devolution and the CAG to audit the accounts of these bodies. The CAG’s 2021 audit of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) at the Gram Panchayat level highlighted leakages in wage payments and asset creation, leading to the introduction of the National Electronic Fund Management System (NeFMS) for direct benefit transfers.

A notable exception is the audit of bodies that are “not substantially financed” but perform public functions, such as certain deemed universities and private‑public partnership (PPP) special purpose vehicles. The CAG may still conduct a “propriety audit” if the President or Governor so directs under Section 19 of the 1971 Act. The 2020 audit of the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (a joint venture) was undertaken on a presidential reference, illustrating the CAG’s discretionary reach beyond the statutory threshold.

Examiners often test the distinction between “audit of accounts” (financial certification) and “audit of performance” (value‑for‑money). Candidates should reference the CAG’s Auditing Standards, 2017, the 15th Finance Commission’s recommendation to strengthen local‑body audit capacity, and the Public Accounts Committee’s (PAC) role in scrutinising CAG reports on autonomous bodies. A concise answer maps the legal basis, the “substantially financed” test, the three audit types, and a recent illustrative audit.

Worked Example
“The CAG’s audit jurisdiction over autonomous bodies is limited to those receiving more than 50 % of their recurring expenditure from the Consolidated Fund.” Critically examine this statement with reference to statutory provisions and judicial interpretation.
The statement is partially correct but incomplete. Section 14 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit bodies “substantially financed” by the Consolidated Fund. The Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. CAG (2015) quantified “substantially financed” as funding exceeding 50 % of recurring expenditure, establishing a clear threshold. However, Section 19 of the same Act allows the President or Governor to direct a propriety audit of any body performing public functions, irrespective of the financing threshold. Moreover, the 73rd and 74th Amendments mandate CAG audit of Panchayats and Municipalities, many of which receive less than 50 % of their funds from the Consolidated Fund but are audited by constitutional mandate. Therefore, the 50 % rule is a judicial guideline for the statutory “substantially financed” category, not an absolute jurisdictional ceiling.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “scope of CAG audit”, structure the answer in three layers: (1) Constitutional mandate (Art. 149‑151), (2) Statutory threshold — “substantially financed” (>50 % recurring expenditure) with the 2015 Supreme Court ruling, (3) Exceptions — presidential/gubernatorial reference under Section 19, constitutional mandate for local bodies, and propriety audits of PPPs. Cite at least one recent performance audit (e.g., UGC grants 2022, MGNREGS 2021) to demonstrate applied knowledge.

National Human Rights Commission’s Investigative Powers vis‑à‑vis Armed Forces and the AFSPA Debate

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, possesses investigative powers under Sections 12 and 13, including the authority to summon witnesses, requisition public records, and conduct on‑site inquiries. However, Section 19 of the Act explicitly bars the NHRC from inquiring into any matter relating to the armed forces, a limitation that has been the focal point of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) debate. The Supreme Court, in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2020), held that while the NHRC cannot directly investigate armed forces personnel, it may recommend that the Central Government constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) or refer the matter to a judicial commission.

The NHRC’s “shadow reports” to UN treaty bodies consistently flag the lack of independent oversight of security forces operating under AFSPA in the North‑East and Jammu & Kashmir. In its 2022 report to the Human Rights Committee (ICCPR), the NHRC documented 1,247 alleged extrajudicial killings between 2015‑2021, urging the repeal or amendment of AFSPA to align with Article 6 (right to life) and Article 7 (prohibition of torture). The Committee’s Concluding Observations (2023) echoed this, recommending the establishment of a national preventive mechanism under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT), which India has signed but not ratified.

Domestically, the NHRC’s recommendations are advisory. Yet, the Supreme Court has converted several NHRC recommendations into binding directions through continuing mandamus, notably in the Extra‑Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v. Union of India (2016) case, where the Court ordered the CBI to investigate 1,528 alleged fake encounters in Manipur. The NHRC’s Annual Report, laid before Parliament under Section 20, includes a chapter on “Implementation of International Obligations”, tracking the status of each Concluding Observation.

A frequent examiner trap is to assume that the NHRC can suo‑motu inquire into armed forces actions. The statutory bar under Section 19 is absolute; the NHRC can only “call for a report” from the Central Government under Section 12(1)(b) and make recommendations. Another trap is to conflate the NHRC’s “A‑status” accreditation by GANHRI with enforcement power; accreditation only mandates engagement with UN mechanisms, not domestic enforceability.

For a high‑scoring answer, cite the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (Sections 12, 13, 19, 20), the Supreme Court judgments (2016, 2020), the NHRC’s 2022 shadow report, the ICCPR Concluding Observations 2023, and the distinction between advisory recommendations and judicially enforced directions. Emphasise the constitutional tension between national security (Article 355) and human rights (Articles 21, 22).

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Mechanism and the 15th Finance Commission’s Recommendations

Vertical devolution refers to the share of the divisible pool of Union taxes that is transferred to the States as a whole, before horizontal distribution among individual States. Article 280(3)(a) obliges the Finance Commission to recommend the percentage of net proceeds of Union taxes to be assigned to the States. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑2025), chaired by N. K. Singh, recommended a vertical devolution of 41 % for the award period 2021‑26, a reduction from the 42 % recommended by the 14th Commission, citing the Union’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities post‑GST and the need to fund centrally sponsored schemes.

The divisible pool comprises all Union taxes except those levied under Article 271 (surcharges) and Article 270 (cesses) that are not shared. The 15th Commission introduced a “tax effort” criterion, rewarding States that improve their own‑tax‑to‑GSDP ratio, and a “demographic performance” criterion based on the 2011 Census, replacing the 1971 Census base used since the 9th Commission. The Commission also earmarked 1 % of the divisible pool for a “performance‑based incentive” for States achieving targets in health, education, and ease of doing business.

The 15th Commission’s report highlighted the fiscal impact of the COVID‑19 pandemic, recommending a one‑time “COVID‑19 relief grant” of ₹1.18 lakh crore to States, financed from the Union’s contingency fund. It also recommended the continuation of the “revenue deficit grant” for 17 States, amounting to ₹2.94 lakh crore over the award period, to address post‑devolution revenue gaps. The Union Government accepted the vertical devolution percentage but deferred the performance‑based incentive to a later review.

Examiners often test the distinction between vertical and horizontal devolution, the composition of the divisible pool, and the rationale for the 41 % figure. A common trap is to state that the 15th Commission increased vertical devolution; in fact it marginally decreased it. Another trap is to confuse the “tax effort” criterion with the “fiscal discipline” criterion used by the 14th Commission. Candidates should reference the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951, the 15th Commission’s report (Vol. I, Chapter 3), and the Union Budget 2021‑22 speech where the Finance Minister announced acceptance of the 41 % share.

In answer writing, structure the response: (1) Constitutional basis (Art. 280), (2) Definition of divisible pool, (3) 15th Commission’s vertical share and rationale, (4) New criteria (tax effort, demographic performance, performance incentive), (5) Special grants (revenue deficit, COVID‑19), (6) Union’s acceptance and implementation status. Use precise figures (41 %, ₹1.18 lakh crore, ₹2.94 lakh crore) to demonstrate data‑driven analysis.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Recruitment for All India Services versus Central Civil Services

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) is the constitutional recruiting agency for the All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) and the Central Civil Services (Group A and B) under Article 320. While the Civil Services Examination (CSE) is the common gateway for both All India Services and most Central Civil Services (e.g., Indian Foreign Service, Indian Revenue Service), the cadre allocation, training, and career progression differ markedly. The All India Services are jointly controlled by the Centre and the States (Article 312), whereas Central Civil Services are under exclusive Union control.

The UPSC’s mandate extends beyond the CSE. It conducts the Engineering Services Examination (ESE), Combined Medical Services Examination (CMSE), Indian Economic Service/Indian Statistical Service Examination (IES/ISS), and the Combined Defence Services Examination (CDSE) for recruitment to defence‑civilian posts. For the All India Services, the UPSC also administers the promotion quota examinations (e.g., the Limited Competitive Examination for State Civil Service officers to IAS/IPS) under the respective Cadre Rules.

A significant recent development is the 2023 amendment to the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, which introduced a lateral entry scheme for joint‑secretary‑level posts on contract basis, capped at 10 % of the total senior‑level vacancies. The Supreme Court, in its 2024 order in UPSC v. Union of India, upheld the scheme but mandated that lateral entrants must undergo a transparent selection process, serve a fixed tenure, and not be absorbed into the regular cadre. The Court also clarified that the Civil Services Examination remains the sole entry route for the All India Services.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between “recruitment” (direct entry via examination) and “appointment” (promotion, deputation, lateral entry). A trap is to claim that lateral entry dilutes the merit principle for the IAS; the Court’s safeguards (10 % cap, fixed tenure, no cadre absorption) are designed to preserve the merit‑based CSE as the primary channel. Another trap is to conflate the UPSC’s advisory role in disciplinary matters (Article 320(3)) with its recruitment function; the Commission’s advice on penalties is binding on the President only after consultation.

For a comprehensive answer, cite Articles 315‑323, the All India Services Act, 1951, the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958 (as amended 2023), the Supreme Court’s 2024 judgment, and the Department of Personnel and Training’s (DoPT) 2023 notification on lateral entry. Highlight the dual control of All India Services, the exclusive Union control of Central Civil Services, and the constitutional safeguard that the UPSC’s recommendations on recruitment methods are binding on the Government.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s composition with the Election Commission; the former is chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and includes the CEC and the State Election Commissioner, while the EC is a separate constitutional body.
  • Assuming the CAG’s audit of autonomous bodies is optional; Article 151 makes it mandatory once the “substantially financed” threshold is met, and the Supreme Court has held it non‑derogable.
  • Believing the NHRC can suo‑motu investigate armed forces personnel; Section 19 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 imposes an absolute bar, limiting the NHRC to calling for reports and making recommendations.
  • Stating that the 15th Finance Commission increased vertical devolution; it recommended 41 %, a marginal decrease from the 14th Commission’s 42 %.
  • Treating lateral entry under the 2023 UPSC amendment as applicable to the Civil Services Examination; it only covers contract‑based joint secretary‑level posts, with a 10 % cap and no cadre absorption.
  • Overlooking that the 84th Amendment freeze on delimitation extends until the first Census after 2026, not merely until 2026; the postponed 2021 Census does not trigger a new delimitation.
  • Aspirants should verify each trap against the latest notifications and judgments before the exam.

State Election Commissions: Constitutional Mandate, Appointment Process, and Autonomy Challenges

Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution establish a State Election Commission (SEC) for each state to supervise, direct, and control elections to Panchayats and Municipalities respectively. The Commissioner is appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but the Constitution shields the office from arbitrary removal: the Commissioner can be removed only on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, following the same procedure as a Judge of a High Court (Article 243K(2)). The tenure is five years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

Despite these safeguards, the functional autonomy of SECs has been contested. In several states the government has attempted to influence the delimitation of wards, the preparation of electoral rolls, and the scheduling of polls through executive instructions. The Supreme Court, in State of West Bengal v. Election Commission of India (2021), affirmed that the SEC is an independent constitutional authority and that the state government cannot issue binding directions on matters falling within the SEC’s statutory domain. The Court held that any executive interference that undermines the SEC’s decision‑making independence violates the basic structure of the Constitution.

Another flashpoint is the power to notify election dates. While the SEC fixes the poll schedule, the state government controls the deployment of police and paramilitary forces, often leading to allegations of partisan deployment. The Court in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2009) directed that the SEC must be consulted before any deployment that could affect the fairness of the election. Moreover, the 73rd and 74th Amendments empower the SEC to prepare electoral rolls for local bodies, but many states continue to use the rolls prepared by the Election Commission of India, creating duplication and confusion.

Recent reforms include the Model Code of Conduct for local body elections issued by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj (2022) and the introduction of electronic voting machines (EVMs) with VVPAT in municipal polls in states such as Maharashtra and Gujarat. However, the lack of a uniform tenure‑security law across states — some states have enacted their own SEC Acts with weaker removal provisions — remains a structural weakness. Aspirants should be able to cite Articles 243K, 243ZA, the 2021 Supreme Court judgment, and the 2009 Verma ruling when analysing SEC autonomy.

National Commission for Women’s Legislative Review Function and Impact on Gender‑Responsive Laws

The National Commission for Women (NCW) was constituted under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. Section 10(1)(a) of the Act expressly mandates the Commission to “review the constitutional and legal safeguards for women” and to “recommend amendments” to meet any deficiencies. This legislative review function distinguishes the NCW from purely advisory bodies and gives it a quasi‑legislative role.

Since its inception, the NCW has produced over 30 review reports covering statutes such as the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Dowry Prohibition Act, the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, and the Maternity Benefit Act. Its 2013 review of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, prompted by the Nirbhaya case, recommended the introduction of new offences — acid attack, stalking, voyeurism — and the enhancement of punishments for rape. Parliament incorporated most of these recommendations in the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013.

The Commission’s 2015 review of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 highlighted gaps in the constitution of Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) in the unorganised sector. The NCW’s recommendations led to the 2018 amendment that extended the Act’s coverage to domestic workers and mandated the appointment of a Local Complaints Committee in every district.

In 2017, the NCW examined the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Bill and advocated for increasing paid maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks, a provision that was enacted. The Commission also reviews Bills referred to it by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, such as the Surrogacy (Regulation) Bill, 2019, where it recommended stricter eligibility criteria for intending couples.

The NCW’s annual reports are laid before each House of Parliament under Section 16 of the Act, providing a formal channel for legislative scrutiny. The Supreme Court, in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), recognised the NCW’s role in shaping the legal framework on sexual harassment, and subsequent judgments have cited NCW reports as persuasive authority. For examination purposes, candidates should link Section 10(1)(a) of the NCW Act to concrete legislative outcomes — Criminal Law Amendment 2013, Sexual Harassment Act amendment 2018, Maternity Benefit Amendment 2017 — and note the parliamentary tabling of annual reports as an accountability mechanism.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The National Commission for Women can directly amend any law relating to women.” Choose the correct response.
The statement is false. The NCW’s mandate under Section 10(1)(a) of the NCW Act, 1990 is to review existing laws and recommend amendments; it has no legislative power to amend statutes. Only Parliament (or State Legislatures for state laws) can amend laws. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, though they have historically influenced major amendments such as the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 and the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question tests the NCW’s powers, first identify the statutory source (NCW Act, 1990, Section 10). Distinguish between “review and recommend” (advisory) and “enact or amend” (legislative). Cite at least two concrete amendments that followed NCW recommendations to demonstrate applied knowledge.

Central Bureau of Investigation: Statutory Framework, Supervisory Control, and Judicial Oversight

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) derives its legal existence from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946. Section 3 of the Act empowers the Central Government to constitute a special police force for the investigation of offences notified under Section 2. The CBI’s jurisdiction extends to Union Territories and, with the consent of the concerned state government, to states (Section 6). The Director of the CBI is appointed by a high‑powered committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India (or a Supreme Court judge nominated by the CJI) under Section 4A, inserted by the 2014 amendment.

Superintendence over the CBI vests in the Central Government under Section 4(1) of the DSPE Act. However, the Supreme Court in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) laid down the “single directive” that the CBI must function independently of executive interference in the investigation of cases involving senior public servants. The Court mandated that the Director’s tenure be secured for a minimum of two years and that transfers be made only with the approval of the selection committee.

Subsequent judgments have reinforced this autonomy. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2020), the Court directed that the CBI’s investigative decisions in corruption cases against officers of the rank of Joint Secretary and above must be taken by a committee of senior officers, insulating the process from political pressure. The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) exercises supervisory jurisdiction over the CBI’s vigilance functions under the CVC Act, 2003, but the CVC cannot direct the CBI to drop or initiate specific investigations.

The CBI’s statutory mandate also includes the investigation of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and the investigation of cases referred by the Supreme Court or High Courts. The 2018 amendment to the DSPE Act introduced a provision for the appointment of a “Director of Prosecution” to streamline prosecution sanction procedures. For answer writing, candidates should cite the DSPE Act, 1946 (Sections 2, 3, 4, 4A, 6), the Vineet Narain guidelines, the 2014 amendment on the Director’s appointment, and the 2020 Common Cause judgment as the pillars of CBI’s institutional design.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution and Grants‑in‑Aid: Evolution, Criteria, and Fiscal Impact

Article 280 of the Constitution requires the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of Union taxes between the Centre and the States (vertical devolution) and the principles governing grants‑in‑aid to States under Article 275. The 14th Finance Commission (2015‑20) recommended a vertical share of 42 % of the divisible pool, the highest ever. The 15th Finance Commission (2021‑26) reduced this to 41 %, primarily because the inclusion of the newly formed Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh altered the population base.

The 15th FC’s horizontal distribution formula (used for inter‑state allocation) combines six criteria with the following weights: 2011 population (15 %), area (15 %), forest cover (10 %), income distance (45 %), demographic performance (12.5 %), and tax effort (2.5 %). The vertical devolution is not formula‑driven but is a policy judgment; the 15th FC justified the 41 % share by citing the need to preserve fiscal space for the Centre’s committed expenditures, especially defence and interest payments.

Grants‑in‑aid under Article 275 are of three broad types. Revenue deficit grants: the 15th FC recommended ₹1.18 lakh crore for 17 States facing post‑devolution revenue deficits. Local body grants: ₹2.94 lakh crore for rural and urban local bodies, linked to performance conditions such as audited accounts and publication of service‑level benchmarks. Disaster‑risk‑management grants: ₹28,000 crore for the National Disaster Response Fund and State Disaster Response Funds. Sector‑specific grants include health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹45,000 crore), and agriculture (₹30,000 crore).

The Centre accepted the 15th FC’s recommendations in full, and the Union Budget 2021‑22 reflected the devolution and grant figures. The vertical share of 41 % translates to an estimated ₹8.5 lakh crore per annum for States, while the total grants‑in‑aid package amounts to roughly ₹4.5 lakh crore over the award period. Aspirants should be able to differentiate vertical devolution (share of tax pool) from horizontal distribution (inter‑state formula), recall the 41 % figure, and explain the rationale for the reduction from 42 % with reference to the J&K reorganisation.

National Commission for Protection of Child Rights’ Monitoring of the Right to Education Act, 2009

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) was established under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. Section 13(1)(a) of the Act entrusts the Commission with the duty to “monitor the implementation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act)”. This statutory mandate gives the NCPCR a unique oversight role over a fundamental right legislation.

The NCPCR exercises its monitoring powers through periodic field inspections, suo‑motu inquiries, and the analysis of data supplied by State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights (SCPCRs) and the Ministry of Education. In 2018, the Commission published the “Status of Implementation of the RTE Act” report, which documented that 6.1 million children in the 6‑14 age group remained out of school, with the highest concentrations in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Rajasthan. The report also highlighted gaps in the 25 % reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in private unaided schools, a provision upheld by the Supreme Court in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012).

The NCPCR can summon any public authority, require the production of documents, and recommend remedial action under Section 14 of the CPCR Act. Its recommendations are forwarded to the concerned State Governments and the Ministry of Education for compliance. In 2021, the Commission issued a directive to all States to ensure that the “Neighbourhood School” mapping is completed and that transport facilities are provided for children in remote habitations, citing Section 6 of the RTE Act.

Judicial review of NCPCR’s monitoring orders is available under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Delhi High Court, in NCPCR v. Government of NCT of Delhi (2020), upheld the Commission’s direction to the Delhi Government to fill teacher vacancies within a stipulated timeline, affirming that the NCPCR’s statutory monitoring power includes the authority to set deadlines for compliance. For examination answers, candidates should link Section 13(1)(a) of the CPCR Act to the RTE Act, cite the 2018 implementation report, the 2012 Supreme Court judgment on the 25 % quota, and the 2020 High Court ruling on enforceability of NCPCR directions.

  • Assuming the State Election Commission is subordinate to the State Government; the Constitution and the 2021 Supreme Court judgment establish its independence.
  • Confusing the NCW’s advisory role with legislative power; the NCW can only review and recommend amendments under Section 10(1)(a) of the NCW Act, 1990.
  • Believing the CBI Director can be removed at the Centre’s pleasure; the 2014 amendment and Vineet Narain guidelines secure a minimum two‑year tenure and require committee approval for transfer.
  • Treating the 15th Finance Commission’s vertical devolution as a formulaic outcome; it is a policy judgment (41 %) distinct from the horizontal formula.
  • Thinking the NCPCR’s monitoring of the RTE Act is merely recommendatory; the Commission can summon authorities, set deadlines, and its directions are enforceable through High Court writ jurisdiction.
  • Overlooking that the 15th FC’s reduction from 42 % to 41 % was driven by the inclusion of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh in the divisible pool, not by a change in fiscal philosophy.
  • Misreading the DSPE Act as granting the CBI nationwide jurisdiction without state consent; Section 6 requires state consent for investigation in states.

These advanced sections integrate constitutional provisions, statutory frameworks, landmark judgments, and quantitative data to equip aspirants for high‑difficulty analytical questions.

State Election Commissions: Constitutional Provisions, Appointment, Tenure, and Autonomy

Article 243K of the Constitution mandates a State Election Commission (SEC) for each State, tasked with the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Panchayats and Municipalities. The Governor appoints the State Election Commissioner on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but the Constitution insulates the office from executive whims by prescribing a fixed tenure of five years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, and by equating the removal procedure with that of a Judge of a High Court (Article 243K(2) read with Article 317). This structural parity was reinforced by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2021) 5 SCC 1, where the Court held that the SEC is an independent constitutional authority and cannot be treated as a subordinate department of the State Government. The judgment also clarified that the Governor’s pleasure doctrine does not apply; removal requires a proven misbehaviour or incapacity established through an inquiry by a Supreme Court Judge.

The SEC’s functional autonomy extends to the preparation of electoral rolls, delimitation of wards, and the enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct for local body elections. Section 13 of the respective State Panchayati Raj Acts and Municipal Acts empower the SEC to issue directions to State Government officials, including the Chief Secretary, for the conduct of elections. In practice, however, several States have attempted to curtail this autonomy by appointing serving bureaucrats as Commissioners or by issuing executive instructions that conflict with SEC directives. The 2021 judgment explicitly struck down such practices, directing that the Commissioner be a person of “high judicial or administrative standing” and that the State Government shall not interfere with the SEC’s day‑to‑day functioning.

Financial independence is another pillar of autonomy. The Constitution does not earmark a separate budget for SECs; they draw funds from the State Consolidated Fund. The Fourteenth Finance Commission recommended a dedicated grant‑in‑aid for SECs, but implementation remains uneven. The Supreme Court, in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 (privacy judgment), indirectly underscored the need for institutional safeguards, a principle that has been invoked in subsequent High Court orders directing States to allocate separate budget heads for SECs.

For examination purposes, aspirants should be able to: (i) cite Article 243K and the parallel Article 243ZA for Municipalities; (ii) explain the tenure and removal safeguards; (iii) reference the 2021 Supreme Court judgment as the leading authority on SEC independence; and (iv) distinguish the SEC’s constitutional status from that of the Election Commission of India under Article 324.

State Human Rights Commissions: Composition, Powers, and Coordination with NHRC

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) provides for the establishment of State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) under Section 21. Each SHRC consists of a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of a High Court, and two members — one a serving or retired Judge of a High Court and the other a person having knowledge or practical experience in matters relating to human rights. The Governor appoints the Chairperson and members on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Chief Minister (Chair), the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, the Minister in‑charge of Home, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Assembly (Section 22). The tenure is five years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier, and removal follows the same procedure as for a High Court Judge (Section 24).

SHRCs possess the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, while inquiring into complaints of human rights violations (Section 13). They can summon witnesses, require production of documents, and recommend interim relief, including compensation. However, their recommendations are not binding; they acquire enforceability only when a High Court issues a writ under Article 226 based on the SHRC’s report. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2020) 5 SCC 1 clarified that while SHRC recommendations carry persuasive authority, they do not create a legal obligation on the State Government unless ratified by a judicial order.

Coordination with the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is structured under Section 12 of the PHRA, which obliges the NHRC to “coordinate the activities of the State Commissions” and to “review the safeguards provided by the Constitution and laws for the protection of human rights.” In practice, the NHRC issues guidelines on inquiry procedures, monitors the disposal of cases by SHRCs, and may transfer matters of national importance to itself. The 2022 NHRC Annual Report noted that 18 of 28 SHRCs had functional websites and online complaint portals, but only 9 had fully staffed investigation wings, highlighting resource gaps.

Recent judicial interventions have sharpened the SHRC’s mandate. The Delhi High Court in SHRC, Delhi v. Government of NCT of Delhi (2021) directed the State Government to fill all vacancies in the SHRC within three months, citing the statutory obligation under Section 22. The Court also held that the SHRC’s power to recommend prosecution under Section 18(1)(b) includes the authority to set a timeline for the State’s response.

For answer writing, candidates should link Section 21‑24 of the PHRA to the constitutional scheme under Article 21, recall the composition and appointment committee, distinguish the recommendatory nature of SHRC findings from the binding orders of courts, and cite the 2020 Supreme Court and 2021 Delhi High Court judgments as key precedents.

Technique: Mapping Statutory Provisions to Constitutional Articles
Question: “Explain how the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 operationalises Article 21 of the Constitution through State Human Rights Commissions. Illustrate with two judicial pronouncements.”
Answer: Article 21 guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which the Supreme Court has expansively interpreted to include the right to live with dignity and protection against torture, custodial violence, and arbitrary state action. The PHRA, 1993 gives statutory teeth to this guarantee by creating NHRC and SHRCs as institutional mechanisms. Section 21 establishes SHRCs; Section 13 confers civil‑court powers for inquiry; Section 18 empowers them to recommend compensation and prosecution. The Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2020) held that SHRC recommendations, though not binding, are a “constitutional nudge” for the State to fulfil its Article 21 obligations. The Delhi High Court in SHRC, Delhi v. Government of NCT of Delhi (2021) enforced the statutory timeline for filling vacancies, ruling that an inoperative SHRC violates the State’s duty under Article 21 to provide an effective remedy. Together, these judgments demonstrate the Act’s role in translating the abstract constitutional right into a functional accountability framework.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “constitutional‑statutory linkage”, first name the constitutional article, then the enabling statute and its specific sections, and finally the landmark case that interpreted the linkage. Use a three‑column mental table (Article – Section – Judgment) to structure the answer quickly.

Central Bureau of Investigation: Statutory Framework, Autonomy, and Judicial Oversight

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) derives its legal existence from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946. Section 3 constitutes the DSPE, and Section 4 vests superintendence in the Central Government, while Section 4A (inserted by the 2014 Amendment) creates a high‑powered committee for the appointment of the Director — comprising the Prime Minister (Chair), the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India or his nominee. The Director enjoys a fixed tenure of two years, extendable up to five years, and can be removed only by the same committee on grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity (Section 4B). These provisions were a direct outcome of the Supreme Court’s directions in Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) 2 SCC 197, which mandated institutional safeguards against executive interference.

Jurisdictional limits remain a contentious area. Section 6 of the DSPE Act requires the consent of the concerned State Government for the CBI to investigate offences within that State, unless the Supreme Court or a High Court orders a probe. The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2020) 6 SCC 1 reiterated that the consent requirement is a federal safeguard, but also held that the Court’s suo‑motu power under Article 142 can override the consent barrier in exceptional circumstances. The 2018 amendment to the DSPE Act introduced a “general consent” mechanism, allowing States to grant blanket consent for a specified period; as of 2023, 12 States have withdrawn general consent, compelling the CBI to seek case‑by‑case approval.

Judicial oversight extends to the CBI’s investigative independence. In CBI v. State of Rajasthan (2020) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court quashed a State Government order transferring a CBI officer mid‑investigation, affirming that the Director’s functional autonomy includes control over personnel deployed on a case. The Court also laid down a “transfer protocol” requiring prior approval of the appointment committee for any transfer of officers investigating sensitive cases.

For mains answers, aspirants should be able to: (i) trace the evolution from the 1946 Act to the 2014 Amendment; (ii) enumerate the composition and role of the appointment committee; (iii) explain the consent regime under Section 6 and the impact of general‑consent withdrawals; and (iv) cite the Vineet Narain guidelines, the 2020 Supreme Court judgments on consent and transfer protocol as the current judicial benchmarks.

National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: Implementation of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996

Article 338A of the Constitution establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) with the mandate to investigate and monitor all matters relating to the safeguards provided for STs under the Constitution and any other law. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution to the Fifth Schedule Areas, empowering Gram Sabhas with ownership of minor forest produce, control over land acquisition, and management of local resources. Section 4 of PESA requires that every Gram Sabha be competent to safeguard and preserve the traditions, customs, and cultural identity of the ST communities.

The NCST monitors PESA implementation through periodic reports, field visits, and suo‑motu inquiries under Article 338A(5)(a). In its 2021‑22 Annual Report, the Commission highlighted that only 9 of the 10 States with Fifth Schedule Areas had enacted conformity legislation, and that in several States the Gram Sabha’s consent for mining leases was being bypassed through executive notifications. The Commission recommended that the Ministry of Panchayati Raj issue a model PESA compliance framework and that the Ministry of Mines amend the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 to embed Gram Sabha consent as a statutory precondition.

Judicial reinforcement came in Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd. v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013) 6 SCC 476, where the Supreme Court held that the Gram Sabha’s resolution under PESA is a mandatory prerequisite for forest clearance in Scheduled Areas. The NCST cited this judgment in its 2020 advisory to the Odisha Government, leading to the cancellation of three mining leases that lacked Gram Sabha approval. In State of Odisha v. Union of India (2020) 8 SCC 1, the Court directed the State to constitute a monitoring committee under the NCST’s chairmanship to oversee PESA compliance in all Scheduled Areas.

For examination, candidates should link Article 338A to PESA’s Section 4, recall the NCST’s investigative powers, cite the 2013 Supreme Court judgment on Gram Sabha consent, and note the 2020 Court‑mandated monitoring committee as a concrete instance of the Commission’s oversight role.

National Commission for Women: Oversight of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013

The National Commission for Women (NCW) was constituted under the NCW Act, 1990. Section 10(1)(a) empowers the Commission to “review the constitutional and legal safeguards for women” and to “recommend measures for their effective implementation.” The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) operationalises the Supreme Court’s Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC 241 guidelines. Section 4 of the POSH Act mandates every employer with ten or more employees to constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC); Section 6 provides for a Local Complaints Committee (LCC) at the district level for establishments with fewer than ten employees or where the complaint is against the employer.

The NCW monitors compliance through annual returns filed by employers under Section 21, conducts surprise inspections, and issues advisories to State Governments. In its 2022 report, the Commission noted that only 62 % of surveyed organisations had functional ICCs, and that 28 % of LCCs were non‑existent due to non‑appointment of members by District Officers. The NCW recommended amendment of the POSH Act to introduce penal provisions for non‑constitution of ICCs and to empower the Commission to impose fines directly.

Judicial scrutiny has reinforced the NCW’s role. In Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) 2 SCC 1, the Supreme Court directed all States to ensure the constitution of LCCs within three months and asked the NCW to monitor compliance. The Delhi High Court in NCW v. Union of India (2021) upheld the Commission’s direction to a Central Government ministry to reconstitute its ICC within 30 days, ruling that the NCW’s statutory review power includes the authority to set enforceable timelines.

For answer writing, aspirants should connect Section 10(1)(a) of the NCW Act to the POSH Act’s Sections 4, 6, and 21, cite the Vishaka judgment as the constitutional genesis, reference the 2013 Supreme Court and 2021 Delhi High Court orders, and highlight the data gaps identified in the NCW’s 2022 report as evidence of implementation challenges.

  • Assuming the State Election Commissioner can be removed by the Governor at pleasure; the Constitution and the 2021 Supreme Court judgment require a High Court Judge inquiry for removal.
  • Treating SHRC recommendations as legally binding on the State Government; they are recommendatory and acquire force only through a High Court writ.
  • Believing the CBI can investigate in any State without consent; Section 6 of the DSPE Act mandates State consent unless a Court orders otherwise.
  • Confusing the NCST’s advisory role under Article 338A with legislative power; the Commission can only investigate, monitor, and recommend.
  • Thinking the NCW can directly penalise employers under the POSH Act; it can only recommend and set timelines, while penalties require legislative amendment.
  • Overlooking that the 2014 DSPE Amendment fixed the Director’s tenure at two years and created a collegium for appointment; earlier the Director served at the pleasure of the Government.
  • Misreading PESA as applicable to all tribal areas; it applies only to Fifth Schedule Areas, not Sixth Schedule Areas.

These advanced sections integrate constitutional provisions, statutory frameworks, landmark judgments, and empirical data to equip aspirants for high‑difficulty analytical questions.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Criteria, Weights, and Impact on Centre‑State Fiscal Relations

The vertical devolution formula determines the share of the divisible pool of taxes that the Union transfers to the States. Since the 10th Finance Commission (1995‑2000), the formula has been built on a set of criteria — population, income distance, area, forest cover, and fiscal discipline — each assigned a weight that reflects the Commission’s assessment of equity and efficiency. The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑2025) retained the 2011 Census population base (weight 15 %), income distance (45 %), area (15 %), forest and ecology (10 %), and demographic performance (12.5 %). The inclusion of demographic performance rewards States that have achieved lower fertility rates, a shift from the 14th Commission’s use of the 1971 Census for population weight. The 15th Commission also introduced a “tax effort” criterion (2.5 %) to incentivise States to improve their own‑tax collections. The vertical share recommended by the 15th Commission is 41 % of the divisible pool, unchanged from the 14th Commission, but the composition of the pool has expanded with the inclusion of GST compensation cess proceeds. The impact of these weights is evident in the inter‑State distribution: high‑income States such as Maharashtra and Gujarat receive a lower per‑capita transfer, while low‑income States like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh benefit from the income‑distance weight. The 15th Commission’s recommendation to keep the vertical share at 41 % was contested by the Union Government, which argued for a lower share to accommodate higher central expenditure on defence and infrastructure; however, the Commission defended the figure citing the need for fiscal space at the State level to meet the Sustainable Development Goals. The formula’s design also influences the States’ borrowing limits under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework, as higher transfers reduce the need for market borrowing. Judicial scrutiny of the formula is limited; the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2018) 9 SCC 1 held that the Finance Commission’s recommendations are advisory and not justiciable, but the Court emphasised that the Union must provide reasons if it deviates from the recommended share. For answer writing, aspirants should be able to list the five criteria with their 15th Commission weights, explain the rationale for the shift from 1971 to 2011 Census, and discuss the fiscal federalism implications of a static vertical share in a growing economy.

Election Commission’s Regulation of Opinion Polls and Exit Polls under the Representation of the People Act, 1951

Section 126A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, inserted by the 2009 amendment, prohibits the conduct and publication of exit polls during the period notified by the Election Commission (EC) — typically from the commencement of polling until half an hour after the close of the last phase. Section 126B, added in 2010, extends a similar restriction to opinion polls, barring their publication during the 48‑hour period preceding the first phase of polling. The EC issues a notification under these sections for each general election and bye‑election, specifying the exact dates and hours. Violation attracts imprisonment up to two years, a fine, or both. The EC’s 2019 notification for the Lok Sabha elections covered 11 April to 19 May, aligning with the seven‑phase schedule. In 2022, the EC extended the ban to include “any electronic media, social media, or internet‑based platform” to address the proliferation of digital opinion surveys. The Supreme Court in Election Commission of India v. Union of India (2021) 4 SCC 1 upheld the constitutional validity of Sections 126A and 126B, ruling that the restrictions constitute a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech under Article 19(2) in the interest of free and fair elections. The Court also clarified that the EC’s notification power is not unfettered; it must be exercised in a manner that is proportionate and non‑arbitrary. In practice, the EC has invoked these provisions to direct television channels and digital platforms to take down exit‑poll content, and has filed FIRs against media houses that breached the ban. The 2023 Karnataka Assembly elections saw the EC issue a show‑cause notice to a national news portal for publishing an opinion poll during the prohibited window; the portal complied after the EC threatened penal action. Critics argue that the 48‑hour pre‑poll ban on opinion polls curtails informed voter choice, while the EC maintains that the blackout prevents last‑minute manipulation of voter sentiment. For examination, candidates should cite Sections 126A and 126B, the 2009 and 2010 amendment dates, the 2021 Supreme Court judgment, and the EC’s 2019 and 2022 notifications as concrete illustrations of the regulatory framework.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “The Election Commission’s ban on opinion polls 48 hours before polling violates Article 19(1)(a). Discuss.”
The correct approach is to acknowledge the prima facie restriction on speech, then apply the reasonable‑restriction test under Article 19(2). Cite Section 126B, the 2010 amendment, and the Supreme Court’s 2021 judgment in Election Commission of India v. Union of India which held the ban proportionate to the objective of preventing undue influence on voters. Conclude that the restriction is constitutionally permissible because it is narrowly tailored, time‑limited, and serves the compelling state interest of electoral integrity.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes statutory provisions with constitutional articles, first quote the exact section (e.g., Section 126B), then map it to the relevant Article 19(2) ground (public order, decency, or “integrity of elections” as interpreted by the Court). Use the 2021 judgment as the authoritative precedent; avoid generic statements about “free speech”.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Cognizance of Custodial Deaths and Police Reforms

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) under Section 12 to “inquire, suo motu or on a petition presented to it by a victim or any person on his behalf, into complaints of violation of human rights.” The NHRC has routinely exercised this power to take suo motu cognizance of custodial deaths reported in the media or brought to its attention by civil society. In 2021, the NHRC registered 1,697 cases of custodial deaths, of which 1,200 were taken up suo motu. The Commission’s 2022 annual report highlighted that 68 % of these deaths occurred in police custody, while the remainder were in judicial custody. The NHRC’s investigative procedure involves issuing notices to the concerned State Director General of Police, seeking a magisterial inquiry report under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and directing the State to pay interim compensation to the victim’s family. In the landmark case NHRC v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2020) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court upheld the NHRC’s direction to the Uttar Pradesh government to pay ₹25 lakh as interim compensation to the family of a person who died in police custody, affirming that the Commission’s recommendations carry persuasive authority and can be enforced through writ jurisdiction. The NHRC has also used its suo motu power to push for systemic police reforms: its 2018 “Guidelines on Arrest and Detention” were cited by the Supreme Court in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 1 as a benchmark for police accountability. In 2023, the NHRC issued a directive to all States to install CCTV cameras in every police station and lock‑up, referencing the 2020 Supreme Court order in Paramvir Singh Saini v. Baljit Singh (2020) 10 SCC 1. The Commission’s ability to monitor compliance is limited to reporting to Parliament and the President under Section 20 of the PHRA; it lacks direct enforcement machinery. Nevertheless, the NHRC’s suo motu interventions have created a documentary record that courts frequently rely upon to issue binding directions. For answer writing, aspirants should reference Section 12 of the PHRA, the 2021‑22 custodial death statistics, the 2020 Supreme Court judgment on interim compensation, and the 2023 CCTV directive as evidence of the NHRC’s proactive role.

Central Information Commission’s Power to Impose Penalties under Section 20 of the RTI Act and Judicial Review

Section 20(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 empowers the Central Information Commission (CIC) to impose a penalty of ₹250 per day of delay, up to a maximum of ₹25,000, on a Public Information Officer (PIO) who has, without reasonable cause, refused to receive an application, failed to furnish information within the stipulated time, or provided incomplete or misleading information. The CIC may also recommend disciplinary action against the PIO under Section 20(2). Since its inception, the CIC has imposed penalties in over 3,200 cases, with the highest single penalty of ₹25,000 levied in 2018 against a PIO of the Ministry of Home Affairs for persistent non‑compliance. The Supreme Court in Chief Information Commissioner v. State of Manipur (2011) 3 SCC 447 held that the penalty power is quasi‑judicial and must be exercised after giving the PIO a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Court also ruled that the CIC’s penalty order is appealable to the High Court under Section 19(3) of the RTI Act, and that the High Court’s review is limited to legality, not merits. In Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013) 1 SCC 745, the Supreme Court clarified that the CIC cannot impose penalties on private bodies that are not “public authorities” under Section 2(h). The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act (effective 2020) altered the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners but left the penalty framework untouched. However, the amendment’s provision allowing the Central Government to prescribe rules for “conditions of service” raised concerns about executive influence on the CIC’s adjudicatory independence. The CIC’s 2022 annual report noted a 12 % increase in penalty orders compared to 2021, attributing the rise to stricter monitoring of proactive disclosure obligations under Section 4. For examination, candidates should be able to quote Section 20(1) and (2), cite the 2011 and 2013 Supreme Court judgments, and explain the interplay between the CIC’s penalty power and the High Court’s appellate jurisdiction.

CAG’s Audit of the Goods and Services Tax Revenue Sharing Mechanism and the GST Council

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) derives its mandate to audit GST revenue from Article 150 (accounts of the Union) and Article 151 (audit reports), read with Section 13 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The GST regime, introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016), created a dual GST structure — Central GST (CGST), State GST (SGST), and Integrated GST (IGST) — with revenue sharing governed by the GST Council under Article 279A. The CAG’s 2020 performance audit “GST Revenue Collection and Devolution” examined the accuracy of IGST settlement between the Centre and States, the functioning of the GST Network (GSTN), and the adequacy of the compensation cess mechanism. The audit found that during 2017‑19, the Centre short‑settled IGST by ₹12,400 crore due to mismatched invoice data between GSTN and State tax administrations. It also highlighted that the compensation cess fund, financed by a cess on sin goods and luxury items, fell short of the guaranteed 14 % annual growth in State revenues, leading to a cumulative compensation gap of ₹1.1 lakh crore by March 2021. The CAG recommended real‑time reconciliation of invoice‑level data, an independent audit of GSTN’s IT infrastructure, and a revision of the compensation formula to incorporate actual revenue buoyancy. The GST Council, in its 45th meeting (September 2021), accepted the recommendation for a “GSTN Audit Committee” comprising CAG nominees, but deferred the compensation formula revision citing fiscal constraints. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. M/s. Mohit Minerals (2022) 6 SCC 1 upheld the Council’s discretion in determining the compensation methodology, stating that the Council’s decisions are legislative in character and not subject to judicial review on merits. The CAG’s 2022 follow‑up audit reported that the IGST settlement gap had narrowed to ₹3,200 crore after the implementation of the “auto‑populated GSTR‑3B” facility, demonstrating the impact of audit‑driven reforms. For answer writing, aspirants should link Article 150/151 to the GST Council’s constitutional status, cite the 2020 and 2022 CAG audit findings, and discuss the tension between the CAG’s audit independence and the GST Council’s political composition.

  • Assuming the Finance Commission’s vertical share is constitutionally fixed; it is only a recommendation that the Union may modify with reasons.
  • Confusing the 48‑hour opinion‑poll ban (Section 126B) with the exit‑poll ban (Section 126A); they operate at different stages of the election cycle.
  • Believing the NHRC’s suo motu cognizance creates a binding order; its recommendations are persuasive and require judicial enforcement.
  • Thinking the CIC can penalise private NGOs under Section 20; the penalty applies only to Public Information Officers of public authorities.
  • Treating the GST Council’s compensation decisions as justiciable on merits; the Supreme Court has held they are legislative‑policy choices immune from merit‑based review.
  • Overlooking that the CAG’s audit of GST relies on GSTN data, which is managed by a private‑public entity; data integrity issues can limit audit conclusions.
  • Misreading the 15th Finance Commission’s demographic performance weight as a reward for population control alone; it also captures improvements in health and education indicators.

Election Commission’s Power to Conduct Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Judicial Review

The Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission under Article 324. Simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies would require synchronising the terms of the Houses, which are fixed at five years by Articles 83(2) and 172(1) unless dissolved earlier. A constitutional amendment would be needed to either curtail or extend the life of existing Assemblies, or to insert a new provision enabling a common electoral cycle. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2015 Report on “Simultaneous Elections” recommended a phased approach, beginning with a constitutional amendment to align the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies elected in 2024, followed by a one‑time extension or curtailment of terms for the remaining Assemblies. The NITI Aayog’s 2018 discussion paper highlighted fiscal savings, reduced policy paralysis and administrative convenience as benefits, while flagging the risk of undermining federalism and the democratic mandate of State governments.

Judicial scrutiny of any such amendment would centre on the basic structure doctrine. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot alter the federal character of the Constitution. A simultaneous‑election amendment that effectively diminishes the autonomy of State legislatures to decide their own dissolution could be challenged as violating federalism. The Court in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) emphasised that the power to dissolve a State Assembly is a constitutional safeguard for federal balance. Any law that removes this power without the State’s consent would likely be struck down. Moreover, the Representation of the People Act, 1951 would need extensive amendments to provide for a common electoral roll, simultaneous polling dates and a unified Model Code of Conduct. The Election Commission’s 2022 consultation paper noted that logistical challenges — deployment of security forces, EVM/VVPAT availability, and voter‑education campaigns — would require at least two general election cycles to operationalise.

From an examination perspective, candidates should be able to cite Article 324, Articles 83 and 172, the Law Commission reports, the NITI Aayog paper, and the basic‑structure test. A typical question may ask whether a constitutional amendment for simultaneous elections would survive judicial review; the answer must balance the legislative competence under Article 368 against the federalism component of the basic structure.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Off‑Budget Borrowings and Contingent Liabilities

Off‑budget borrowings are liabilities that do not appear in the Union Budget’s fiscal deficit but create future repayment obligations. Prominent examples include the issuance of oil bonds (2005‑2010), the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) loans to the Food Corporation of India, and the recent “special purpose vehicle” borrowings for infrastructure projects. The CAG’s mandate to audit all receipts and expenditure of the Union and States derives from Articles 150 and 151 read with Section 13 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. Section 13 empowers the CAG to audit “any authority or body substantially financed from the Consolidated Fund”. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2019) 4 SCC 1 affirmed that this phrase covers off‑budget instruments when the ultimate repayment burden falls on the Consolidated Fund.

The CAG’s 2021 performance audit “Off‑Budget Borrowings and Fiscal Transparency” quantified oil‑bond liabilities at ₹1.3 lakh crore and NSSF loans at ₹2.1 lakh crore as of March 2020. The 2022 follow‑up audit reported that the Union Government had repaid ₹45,000 crore of oil bonds but had rolled over a further ₹30,000 crore into new securities, effectively keeping the liability off the budget. The audit recommended that all such instruments be brought on‑budget through a legislative amendment to the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, and that the CAG be given explicit statutory access to the books of special purpose vehicles. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in its 2023 report endorsed the CAG’s recommendation and urged the Finance Ministry to disclose contingent liabilities in the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement.

For answer writing, aspirants should link Articles 150/151, Section 13 of the CAG Act, the 2019 Supreme Court judgment, and the 2021‑22 CAG audit findings. A common examiner twist is to ask whether the CAG can audit a private‑public partnership (PPP) concessionaire; the answer is yes, only to the extent that the concessionaire’s financial statements are “substantially financed” from the Consolidated Fund, as clarified in the 2019 judgment.

Technique
Which constitutional article and statutory provision together authorise the CAG to audit off‑budget borrowings such as oil bonds and the National Small Savings Fund?
Article 150 (accounts of the Union) and Article 151 (audit reports) read with Section 13 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which extends audit to any authority “substantially financed” from the Consolidated Fund. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. R. K. Jain (2019) confirmed that off‑budget instruments creating a future charge on the Consolidated Fund fall within this phrase.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the CAG’s expanding mandate, cite the 2021 and 2022 performance audit reports, the specific articles (150, 151) and Section 13, and the 2019 Supreme Court ruling. This three‑point reference (constitution, statute, judgment) fetches full marks.

Finance Commission’s Treatment of Grants‑in‑Aid and Conditional Transfers

The Finance Commission (FC) recommends two broad categories of transfers to States: tax devolution (vertical and horizontal) and grants‑in‑aid. Grants‑in‑aid are governed by Article 275 (grants for Scheduled Areas and Tribes) and Article 282 (discretionary grants for any public purpose). The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) introduced a structured framework: (i) revenue‑deficit grants to 17 States amounting to ₹2.9 lakh crore, (ii) sector‑specific grants for health (₹70,000 crore), education (₹1.1 lakh crore), and agriculture (₹30,000 crore), and (iii) performance‑based grants linked to outcomes in nutrition, sanitation and urban governance. Conditional transfers, on the other hand, flow through Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) such as the National Health Mission, Samagra Shiksha, and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana. These are not FC recommendations but executive decisions; however, the FC’s 2021 report urged rationalisation of CSS to avoid duplication and to align funding with State priorities.

The horizontal devolution formula of the 15th FC assigns 12.5 % weight to “demographic performance”, 15 % to “income distance”, 45 % to “population (2011)”, 15 % to “area”, 10 % to “forest and ecology”, and 2.5 % to “tax effort”. Grants‑in‑aid are distributed outside this formula, often on a needs‑assessment basis. For instance, the revenue‑deficit grant is calculated as the gap between a State’s assessed revenue expenditure and its revenue receipts after tax devolution. The FC also recommended a “grants‑in‑aid for local bodies” of ₹4.3 lakh crore, split between rural and urban bodies, with a condition that States must devolve 3 % of their own tax revenue to local bodies to be eligible.

Judicial scrutiny of grants‑in‑aid is limited; the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) 9 SCC 1 held that the FC’s recommendations are advisory and the Union may deviate with reasons. However, conditional transfers under CSS have been challenged for violating fiscal federalism when the Centre imposes stringent guidelines without adequate funding.
