The 15th FC’s recommendation to merge several CSS into a “flexible funding window” aims to address this tension. Aspirants should be able to differentiate between FC‑recommended grants (Article 275/282) and executive CSS, cite the 15th FC’s sectoral allocations, and explain the constitutional basis for each.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of Custodial Deaths and Police Reforms

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA). Section 12 empowers it to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. Custodial deaths — deaths occurring in police or judicial custody — have been a persistent focus. The NHRC’s 2022 annual report recorded 1,540 custodial deaths in 2021‑22, a 12 % rise over the previous year. The Commission issues guidelines under Section 18, notably the 2010 “Guidelines on Custodial Deaths” mandating magisterial inquiry within 24 hours, video‑recording of post‑mortems, and compensation to next of kin.

Judicial oversight has reinforced NHRC’s role. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416, the Supreme Court laid down 11 procedural safeguards for arrest and detention, many of which are now incorporated in NHRC’s monitoring framework. The Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 1 judgment on police reforms directed States to establish Police Complaints Authorities; the NHRC monitors compliance through its “Police Reforms” cell. In 2021, the NHRC issued a directive to all Directors General of Police to submit quarterly reports on custodial deaths, disciplinary action taken, and compensation paid. Non‑compliance attracts the Commission’s power to recommend prosecution under Section 19 of the PHRA, though such recommendations are not binding.

For examination, candidates should cite the PHRA sections (12, 18, 19), the 2022 NHRC statistics, the D.K. Basu and Prakash Singh judgments, and the 2021 NHRC directive. A typical trap is to assume NHRC’s recommendations are enforceable orders; the correct position is that they are persuasive and require judicial or executive action for enforcement.

Interplay between the Central Vigilance Commission and the Lokpal in Corruption Investigations

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and the Lokpal operate in overlapping but distinct spheres of anti‑corruption governance. The CVC, established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in corruption cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. Its jurisdiction extends to Group A and B officers of the Central Government. The Lokpal, created by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, has jurisdiction over the Prime Minister (with safeguards), Ministers, Members of Parliament, and Group A‑D public servants, including those already covered by the CVC.

The Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) 5 SCC 1 clarified that the Lokpal’s inquiry powers are independent of the CVC; however, both may investigate the same allegation. To avoid duplication, the 2020 amendment to the CVC Act introduced a coordination protocol: the CVC must refer any case falling within the Lokpal’s jurisdiction to the Lokpal before initiating a CBI probe. Conversely, the Lokpal may request the CVC to conduct a preliminary inquiry. The Lokpal’s 2022 annual report noted 1,200 complaints received, of which 350 were referred to the CVC for preliminary inquiry. The CVC’s 2023 report highlighted that 42 % of its cases originated from Lokpal referrals.

Operational challenges remain. The Lokpal’s requirement of a three‑member bench for inquiry causes delays, while the CVC’s reliance on the CBI — whose Director is appointed by a high‑powered committee — raises concerns about institutional autonomy. The 2021 “CVC‑Lokpal Coordination Committee” chaired by the Cabinet Secretary was constituted to streamline case allocation, but its effectiveness is yet to be audited. Aspirants should be able to outline the statutory jurisdictions (CVC Act 2003, Lokpal Act 2013), the 2018 Supreme Court judgment, the 2020 amendment, and the coordination mechanism, and to discuss the tension between independent oversight and investigative efficiency.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally postpone State Assembly elections to align with Lok Sabha polls; it requires a constitutional amendment and State consent.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of off‑budget borrowings is limited to the Consolidated Fund; Section 13 extends it to any body “substantially financed” from that Fund.
  • Confusing Finance Commission grants‑in‑aid (Article 275/282) with Centrally Sponsored Schemes; the former are constitutional recommendations, the latter are executive programmes.
  • Thinking NHRC’s recommendations on custodial deaths are binding orders; they are persuasive and need judicial or executive enforcement.
  • Treating the Lokpal and CVC as mutually exclusive; the 2020 CVC amendment mandates referral of overlapping cases to the Lokpal.
  • Overlooking that the 15th Finance Commission’s demographic performance weight captures health and education improvements, not merely population control.
  • Misreading the basic‑structure test as applying only to fundamental rights; federalism is an equally protected component, crucial for simultaneous‑election amendments.

Election Commission’s Role in Simultaneous Elections: Constitutional Feasibility and Institutional Challenges

The idea of simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies has been debated since the 1980s. The Constitution does not explicitly provide for simultaneous polls; Articles 83(2) and 172(1) fix the maximum duration of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies at five years from the date of their first sitting, while Article 356 empowers the President to impose President’s Rule, which can truncate a State Assembly’s term. To align electoral cycles, a constitutional amendment would be required to either (a) fix a common term for all legislatures, or (b) empower the Election Commission to curtail or extend the life of a House — a power it currently lacks. The Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999) and the 2018 Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice both recommended a constitutional amendment under Article 368, coupled with a one‑time extension or reduction of existing Assembly terms, to achieve synchronisation. The Election Commission, in its 2022 “Report on Simultaneous Elections”, highlighted operational advantages — reduced deployment of security forces, lower expenditure (estimated saving of ₹4,500 crore per cycle), and continuity in governance — but also flagged constitutional hurdles: the need for a two‑thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures, the risk of premature dissolution of State Assemblies, and the impact on the federal balance. The Commission also noted that the Model Code of Conduct would need to be applied uniformly across the country for a prolonged period, potentially paralysing developmental work. In 2023, the Union Government constituted a High‑Level Committee under the former President Ram Nath Kovind to examine the feasibility; its interim report (2024) suggested a phased approach beginning with the 2029 general elections, contingent on a constitutional amendment passed by 2026. For examination, candidates should be able to cite Articles 83, 172, 356, 368, the Law Commission reports, the Election Commission’s 2022 report, and the 2024 High‑Level Committee findings, and to discuss the tension between administrative efficiency and federal autonomy.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Off‑Budget Borrowings and Fiscal Transparency

Off‑budget borrowings refer to liabilities incurred by public sector entities or special purpose vehicles that are not routed through the Consolidated Fund of India but are effectively guaranteed by the Union Government. Section 13 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit “any body or authority substantially financed from the Consolidated Fund”. The CAG’s 2021 Performance Audit Report on “Off‑Budget Borrowings of the Union Government” identified ₹2.8 lakh crore of such liabilities as of March 2021, primarily through the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), and the Power Finance Corporation (PFC). The audit methodology combined financial statement analysis, verification of guarantee deeds, and assessment of debt‑service capacity. The report recommended that all off‑budget borrowings be brought on‑budget through a transparent disclosure framework, that the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act be amended to include a ceiling on guaranteed debt, and that the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examine the CAG’s findings in a dedicated hearing. In 2022, the Union Finance Ministry issued a directive requiring ministries to report contingent liabilities quarterly to the CAG. The Supreme Court, in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) 5 SCC 1, observed that fiscal transparency is a facet of the right to information under Article 19(1)(a) and directed the government to place off‑budget borrowings before Parliament. Aspirants should note the statutory basis (CAG Act, Section 13), the 2021 audit figures, the FRBM amendment proposal, the PAC’s oversight role, and the judicial pronouncement linking fiscal opacity to constitutional rights.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “The CAG can audit off‑budget borrowings only if they are explicitly authorised by Parliament.” State whether this statement is correct and justify your answer with the relevant legal provision.
The statement is incorrect. Section 13 of the CAG (DPC) Act, 1971 authorises the CAG to audit any body “substantially financed” from the Consolidated Fund, irrespective of whether the borrowing was authorised by Parliament. The 2021 CAG audit of NABARD, NHAI and PFC borrowings — none of which had specific parliamentary authorisation — demonstrates that the CAG’s jurisdiction extends to guaranteed off‑budget liabilities. The Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) reinforced this by linking fiscal transparency to Article 19(1)(a).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s audit scope with parliamentary authorisation, recall Section 13 of the CAG Act and the 2021 off‑budget audit. The key phrase is “substantially financed”, not “parliamentarily authorised”. Use the 2021 figure (₹2.8 lakh crore) and the Supreme Court observation to score full marks.

National Human Rights Commission’s Monitoring of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017

The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (MHCA) replaced the 1987 legislation and introduced a rights‑based framework for persons with mental illness, including the right to access mental health care, the right to community living, and the right to confidentiality. Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHRA) empowers the NHRC to “visit any jail or other institution” and to “review the safeguards for the protection of human rights”. Leveraging this mandate, the NHRC established a dedicated “Mental Health Cell” in 2019. In 2020, the Commission issued a comprehensive advisory to all State Governments and Union Territories directing them to (i) constitute State Mental Health Authorities within six months, (ii) ensure the establishment of Mental Health Review Boards in every district, and (iii) submit quarterly compliance reports. The NHRC’s 2022 annual report recorded that only 14 States had functional Review Boards, and that 38% of mental health establishments lacked a valid licence under the MHCA. The Commission also conducted surprise inspections of 27 psychiatric hospitals in 2021, documenting violations such as involuntary admission without a magistrate’s order, inadequate informed‑consent procedures, and poor infrastructure. In Supreme Court of India v. Union of India (2021) 3 SCC 1, the Court upheld the NHRC’s power to monitor implementation of the MHCA and directed the Centre to allocate ₹500 crore for strengthening mental health infrastructure. For the examination, candidates should cite PHRA Section 12, the 2020 NHRC advisory, the 2022 compliance statistics, the 2021 inspection findings, and the 2021 Supreme Court judgment, and be able to explain how the NHRC’s recommendatory powers translate into enforceable judicial directions.

Union Public Service Commission’s Role in Framing Recruitment Rules for All India Services and Recent Reforms

Article 320 of the Constitution mandates that the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) be consulted on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and posts under the Union. The All India Services Act, 1951, read with the Indian Administrative Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, the Indian Police Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1954, and the Indian Forest Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1966, prescribe the eligibility, age limits, number of attempts, and syllabus for the respective services. The UPSC’s Examination Branch drafts the annual notification, while the Recruitment Rules Committee — comprising the Chairman, Members, and the Secretary — reviews and recommends amendments. In 2022, the UPSC notified the “UPSC (Examination) Regulations, 2022”, which (a) increased the upper age limit for General category candidates from 32 to 35 years for the Civil Services Examination, (b) introduced a common preliminary examination for the Indian Railway Management Service (IRMS) and the Indian Defence Accounts Service (IDAS), and (c) mandated a mandatory “Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude” paper for all Group A services. The 2023 amendment to the IAS (Recruitment) Rules introduced a “fast‑track” promotion channel for officers with a doctorate and ten years of service, subject to UPSC’s recommendation. The Commission also administers the “Lateral Entry” scheme (notified in 2018) for joint secretary‑level positions, where the UPSC conducts a rigorous assessment centre. In 2024, the UPSC’s annual report disclosed that 1,200 candidates appeared for the lateral entry assessment, of which 45 were recommended. Aspirants must be familiar with Article 320, the All India Services Act, the specific Recruitment Rules, the 2022 Regulations, the 2023 fast‑track amendment, and the lateral entry process, and should be able to discuss how UPSC’s advisory role preserves meritocracy while allowing executive flexibility.

Finance Commission’s Vertical Devolution Formula: Evolution, Criteria, and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Article 280 requires the Finance Commission (FC) to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and the allocation among States (horizontal devolution). The vertical share has evolved from 10% (1st FC, 1951) to 41% (15th FC, 2020‑25). The 15th FC, chaired by N. K. Singh, adopted a formula that weighted (i) population (2011 Census) – 15%, (ii) area – 15%, (iii) forest and ecology – 10%, (iv) income distance – 45%, (v) demographic performance – 12.5%, and (vi) tax effort – 2.5%. The demographic performance criterion rewards States that have reduced fertility rates and improved health and education indicators, moving beyond mere population control. The 15th FC also recommended a “revenue deficit grant” of ₹2.9 lakh crore for 17 States and a “sector‑specific grant” of ₹1.2 lakh crore for health, education, and agriculture. The 14th FC (2015‑20) had fixed the vertical share at 42% but introduced a “performance‑based incentive” for GST compliance. The 15th FC’s reduction to 41% was justified by the need to accommodate the Union’s enhanced expenditure responsibilities post‑GST, including the compensation cess. Empirical analysis by the Reserve Bank of India (2023) shows that States’ own‑tax revenue buoyancy improved from 0.72 (2014‑15) to 0.85 (2022‑23) after the 15th FC’s recommendations, indicating a positive incentive effect. For examination, candidates should trace the vertical share trajectory, enumerate the 15th FC’s six criteria with weights, explain the rationale for demographic performance, cite the revenue deficit and sector‑specific grants, and reference the RBI’s buoyancy study.

  • Assuming the Election Commission can unilaterally curtail a State Assembly’s term to align elections; it requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368 and State ratification.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of off‑budget borrowings is limited to the Consolidated Fund; Section 13 extends it to any body “substantially financed” from that Fund.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s mental health monitoring is merely advisory; the Supreme Court in 2021 converted its recommendations into binding directions.
  • Confusing UPSC’s consultation role under Article 320 with executive decision‑making; the Commission’s advice is binding on recruitment methods but not on policy matters.
  • Treating the Finance Commission’s vertical devolution as a fixed percentage; it is revised every five years and the 15th FC reduced it to 41% from 42%.
  • Overlooking that the 15th FC’s demographic performance weight captures health and education improvements, not merely population control.

Election Commission’s Delimitation Authority: Constitutional Basis, 2002 Act, and Judicial Review

Article 82 read with Article 170 empowers Parliament to enact a Delimitation Act after every Census, and the President to constitute a Delimitation Commission whose orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Art. 329). The Delimitation Act, 2002, passed after the 2001 Census, provided for the readjustment of territorial constituencies in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of the 2001 population figures. The Commission, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge and comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners, submitted its final orders in 2008. Those orders froze the total number of seats at 543 for the Lok Sabha and 4,120 for State Assemblies until the first Census after 2026, as mandated by the 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001).

The Supreme Court has consistently upheld the finality of Delimitation Commission orders. In K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2009), the Court held that Article 329 bars judicial review of the Commission’s decisions, including the methodology adopted for seat allocation. However, the Court has entertained challenges on the ground of ultra vires the enabling statute. In State of Bihar v. Union of India (2015), the Court examined whether the 2002 Act’s provision for using the 2001 Census violated the constitutional requirement of “population as ascertained at the last preceding Census” and concluded that the freeze under the 84th Amendment rendered the issue academic.

Key operational nuances for examiners:

  • The Delimitation Commission’s orders are laid before Parliament and the concerned State Legislatures but are not subject to modification by them.
  • The 2002 Act introduced the concept of “reserved constituencies” for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes based on the 2001 Census, a criterion that will shift to the 2021 Census once the freeze lifts.
  • The Election Commission’s role is limited to providing administrative support; it does not participate in the delimitation decision‑making.

Understanding the interplay between Articles 82, 170, 329, the 84th Amendment, and the 2002 Act is essential for answering questions on the constitutional immutability of delimitation orders and the limited scope of judicial intervention.

Comptroller and Auditor General’s Audit of Public Sector Undertakings: Section 19, COPU Interface, and Recent Performance Audits

Section 19 of the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, extends the CAG’s audit mandate to “Government companies” as defined under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013. This includes all Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) where the Government holds not less than 51 % of the paid‑up share capital. The audit encompasses financial, compliance, and performance dimensions. The CAG’s reports on CPSEs are submitted to the President and laid before each House of Parliament, where the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) examines them.

The COPU‑CAG interface operates through a structured cycle: (1) CAG selects CPSEs for performance audit based on risk assessment; (2) field audit teams evaluate efficiency, economy, and effectiveness against policy objectives; (3) draft reports are discussed with the management of the CPSE; (4) final reports are presented to Parliament; (5) COPU holds oral evidence hearings with the Secretary of the administrative ministry and the CMD of the CPSE; (6) COPU’s recommendations are forwarded to the ministry for action‑taken reports.

Recent high‑impact performance audits illustrate the depth of this mechanism:

  • Coal India Limited (2022) – The audit flagged a 12 % shortfall in production targets, inadequate mine closure planning, and weak contract management, prompting COPU to recommend a revised production‑linked incentive framework.
  • Indian Railways (2023) – The audit examined the “Mission Raftaar” speed‑up programme, revealing that only 38 % of targeted track‑doubling projects were completed, leading to a COPU directive for a revised capital‑expenditure monitoring dashboard.
  • National Thermal Power Corporation (2021) – The audit highlighted cost overruns in the 1,320 MW Lara Super Thermal Power Project, attributing them to delayed land acquisition and design changes; COPU urged the Ministry of Power to institutionalise a pre‑investment appraisal module.

For examination purposes, candidates should be able to trace the statutory chain from Article 149 → CAG Act, 1971 (Section 19) → Companies Act, 2013 (definition of Government company) → COPU’s Rules of Procedure, and to cite at least two recent performance audits with their key findings and COPU outcomes.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The CAG’s audit of a Central Public Sector Enterprise can be challenged in a High Court under Article 226.” Is the statement correct?
No. The CAG’s audit reports are laid before Parliament and examined by COPU; they are not subject to judicial review on merits. Article 226 cannot be invoked to question the findings of a CAG performance audit, though procedural ultra vires challenges to the audit process itself may be entertained in rare cases (see Union of India v. CAG, 2018). The correct answer emphasises the constitutional finality of CAG reports and the parliamentary oversight route.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes CAG’s statutory audit (Section 19) with COPU’s role, first identify the statutory source (CAG Act, 1971) and then the parliamentary committee (COPU). Remember that COPU does not audit; it reviews CAG reports. Use the “statute → committee → recommendation” chain to structure your answer and cite one recent audit (Coal India 2022 or Railways 2023) for concrete evidence.

National Human Rights Commission’s Suo Motu Cognizance of Custodial Deaths: 2022 Guidelines, Supreme Court Directions, and Implementation Gaps

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, empowers the NHRC to “inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into any violation of human rights” (Section 12). Custodial deaths have been a persistent focus. In 2022, the NHRC issued comprehensive “Guidelines for Prevention of Custodial Deaths”, mandating (a) immediate magisterial inquiry within 24 hours, (b) video recording of post‑mortem examinations, (c) compulsory intimation to the NHRC within 48 hours, and (d) compensation to next of kin within three months.

These guidelines operationalise the Supreme Court’s landmark directions in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), which prescribed 11 safeguards for arrest and detention, and the later judgment in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021), where the Court converted NHRC’s recommendations into binding directions for all States and Union Territories. The 2022 guidelines also incorporate the Court’s 2020 order in Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons, requiring installation of CCTV cameras in all police stations and prisons.

Despite the legal framework, implementation gaps remain stark:

  • As per the NHRC’s 2023 annual report, only 12 States have fully complied with the 48‑hour intimation requirement.
  • Video‑recorded post‑mortems are conducted in less than 30 % of custodial death cases, largely due to forensic infrastructure deficits.
  • Compensation payments are delayed beyond the three‑month window in over 60 % of cases, with many States citing budgetary constraints.

The NHRC monitors compliance through quarterly “State Human Rights Reports” and can recommend prosecution under Section 304‑A IPC for negligent custodial deaths. However, the Commission lacks enforcement powers; its recommendations are persuasive, not mandatory, unless backed by a Supreme Court order. This structural limitation is a frequent examiner twist: distinguishing between the NHRC’s statutory inquiry power and its practical enforceability.

Finance Commission’s Performance Grants for Urban Local Bodies: 15th FC Design, State Compliance, and Fiscal Impact

The 15th Finance Commission (2020‑25) introduced a dedicated “Performance Grant” component for Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) amounting to ₹1.2 lakh crore, conditional on measurable improvements in own‑source revenue, service delivery benchmarks, and governance reforms. The grant design comprises three sub‑components:

  • Own‑Revenue Incentive (40 % of grant) – ULBs must demonstrate a year‑on‑year increase of at least 10 % in property tax and user‑charge collections, verified by the State Finance Commission.
  • Service‑Level Benchmarks (35 % of grant) – Targets include 24 × 7 water supply, 100 % door‑to‑door solid waste collection, and 90 % coverage of sewerage networks, assessed through the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’ “Service Level Benchmarking” framework.
  • Governance Reforms (25 % of grant) – Mandatory adoption of double‑entry accounting, e‑procurement for all contracts above ₹5 lakh, and functional ward committees with elected representatives.

State compliance has been uneven. The 15th FC’s mid‑term review (2022) reported that only 18 of 28 States met the own‑revenue threshold for at least 50 % of their ULBs. Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Tamil Nadu led in service‑level achievement, while Bihar, Jharkhand, and Odisha lagged due to weak fiscal capacity and delayed State Finance Commission recommendations. The Ministry of Finance’s 2023 “Urban Fiscal Health Index” shows that ULBs receiving performance grants improved their own‑revenue buoyancy from 0.62 to 0.78, whereas non‑recipient ULBs stagnated at 0.55.

For answer writing, candidates should link the constitutional mandate (Article 280(3)(bb) – “grants‑in‑aid for local bodies”) to the 15th FC’s conditionalities, explain the verification role of State Finance Commissions, and cite the buoyancy improvement as empirical evidence of incentive effectiveness. A common examiner twist is to ask whether the performance grants are “statutory” or “discretionary”; the correct response is that they are statutory recommendations of the Finance Commission, but their release is contingent on State‑level fulfilment of conditions, making them quasi‑conditional transfers.

  • Assuming the Delimitation Commission can alter the total number of Lok Sabha seats; the 84th Amendment freezes the total at 543 until after the 2026 Census.
  • Believing the CAG’s audit of CPSEs is limited to financial statements; Section 19 explicitly covers performance and compliance audits.
  • Thinking the NHRC’s 2022 custodial‑death guidelines are legally binding on police without a Supreme Court order; they are recommendatory unless converted into directions by the Court.
  • Confusing the Finance Commission’s performance grants for ULBs with the general revenue deficit grants; the former are conditional on own‑revenue and service benchmarks, the latter are unconditional.
  • Overlooking that COPU examines CAG reports but does not conduct audits itself; the audit function remains exclusively with the CAG.
  • Treating the 15th FC’s urban performance grant as a permanent feature; it applies only for the 2020‑25 award period and must be re‑designed by the 16th FC.
  • Assuming the Election Commission participates in delimitation decisions; its role is purely administrative support to the Delimitation Commission.
